name: Kansas Reflector
title: National health experts dissect election wins, effects on healthcare policy
description: TOPEKA — A national health expert expects Democrats to quickly move to reverse Medicaid cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to restore Affordable Care Act premium subsidies, which led to millions of people losing health insurance coverage.  “The size of this blue tsunami means huge expectations for Democrats, especially on healthcare […]
text:
Janice Martin says, "Thank you, Jesus," after the news broadcast announced Adam Hamilton's win at Cindy Holscher's watch party Nov. 3, 2026, in Lenexa. As Democrats claimed wins across the country, political anaylsts began to consider what the new landscape in Washington, D.C., might mean for healthcare policies. (Photo by Baya Burgess/ Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A national health expert expects Democrats to quickly move to reverse Medicaid cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to restore Affordable Care Act premium subsidies, which led to millions of people losing health insurance coverage. 
“The size of this blue tsunami means huge expectations for Democrats, especially on healthcare because this was very much a healthcare election,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a national nonpartisan healthcare policy institute, on a Thursday webinar during which KFF experts talked about what happens next after Tuesday’s election.
Healthcare was a key issue for Adam Hamilton, Kansas’ Democratic candidate and presumed winner of the U.S. Senate race against incumbent Republican Roger Marshall. 
The big question as election results are finalized is whether Democrats can meet high expectations set for addressing healthcare issues, Levitt said. 
Democrats will really only have the next year to make changes, because 2028 will be a presidential election year, in which Congress tends “not to do a lot,” he said.
“I would say the expectations for what Democrats can accomplish on healthcare should be tempered by the fact that President Trump will still be in the White House and has a veto pen,” he said. 
Levitt still expects Democrats to promptly tackle the core issues of Medicaid and ACA premiums. 
“I also expect President Trump to veto any bill that the Democrats pass to do this, if they are able to pass it,” Levitt said. “That takes us to the second path, which is kind of a game of 3D chess for Democrats to try to figure out what and how they can get President Trump to agree to restore some of these healthcare cuts.”
That could look like a delay of implementing ACA subsidy cuts or including Trump priorities such as health care savings accounts, he said. 
A third path could look like “populist healthcare ideas” that might pull in bipartisan support, such as addressing drug prices, which tends to be popular with both sides, price transparency and breaking up big insurance conglomerates. 
Amanda Seitz, Washington health policy reporter, said President Donald Trump shifted messaging several times in the first few days, appearing at times conciliatory and willing to work with Democrats, and then giving tours of his in-progress ballroom. 
She said it’s doubtful Trump will go along with reversing cuts to Medicaid. 
“Republicans really do view that as a signature achievement of this administration so far,” Seitz said. “However, I think we should be watching the rulemaking around Medicaid over the next couple weeks and months.”
The definition of Medicaid frailty is being challenged in court, and Medicaid work requirements are expected to go into effect Jan. 1. 
“There’s going to be a lot of pressure now on this administration to take a look at that again, especially when you have state legislatures that are now turning Democratic as well,” Seitz said. 
Democrats have created an 84-page working paper outlining healthcare policy, published by Politico in September, said Julie Rovner, chief Washington correspondent for KFF Health News. But she asked whether they have a plan to pay for what they outlined.  
Levitt said that’s typically the sticking point on any legislation, and healthcare changes will be no exception.
“We’re talking about almost a trillion dollars over 10 years in the Medicaid cuts, hundreds of billions of dollars for restoring the ACA premium subsidies, and I think that’s going to be a big fight,” he said. “Probably a big fight among Democrats, even whether they should try to pay for it. Republicans didn’t pay for all of the tax cuts they passed, and if this is a bill that the president is likely to veto anyway, why fight over how to pay for it?”
However, Levitt said, Democrats are unified on those issues, as well as reversing tax cuts for wealthy people. 
“That will be the first big fight, is whether Democrats pay for it, how they pay for it, and procedurally how they’re even going to proceed,” he said. 
Rovner asked how sure anyone is that Trump will veto such bills. 
“He’s obviously thinking about his legacy, and we know he likes to think about his legacy in terms of physical buildings like the ballroom and the reflecting pool,” she said. “Trump has proved very unpredictable in the past.”
Rovner pointed out that incoming senator from Michigan Abdul el-Sayed had said he’d be happy to name his health plan after Trump if it would get the president to sign it.
Levitt said he’s not sure Trump is particularly attached to Medicaid cuts. 
“He said during the 2024 campaign that he wasn’t going to cut Medicaid,” Levitt said. “He wasn’t going to cut Medicare, right? So I doubt that was a priority for him. I don’t think we can necessarily predict exactly what President Trump would do on the Affordable Care Act.”
There also could be a shift from Republicans left in Congress, as the ACA premiums affected middle-income people above four times the poverty level, such as farmers, ranchers and small-business owners, traditionally Republican constituencies, Levitt said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Two Kansas GOP legislative leaders accuse governor of misconduct in Walk of Honor selections
description: Two members of the Kansas Legislature allege Gov. Laura Kelly ignored state law by unilaterally selecting people to be added to the Capitol's Walk of Honor.
text:
Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly speaks Oct. 29, 2026, during a ceremony at the Capitol honoring eight people added to the Kansas Walk of Honor. Two Republican members of the Kansas Legislature claim she violated state law by unilaterally choosing eight new inductees. (Photo by Kansas Governor's Office)TOPEKA — The Republican House speaker and Senate majority leader Friday accused Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly of breaking Kansas law by personally selecting a group of people honored with bronze plaques at the Capitol.
Kelly, who completes her second term as governor in January, celebrated Oct. 29 the addition of seven women and one man to the Kansas Walk of Honor. The class included basketball pioneer James Naismith, educator Lucinda Todd, abolitionist Clarina Nichols and Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation Chairwoman Minnie Evans.
House Speaker Dan Hawkins and Senate Majority Leader Chase Blasi, both Wichita Republicans, said the governor failed to adhere to Kansas statute when she unilaterally chose honorees and directed placement of sidewalk markers without consulting the Kansas Legislature.
“The governor bypassed the statute and installed these unlawfully and, in addition, had a ceremony already,” Hawkins said.
Blasi, who serves on the Legislature’s capitol preservation committee, said he would welcome legal analysis of the governor’s actions. He suggested the joint preservation committee should be allowed to add its voice to discussion of memorials placed on the Capitol grounds “as the law requires.”
“The governor has decided to unlawfully violate the law and do whatever she wants,” he said.
Kelly’s staff didn’t respond to a request for comment, but she has said responsibility for selecting recipients fell to the state’s governors.
“The honorees being added to the Kansas Walk of Honor have always been an important part of Kansas history,” Kelly said in a statement last week. “They broke down barriers, challenged injustice, led industries and opened doors for generations to follow. Their contributions have shaped our state and our nation, which is why their names will forever be embedded in the sidewalks around the Statehouse, ensuring their stories live on in perpetuity.”
Kansas hasn’t applied a rigid selection formula or a mandatory legislative voting process for designation of these honorees. Since the Walk of Honor was established by GOP Gov. Sam Brownback in 2011, decisions involved the state’s governor in coordination with the Kansas Historical Society. The Kansas Historical Foundation finances the memorial plaques.
The governor was joined at last month’s ceremony on the Capitol steps by representatives of the Kansas Historical Society, Capitol Preservation Committee, family members of honorees and private donors to the project.
“Over the last 15 years, we have honored 17 Kansans from all walks of life who have made a significant impact on the state and to the country. We are pleased to include these eight new honorees,” said Patrick Zollner, executive director of the Kansas Historical Society.
The new honorees included Naismith, who invented basketball in 1891 and became the University of Kansas’ first head basketball coach. Todd, a civil rights advocate and teacher from Litchfield, was part of the families challenging school segregation in the landmark 1954 decision by the U.S. Supreme Court in Brown v. Topeka Board of Education.
Nichols was a women’s rights advocate who helped secure constitutional recognition of married women’s property rights and rights in child custody matters. Evans, who served as tribal chairwoman of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, defended tribal sovereignty and helped defeat federal efforts to terminate the standing of tribes, including the Potawatomi.
Kelly paid tribute to Georgia Neese Clark Gray, a Richland native and Washburn University graduate who became the first woman to serve as U.S. treasurer. She was appointed by President Harry Truman in 1949.
The governor selected for recognition Olive Ann Beech, an aviation executive from Waverly. She built Beech Aircraft into a major manufacturer and was the first woman to lead a Fortune 500 company.
Another addition was Mary Skubitz, a labor rights advocate who helped lead a 1921 march in which thousands of women joined striking coal miners protesting unfair labor practices in Kansas coalfields. The list included Kay McFarland, the first woman appointed to the Kansas Supreme Court and the first woman to serve as the Supreme Court’s chief justice.
Previously, Kelly selected U.S. Sen. Pat Roberts, who represented Kansas in Congress from 1981 to 2021.
Brownback, the Republican governor who created the Walk of Honor program, chose the 16 other people honored in this way. His list included 14 men and two women.
He started with U.S. Sen. Bob Dole in 2011, before selecting Vice President Charles Curtis, aviator Amelia Earhart and Nobel Prize winner Jack Kilby in 2012.
In 2015, Brownback’s list was expanded to aviation executive Clyde Cessna, automaker Walter Chrysler, physician Samuel Crumbine, artist John Steuart Curry, photographer Gordon Parks, journalist William Allen White and President Dwight Eisenhower.
In 2016, Brownback included entrepreneur Fred Harvey, U.S. Sen. Nancy Landon Kassebaum, Gov. Alf Landon, cattle transport executive Joseph McCoy and psychiatrist Carl Menninger.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Von Gillern concedes; jockeying begins for speakership of Nebraska Legislature
description: OMAHA — An incumbent state senator eyed as the frontrunner for speaker of the Nebraska Legislature has conceded his Omaha-area race in a rematch with his 2022 challenger. State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, in a statement Friday, congratulated state Sen.-elect Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha. Since joining the Legislature in 2023, von Gillern has served [[...]
text:
State Sen. Brad von Gillern and Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek are facing off again for to represent west-central Douglas County's Legislative District 4. They are pictured in Omaha in early October 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — An incumbent state senator eyed as the frontrunner for speaker of the Nebraska Legislature has conceded his Omaha-area race in a rematch with his 2022 challenger.
State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, in a statement Friday, congratulated state Sen.-elect Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha. Since joining the Legislature in 2023, von Gillern has served in leadership positions for the Revenue Committee, including the first two years as vice chair to former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn before becoming chair.
“I wish Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek success as she heads to Lincoln to be our representative and will do all that I can to tee her up to succeed,” von Gillern wrote. “Her success is Nebraska’s success. The job is difficult and thankless, but vastly rewarding.”
State Sens. Rob Clements of Elmwood, left, and Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn talk with reporters after a meeting of the Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board at the Nebraska State Capitol on Oct. 30, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The Douglas County Election Commission released updated results 12:15 p.m. Friday with 8,000 more ballots counted (about 7,000 are left). In Legislative District 4, 645 more ballots were counted.
In the latest results, Maxwell-Ostdiek’s lead expanded by almost 80 votes. She leads with 9,099 votes (51%) to von Gillern’s 8,729 votes (49%). In 2022, von Gillern won the election with 8,710 votes, a margin of 4.8 percentage points over Maxwell-Ostdiek that year.
The New York Times has not yet called the LD 4 race for Maxwell-Ostdiek, nor the winners in three other legislative races (LD 14, LD 18 and LD 36). However, with von Gillern’s announcement, all four second-place finishers now have conceded. All newly elected lawmakers, including Maxwell-Ostdiek, have started new senator orientation, or “senator school,” already.
The Nebraska Board of State Canvassers, composed of State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg, Secretary of State Bob Evnen, Gov. Jim Pillen, Attorney General Mike Hilgers and Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley, meets to certify Nebraska’s May 12 primary election. At the podium, speaking to the board, is Deputy Secretary of State Wayne Bena. June 8, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Final results will be released in the coming weeks. The Nebraska Board of State Canvassers — consisting of the state’s constitutional officers — will finalize the election in early December.
Maxwell-Ostdiek also released a statement Friday saying she was “honored to have earned the trust of District 4 voters.”
“This campaign has been an unforgettable experience, and I am deeply grateful to everyone who helped make this victory possible,” Maxwell-Ostdiek wrote.
Speaker of the Legislature
Multiple lawmakers viewed von Gillern as the leading contender to succeed term-limited state Sen. John Arch of La Vista as speaker of the Legislature, a post he held for four years in turbulent times.
State Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, left, meets with State Sen. Paul Strommen of Sidney. March 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In Nebraska’s one-house Legislature, the speaker sets the daily debate schedule, and the speaker’s election is the first vote cast by senators each year. Under legislative rules, leadership votes are via secret ballot.
One lawmaker had already voiced her intention to seek the role regardless of von Gillern’s election: state Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha. Another, state Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, had said he would pursue the top role only if von Gillern lost. Jacobson has long said he wanted the Revenue Committee chairship but was willing to step up for speaker if needed.
The Nebraska Examiner can confirm one other legislator is considering the role: state Sen. Teresa Ibach of Sumner. Ibach said in the past 48 hours she’s had conversations with colleagues who encouraged her to seek the top spot, but she has not made a final call.
State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, center, meets with, from left, State Sens. Dave Murman of Glenvil, Barry DeKay of Niobrara, Steve Halloran of Hastings, Steve Erdman of Bayard and Brian Hardin of Gering. Feb. 23, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Kauth, Jacobson and Ibach all have legislative leadership positions already:

Kauth is chair of the Business and Labor Committee.
Jacobson is chair of the Banking, Commerce and Insurance Committee, and he is vice chair of the Revenue Committee.
Ibach is vice chair of the Executive Board (an internal high-ranking committee that handles day-to-day affairs of the legislative branch) and the Agriculture Committee.

Lawmakers have said other legislators have discussed or are looking for other names, too.
‘One of the best experiences of my life’
Von Gillern, in his concession, thanked his wife, Mary, for joining him in the campaign and service, describing her as an “integral part of this service to our great state.” He also extended his “deepest gratitude” to supporters, some of whom gave time, resources, prayers and encouragement.
“All of it mattered,” von Gillern said.
State Sen. Teresa Ibach of Sumner, center, talks with State Sen. Steve Erdman of Bayard. State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln watches to Ibach’s left. July 29, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Von Gillern said he launched his reelection bid one year ago to “finish the job,” including reforming the tax code, keeping neighborhoods safe and growing the economy. He said lawmakers “were able to accomplish a great deal” toward those efforts.
“Unfortunately, the voters wanted a change in this seat,” von Gillern wrote.
“I appreciate the feeling that tax relief did not replace the need and desire for tax reform,” von Gillern continued, “and I understand that national politics far from Nebraska increased the cost of goods we rely on right here in District 4.”
Von Gillern said he ran a positive and energetic race, worked his “tail off” each day to share his vision and knocked on close to 10,000 doors. He said he truly enjoyed talking with thousands of Nebraskans, including on porches where he said he earned some of his “fondest memories” that he’ll remember forever.
“It was an honor and one of the best experiences of my life,” von Gillern said. “I commit to wrap up the final days of my term just like the previous days, by working hard to ensure that this next 110th (Legislature) is productive and beneficial to Nebraskans.”
‘Earned the trust of District 4 voters’
Maxwell-Ostdiek thanked von Gillern for his “longstanding contributions to our community” as well as his legislative service. She said she wishes von Gillern and his wife well and looks forward to working with von Gillern during the transition.
Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha, a 2026 candidate for Legislative District 4, talks with volunteers for her campaign in her west Omaha neighborhood on Oct. 4, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The senator-elect will be the lone registered nonpartisan in the Legislature next year.
“(I) want to be clear that I intend to represent all of my District 4 neighbors, regardless of their party or who they supported this election season,” Maxwell-Ostdiek wrote.
“The voters of this district elected me because property taxes are too high, the cost of living is rising too quickly, the state is in a budget crisis and Nebraskans don’t feel heard,” she continued. “I will work every day to deliver progress on these issues, and look forward to getting started.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Federal appeals court finds Florida’s Medicaid termination letters insufficient
description: Florida has lost another round in a  long-running legal battle over how the administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis removed people from Medicaid. A federal appeals court ruled this week that the DeSantis administration did not provide adequate notice to people it claimed were no longer financially eligible before dropping them from the safety net program […]
text:
(iStock Getty Images Plus)Florida has lost another round in a  long-running legal battle over how the administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis removed people from Medicaid.
A federal appeals court ruled this week that the DeSantis administration did not provide adequate notice to people it claimed were no longer financially eligible before dropping them from the safety net program following the end of the public health emergency caused by COVID-19.
The 23-page decision, written by U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa, upholds a permanent injunction issued earlier this year by U.S. District Judge Marcia Morales Howard in Jacksonville.
Howard wrote a scathing 273 page opinion ordering Florida to clearly explain in its Medicaid termination letters why the state determined people were no longer financially qualified for the program.
“After a six-day bench trial, the district court found that the notices did not ‘unambiguously communicate the State’s decision to terminate benefits, the reason for that decision, or to whom it applies,’ and that the other available sources did not cure those deficiencies,” Lagoa wrote in the ruling issued Thursday. “We agree.”
The Florida Agency for Healthcare Administration (AHCA), which administers the Florida Medicaid program and one of the defendants in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to the Florida’ Phoenix’s email request for comment on the ruling.
The Department of Children and Families, the state agency charged with determining Medicaid eligibility, also did not respond to Phoenix’s request for comment.
It’s not clear whether the state plans to seek review by the U.S. Supreme Court — an action that would need to be started before DeSantis leaves office in early January. Also unclear is how Gov.-Elect Byron Donalds views the litigation.
‘Crystal clear’ standard
The National Health Law Program and Florida Health Justice Project filed the legal challenge on behalf of plaintiffs who were erroneously removed from the program. Both groups lauded the ruling.
“It is unfortunate that it took three years and extensive state resources to confirm the non-controversial proposition that Medicaid enrollees must be informed of the grounds upon which the state is ending their health care coverage before the coverage ends,” Florida Health Justice attorney Lynne Hearne said in a written statement Friday to the Florida Phoenix.
“The good news is, going forward it is crystal clear that this is the standard for all Medicaid termination notices.”
National Health Law Program senior attorney Katherine DeBriere said the ruling comes as states prepare to implement eligibility changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which changes who qualifies for Medicaid and brings even more “urgency” to well-designed notices that explain coverage decisions.
“Florida has already begun issuing notices to immigrant enrollees noting coverage terminations,” DeBriere said in a prepared statement. “As states prepare for a new wave of Medicaid paperwork and notices under OBBBA, they should heed this decision.” 
“People need enough information to understand why the state proposes to end their coverage and to challenge mistakes,” she added. “States must build those protections into their systems now. Confusing notices and inaccessible explanations put people’s health care at risk.”
Medicaid is a health care program jointly administered and paid for by the state and federal governments. Financial eligibility for Medicaid hinges on several factors, including the qualifying eligibility category; the size of the family unit and allowable income limits based on that; and the recipient’s reported income.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal government increased by 6.2% its contributions to the Medicaid program to help foot the costs of the growing number of people who qualified due to the financial downturn.
With the additional federal funding came the requirement the states couldn’t disenroll anyone from Medicaid until the public health emergency expired.
That occurred on March 31, 2023. Florida started its Medicaid unwinding the following day. And by the following year, DCF redetermined the Medicaid eligibility of more than 4 million people.
Howard’s initial ruling focused on termination notices sent to children, parents (and other caretakers of children), pregnant women, and former foster children under age 26. They are all part of the “family related Medicaid” category of beneficiaries, described by Howard as some of the state’s “most vulnerable citizens.”
Court rules Florida Medicaid termination letters fly in face of federal law

Howard found that the state did not provide enough case-specific information for recipients to understand how DCF reached its decision that they no longer qualified, making it “difficult, if not impossible, for the recipient to understand the State’s intended action as to each enrollee or the reasons for that action.”
Bad notices
The named plaintiff in the underlying case is identified in court papers Chianne D, who received an 11-page notice in April 2023 that she and her newborn son were being disenrolled for financial reasons. The notice contained eight pages discussing health-benefit criteria. One section of the letter said that neither she nor her newborn son, S.D., were eligible for Medicaid benefits because Chianne D’s household income was too high. Several pages later, a different section of the letter advised that S.D. was eligible. 
The notice didn’t include the size of Chianne D’s family or the qualifying income corresponding to the family’s size. Neither did it disclose what Chianne D’s reportable monthly income was or the Medicaid eligibility category assigned her.
Calling the DCF call center didn’t provide clarification. The court record indicates a DCF agent acknowledged to Chianne D that S.D.’s Medicaid “remained open” but the agent also told her that S.D. was being terminated because her income was too high.
Ultimately, the state determined that Chianne D.’s own coverage had been incorrectly terminated and that she remained eligible for Medicaid.
In confirming Howard’s decision on appeal, Lagoa wrote, “When a trained DCF employee could read the notice and come away with the wrong answer about whose coverage was ending, the district court did not err in finding that the notice did not reasonably convey DCF’s decision to its intended recipient.”
It wasn’t the only example of flawed determination letters plaintiffs highlighted during the six-day hearing in Jacksonville.
A.V. received an eight-page termination notice from the Medicaid program because of income limits. But the notice didn’t say what family size the state used for A.V’s family. Ultimately, A.V. , who had been on a Medicaid program called Medically Needy learned the state assigned a family size of six instead of her actual family of eight. 
The smaller family size figure lowered the allowable monthly income A.V. could earn to qualify for the Medically Needy program. Moreover, the state incorrectly inflated A.V’s reported monthly income. 
‘This is pretty bad’
Attorney Andy Bardos represented the DeSantis administration on appeal. Appearing before Lagoa and U.S. Circuit Court judges Adalberto Jordan and Robin Rosenbaum, he defended the state’s termination notices.
Bardos argued Florida needed to adhere only to minimum due-process requirements such as the information about the state’s intended action, the date when the action would occur, and a statement of the reason why.
“With nothing else?” Jordan asked.
“We think that’s the minimum requirement of due process,” Bardos replied.
Jordan offered that perhaps the state notices could have included additional information steering people to a website where they could input pertinent information like their income and family size to ensure the determination was accurate, but didn’t.
“This is pretty bad,” Jordan told Bardos at the time.
Jordan wasn’t the only judge who appeared skeptical during the arguments.
Lagoa, once a DeSantis appointee to the Florida Supreme Court, told Bardos that “it’s clear” Medicaid notices must provide the recipient with meaningful notice and the opportunity to be heard.
“You cannot be heard if you don’t know what you’re objecting to. Because, by the way, I don’t think you would like a trial judge to issue an order just telling you ‘denied’ and not tell you the basis. Correct? Because you wouldn’t be able to have meaningful appellate review.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont keeps Brokman as chief, mulls changes in cabinet
description: Gov. Ned Lamont asked for the resignations of his cabinet Friday, the first step to assessing what changes he intends to make before Jan. 6.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont, fresh off a landslide reelection victory Tuesday, asked for the resignations of his cabinet Friday, the first step to assessing what changes he intends to make in the weeks before beginning his third term as governor on Jan. 6.
In a brief interview, the governor said the new term offers “a chance to make some changes and inject more energy in some of our departments.” He declined to say which agencies were getting a hard look.
His chief of staff, Matt Brokman, who took a leave from the Capitol to work on Lamont’s reelection campaign, has returned to the Capitol and will remain his top aide, Lamont said. Brokman has been chief since July 2004.
Cathryn Vaulman, the governor’s communications director, noted that Lamont made the same request for resignations after winning his second term in 2022.
“As was the case in 2022, Gov. Lamont is taking this opportunity to evaluate agency leadership and ensure the administration is aligned on goals for the upcoming term,” she said. “All commissioners must go through the nomination and approval process at the start of the next session.”
Lamont has signaled education reform will be a priority in his third term, inviting speculation as to whether he will seek a new education commissioner, an appointment that technically belongs to a state Board of Education, albeit with the governor’s input. 
Charlene M. Russell-Tucker, the current commissioner, made a strong pitch to remain four years ago when he was considering a change then.
Last April, he signed an executive order creating a Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability. As chair, Lamont chose his deputy chief of staff, Natalie Wagner, with Russell-Tucker as vice chair. The commission’s recommendations are due in January.
After his reelection in 2022, Lamont made his first changes 13 days after the election, announcing the long-planned departures of his chief of staff, Paul Mounds, and general counsel, Nora R. Dannehy.
His well-regarded economic development commissioner, David Lehman, left then to rejoin the private sector. A month later, he appointed a new commissioner of social services, Andrea Barton Reeves.
Lamont has at least one commissioner whom he inherited from his predecessor, Gov. Dannel P. Malloy. Jorge Perez has been the banking commissioner since February 2015.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas governor proposes spending hikes for Medicaid, SNAP, school vouchers in $7B budget
description: Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders unveiled her nearly $7 billion state budget for the coming fiscal year Friday, promising a fifth round of income tax cuts if the Legislature approves her proposal. New spending items include $70 million for school vouchers, $20 million for early childhood education, $25 million for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Pr[...]
text:
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders presents her fiscal year 2028 budget proposal to state lawmakers at the Capitol's Multi-Agency Complex on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders unveiled her nearly $7 billion state budget for the coming fiscal year Friday, promising a fifth round of income tax cuts if the Legislature approves her proposal.
New spending items include $70 million for school vouchers, $20 million for early childhood education, $25 million for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and $150 million for Medicaid.
The state budget for the current fiscal year, which began July 1, totals $6.7 billion. Sanders’ proposed fiscal year 2028 budget would give the state a $449 million surplus, Finance and Administration Secretary Jim Hudson said, though future tax cuts would lower that number.
The state netted a $655 million surplus from the fiscal year that ended June 30, and the state has about $4 billion in reserves.
Sanders, a Republican, won a second term Tuesday, and her party will maintain its legislative majority. She told lawmakers Friday that she saw the election as an endorsement of Republican fiscal values.
“Budgets show our priorities: education, public safety, public health, care for our most vulnerable and tax cuts,” Sanders said.
Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families praised the proposed investments in early childhood education, Medicaid and SNAP in a news release but said the proposed budget is “light on details.”
“We do not believe it goes far enough to address the needs of Arkansans,” the organization wrote. “And the push for additional income tax cuts does not make life more affordable for most Arkansans and instead threatens important programs and services.”
Arkansas Explained: What’s happening with the state’s school voucher program?

Sanders faces a changed lawmaking landscape next year after Democrats flipped 10 House seats Tuesday, breaking Republicans’ decade-long supermajority and requiring bipartisan support for most budget bills.
Democratic and some Republican lawmakers have questioned the growing cost of the state’s school voucher program created in 2023, the year Sanders took office.
School vouchers remain one of Sanders’ signature policies, and her proposed budget allocates $70 million more to the program for fiscal year 2027. That would bring its total cost to more than $379 million.
Lawmakers from both parties praised the annually recurring $20 million Sanders proposed for early childhood education. Last year, a task force came to the rescue of Arkansas’ financial aid program for low-income families seeking child care after providers said proposed changes to the program could force them out of business.
Sanders said investing in early childhood education would “build on the achievements of the LEARNS Act,” the 2023 law that created the voucher program for K-12 students.
“I’m confident this will be another opportunity to transform Arkansas education and set our students up for success from cradle to career,” Sanders said.
The top Democrat in the House, Rep. Andrew Collins, said the budget doesn’t go far enough in funding early childhood education and that the new Medicaid funding won’t cover badly needed increases in reimbursement rates.
“While I truly appreciate these advancements, the budget still falls far short of where we need to be,” he wrote in a Facebook post.
 Medicaid and SNAP

Last year’s federal tax and spending cut legislation, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, will cut Medicaid spending by $900 billion over the next decade. More than 800,000 Arkansans are covered by Medicaid, the federally funded, low-cost insurance program for low-income people and people with disabilities.
Sanders’ proposed budget includes not only a $150 million increase for the Department of Human Services to administer Medicaid, but also $200 million in one-time surplus funds and another $75 million in dedicated interest earnings for the program.
Hudson reiterated past statements to lawmakers that Medicaid claims spiked this year, but he said he’s confident the state has “the ability to meet the ongoing operational needs of Medicaid” until the current fiscal year ends June 30, 2027.
Families of Arkansas children with disabilities say more action needed on waitlist

The Department of Human Services’ increased Medicaid administrative funding includes $34 million for supportive living services that families of Arkansans with complex disabilities have been requesting for years.
Sanders announced in September that the state would fund in-home care for the thousands of families on the waitlist for Medicaid coverage of these services. She estimated this would cost $17 million for the second half of fiscal year 2027.
The future of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion is expected to be one of the Legislature’s top priorities next year. The Trump administration rejected a five-year renewal of the program in July and said Thursday that the program would stay in effect for the first half of 2027 while Arkansas officials consider a new model. 
Additionally, Sanders’ proposed budget’s new $25 million for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program will address higher administrative costs required by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The federal legislation requires states with error rates above 6% to pay at least 5% of SNAP benefit costs beginning in fiscal year 2028. 
Sanders’ proposed budget sets aside a one-time $50 million allocation for the state’s potential share of SNAP benefit costs because Arkansas’ rate of overpaying or underpaying those benefits has been consistently above 6%.
Arkansas is the nation’s most food-insecure state. Democrats and community advocates said earlier this year that the SNAP funding shortfall was one reason not to cut taxes, especially when the lower and middle classes see little savings.
The state’s top income tax rate dropped from 7% to 4.9% under Sanders’ Republican predecessor Asa Hutchinson, who served from 2015 to 2023. The four tax cuts implemented during Sanders’ first term have lowered the top rate to 3.7%.
Hudson said Friday that the state’s revenues of $214.4 million are nearly 10% above what his office forecast for this point in the fiscal year, even accounting for the tax cut Sanders signed in May that was retroactive to Jan. 1.

Arkansas Explained: What’s happening with state tax cuts?


 LEARNS opponent named Joint Budget co-chair

Republican Sen. Jimmy Hickey was chosen as the next Senate co-chair of the powerful Joint Budget Committee Thursday, succeeding former chairman Sen. Jonathan Dismang, who resigned in September.
The committee oversees all appropriations and budgetary matters that come before the Legislature. Hickey’s selection to the post comes as the state faces questions about the cost of school vouchers and changes to its Medicaid expansion program.
The senator from Texarkana previously chaired the Senate Revenue and Tax Committee, and is a past president pro tempore.
Sen. Jonathan Dismang (left), R-Searcy, and Sen. Jimmy Hickey (right), R-Texarkana, on the Arkansas Senate floor on Monday, March 31, 2025. (Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)
Hickey, a former banker, has split with Sanders on several occasions since she took office. He was one of two Republican senators who voted against the LEARNS Act, and he requested an audit of Sanders’ office’s 2023 purchase of a $19,000 lectern.
Hickey led the opposition to the nomination of Republican Sen. Breanne Davis of Russellville, a Sanders ally and a lead sponsor of the LEARNS Act, as the next Senate president Thursday. He nominated Republican Sen. Ron Caldwell of Wynne to the post three times, resulting in three deadlocked votes, before senators agreed to elevate Republican Sen. Joshua Bryant of Rogers to the top job.
Reporter Ainsley Platt contributed to this article.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: McKee submits names of three more judges to Rhode Island Senate
description: Gov. Dan McKee delivered three more judicial nominations to Rhode Island Senate leaders Friday afternoon, naming two new Superior Court justices and a chief judge for the District Court. McKee nominated District Court Associate Judge Debra Saunders to become the court’s chief judge and Family Court Magistrate Denise Cassisi Finkelman and employment attorney [...]
text:
The exterior of the Frank Licht Judicial Complex in downtown Providence. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Gov. Dan McKee delivered three more judicial nominations to Rhode Island Senate leaders Friday afternoon, naming two new Superior Court justices and a chief judge for the District Court.
McKee nominated District Court Associate Judge Debra Saunders to become the court’s chief judge and Family Court Magistrate Denise Cassisi Finkelman and employment attorney Carly B. Iafrate to become associate justices on the Superior Court.
“These three nominees have demonstrated strong character, sound judgment, and the highest integrity. I’m confident they will serve Rhode Islanders well on the bench,” McKee said in a statement.
The three nominations come as the Senate begins reviewing judicial appointments, including eight magistrate nominees and McKee’s selection of Superior Court Judge Luis Matos for the Rhode Island Supreme Court. McKee leaves office in January.
RI Senate begins judicial nominations process. House hearing on McKee’s Supreme Court pick pending

Matos’ nomination requires approval from the House of Representatives in addition to the Senate. No hearings have been scheduled by the House Committee on Judiciary as of Friday.
McKee’s latest nominations were not formally transmitted to the Senate Friday, chamber spokesperson Greg Paré said in an interview.
“We recessed yesterday, so our desk is open,” Paré said. “We can receive the letters and then just refer them to committee.”
The Senate Committee on Judiciary is scheduled to meet Nov. 17 and 18 to consider nominees.   If advanced by the 10-member panel, the nominees will proceed to the floor for full confirmation.
Saunders would fill the District Court chief judge vacancy created by the Oct. 9 retirement of Jeanne E. LaFazia, who stepped down after 16 years on the bench.
A District Court associate judge since 2023, Saunders previously spent 15 years as clerk of the Rhode Island Supreme Court, supervising the Clerk’s Office and its nine-person staff. She oversaw the court’s appellate process and attorney licensing, and directed the transition to the Uniform Bar Examination, according to her resume.
She also served as deputy general counsel for the Supreme Court, advising on legal issues involving court operations, personnel, budgets, security and technology. Earlier in her career, she prosecuted misdemeanor and felony cases as a special assistant attorney general.
“I am deeply honored to be selected for this role, and I’m grateful to Governor McKee for his trust and belief,” Saunders said in a statement. “I look forward to serving the people of Rhode Island with the fairness, integrity, and an unwavering commitment this role demands.”
Finkelman would fill the Superior Court vacancy created by Joseph Montalbano’s ascension to presiding justice of the state’s top trial court in April.
A Family Court magistrate since 2021, Finkelman has presided over cases involving custody, placement, child support and contested divorces. Before joining the Judiciary, she ran her own law practice, representing clients in litigation, mediating Family Court disputes and serving as a guardian ad litem for children involved in domestic cases.
“I’m beyond honored and grateful to be chosen for this extremely important role,” Finkelman said in a statement. 
She is the wife of state Rep. Alex Finkelman, a Jamestown Democrat.
Iafrate would fill the Superior Court seat formerly occupied by Jeffrey Lanphear before his retirement in April.
Among the finalists to fill Montalbano’s vacant spot, Iafrate is a labor and employment lawyer who has operated a private practice since 2003, her resume notes. Iafrate helped negotiate the three-year contract the state reached with multiple public employee unions in 2024. That same year, she represented then-Senate Majority Whip Valarie Lawson before the Ethics Commission over whether her former career as a teacher and her position as president of a state teachers’ union prevented her from voting on pension-related legislation.
Iafrate said in a statement she looks forward to the Senate vetting process.
“I will work tirelessly to protect the integrity of the Superior Court and fairness for all in Rhode Island,” she said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham, Gov.-elect Haaland begin transfer of power after historic victory
description: Outgoing New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham met with her successor, fellow Democrat Deb Haaland, Friday morning on the fourth floor of the Roundhouse in Santa Fe to offer some parting advice.
text:
From left to right: New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland, Lt. Gov. Howie Morales and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham address reporters at the Roundhouse in Santa Fe on Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Outgoing New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham met with her successor, fellow Democrat Deb Haaland, Friday morning on the fourth floor of the Roundhouse in Santa Fe to offer some parting advice.
“This job places you at the center of America’s heartbeat,” Lujan Grisham said at a Friday news conference with Haaland, outgoing Lt. Gov Howie Morales and incoming Lt. Gov. and current state Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard. “I want the governor-elect and the lieutenant governor-elect to take every opportunity to advance everything they can that makes a difference for New Mexicans; to get through the tough times, and there will be many; and to celebrate all of the things that really matter.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lujan Grisham said she was glad to be in a position where she was handing over control of the state’s executive branch to someone she has long known and respected. The transition marks the second one between the two as Haaland also succeeded Lujan Grisham in Congress representing the state’s 1st Congressional District after the latter was elected governor in 2018.
“This is a gift, I believe, to New Mexico — a true New Mexican who understands what we can do and accomplish,” Lujan Grisham said.
Haaland, who Tuesday became the first Native American woman to be elected governor in U.S. history, was visibly emotional as she embraced Lujan Grisham in the lobby of the governor’s office.
Even as New Mexico has continued to struggle in recent years with poor national rankings in regard to metrics such as crime, education and child welfare, Lujan Grisham oversaw significant growth in the state’s trust funds, established scholarships for tuition-free college degrees and pioneered the first-in-the-nation universal childcare program.
Once she’s sworn in in January, Haaland has pledged to sign an executive order implementing a moratorium on new large-scale data center developments while the state Legislature crafts guardrails around such projects. Earlier this week, she also said she would prioritize naming a new leader for the state’s beleaguered child welfare agency. Beyond that, she has said she’ll immediately get to work on a state budget for the 60-day legislative session that starts Jan. 19.
“The only real promise I made to New Mexicans is that I’ll work as hard as I can to ensure that we are lifting New Mexicans up across the state,” she said Friday.
Day after historic win, New Mexico Gov.-elect Haaland starts accepting resumes

Haaland added that she will “protect and expand Gov. Lujan Grisham’s legacy,” particularly as it relates to universal childcare and early childhood education.
“She has also done a phenomenal job on lifting so many New Mexicans out of poverty,” Haaland said. “I’m also excited to build upon the accomplishments of this current administration with investments in healthcare, affordable housing, affordability in general for New Mexico families across this state.”
Lujan Grisham and Haaland spoke alongside their running mates, who can often get overlooked in conversations about the state’s leadership. Both mentioned the important, behind-the-scenes role a lieutenant governor often plays.
When Lujan Grisham signed the universal childcare program into law earlier this year, for instance, she credited Morales for taking up the issue when he was a state senator and continuing to prioritize it after he joined her administration.
At Friday’s news conference, he said he told his successor to continue a practice that she and Haaland employed on the campaign trail: traveling outside of Santa Fe and Albuquerque to hear the concerns of New Mexicans everywhere.
“New Mexico is very much a rural state,” he said. “Those relationships will be so instrumental when you come into the legislative session that you’re prepared to advocate for the smallest parts of the state.” 
Garcia Richard, who attended the same Silver City high school as Morales, said she planned to do so and to continue Morales’ tradition of working closely alongside the governor.
“A lieutenant governor is only as effective as their relationship with the governor,” she said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota sues Trump administration over new Medicaid work requirements, again
description: Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, along with attorneys general from Washington, New Mexico and Oregon, is suing the Trump administration over new Medicaid work requirements passed in H.R. 1., the 2025 tax and spending law also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The states, which filed the lawsuit Thursday, are employing a legal […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C., in December. Minnesota, along with three other states, sued Oz and the Trump administration Thursday over new Medicaid work requirements. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, along with attorneys general from Washington, New Mexico and Oregon, is suing the Trump administration over new Medicaid work requirements passed in H.R. 1., the 2025 tax and spending law also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
The states, which filed the lawsuit Thursday, are employing a legal strategy based on an argument successfully used by conservative states to oppose Obamacare’s Medicaid expansion.
Around 1.2 million Minnesotans are enrolled in Medicaid, the public health insurance program jointly funded by the federal government and state government which serves low-income, disabled, elderly and pregnant people.
The Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare, expanded Medicaid to cover adults who make between 100% and 138% of the federal poverty line in many states, including Minnesota. The federal government foots the bill for 90% of the care for those adults, instead of the usual 50-50 split between federal and state funding for other Medicaid recipients. Over 200,000 people are in the Medicaid expansion population in Minnesota, as of 2025.
New work requirements in OBBBA make those Medicaid expansion recipients prove that they work or volunteer if they’re able to, starting in 2027. The work requirements, set to take place on Jan. 1, are expected to lead to people losing Medicaid, which is the main way OBBBA lowers spending on the program.
In June, Minnesota joined 25 Democratic-led states in suing the Trump administration over its implementation of the work requirements, arguing that the administration’s new “medically frail” designation was too narrow and would make it too difficult for ill and disabled people to remain on Medicaid. On Oct. 29, a federal judge granted the states a partial victory, ruling against the administration’s narrow definition but upholding other restrictions — and upholding the work requirements in general.
The new lawsuit references a 2012 Supreme Court decision, National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, centering on Congress’s power to enact provisions of the Affordable Care Act. In that decision, the Supreme Court decided that Congress does not have the authority to threaten states with complete loss of federal Medicaid funding if states don’t comply with the expansion. As a result, 10 states were able to forego the expansion.
In the Thursday lawsuit, the states argued that the OBBBA work requirements “dramatically reshaped and redefined” Medicaid “into a vehicle to encourage work, yet did so under the guise of merely amending it,” and that forcing states to administer those changes under threat of all federal Medicaid funding would contradict the Supreme Court’s 2012 decision.
The state is in the process of implementing the new work requirements, and has encouraged Medicaid recipients to use a renewal tool to help the department prepare for the requirements.
According to the Minnesota Department of Human Service’s 2026 supplemental budget, which was passed by the state Legislature, the new work requirements will cost the state $1 million to implement and will save the state $1 million in the 2027 fiscal year and $3 million across both the 2028 and 2029 fiscal years — i.e., $1 million to $1.5 million per year in the next three years.
Budget officials have also previously said that new work requirements may cause some of the expansion recipients to switch from being eligible based on income to being eligible based on disability to avoid the administratively burdensome requirements. Their healthcare would then be funded roughly equally by the state and federal government, meaning the state would pay for more of their care than previously — a win for the federal budget, a loss for Minnesota.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Arrest in Eve Rogers case raises medication misuse, access issue
description: Experts cited concerns after reports of "loose medication" and Benadryl misuse in arrest warrant in overdose death of 12-year-old Eve Rogers.
text:
In the hours after 12-year-old Eve Rogers was found dead in her Enfield home by her mother in March, police responding to the scene discovered “loose medication and/or vitamin pills” on the floor, in a pill organizer and elsewhere in the child’s room, according to documents.
A search of the other children’s rooms also yielded sightings of loose medication. When questioned about the use of medication, pill organizers given to the children and the use of allergy medicine and sleep aids, Eve’s mother, Melanie Federline, contradicted herself and her husband, Anthony Federline, and admitted to not being sure if her daughter had taken a sleep aid the night before, an arrest warrant states.
Although no one has been charged with her death, police arrested Melanie Federline last month for risk of injury to a child. Rogers’ stepfather, Anthony Federline, was also arrested shortly after the girl’s death and charged with sexual assault after police discovered evidence of an assault and his DNA on her body.
Since Melanie Federline’s arrest, details in the arrest warrant about loose pills and the use of allergy medicine in the home as a sleep aid have alarmed physicians and child welfare experts. They say that the careless way that Federline handled medications around Rogers and her siblings can serve as warning to parents and an opportunity to spread information about the potential dangers of medication as well as the use of antihistamines in kids.
Rogers died of “acute diphenhydramine, fluoxetine and bupropion intoxication,” according to the Office of the Medical Examiner, generic names for the antihistamine Benadryl and the antidepressants Prozac and Wellbutrin. The child had 23,000 nanograms per milliliter of diphenhydramine in her system, about five times the lethal dose, according to the warrant. 
The cause of death is undetermined, meaning it was unclear if ingesting the lethal amount was accidental, or the result of a suicide or homicide.
“It’s heartbreaking when you see that a 12-year-old had died who deserved to be in a safe environment where she was growing up,” said Sen. Saud Anwar, D-South Windsor, a physician and co-chair of the legislature’s Public Health Committee. “And while we worry about the sleep medications, literally every medicine has risks associated with it, so we need to have a comprehensive way of preventing accidental overdose of our children, not from Benadryl like in this case or sleep aids, but actually every medicine.”
A week prior to her death, Rogers had been picked up by police in the middle of the night after leaving her home without her parents’ knowledge and stealing a drink from a gas station. The incident prompted an investigation from the state’s Department of Children and Families.
Anwar said the information in the warrant on medication in the home raised questions about how thoroughly DCF had checked out the family home in the week preceding Rogers’ death.
Asked about whether there was a home visit this week, DCF referred The Connecticut Mirror to previous statements about their investigation that did not include that information. 
The statements said, in part, that is it DCF’s policy and best care practice to interview all adults and children in the home and that “we spoke to all household members in-person and collateral contacts were made pertaining to the allegations in the 3/11/26 report. The investigation into that specific incident has been closed.”
The warrant for Melanie Federline’s arrest details a household in disarray, including “a trash can overflowing with old and moldy food, kitchen pans containing old food, bowls containing old milk and cereal on the first floor.”
In addition to the loose pills in Rogers’ room, there were “hundreds of used pill capsules with the medication removed, as well as loose, unused medications that were not stored in medication containers.” Dozens of sex toys were found in the home, including a vibrator in Rogers’ room which Melanie Federline said she purchased for her.
The warrant also noted that Federline should have reasonably noticed how quickly the supply of diphenhydramine sleep aid pills were diminishing, and given her daughter’s history of self-harm and suicidal thoughts, taken more care with how she handled the medication and followed medical advice from Rogers’ therapist.
The warrant says that Melanie Federline often gave Rogers Benadryl — the brand name for diphenhydramine — to sleep. Other medications like Lorazapam, Wellbutrin and Adderall were being used by Rogers or other household members, as well as a “Sleep Aid” medication and melatonin. 
The warrant also described a complaint to the Massachusetts Department of Children and Families in 2017 in which Melanie Federline said she gave her daughter NyQuil to “make her go to sleep,” something she did “often and did not consult a pediatrician.” 
Melanie Federline also told Enfield police in March that Rogers sometimes took Benadryl for help sleeping.
Dr. John Brancato, director of emergency medicine at Connecticut Children’s Hospital, said that Benadryl should not be given to children as a sleep aid, and in recent years has not been recommended for use in children even to treat allergies because of its side effects.
“I think for many years, people would give their kids Benadryl because a dose of Benadryl is known to cause for many people some drowsiness. And it says so right on the bottle. The problem with it is that it’s not hard to overdose Benadryl, and it can be really pretty toxic,” he said.
A Benadryl overdose can cause hallucinations, agitation and seizures. Brancato said that in the last six months, Connecticut Children’s has seen around 40 kids who came in because of a Benadryl overdose.
“In the last couple of years there’s been a really big push for us from the standpoint of antihistamine use to encourage the use of much safer second generation antihistamines like cetirizine,” also known by its brand-name Zyrtec, which has the same allergy-treating benefits as Benadryl but with a better safety profile. Cold medicines are not recommended at all in kids under 2 years old.
Brancato said that many parents struggle to help their children sleep, but recommended they start with some adjustments to routines and behaviors, “lots of things that sound like common sense and yet people don’t always do them.” The list includes keeping screens away from kids before bedtime, eating earlier in the evening because an active metabolism can keep some kids up, and ensuring kids get plenty of fresh air and activity during the day so they are tired enough to sleep at night.
Brancato also advises parents to keep drugs out of the reach of children, even over-the-counter medications that are safe in small doses.
“I took care of a child many years ago in my training who died from liver from acetaminophen overdose,” or the generic name for Tylenol, a drug that he said is safe at the correct dose.
Many children’s medications also have flavorings to get children to take them, increasing risks of accidental overdose. Brancato said parents should consider putting medications in a lock box or at least in a place children can’t get to them.
“With increasing numbers of kids with mental and behavioral health problems, that’s a huge risk: to have things that are thought to be safe available in the house,” he said, not just for younger kids who may not understand what they are ingesting, but also for “kids who may actually be at risk for wanting to hurt themselves” by overdosing on drugs. 
Child Advocate Christina Ghio, whose office investigates suspicious child deaths, echoed Brancato’s call for vigilance. 
“We need to think about the fact that really any medication that is taken outside of what is the recommended dosage can be dangerous to children, and so we want parents to be aware of that reality, and to store their medications safely,” she said. “We know 16 kids a day, on average, go to the emergency room with self harm or suicidal ideation every day in Connecticut, and so if there’s something that’s accessible to them, that’s a risk, right? And we want to reduce risk as much as possible.”
Anwar said he hoped that Ghio would be able to get answers. 
“That’s where the child advocate would have a better opportunity to find out if DCF had visited the home and what kind of an analysis they had. What was the risk assessment that they had identified in that case?” he said. “And while they were visiting and doing a site visit, did they actually see medications around? Was that documented? Was a warning given to the parent?”
It remains unclear what role access to medication played in Rogers’ death. But depending on what Ghio’s office finds, Anwar said there could be opportunities to pursue legislative solutions to act and create more safeguards for children in the future.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bridgeport Art Trail rolls into its 18th year
authors: Alisha Martindale | Special to The Connecticut Mirror
description: This weekend, the Bridgeport Art Trail will feature more than 200 artists, spanning 30+ sites, multiple studios, stores and galleries.
text:
On an unseasonably hazy evening in early November, Bridgeport welcomed curious cultural enthusiasts from all corners of Connecticut to experience the soul of the city, through the lens of creative visionaries past and present. 
As part of the 18th Annual Bridgeport Art Trail, which features over 200 artists and spans more than 30 sites across the city, multiple studios, stores and galleries opened their doors to what is anticipated to be more than 5,000 visitors in search of community, connection and inspiration between Nov. 5 and 8.
“That it’s sustained 18 years is pretty amazing,” said Suzanne Kachmar, director of City Lights Gallery and a founder and organizer of the Art Trail. “People — the artists and the community — embrace it. I think it bridges art and community, which for me is very important.”
Attendees at the Housatonic Museum of Art enjoy a highly spirited and passionate lecture about F. Luis Mora’s work by guest curator, Dr. Cynthia Roznoy, on Nov. 5, 2026. The event was part of the kickoff of the 18th annual Bridgeport Art Trail.  Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
Kachmar said she has always seen the arts as a sign of civic vitality, and she seeks to use the Art Trail as a way to amplify the work artists are doing to improve and knit together the city. Growing up in Stratford, she savored the American Shakespeare Theatre, which went up in flames in 2019. Her mom was a founding member of Stratford’s Polka Dot Playhouse.  
“It’s the ‘Horton Hears A Who’ theory,” she said. “We need to collectively let people realize we’re here. I’m still shocked, honestly, that people want to be a part of [the Art Trail]. It’s like an artist’s homecoming. It’s like an artists’ holiday. It’s all in Bridgeport, and it’s all wonderful.”
Multimedia artist, Joseph Fekieta stands in front of his sculpture made of recycled materials and tilted, “Renewal 1,000,000 AD” Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
Museum guests and campus students alike enjoyed live music, fresh pasta, lively conversation, and even warm embraces together during the Housatonic Museum of Art’s Bridgeport Art Trail Launch Celebration. Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
As part of the Art Trail launch Thursday night, the Housatonic Museum of Art welcomed visitors to its Burt Chernow Galleries for a celebration of the city’s vibrant arts community. That included guided tours of “Making His Mark in Connecticut: The Creative Process of F. Luis Mora,”  an exhibition of selected artworks by Uruguayan-born artist F. Luis Mora. 
The featured exhibition explores the main themes of “America 250” through the lens and creative process of Mora, the first Hispanic member of the National Academy of Design, who lived in Gaylordsville, Conn. between 1912 and 1913. Visitors can see his preparatory sketches alongside the finished works, offering insight into the evolution of his practice. 
As part of the celebration, attendees went on guided tours of the work by guest curator, Dr. Cynthia Roznoy, who spent time educating guests on the exhibition.
Museum guest and Bridgeport resident Andreyah Black enjoys a highly spirited and passionate lecture about F. Luis Mora’s work by guest curator, Dr. Cynthia Roznoy, on Nov. 5, 2026. The event was part of the kickoff of the 18th annual Bridgeport Art Trail.  Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
Museum guest and Bridgeport resident Andreyah Black said she’s an “an art aficionado,” and was eager to jump into the Art Trail’s festivities.
When asked what her favorite painting was at the exhibit, she motioned to Mora’s painting “Jeanne Cartier.” 
“I love the colors” she said, pointing to how her outfit and makeup seemed exactly right for the occasion.
Jennier Reynolds-Kaye, director of the Housatonic Museum of Art, and Andrew Pelletier, campus director, tutor and academic support for the CSCU Housatonic Community College, warmly welcome museum guests to the museum during the kickoff of the Bridgeport Art Trail on Nov. 5, 2026. Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
Outside the galleries, museum Director Jennifer Reynolds-Kaye and CT State Housatonic Campus Director Andrew Pelletier welcomed museum guests from the hazy drizzle outside.
When asked about the importance of the Bridgeport Art Trail, Reynolds-Kaye called it a tremendous and meaningful event for both the museum and the city.”
“It’s such an honor to be part of it,” she said. “It really brings much-needed attention to the incredibly vibrant arts community that’s in Bridgeport, both the artists, the galleries and the Housatonic Museum of Art.” 
Museum guest and local sculptor / painter John Bright, owner of Brightworks Gallery in Bridgeport, stops in to support and enjoy the launch festivities at the Housatonic Museum of Art.  Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
Nearby, attendee and local sculptor and painter John Bright, owner of Brightworks Gallery in Bridgeport, stops in to support and enjoy the launch festivities at the Housatonic Museum of Art.
“I’m following the Art Trail since I’m in it, my gallery is going to be open on Sunday,” he said. He said his work is also on display at Schelfhaudt Gallery, which will be open Saturday.
Five minutes down the road at the City Lights Gallery, the nonprofit run by Kachmar, guests and artists enjoyed a more intimate experience centered around a theme. The spirit of the evening, in the words of participating artist Ellen Tresselt, was “We’ve all had enough … of everything!”
When asked why she founded the Art Trail and continues to run it today, Kachmar said that “I believe that art should serve the community, and that also the arts can connect people. I’m a natural dot connector.”
“We’ve got Norwalk, Westport and New York and Boston and New Haven, and we had to make our noise together so we could have a presence,” she said.
Artist Ellen Tresselt with her work, a paper collage made of origami paper and titled, “White Gaze,” at opening festivities for the 18th annual Bridgeport Art Trail at City Lights Gallery on Nov. 5, 2026. “My understanding of this exhibit is it has to do with timeliness,” she said. “I know what my piece is about, my piece is a political piece. I think it’s really a lot of social commentary — how people are feeling about everything! I think a lot of this work has come out of frustration and a feeling of being fed up with the status quo.” Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
Artist Francis Pressley, who has been an 18-year participant of the Bridgeport Art Trail, pictured at City Lights Gallery on Nov. 5, 2026. Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
And the community came out, for a wonderfully noisy presence that kicked off a weekend jam-packed with artist panels, museum visits, and hundreds of open studios across the city. 
One such artist, Francis Pressley, said this will be his 18th year participating. In that time, he has become a close artistic colleague of Kachmar’s.
“I’ve always admired Hillary,” he said when asked about his jubilant portrait of Hillary Clinton on wood. “I always thought she was a little bit brighter than her husband …  much more ambitious, so I painted her! I also was working on just wood, seeing the texture of the wood and what I could do with it, and then you know, it was Hillary!”
“American’t Contemplation,” by artist  Iyaba Ibo Mandingo, is installed beside some of Kachmar’s own artwork at City Lights Gallery. The show is part of the 18th annual Bridgeport Art Trail, which kicked off Nov. 5, 2026.  Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
While the artist Iyaba Ibo Mandingo was himself away, his partner Jacinth Stevenson attended the gallery event in support and representation of Mandingo’s acrylic work “American’t Contemplation”.
A multimedia artist, storyteller and puppeteer, Mandingo was born in Antigua and he left when he was 11. He said he feels Antigua played a major role in the artist that he is today, Stevenson said. This year, that meant that he was at Antigua’s art week, which happens to take place at the same time as Bridgeport’s.
“I’m here to represent!” said Stevenson. When asked about the subject of the work, she said that “it’s about the struggles of men in this particular diaspora, with “vibrant colors to represent the island culture of Antigua.”
Attendees at City Lights Gallery at the kickoff to the 18th annual Bridgeport Art Trail on Nov. 5, 2026. Credit: Alisha Martindale / CT Mirror
The 18th annual Bridgeport Art Trail runs from Nov. 5-8 across the city of Bridgeport. To learn more, including a map and full schedule of events, click here. 
CT Mirror Arts and Culture Editor Lucy Gellman contributed to this story.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Regents to review two candidates to lead Center for Intellectual Freedom
description: The overseeing committees for the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa moved ahead two candidates for the center’s top role Friday after a finalist’s rejection of a job offer caused a national search to continue. Members of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa’s executive committee and full advisory […]
text:
Panelists speaking Dec. 6, 2025, at the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, from left, are center Interim Director Luciano de Castro, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education David Barker, state Rep. Taylor Collins, state Sen. Kerry Gruenhagen and Regent Christine Hensley. The center's advisory council approved two candidates to be interviewed by the board of regents for the director job. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The overseeing committees for the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa moved ahead two candidates for the center’s top role Friday after a finalist’s rejection of a job offer caused a national search to continue.
Members of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa’s executive committee and full advisory council met Friday afternoon to discuss finalists for the permanent director position, a job that was supposed to be already filled by a previously selected candidate.
Executive Committee Chair Mark Bauerlein told the advisory committee that the executive committee completed interviews with two candidates for the director job and its recommendation was to move both forward as finalists for the board of regents to interview. The advisory council gave unanimous approval to send the candidates ahead.

“The board of regents will interview the finalists in closed session at next week’s meeting, and all of the identities will continue to remain confidential before and during the interview process because they did sign confidentiality documents,” said Regent Chris Hensley, chair of the board of regents committee overseeing the center.
Discussion of the center director position is scheduled for Nov. 11 at the board’s meeting at Iowa State University, according to the board’s meeting agenda.
The original candidate chosen for the position, Carson Holloway, informed the board Tuesday he had chosen to go with another job offer at the University of Florida. Holloway was a department head and professor at the University of Nebraska at Omaha at the time he was interviewing for the position in Iowa.
With Holloway’s decision, the national search for a new center director has now lasted close to five months, having launched in mid-June with the original goal of selecting a permanent director in September. University of Iowa professor Luciano de Castro served as interim president from the center’s establishment in summer 2025 to Oct. 22 of this year.
