name: West Virginia Watch
title: Changes for WV childcare subsidy program likely in 2027 as Morrisey, lawmakers eye pricetag
description: A program used by thousands of working parents in West Virginia to pay for childcare could see changes next year. The state pays for the childcare subsidy program through federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families dollars, an anti-poverty program under scrutiny by Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Other federal dollars are used, too. The governor has already […]
text:
Eleven thousand children are enrolled in West Virginia’s childcare assistance program, available to parents who are working or enrolled in school. (Photo by Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent)A program used by thousands of working parents in West Virginia to pay for childcare could see changes next year.
The state pays for the childcare subsidy program through federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families dollars, an anti-poverty program under scrutiny by Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Other federal dollars are used, too.
The governor has already signaled there could be modifications to the childcare assistance program after his administration announced a $40 million structural deficit in TANF funding. 
“The Department of Human Services continues to evaluate a range of options to ensure the TANF program operates within its available resources. No final decisions have been made regarding potential program or funding changes,” Lars Dalseide, the governor’s communications director, said on Thursday. 
“The Governor’s Office will work with the Legislature to develop sustainable solutions that do not rely on one-time federal funding,” he said. 
Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, speaks on the House of Delegates floor on Jan. 23, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
House Health Chair Evan Worrell, who has supported the child care subsidy, said on Thursday he is expecting changes to the child care subsidy in the next legislative session. 
“Everything’s on the table for what those changes could be, and I’ll say eligibility is a portion of that,” said Worrell, R-Cabell.
Right now, eligible parents and caregivers must be below 85% of the Federal Poverty Level, which is a yearly annual income of about $28,000 for a family of four. Parents must also be working on furthering their education to receive the childcare financial assistance.
More than 11,000 West Virginia children are enrolled in the childcare subsidy program.
As lawmakers consider how to pay for the program, Worrell said one consideration may be changing the income requirements for parents that would reduce eligibility. He isn’t advocating for that, but noted it could be considered during budget discussions early next year.
“It comes down to funding, right? We have Medicaid cuts coming through from the (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), but the governor’s budget will kind of show us what that priority is on his side, and we’ll have to adjust to that accordingly,” said Worrell, who also serves on the House Finance Committee.
“It will be a conversation in our caucus of what are our priorities?” he added.
Potential changes to childcare assistance come after lawmakers just passed their first-ever landmark childcare bill, which included mandates for the subsidy program. Morrisey declined to sign the legislation, letting it become law without his approval. 
Republican-sponsored House Bill 4191 was meant to help stabilize West Virginia’s struggling childcare industry as many providers serve children using child assistance across the poor state.  
In Clay County, 70% of young children at the county’s only childcare center are enrolled in the financial assistance program. 
Worrell believes that West Virginia should use state dollars to run the childcare subsidy program instead of relying on federal funds. He estimates it will cost $20 million in the state dollars.
“I strongly believe in (House Bill) 4191 and its passing. But, I also will be advocating to make sure that the funding for 4191 is put into our general revenue budget, so we are not relying on federal TANF funds to pay for that,” he said. 
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, speaks on the House of Delegates floor on March 5, 2026.(Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, has led childcare reform efforts in the Legislature. She worries about the assistance program’s future under Morrisey.
“The state has underinvested in childcare by over 50% over the last 12 years. So it’s about time that we start putting our money where our priorities are, which needs to be with children in West Virginia,” Young said. 
Lawmakers want answers delayed child care changes
The state Department of Human Services hasn’t implemented all of lawmakers’ childcare requirements despite a July 1 deadline. The Morrisey administration has said the delays were because lawmakers didn’t include state funding with their mandates. 
On Monday, lawmakers are scheduled to hear from Human Services Deputy Secretary Christina Mullins about progress on the bill during legislative interim meetings at the state Capitol in Charleston. 
“House Bill 4191 has been a little bit of a consternation with the agency as far as trying to pay for it and make it work how it’s supposed to,” Worrell said.  “We want to try to understand before we go into session, what are the pain points? What are the issues with getting it done?”
Among the bill’s requirements, lawmakers mandated that the Department of Human Services reimburse childcare providers who serve kids using the state’s childcare subsidy by the total enrollment rather than daily attendance. This was supposed to stabilize centers’ finances. 
“If the Legislature believes in enrollment versus attendance, which is what they codified, then they should put the money where their mouth is and fund the $20 million for that general revenue,” Worrell said. 
Morrisey will ask lawmakers for a $10 million to $15 million supplemental appropriation to maintain current TANF program operations through this fiscal year. Along with the childcare subsidy program, the federal funds pay for the school clothing allowance program, foster care services and more.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Incumbents, Republicans prevail in Alabama’s congressional elections
description: Incumbents and Republicans largely held onto seats in Alabama’s congressional delegation, though as in other races Democrats kept some margins closer than previous elections.  U.S. Rep. Dale Strong, R-Madison, was re-elected Tuesday night with 142,080 (53.2%) votes in unofficial returns. Democratic nominee Andrew Sneed received 124,763 (46.7%) votes in unoff[...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 13, 2026. Incumbents and Republicans largely maintained seats in Alabama's congressional delegation during Tuesday's election. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)Incumbents and Republicans largely held onto seats in Alabama’s congressional delegation, though as in other races Democrats kept some margins closer than previous elections. 
U.S. Rep. Dale Strong, R-Madison, was re-elected Tuesday night with 142,080 (53.2%) votes in unofficial returns. Democratic nominee Andrew Sneed received 124,763 (46.7%) votes in unofficial returns.
Strong thanked voters in a social media post on Wednesday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I am grateful for the opportunity to serve and represent the Fifth Congressional District. I will continue the work to keep North Alabama the best place to live, work, play, and raise a family,” the statement said.
According to Strong’s campaign website, his priorities included supporting law enforcement and anti-abortion policies and cracking down on immigration.
Sneed thanked supporters in a statement posted to social media Tuesday night.
“My family, my team, and I are so thankful to all of you for the incredible outpouring of support this last year and half. I am so sorry we couldn’t deliver this win for North Alabama,” the statement said.
Sneed campaigned on affordability, opposing school voucher programs and supported a “responsible moratorium on new data center construction in North Alabama.”
In Alabama’s 6th Congressional District, U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover, won re-election for his 7th term. Palmer received 149,921 (57.4%) votes to his Democratic opponent Maurice Mercer’s 110,957 (42.5%) votes in unofficial returns.
Palmer said in a statement Wednesday “I will continue to put the people of Alabama’s 6th Congressional District and the conservative values we share at the forefront of every decision I make in Congress.”
According to Palmer’s campaign website, his priorities included protecting Second Amendment rights, economic growth and religious freedom.
In a social media post Wednesday night, Mercer thanked supporters and said that while the results weren’t what he hoped for, he was glad that the Republican margin was reduced.
“His last two challengers received 29% and 15% of the vote, respectively 2024 and 2022, and last night we secured just above 42%, approximately 110,000 votes in a district naysayers said I wouldn’t cross 30%,” the statement said.
Mercer ran on affordability, increasing public safety and improving access to healthcare. U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, won re-election to Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District with 124,422 (53.7%) votes in unofficial returns defeating Alabama Rep. Rhett Marques who had 107,049 (46.2%) votes in unofficial returns, overcoming a Republican gerrymander.
In Alabama’s 1st Congressional District, Republican nominee former U.S. Rep. Jerry Carl defeated Democratic nominee Clyde Jones.
In a short social media post Tuesday night, Carl said he “look(s) forward to doing great things for each one of you in Washington DC.”
According to election data, Carl received 137,000 (59%) votes to Jones’ 94,900 (41%) votes in unofficial returns. Carl campaigned improving the business environment in Mobile and Baldwin Counties and affordability.
Jones congratulated Carl for his win in a statement Wednesday night but said the work isn’t over yet.
“It will be up to all of us to ensure that Mr. Carl works on our behalf for the next two years,” the statement said. “It will be up to us to ensure that our voices are heard loud and clear as they were on the campaign trail.”
Jones ran on improving access to healthcare, immigration reform and supporting veterans.
U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, also won re-election to Alabama’s 7th Congressional District defeating Republican nominee Ammie Akin. Election data shows Sewell received 174,823 (69.4%) votes and Akin received 77,085 (30.6%) votes in unofficial returns.
Sewell said in a social media post Wednesday “I am so grateful to the amazing people of AL-07 for entrusting me to represent them in Congress.”
Sewell campaigned on affordability, protecting voting rights and protecting public schools.
Akin said in a statement posted on social media Tuesday night “the campaign may be over, but the work that brought me into this race is far from finished.”
“For nearly 25 years, I’ve dedicated my life to serving families, strengthening communities, and helping people overcome barriers. That commitment was never dependent on an election, and it certainly doesn’t end with one,” the statement said. “I’m taking everything I’ve learned, every relationship I’ve built, and every story I’ve heard into whatever comes next.”
Akin ran on strengthening education, creating safe communities and affordability.
In Alabama’s 4th Congressional District, U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville, won re-election for his 16th term in office. Unofficial election results show Aderholt received 160,008 (74.8%) votes, the most of any Republican candidate running for Congress. His opponent Amanda Pusczek received 53,633 (25.1%) votes in unofficial returns.
Aderholt thanked voters in a statement on social media Tuesday night for the high number of votes.
“That is an incredible testament to the people of Alabama’s Fourth District, and I am humbled by your continued support. I look forward to continuing to work every day to deliver results for our district and the people I am privileged to represent,” the statement said.
Aderholt ran on expanding economic opportunities, “standing up against the liberal agenda,” and supporting anti-abortion policies. 
Pusczek said in a statement posted to social media Tuesday night “while the outcome tonight wasn’t what we hoped for, the movement we built together across North Alabama does not end here.” She ran on addressing gun violence, expanding ballot access and helping rural hospitals in Alabama.
U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Saks, won re-election to Alabama’s 3rd Congressional District with 141,800 (63.9%) votes in unofficial returns. His opponent Lee McInnis received 79,926 (36.%) votes in unofficial returns.
Rogers thanked voters in a short social media post Tuesday night.
“Thank you #AL03! Honored to be reelected as your representative in Congress,” the post said.
Rogers told the Alabama Reflector in a statement last month his priorities were “lifting up our communities and advancing conservative policies.”
McInnis said in a statement Wednesday morning “those of you who know me know I’m already looking at the data to see what we need to do to set the stage for the next round.”
McInnis ran on access to healthcare and affordability.
In the U.S. Senate race, U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, defeated Democratic nominee Everett Wess. Unofficial election results show Moore received 917,860 (54.7%) votes and Wess received 758,465 (45.2%) votes.
Moore thanked voters in a statement Wednesday afteroon.
“As our team and I prepare to enter the U.S. Senate in January, we are thankful for your prayers and encouragement,” the statement said. “We are committed to working for all of our state with the same focus and dedication we’ve had in serving South Alabama, and we look forward to making you proud.”
Moore’s priorities included protecting Second Amendment rights, supporting law enforcement and “stand(ing) with President Trump).
Wess said in a video statement on social media that “this is not the end.”
“We need to continue to register voters, we need to continue to activate voters, we need to go into some of the smaller counties, in my opinion, and let the people know that we are Americans, we are people, we are human, we want what’s best for Alabama,” the video said.
Wess campaigned on creating safe communities, affordable healthcare and protecting citizen rights.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginians footing the bill for war and big oil
description: No matter which party is in power, it’s a common misconception that the president of the United States has a significant impact on the price of gas at the pump. While that’s usually true, we’re living in an inflation crisis that can be pinpointed to the national and international policy of one person: the current president. West Virginians are paying the pri[...]
text:
Regular unleaded gas is $4.159 per gallon at the ParMar Store at 1503 Washington Street E in Charleston, West Virginia, on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)No matter which party is in power, it’s a common misconception that the president of the United States has a significant impact on the price of gas at the pump. While that’s usually true, we’re living in an inflation crisis that can be pinpointed to the national and international policy of one person: the current president. West Virginians are paying the price.
Normally in the weeks leading up to midterm elections when there are palpable issues people are concerned about, you’d think that the president would talk about how they’d address the issue. Unfortunately in the lead up to the midterms this week, there wasn’t a lot of focus on how national policy is making lives better for everyday West Virginians.
Two weekends ago at a campaign rally in Georgia, President Donald Trump pivoted from supporting his chosen candidates to talking about the Iran War and how it’s supercharging profits of American oil companies.
“Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happening in the Middle East… ‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ That’ll be the headline. But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn, I’m going to say it.’ We’re making a freaking fortune. Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time. And those pump prices are going to come down.”
We learned just a week later who is pocketing that “freaking fortune.” On Friday, ExxonMobil and Chevron reported tremendous increases to their bottoms lines. ExxonMobil’s profits doubled from the same period last year, while Chevron’s nearly tripled.
So who, exactly, is making a freaking fortune while United States soldiers have died and civilians in Iran and other Middle Eastern countries have died? Are those skyhigh profits trickling down to West Virginians? 
I don’t know about you, but I’m willing to bet nearly none of my neighbors, friends and family have benefited from the war. During his State of the Union speech this year, the president bragged about low gas prices. So what did he do? Go to war and get a major oil shipping lane closed. Now we’ve seen gas prices rise at the pump, and high diesel costs have led to increases in the price of goods because of transportation costs. If it feels like your dollar is worth a lot less than it used to be not even that long ago, that’s because it’s true. 
In fact, the latest inflation numbers in October were higher than usual. 
When national leaders boast about corporate profits, while cutting public goods and social support systems like food assistance and healthcare, they’re showing what their priorities are, and that’s not West Virginians. I’m inspired by how the election went, and I hope that leaders are starting to learn that they should put people’s concerns first, not corporations’.

title: Commentary: What to expect from complete Democratic dominance in the Colorado Legislature
description: Democrats in Colorado have enjoyed trifecta control of the state Capitol for eight years. It’s the longest period of one-party dominance in state history. On Tuesday, they deepened their control of Colorado politics even further. Voters installed new Democrats in every statewide office, and, based on unofficial results, state legislative leaders expect to ha[...]
text:
Colorado Senate President James Coleman delivers a speech on the opening day of the Colorado Legislature in January at the Colorado Capitol. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Democrats in Colorado have enjoyed trifecta control of the state Capitol for eight years. It’s the longest period of one-party dominance in state history. On Tuesday, they deepened their control of Colorado politics even further.
Voters installed new Democrats in every statewide office, and, based on unofficial results, state legislative leaders expect to have supermajorities for the first time in both the House of Representatives and Senate. That means they can override a governor’s veto and refer constitutional amendments to the ballot.
Plus, they don’t expect many vetoes. Term-limited Gov. Jared Polis, though he is a Democrat, often clashed with Democratic state lawmakers and vetoed or threatened to veto many of their marquee bills. They expect his successor, Phil Weiser, the state attorney general who won election Tuesday, to be more sympathetic to their agenda.
That creates a blue juggernaut never before seen at the state Capitol.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado had been growing averse to Republicans over the last decade, but this year’s nationwide anger toward the Trump administration juiced that trend.
“I think Democrats won huge margins last night nationally and in Colorado because folks don’t like what the federal government with Trump is doing,” Democratic state Rep. Kyle Brown of Louisville, who sits on the powerful Joint Budget Committee, said Wednesday. The state Legislature in the last two years has worked to mitigate damage done by national Republican policies, he said, especially related to healthcare access.
“These victories last night will give us the ability to continue that work and hopefully build upon it so that families across Colorado can afford healthcare and that we can continue to make gains on affordable housing and any number of issues that are plaguing working families and making it harder for folks to get ahead,” Brown said.
The Democratic agenda abounds with ideas to bring down costs for housing, healthcare, childcare and other necessities. Senate President James Coleman of Denver said he thinks Democrats will be “laser focused on bringing down costs for Colorado families.”
Supermajority status will help with that mission, but Coleman said it’s not necessarily a tactical windfall.
“Having a supermajority, it gives us more tools to deliver for Colorado families, but it’s not going to change our approach to responsible, effective governance,” he said, adding that he expects relations with a Weiser administration to be productive.
“We’ve been in contact — constant contact — with now Gov.-elect Weiser and his team,” Coleman said. “We look forward to finding ways when we can collaborate more and communicate with each other and be on a similar page when it comes to decisions that we believe are going to benefit every Coloradan.”
The commitments Weiser made as he ran for governor suggest there will be strong policy agreements between the executive and legislative branches.
“We aligned with his campaign, otherwise we wouldn’t have voted for him,” Coleman said.
Coleman said he’s broadly focused on K-12 and higher education, and bringing down costs of living.
“For me it is about fully funding our education system,” he said. “We’ve increased education funding for those past two years by $400 per pupil, per kid, in the state of Colorado, and that’s great. But when you’re almost dead last in the country with funding public education, that’s a very low bar.”
He’s looking for ways to bring down rising costs for childcare and housing, too.
“People are trying to figure out where they can afford to live,” he said, adding that potential solutions could involve investments in rental assistance, down payment assistance or other programs to help first-time home owners. The state could even act to limit the rising costs of groceries, Coleman said.
One clue to legislation Democrats might introduce when the next general assembly convenes in January is the list of bills Polis resisted or vetoed, such as those related to accountability for lawless federal immigration agents; robust consumer protections around AI; surveillance pricing and wage regulations; and the Worker Protection Act, which would ease union formation. Polis vetoed that bill twice.
All of these policies are on state Rep. Javier Mabrey’s agenda. Passing the Worker Protection Act is the Denver Democrat’s top priority.
“We need to make it easier to form a strong union in Colorado,” he said. “Colorado is the only blue state in the country that is not a free bargaining state. And we have lower union density in Colorado than in Alabama.”
The bill would repeal the state’s 80-year-old Labor Peace Act, which says Colorado workers who are organizing have to hold a second union election to decide whether workers who don’t support the union would have to pay fees. Mabrey said he expects Weiser would sign the measure, which is opposed by business leaders.
Previous attempts by Democrats in the Legislature to regulate AI were largely thwarted by Polis, Mabrey said.
“Gov. Polis was really hard to work with if you were trying to regulate Big Tech,” Mabrey said. In the new General Assembly, he’ll have opportunities to enact such legislation. “I think we really need to step up and do something about the rise of AI in the economy.”
Weiser is widely viewed as more progressive than Polis, but some Democrats are wary of his tendency to promote business interests. If that trait leads to vetoes, legislative Democrats for the first time will have the power to override them.

title: Commentary: We used to call leaf-peeping ‘going for a ride’
description: I saw something the other day about “leaf-peeping.” Apparently, this is an activity now. You can plan a trip around it, consult a map, book a room, and purchase clothing suitable for looking at a tree. We used to call it going for a ride. Somebody would look out the window after Sunday dinner and […]
text:
Fall foliage in Pine Mountain State Resort Park in Bell County. (Photo by Wayne Knuckles for Kentucky Lantern)I saw something the other day about “leaf-peeping.”
Apparently, this is an activity now. You can plan a trip around it, consult a map, book a room, and purchase clothing suitable for looking at a tree.
We used to call it going for a ride.
Somebody would look out the window after Sunday dinner and say, “Let’s go see if the leaves are turning.”
That was the planning committee’s entire report.
Nobody checked an app. Daddy might have checked the gas gauge, although sometimes that appeared to be more of a suggestion than an instrument.
Then everybody got in the car.
In the mountains, a fall drive didn’t require much navigation. You picked a road that went uphill and stayed on it until somebody said, “I don’t believe we’ve ever been this way.”
This was generally followed by somebody else saying, “Yes, we have.”
A discussion would develop.
The leaves were beautiful, but occasionally they had to compete with a marital hearing about whether that was the same barn we passed coming back from somebody’s funeral.
There was always something to see.
A hillside gone yellow. A red maple standing by itself like it had dressed up for church. A little house with smoke coming out of the chimney and a dog who considered traffic a personal insult.
You slowed down.
Partly for the scenery. Partly because there might be a tractor around the next curve, and its operator had no particular interest in your afternoon schedule.
Sometimes you stopped at a roadside stand.
Apples tasted better when they came out of a wooden basket beside the road. I cannot prove that scientifically, but I am willing to participate in further research.
If there was cider, you bought some.
If there were fried apple pies, the trip had fulfilled its purpose.
What I remember about those rides is how little pressure there was to accomplish anything. We weren’t trying to reach an overlook before a reservation. Nobody needed a photograph proving we had enjoyed ourselves.
We could look at a mountain without immediately turning our backs to it and holding up a telephone.
Sometimes nobody said much for miles.
Then somebody would point out an old homeplace, and a story would start. Who lived there. Who married whom. Who moved to Ohio and eventually came back.
You learned a surprising amount of family history from the back seat of a car, provided you could hear over the argument about the barn.
I understand the appeal of a fall getaway. These mountains deserve the attention.
But I’d hate for us to think enjoying the fall requires a reservation.
Pick a road. Take somebody whose company you enjoy. Leave enough time to stop when something catches your eye.
The leaves won’t stay much longer.
And if you pass a little stand selling fried apple pies, pull over.
You can admire the scenery while you eat. That way, if the colors aren’t quite what you hoped, you still have a perfectly good reason to declare the trip a success.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: GOP lawmaker seeks Senate investigation, possible expulsion of Sen. Louise Lucas
description: Republican state Sen. Bryce Reeves of Spotsylvania wants the Virginia Senate to investigate Democratic Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth and consider expelling her after federal prosecutors accused her of using her legislative influence to benefit a cannabis business she co-owns.  Reeves prefiled Senate Resolution 173 on Oct. 30 for the 2027 General Assembly s[...]
text:
State Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, faces federal charges tied to a cannabis business she co-owns. A resolution filed by Republican Sen. Bryce Reeves seeks a Senate investigation and consideration of possible expulsion. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Republican state Sen. Bryce Reeves of Spotsylvania wants the Virginia Senate to investigate Democratic Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth and consider expelling her after federal prosecutors accused her of using her legislative influence to benefit a cannabis business she co-owns. 
Reeves prefiled Senate Resolution 173 on Oct. 30 for the 2027 General Assembly session, which is scheduled to begin in January. 
The measure would direct the Senate Committee on Privileges and Elections to examine allegations behind five federal charges against Lucas, including racketeering, marijuana distribution, money laundering and honest-services fraud conspiracies, and maintaining drug-involved premises. 
In an interview with The Mercury Thursday, Reeves said the Senate has a responsibility to investigate possible misconduct independently of the criminal proceedings. He said his proposal was motivated by that obligation and his concerns about financial disclosures, rather than personal animosity toward Lucas. 
“She’s innocent until proven guilty, but there is enough circumstantial evidence, I think, that the Senate needs to investigate and figure out what’s going on,” Reeves said. “If we can’t police our own house, what does that say about us as an institution?”
The resolution could set the stage for a separate vote on expulsion, although it acknowledges Lucas’ presumption of innocence and calls for any disciplinary action to be based on committee findings “supported by evidence.”
Lucas, who serves as the Senate’s president pro tempore, did not respond to an inquiry from The Mercury seeking comment. 
Under Reeves’ proposal, the committee would seek recordings, transcripts, financial and ownership records, economic interest disclosures and legislative documents. Senators would examine whether the alleged conduct violated Virginia’s marijuana distribution laws or the General Assembly Conflict of Interests Act. 
In the interview, Reeves pointed to allegations that Lucas had failed to disclose business interests on required financial filings. He said that her position as the chair of the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee, which oversees much of the chamber’s work on taxes and spending, made scrutiny particularly important because of the responsibility its members have for the state budget. 
State Sen. Bryce Reeves, R-Spotsylvania, has filed a resolution seeking a Senate investigation into allegations against Democratic Sen. Louise Lucas and consideration of disciplinary action, including possible expulsion. (Photo courtesy Bryce Reeves)
The resolution singled out two conversations cited in the indictment. 
In one, Lucas allegedly discussed making past marijuana-related conduct legal. In another, prosecutors allege, she discussed disqualifying a prospective marijuana license applicant until money owed to her was repaid. 
The resolution calls for reviewing the underlying recordings and other evidence to determine the statements’ authenticity, context and legal significance. It cautions against treating the indictment or statements quoted in it as proof of guilt or a violation of state law. 
The committee would hold hearings as needed, provide procedural protections and report its findings and recommendations to the Senate. Any proposed disciplinary action would require another resolution specifying the action. 
Options include reprimand, censure or expulsion. The committee could also recommend referring the matter to the attorney general. 
Under the Virginia Constitution, expelling a senator requires a two-thirds vote of the chamber’s elected membership — 27 votes in the 40-member Senate. 
Reeves said he expected the panel would probably consider the matter in January and acknowledged that its review may not result in expulsion.
“It might not lead to that, maybe she’s not guilty of some of these things. I don’t want to say one way or the other. I’m just saying we need to look at it, that’s our job,” he said.  
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, could not be reached for comment Thursday. 
The federal indictment unsealed Oct. 22 charged Lucas and six others, including relatives and business associates. Prosecutors allege she helped operate a marijuana distribution enterprise, laundered proceeds and used her public office for personal financial gain. 
One allegation centers on a $750,000 payment Lucas allegedly made in 2022 for an ownership interest in a business tied to another person’s anticipated recreational marijuana license. Prosecutors allege she failed to disclose the interest and used her position in discussions involving the prospective license.  
None of the allegations have been proven in court. Reeves’ proposal would allow the Senate to examine possible legislative misconduct while the federal criminal case proceeds. 
Lucas has served in the Senate since 1992 and as president pro tempore since 2020. Following her indictment, Lucas accused federal authorities of trying to intimidate her and vowed to not back down. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger defended Lucas’ right to present a defense and questioned the timing of the indictment, which came less than two weeks before the midterm elections. Federal authorities have said the investigation began before President Donald Trump returned to office. 
House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Scott, called the allegations serious and said they should be resolved in court. 
The investigation became public in May, when federal agents searched Lucas’ Portsmouth legislative office and cannabis businesses. Prosecutors allege the operation involved The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe, businesses connected to Lucas and her associates. 
The indictment also includes firearms and wire fraud charges against other defendants. 
Reeves’ resolution would put the matter before the Senate committee responsible for reviewing potential disciplinary action. Any recommendation would go to the full Senate, where Democrats currently hold 21 seats. 
Reaching the 27 votes required for expulsion would take at least eight Democratic votes if all 19 Republicans supported it.  
Reeves said he was certain some Democratic colleagues would support action if Lucas were convicted in the criminal case, even if the Senate’s review found no basis for discipline.
“Maybe there’s nothing there,” he said. “And then if the court case drags on and eventually she’s convicted, then that’s a whole other deal, right?”
Virginia Mercury reporter Shannon Heckt contributed to this story.

title: Voter turnout for Virginia constitutional amendments transcended partisanship
description: As Democrats nationwide and in Virginia flipped partisan control of the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate, three civil rights-based state constitutional amendments prevailed across party lines.  The statewide ballot referendums asked voters if they wanted to enshrine reproductive rights, same-sex marriage protections and voting rights restoration[...]
text:
At a Virginians For Reproductive Freedom victory party in Richmond, Chrisi West smiles shortly after voters approved an amendment to enshrine reproductive rights into the state's Constitution. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)As Democrats nationwide and in Virginia flipped partisan control of the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate, three civil rights-based state constitutional amendments prevailed across party lines. 
The statewide ballot referendums asked voters if they wanted to enshrine reproductive rights, same-sex marriage protections and voting rights restoration for formerly incarcerated people into Virginia’s Constitution. The answer was a resounding “yes,” with roughly 60% of voters backing each amendment. 
The reproductive rights amendment garnered over 62% of voters’ approval, outperforming the margin of Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Warner’s statewide win by over 12,000 votes —- and signaling GOP and independent voters also backed the referendum.  
A KFF Health News poll found between 30% and 42% of voters in four states with abortion rights ballot measures in 2026, including Virginia, said those amendments were a major motivating factor in participating in this year’s elections. 
“We know that our amendments are not partisan,” said Virginians For Reproductive Freedom campaign manager Han Jones. “Everyone was deciding singularly. A lot of times that’s going to be informed by their life experience, their communities, their personal stories.”
Kacia Kriener Putman, who supports Virginia’s proposed reproductive rights constitutional amendment, stands outside the Bank Street entrance to the Virginia State Capitol with her children in January 2026. (Photo courtesy of Putman)
With the passage of Ballot Question 1, Virginians will have stronger protections for contraceptives or fertility treatments and abortion access. 
The latter was the more controversial portion of the amendment and received robust debate in the state legislature during the two years it had to pass before it could make it to ballots statewide. 
Opponents argued that reducing the number of physicians needed to approve rare late-term abortions made it too easy for people to get the procedure. Proponents said the measure was critical in emergency situations or for rural patients who already travel further for healthcare. 
Having survived her own life-threatening pregnancy emergency with her first child, Alexandria resident Kacia Kriener Putman said she knows firsthand how complicated pregnancies can be. Virginia’s law allowing abortion was the reason she felt safe to have a second child. 
Putman and her family felt excited on Election Night ahead of the amendment’s victory and have experienced relief in the days since, she said. 
“One thing we kept reflecting on over and over is that women might be dying (from pregnancy complications), but they will not be dying in Virginia — at least not from something that can be preventable.”
For Chesterfield County residents Rachel Leyco and Jenn Jackson, Ballot Question 1 and Ballot Question 2 — on whether to lift Virginia’s ban on same-sex marriage — resonated most. Fifty-seven percent of voters approved the second measure.
Virginia previously didn’t recognize their marriage, the couple said. When they became parents, they had to travel out of state so Leyco could legally adopt her own biological children. 
Rachey Leyco and Jenn Jackson sit on the porch of their Chesterfield County home with their sons in the summer of 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
The couple had used Leyco’s eggs paired with a sperm donor for Jackson to carry the pregnancies, a type of assisted reproduction that Ballot Question 1 preserves access to statewide. 
The couple’s sons, age and age, called witnessing the amendment’s approval by voters “cool.” Their mothers likened it to a “sigh of relief” for families like theirs. 
“It was truly an honor to share our story alongside many others,” Jackson said. “We are both humbled and so very grateful that the citizens of the commonwealth showed up for us.”
The state’s 2006 ban has been dormant since the Supreme Court ruled to protect such unions nationally in 2015. 
After the high court overturned federal abortion protections in 2022, Justice Clarence Thomas suggested overturning the gay marriage statute, too.
The move had a chilling effect on the community, Virginians For Marriage Equality manager Narissa Rahaman noted. Some queer couples rushed their marriage plans to ensure they wed before the right could be stripped from them, Rahaman said. 
The amendment represents “a new era for LGBTQ Virginians,” Rahaman added. Virginians will be able to “look at their constitution and not see discriminatory language in it.” 
Voting rights were on the ballot too.
Quadaire Patterson and wife Santia Nance stand with daughter Trinity on the porch of their Henrico County home in the summer of 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
With 56% of the vote, Ballot Question Three will now allow for automatic restoration of voting rights to people with felony convictions who have completed their sentences. 
People will still have to register to vote if they wish to do so, but moving forward, they have the option. 
Virginia’s constitution has historically disenfranchised people with felony convictions unless a governor pardons them or individually restores their rights. 
The subjective process has not always been clear and restorations have ebbed and flowed across gubernatorial administrations. Proponents argued that taking it out of governors’ hands and making it contingent upon completing a sentence would be more just. 
“If a judge didn’t give you a life sentence, we shouldn’t give you a life sentence as a society,” Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, said in a recent call with The Mercury. “Once you’ve been adjudicated for your crime and you’ve served your time, then your right should be restored.” 
The republican state lawmaker had previously carried the ballot measure in a past legislative session and has continued to support his Democratic colleagues in getting it to voters. 
Beyond allowing returning citizens to take part in the democratic process, Virginians For the Right to Vote campaign manager Amber Brown emphasized that the amendment also cements voting rights for all Virginians. 
“We made sure Virginians knew they should have the fundamental right to vote because it was not explicitly stated in our Constitution,” she said. “We wanted the people to understand that the bigger picture was about the fundamental right to vote and ensuring our state Constitution reflected that fundamental right.” 
Henrico County resident Quadaire Patterson knew voting for the first time was important to him, but he didn’t anticipate the emotional magnitude of the experience on Election Day. 
Following his release from prison two years ago, he has helped shape and advocate for several law changes, despite being unable to vote himself. He was among about 60,000 Virginians that Gov. Abigail Spanberger restored rights to over the summer, so voting for the voting rights amendment was extra special for him. 
At a (location) watch party with other supporters of Ballot Question 3, Patterson said he cried as he “thought of the many ways this will change the atmosphere in prison and the communities (people) will return to.” 
 Legal challenges two Question 1 and 2 loom, but campaigns are confident

Opponents are seeking to strike down two of the three amendments. 
A court hearing is set for Nov. 13 in a case by the Founding Freedoms Law Center argues the ballot language was “misleading” and that the proper procedure for amending the constitution was not followed. 
A separate but similar lawsuit carried by Liberty Counsel was dismissed over the summer, but plaintiffs are seeking an appeal. 
The Family Foundation also filed a case on behalf of a pastor in Prince William County that challenges the marriage amendment on the same grounds. 
The language of the amendment affirms that “two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, or race.” 
Rahaman said Virginians For Marriage Equality will intervene in the challenge to Question 2.

title: At SCC hearing, Virginians say Dominion-NextEra merger could mean higher bills, new risk
description: In downtown Richmond outside the State Corporation Commission, dozens of protestors shouted their opposition to the NextEra-Dominion Energy merger, as public testimony in the case proceeded inside the SCC courtroom.  Some demonstrators held aloft effigies of the three SCC commissioners, while others gave speeches outlining their concerns about the deal, sayi[...]
text:
Protesters of the NextEra-Dominion Energy merger speak outside the State Corporation Commission in Richmond on Nov. 5. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)In downtown Richmond outside the State Corporation Commission, dozens of protestors shouted their opposition to the NextEra-Dominion Energy merger, as public testimony in the case proceeded inside the SCC courtroom. 
Some demonstrators held aloft effigies of the three SCC commissioners, while others gave speeches outlining their concerns about the deal, saying it would create a monopoly and urging commissioners to reject the $67 billion proposal.
“This is trickle up capitalism. And we are seeing people suffer,” said Rev. Daniel Ray Wilson outside the SCC doors. “While people get richer, they do things that they don’t even need to be doing, like buy islands, or dump millions upon millions into flying cars.” 
The final in-person public testimony hearing highlighted Dominion ratepayers’ key gripes ahead of the proposed merger’s litigation process, chiefly spiking electricity bills.
In recent years Dominion’s base rates have increased and riders have been added to bills to cover the costs of several energy generation projects. Opponents fear the merger will only worsen their utility costs as demand grows.
“The case before you is perhaps the most consequential decision this commission will make, in a generation, or in maybe many generations,” Sen. Kannan Srinivasan, D-Loudoun, said in his testimony. “And we cannot discuss it without addressing what is driving the energy demand: data centers.”

“People are struggling to make ends meet right now as it is, and this is just an additional thing on top of that,” testified Jessica Schneider, a member of the Chesterfield Board of Supervisors. “NextEra has shown they have a history of turning off people’s utilities, which is not something that I am in favor of at all.”
The merger would create the largest regulated utility in the world with 10 million customers, 110 gigawatts of power, and a connection queue of 130 GW. 
The crux of what the three commissioners will have to consider when making their determination on this merger is whether “adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized” by the combining of the two companies.
SCC staff testimony pre-filed ahead of the public hearing outlined policy recommendations and changes to quell concerns over investment protections called “ring fencing” and the volatility of the unregulated branch of the NextEra’s business. 
Ultimately staff recommended against the commissioners approving the deal.
In the joint petitioners rebuttal testimony earlier this week, Dominion agreed to some of those changes but rejected or altered others.
The three State Corporation Commission commissioners sit in the courtroom for the NextEra-Dominion Energy merger case. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
Thursday’s hearing also drew supporters of the project.
Virginia Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Brad Hall said that the creation of the energy titan would fuel job creation and economic growth in the state. 
In response to the concerns about bill costs, Hall pointed to the four-year, $10 monthly bill credits as part of immediate relief the companies have offered.
“I believe these two companies coming together with a capital buying power that they’ll have, and the amount of investments that they’re gonna make into generation, which will help customers in the long run,” Hall said.
Two days of telephonic public testimony will follow the in-person hearing, taking place Nov. 9 and 10. Written testimony can be submitted until Nov. 12 on the SCC website. 
Commissioner Samuel Towell told the crowd that 2,400 written comments have been submitted as of the time of the hearing.
At a meeting of the Energy Commission of Virginia on Thursday, lawmakers had a lengthy debate over a drafted letter some legislators  intended to send the SCC, detailing the potential risks of the merger that they’d learned from experts over the last several months. 
However, some members of the board felt the letter was an improper attempt to legislate while litigation was on-going. The motion to send a revised version of the letter did not receive enough votes to pass.
The evidentiary portion of the case is set to begin on Nov. 17. The SCC commissioners have until Jan. 11 to make their determination on if the merger should be approved. 
Regulators in North Carolina and South Carolina, as well as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and federal anti-trust officials, will have to give approvals for the merger in order for it to be completed.

title: In this year’s midterms, the rest of the country learned what Virginia has known for a while
description: Maybe the rest of America finally caught on to what Virginia has known for 10 years. Voters handed Democrats a historic, sweeping victory not only in swing-state contests but in the most reliably Republican states Tuesday. And the reason is unambiguous: President Donald Trump. Welcome aboard. We in the Old Dominion have been waiting for […]
text:
President Donald Trump rallied with Iowa Republicans at the Five Flags Center in Dubuque on Nov. 1, 2026, two days before Election Day. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Maybe the rest of America finally caught on to what Virginia has known for 10 years.
Voters handed Democrats a historic, sweeping victory not only in swing-state contests but in the most reliably Republican states Tuesday. And the reason is unambiguous: President Donald Trump.
Welcome aboard. We in the Old Dominion have been waiting for you.
Democrats won Congress. Now they have to figure out how to deal with Trump.

I can hear the dissent now. Oh, you’re just a blue state filled with heathen liberals, and that’s why y’all voted against President Trump each of the three times he’s been on your ballot. Y’all wouldn’t know how to vote any other way than Democrat.
Well, Trump’s winless record in Virginia would be correct, but the rest doesn’t hold water. Look no farther than 2021 when Republican Glenn Youngkin led a resounding red-wave election that swept Democrats out of all three statewide offices and control of the House of Delegates.
That Republican rebound came one year after Democrat Joe Biden won Virginia by 10 percentage points en route to denying Trump reelection. That’s how quickly things changed here, and that doesn’t happen in indelibly blue states like California and Illinois.
Last year, with Trump back in office, the process reversed itself. A majority of Virginia voters recoiled at Trump’s presidency after just a few months, and Democrats roared back in a preview of this year’s nationwide blue tsunami.
Democrat Abigail Spanberger trounced her GOP opponent to become the first woman governor in Virginia’s 400-plus years either as a state or a British colony. Two other Democrats easily won the offices of lieutenant governor and attorney general, and Democrats took a sizable House of Delegates majority.
It’s not that Virginia won’t elect Republicans. The state had a good record of that from the 1990s right into the mid-2010s.
For 20 consecutive years, through 2019, Republicans had a lock on the House of Delegates.
Over a 32-year span beginning in 1994 and running through 2025, Republicans and Democrats each held the governor’s office for 16 of those years.
Doesn’t get much more balanced than that.
The trouble for Republicans in Virginia has a direct nexus to Trump’s ascent from reality-TV celebrity to the world’s most powerful office in 2016. To voting majorities in Virginia, he came across as a ridiculous, mean-spirited carnival barker with orange face paint who used empty promises and dog whistles to exploit voters’ fears and biases.
Virginians didn’t need Jan. 6, 2021, to know the depth of his contempt for the Constitution. We had watched it up close for four years.
To understand his appreciation for gratuitous cruelty, Virginia didn’t need to see him outfit thugs with federal badges and guns and give them carte blanche to attack and abduct undocumented immigrants and sometimes citizens without due process of law.
We weren’t surprised when he threatened allies abroad and drove up costs at home with tariffs he imposed on a whim while a Republican Congress sat mute.
Virginians suffered disproportionately as he outsourced the dismantling of whole federal departments and mass firings of government employees to the world’s richest person, but no one doubted his carefree capacity for such harm.
When he launched a surprise war overnight against Iran more than eight months ago, the world was mortified, including Virginia. But we knew that his lack of impulse control made such a thing possible if not likely. 
Nor was it a shock to see that he either hadn’t considered that Iran’s closure of the primary shipping artery for a fifth of the planet’s oil supply would trigger prohibitive fuel price increases, or he didn’t care.
All of which led us to Tuesday, and a historic reckoning that Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis called “as close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last hundred years.”
There’s more than a little hyperbole in that statement. Political waves ebb and flow for both parties. But with Trump, this phenomenon is not new. It has played out before in microcosm in Virginia.
When Trump began his first term, Republicans controlled both chambers of Virginia’s General Assembly and had a 7-4 majority in the state’s 11-seat U.S. House delegation. By the time Trump grudgingly left the White House in January of 2021, Democrats regained every elective office or institution of state or federal government in Virginia for the first time since 1968.
Now, the pain starts anew — and at a national scale — for the GOP.
Warner wins fourth term, Luria ousts Kiggans in VA-02, Taylor triumphs in VA-01

Democrats will hold eight of the state’s 11 House seats when the 120th Congress convenes in January. Democrats Shannon Taylor and Elaine Luria unseated GOP incumbents Rob Wittman and Jen Kiggans in the 1st and 2nd U.S. House districts, respectively, helping their party win a robust majority of at least 259 — perhaps more — of the 435 seats.
But this week, the whole country — including states where the Democratic label has been an instant disqualifier — joined Virginia in shifting away from Trump’s party.
In Texas, whose GOP leaders had been so obsequiously loyal to Trump that they started a round of preemptive gerrymandering last year in a vain bid to contain this fall’s blue tsunami, Democrats won the governorship and a Senate seat.
A United Methodist pastor became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932.
In South Carolina, Republican Darlene Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, lost her bid to keep the seat in her family and her party to pediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat.
And in Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom held a thin but shocking lead over GOP incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. The last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate was John C. Stennis, a one-time Dixiecrat who was more conservative than most of his GOP colleagues when he was last elected in 1982.
We are a nation exhausted from a temperamental man-toddler vested with immense power and a Republican Congress  lacking the spine to protect Americans from his more destructive proclivities.
Frustration gathered steam for two years and made landfall Tuesday as a category 5 political disaster, splintering Trump’s Republican support system and promising some measure of restraint on him during his two remaining lame-duck years in office.
Finally, working-class Americans in parts of the nation that have been unstintingly loyal to Trump realized that, for all his bluster, braggadocio and nonsense, their lives were getting harder. So, for the first time in generations, they gave Democrats a chance.
As has been Virginia’s experience, that doesn’t mean they will still favor Democrats in the next election. But it was a statement that had to be made, and it was made at the ballot box.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Commentary: Dumping trash in Virginia or Pennsylvania is not the answer for Montgomery County
authors: Kit Gage, Vivian E. Thomson, Dani Wilches Venegas
description: Closing Montgomery County's resource recovery facility and sending county trash to an out-of-state landfill may seem attractive, write Kit Gage, Virginia Thomson and Dani Wilches Venegasclos, but it has higher costs, health and environmental justice impacts.
text:
Closing Montgomery County's resource recovery facility and sending county trash to an out-of-state landfill may seem attractive, write Kit Gage, Virginia Thomson and Dani Wilches Venegasclos, but it has higher costs, health and environmental justice impacts. (Photo courtesy Montgomery County Department of Environmental Protection)Montgomery County Council members face a momentous trash management decision. They will soon vote on County Executive Marc Elrich’s push to close the county’s resource recovery facility (RRF) and export 600,000 tons a year of trash to an out-of-state landfill.
But landfilling our waste would have worse environmental, public health, cost, and environmental justice impacts than operating the RRF, according to Nature Forward, the League of Women Voters of Montgomery County, and the City of Gaithersburg.
Waste hierarchies in the U.S. and in the European Union rank landfilling as the worst option. Arlington County and the City of Alexandria in Virginia say their RRF is the “most environmentally sustainable means of disposing of waste … after reduction, reuse and recycling.” Following EU rules, green countries like Denmark, Sweden and Germany have rejected landfilling and use RRFs.
Montgomery County’s most recent greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory shows that landfilling county waste produces almost twice as much GHG per ton as using the RRF. That result is consistent with many scientific studies. Fairfax County, Virginia, found that landfilling its trash would produce six times more greenhouse gases than using Fairfax’s RRF. If the Montgomery RRF closes, its electricity generation would be replaced with fossil fuel-powered electricity.
Landfills produce methane, an especially potent GHG that is also explosive and contributes to ambient ozone, which harms public health and causes crop losses. Reducing methane emissions is the most effective and timely action we can take to reduce global warming.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Landfill gas collection systems are leaky and are inefficient at capturing methane and other toxic air pollutants. The US EPA says many landfill operators are violating their landfill gas collection requirements.
Montgomery County’s studies show that the RRF has no measurable influence on local air quality. New research indicates that RRFs may destroy PFAS, or “forever chemicals.”
When the RRF’s air emissions exceeded allowable limits in 2025, the incidents were identified, disclosed publicly, and resolved. A county analysis shows that those exceedances posed very low health risks, 20 to 300 times below target levels.
Landfills emit toxic gases, including carcinogens like benzene and vinyl chloride. Landfills can produce hundreds of thousands of gallons of polluted liquid a week. One Virginia landfill mentioned as a possible place for Montgomery County’s trash has closed, is bankrupt, and will require an estimated $173 million to clean up.
Virginia and Pennsylvania are among the states with the highest number of landfills violating federal environmental standards, according to the Environmental Defense Fund. Montgomery County could not require clean-up at an out-of-state landfill.
Trucking produces carcinogenic diesel exhaust. A 2025 county study says the Derwood trash transfer station already suffers from elevated levels of diesel fumes.
Updating the RRF will require significant investment, especially since, according to council members, the county executive has deferred needed upgrades. But the county says using the RRF is either far cheaper than landfilling or roughly the same cost. The RRF’s costs are predictable and are somewhat offset by the sale of electricity and valuable recyclable metals. Arlington County and the City of Alexandria lease their RRF to Reworld in a financially advantageous arrangement.
In contrast, landfilling means losing control of costs. Those charges are unpredictable and would naturally rise because of inflation and predicted waste stream increases.
To reduce landfilling costs, the county executive advocates an “advanced waste processing” facility. But we don’t have details on the cost, feasibility, location, or benefits of that facility. No such facility exists at the scale needed for Montgomery County.
Guiding principles in the EU and in Japan say waste should be disposed of close to its point of origin. Exporting our trash would violate this proximity principle and would shift our pollution to more vulnerable communities. The RRF is in an affluent, disproportionately white part of Montgomery County. All landfills examined in the county’s 2025 study have environmental justice strikes against them.
We must find another solution for the RRF’s 150,000 tons/year of ash, which goes to a mixed waste landfill near a low-income, minority community in Henrico County, Virginia. An ash monofill in Fairfax County shows lower environmental justice vulnerability and would better protect against soil and groundwater contamination than the Henrico landfill. Perhaps the ash could be reused.
Montgomery County can upgrade its RRF, find a better ash treatment option and expand waste reduction and recycling efforts. In so doing, the county will make fairness, accountability, and greenhouse gas reductions the pillars of its waste management strategy.
