name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia Democrats ride national blue wave into power in history-making election
authors: Maya Homan, Alander Rocha, Ross Williams
description: Within an hour of polls closing Tuesday, it was clear that Democrats had made a strong showing and that U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff would be re-elected by a large margin. But what unfolded after that far exceeded what even the most optimistic Georgia Democrat could have imagined. By about 9 p.m., it became apparent that […]
text:
Voters file into the Jefferson Park Recreation Center polling place in south Fulton County. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderWithin an hour of polls closing Tuesday, it was clear that Democrats had made a strong showing and that U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff would be re-elected by a large margin.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks to supporters in Atlanta Tuesday night after winning reelection. Julia Beverly for the Georgia Recorder
But what unfolded after that far exceeded what even the most optimistic Georgia Democrat could have imagined.
By about 9 p.m., it became apparent that not only would former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms become Georgia’s first Democratic governor since Roy Barnes left office in 2003 but that the entire slate of Democratic statewide candidates would share in the victory, flipping offices like agriculture and insurance commissioners that had been considered relatively safe for Republicans. House Democrats are also poised to take control of the state House of Representatives for the first time in more than two decades.
“I’ve been at these elections a lot of times when we went home crying, and so it was hard for me to believe when the results came in as early as they did,” House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley, who could be in line to be the chamber’s next speaker, told reporters Wednesday. “I’m like, OK, is that really real? And then they kept coming, kept coming, kept coming. So it was overwhelming. I was so very excited.
“We’re excited not only for the Democrats, but for the people of Georgia, because this shows people that elections matter and that your voices can be heard and your votes will matter,” she added.
What happened on Tuesday will be discussed by Georgians for years – and shape the state’s future for generations, starting by transforming the state government next year. As the dust settles in the aftermath, here are five of the biggest initial takeaways from a historic election.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
How far did the blue wave reach?
Democrats have a lot to celebrate, with victories this year far exceeding the traditionally blue stronghold of metro Atlanta.
Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms celebrates her victory on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Bottoms made gains across middle and southwest Georgia, winning over a majority of voters in eight counties where voters picked Republican Gov. Brian Kemp in the 2022 midterms: Burke, Clay, Fayette, Houston, Jefferson, Peach, Sumter and Washington.
Emory University political science professor Andra Gillespie said that Democratic candidates made strides with many key groups, including independents and white voters in the state.
“The national mood was sour, and Democrats were able to ride that wave in places that we didn’t expect,” she said. “But I think it remains to be seen whether or not voters who were dissatisfied with Trump are going to stick with Democrats.”
But Georgia Republicans did have one bright spot in all the election news, managing to hold on to their nine seats in the U.S. House even as a number of congressional seats across the country flipped Democratic. But Gillespie noted that the margins of victory in many House districts were much tighter this year than they normally are, signaling widespread dissatisfaction with GOP leadership.
“I think Republicans should heed the margins and recognize that there was discontent in their districts even when they won, and that voters in their districts contributed to the Democratic sweep of the statewide offices,” she said.
The energy benefited down-ballot Democrats too, bringing a wave of new lawmakers to the Legislature and changing the balance of power.
Even before the polls closed, some conservative voters said they felt the tide changing. Joel Pirtle, a 50-year-old IT manager from Henry County who voted for Collins and Jackson, said that he would not be surprised if Democrats managed to flip his state representative’s seat, which is currently held by Republican state Rep. Noelle Kahaian. Kahaian did end up losing her seat to truck driver Mishael White, who is a Democrat, by nearly 8 points, according to unofficial results from the secretary state’s website.
“I’m seeing Georgia going more and more Democrat, so I would not be surprised if it does. I don’t necessarily agree with it, but we’ll see what happens when it does. If it works out, great. If it doesn’t, then we’ll vote again,” Pirtle said.
Trump was on the ballot
President Donald Trump gestures to the crowd at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
In the weeks leading up to the election, Trump made stops across the country, including in Georgia, where he held two rallies last month calling on the GOP faithful to vote as if he were on the ballot.
His intention was to fire up low propensity voters who support Trump but inconsistently turn out to support other Republican candidates.
He may have achieved the opposite. Many Democratic and independent voters who were interviewed at the polls said they were encouraged to get out and vote in opposition to Trump.
Woodstock retiree Judi Smith, who is 74, said she voted for Ossoff and Bottoms because she said she wanted to send a message to the Trump administration.
“I just want Trump and all of those people out of office,” she said.
“Everything about Trump, all of those people, all of that corruption, it just needs to be over and done with,” she added. “And all of the hatred that they have sown in this country, it’s just horrible.”
Voters in Henry County who backed Democrats said that a change of party control was overdue. Keisha Thompson, a 48-year-old federal employee who saw many of her former colleagues lose their jobs due to funding cuts from the Trump administration, said she had a simple goal.
“We just need to make some change. We need to change it from whatever color it is to blue,” Thompson said.
Trey Hood, a political science professor at the University of Georgia, said that Democrats outperformed Republicans because of what he called a “national repudiation of Trump.” He said they tied current economic issues like high gas prices due to the war in Iran to the White House.
Some Republican voters said Trump had no influence on their decisionmaking.
“It’s got nothing to do with Trump,” said Brad Baldwin, a 65-year-old retiree in Henry County who voted straight Republican. “No, no, no. I vote for a guy I want to vote for. I don’t care if he likes Trump, hates Trump. I can’t wait for Trump to get out of office just so people will shut up about it.”
Split-ticket voters were not a significant factor
Gov. Brian Kemp speaks in Roswell on Oct. 27, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
During the 2022 midterm elections, Georgians chose Kemp, a Republican, and U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, a Democrat, during the same election, largely thanks to independent and split-ticket voters who helped both candidates across the 50% minimum threshold amid tight electoral margins.
But this year, split-ticket voters weren’t the tiebreaking force they had been in 2022, with independents breaking “very hard for the Democrats this election cycle,” Hood said.
“There’s hardly any roll off if you go downballot, down the constitutional offices in Georgia. I mean, the margin is almost the same. So it was just people checking the Democratic box all the way down the ballot,” Hood said.
Ossoff, who was running as an incumbent, won with nearly 60% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the secretary of state’s office. Bottoms received more than 54% of the vote, numbers that Gillespie said signal widespread enthusiasm among Democratic base voters and gains among demographics that have tilted towards Republicans in recent elections.
“The reason why [Democrats] won this time is they were able to get over the hump with white voters in ways that we have not seen them do, even in the elections of Joe Biden, Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff in previous cycles,” Gillespie said.
That’s not to say that every voter cast their ballot along party lines, though. Jordan Fuller, a 36-year-old tech support worker in Union City, said he doesn’t vote consistently for either party. He cast his vote for Ossoff and the Republican nominee for governor Rick Jackson this year, citing his disapproval of Bottoms’ mayoral record.
“I’ve already experienced Keisha,” he said. “She was the mayor of Atlanta, and I’m not much of a fan of how she handled some things.”
But other independent voters turned away from Republican candidates altogether. Gillespie said the data shows Democrats overperforming among independent voters in this election cycle.
About 1.3 Georgians turned out to vote on Election Day, including many voters in conservative Whitfield County. But not enough Republican voters turned out statewide to offset the lead Democrats built up during early voting and continued to build on Tuesday. Ignacio Perez/Georgia Recorder
Steve Bigler, a Gwinnett County voter, said he has voted for candidates of both parties throughout his life, but he went into this year’s election hoping to enact some guardrails against Trump’s policies in the federal government.
He supported both Kemp and Warnock in 2022 and would have voted for Kemp again if that was an option. But he said Jackson’s early campaign ads, including one where he warned that immigrants who broke the law would end up “deported or departed,” made him uneasy.
“I believe in supporting law enforcement and all that,” Bigler said. “But come on, let’s just get a little humanity into our politics.”
Conrad Gill, another Gwinnett County resident, chose Ossoff in the Senate race and voted for Bottoms in the governor’s contest, fearing that Jackson would be too closely tied to Trump and his policies.
“I was leaning toward Jackson until the ad came out about his affiliation with Trump and his statements about ‘he’s going to be Trump’s man, he’s going to be Trump’s best friend as a governor’ and all of that,” Gill said. “I didn’t want to vote for him based on that because I don’t think Trump is doing a good job. I don’t think he’s honest. I don’t think he’s fair. I think he’s very corrupt.”
But Gillespie said it remains to be seen whether this year’s midterm election results were an outlier or part of a larger political realignment within Georgia.
Future support from independent voters, she added, will likely depend on “whether or not [Democrats] are going to deliver on the policy promises that they [made], and whether or not they’re going to look like they can govern effectively. If they don’t govern effectively, then what I suspect is that independent voters could possibly defect.”
What’s next for the parties?
Georgia GOP chairman John McKoon speaks at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Outgoing Georgia Republican Party Chair Josh McKoon said that in the short term, the state party will help Republican state Rep. Mike Cheokas keep his seat in a runoff.
But in the long term, the plan is to do a thorough review of the election results to develop a platform that better resonates with voters ahead of 2028, when he feels prospects for Republicans will be “very positive.”
While Democrats ran on making life more affordable for Americans, McKoon thinks that Democrats will “pursue a far-left agenda that is totally out of touch with where most Georgians are.”
“I think there’s going to be a lot of anger with national Democrats by the time 2028 rolls around here at the state level,” McKoon said.
Georgia Democratic Party Chair Charlie Bailey speaks at an event marking the third anniversary of the Dobbs decision. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
He hopes that when 2028 comes around, voters will be ready to “take a fresh look at Republicans and probably realize there is a reason that Republicans have run this state for two decades.”
House Minority Leader Carolyn Hugley, who is in line to become the next speaker, said House Democrats plan to stick to the pocketbook issues that she acknowledged is ushering her party into power, at least for now.
“What Georgia citizens have told us is affordability is the number one issue. And so you can expect the issues that we put forth in this first legislative session are going to be focused on meeting that challenge of affordability,” Hugley told reporters this week.
For his part, Democratic Party of Georgia Chair Charlie Bailey said he hopes to use the wins in Georgia to boost the state’s importance in the eyes of national Democratic groups and PACs.
“We will certainly be making the argument, as we have been for at least as long as I’ve been chair, that we have to expand into the South if we’re going to be a truly national party with a national, governing majority,” Bailey said in a Zoom call with reporters Wednesday. “We are the ultimate battleground in Georgia, but we’ve got to kind of lock it down here, you know?”
To do so, Bailey said Democrats will expand into year-round organizing in Georgia for the first time.
“That’s going to take a lot of resources, and we’ll be leaning on our partners to send those resources down here, and I’m optimistic we’ll get some takers,” he said.
Georgia Recorder Editor Jill Nolin contributed to this report.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin Deflection Initiative aims to keep people out of  the criminal justice system
description: School districts often identify students they call “at-risk” who might have a learning disability or low reading or math scores in order to  provide them additional resources and attention to help them keep pace with their classmates and avoid dropping out. In the Wisconsin Deflection Initiative, the “at-risk” people are in the community at large. […]
text:
The Wisconsin Deflection Initiative offers peer support, job counseling and other services to help keep people from becoming entangled in the criminal justice system. (Getty Images)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
School districts often identify students they call “at-risk” who might have a learning disability or low reading or math scores in order to  provide them additional resources and attention to help them keep pace with their classmates and avoid dropping out.
In the Wisconsin Deflection Initiative, the “at-risk” people are in the community at large. They might have mental health or addiction issues, and the objective is to provide support to create stability and help them steer clear of the criminal justice system.
Eau Claire County is one of roughly 11 counties in the state that have a deflection program under the Wisconsin Deflection Initiative. The county started the program in 2024 under an opioid abatement efforts law enforcement grant that involves a partnership between the sheriff’s office, the public health department, human services, and criminal justice services.  
“Deflection, in its truest form, is really to try to be a preventative program that we can intervene when people are having difficulties in their lives before a major kind of event happens,” said Brianna Marsden, recovery and justice service manager for the Eau Claire County Department of Human Services
It’s a voluntary program for people who are at least 18 years of age, live in the county, have completed an assessment, have agreed to case management, and have no warrants or pending felony charges.
The Eau Claire County’s deflection program website states that the program “prioritizes connecting people experiencing substance use and/or mental health challenges with the care and resources they need—particularly in low-level, non-violent situations—while promoting healthier outcomes for individuals, families, and communities.”
With so many jails and prisons in Wisconsin filled with people who also have addiction and mental health problems, the deflection program offers a proactive, preventive alternative to incarceration.
“We’re really trying to look at where there are the gaps in our system and how can we help that? How can we prevent these bigger things from happening in people’s lives?” said Marsden.
Those “bigger things” could be accruing a large financial debt or having felony charges, spending time in jail, losing a job or acquiring a social stigma that shadows one’s life.
Currently, Marsden said, there are about 30 people in the deflection program in Eau Claire County, and a total of 50-60 have been served since the program began.
It’s often law enforcement personnel responding to a crisis who make a referral to the deflection program.
“Law enforcement gets sent to many different calls throughout their day, and the vast majority aren’t criminal in nature,” said Eau Claire County Sheriff Dave Reiewestahl. “Whether it’s mental health, substance use, there’s a variety of reasons why we get called, and the hope is that we can pair that person up with somebody in peer support and a case manager, you know, walks alongside that person, so they don’t get involved in the criminal justice system.”
People can also apply for the program or self-report online.
“We get some of our people already connected to some resources in our community, like sober living, who could use a little bit more support, or they’re already connected with peer support from our jail, and community members can send in referrals for other community members,” Marsden said.
To promote the deflection program, the county has also produced informational videos airing at Kwik Trip gas pumps and ads on city buses and social media.
“It’s low-barrier, free services for individuals,” said Marsden. “You don’t have to have Medicaid. You don’t have to have insurance. We’re not charging you for anything. It’s really trying to be in that space to help people when they’re ready for help.”
After applicants fill out an  online application, they receive a call within 72 hours to determine interest in the program. Then there is an  intake meeting where participants sign an informed consent form and are connected to  peer support specialists. The specialists often have struggled with the same kinds of problems facing  their clients, but have received training to become mentors. 
Marsden said the pillars of the deflection program are case management, helping to secure resources and peer support.
The concept of flagging “at-risk” students, she said, is very similar to the deflection program effort to help “at-risk” people in the community.
“We know something is going to likely happen if we don’t intervene,” she said, “so let’s just intervene so that nothing really big or significant happens.” 
The power of peer support
Emily Nichols is a certified recovery coach and operations manager for At the Roots LLC, which provides services through certified peer support specialists and certified recovery coaches.
“The provider often helps with practical things,” she said. “That might include rides. It might be setting up or getting to appointments. It might be completing paperwork or following up on leads for things like housing. Because we know those are the barriers that often derail somebody’s recovery, and once that recovery is derailed, they’re definitely at risk for becoming involved in the legal system.”
Nichols said it makes a huge difference that the peer support and recovery coaches working with clients know first hand what their  clients are going through.
“Even if somebody is maybe wary of the system, oftentimes peer support or recovery coaching is an easier way for them to kind of get the help and support that they need without feeling like they’ve kind of been sucked into the system,” she said. “I think it’s easier for people to talk to folks who have been where they are and have actually been successful, to kind of keep that hope alive.”
Her agency does a brief screening with potential clients and asks such basic questions as: “Are you going to answer the phone when we try and get hold of you?”
The agency matches the participant with someone who has a similar demographic and life experience, and they meet once a week.
“Oftentimes we’re meeting with individuals before they’ve done their intake into deflection because we’re trying to get them help as quickly as we can,” she said. “We do some goal setting with the person, kind of figure out if they have any basic needs they need met, and then kind of get talking about recovery capital and what they have going on in life.” 
Help can mean different things to different people, from processing past trauma to working on communication skills to getting their most basic needs for food and housing met, she said. 
The goal is to help clients manage their lives and not live in a constant state of crisis, but there are times when additional help is needed. Mentors have given clients rides to appointments, helped them deal with the social service bureaucracy and apply for benefits. 
“We have people who have said they truly have just never felt listened to before,” Nichols said. “So it was the first time they had somebody who would listen to them without judging or offering unsolicited advice. We’ve had individuals who came to us unemployed and with engagement from the cops, and after six months of the program, some of them have done things like enroll at the technical school. We’ve had people get jobs.”
Some clients, she added, worked on interview skills through the program and were successful in finding employment. Others began attending recovery meetings,  “which, while that sounds like a small thing, it’s helping them build a healthy community, which replaces some of the relationships that maybe they need to leave behind them.”
“I think the biggest thing from our perspective is if we can reduce the level of harm that people are facing, whether that’s with the legal system, or it’s by stopping or reducing drug use,”  Nichols said.  
“We’ve extended people’s opportunity to survive and exist … you cannot put a price on that,” she said.
Nichols thinks the most important thing  the deflection program offers clients is community connection,  helping them feel secure and participating and living in the community, and confidently exploring interests without falling back into destructive habits.
“Oftentimes, the people that end up in the deflection program just don’t have anyone else who is supportive of them in that way, and we do very little advice giving, and a lot of guided listening,” she said. 
‘This has helped me the most’
Mae is a young woman who has struggled with addiction. She had recently been released from jail when she learned about deflection. At first she was skeptical and asked, “What’s the catch?”
But then Mae, who meets with a therapist, sat down with her peer support specialist and liked the fact that the woman helping her had similar experiences.
“It was great because I was able to relate to her on different things during our meetings, like domestic violence things, recovery-related things, mental health and substance abuse,” she said. “It didn’t feel clinical. Out of everything that I’ve tried, that’s like recovery-related oriented stuff, this has helped me the most and I feel the most supported and the most seen and understood.”
Mae meets one hour a week with her peer specialist, and they talk about how her week has gone. They work on positive self-talk and learning coping skills to support Mae’s recovery and also address her anger.
The peer specialist doesn’t just find resources for Mae; she shows her how to research and look for resources herself.
 “She shows me, and we do it together so that I don’t feel like I don’t know how to look and find resources on my own when we are done meeting,” Mae said.
In two months, Mae will leave the deflection program and transfer to Comprehensive Community Support (CCS), a voluntary Medicaid-funded community-based psychosocial rehabilitation program, where she will keep her peer specialist and have a team to support her as she pursues recovery.
“I would not have known about it (CCS) if it wasn’t for being in the deflection program,” she said.
Mae knows another person in deflection, also struggling with addiction, who was referred to by a law enforcement officer, and she says that person is doing well.
“And I hear people talk about it (deflection) in support groups or recovery groups like NA (Narcotics Anonymous) or AA (Alcoholic Anonymous), and they also speak highly of it,” she said.
Just being able to talk about her pursuing recovery, she said, is growth because in the past she’s always pretended not to have a problem.
“I’m getting more comfortable talking about it,” Mae said. “I think that’s part of just accepting what I’m going through and being okay with it and coming out on the other side, because I haven’t been this far yet in my mental health and substance use recovery. It’s like coming through on the other side and being OK to talk about it and accepting myself and what I’m going through and giving myself grace.”
Mae has been so inspired by her growth and working with her peer support specialist that she envisions herself one day being a certified peer specialist herself.
Sheriff support
Sheriff Dave Riewestahl is very supportive of the deflection program.
“Historically, law enforcement has really three options when responding to the needs of the community,” he said. “We can leave that person there. We can arrest that person if they’ve committed a crime, or if they’re having a medical or mental health emergency, they get to go to the hospital,” he said.  
“Deflection gives our staff a fourth option. Yes, that person remains in the community, but we don’t just walk away. We’re able to get them linked up with DHS, with a case manager, and start working on that individual’s needs.” Peer support, he said, seems to be the  … “secret sauce”:  “They have a greater rapport, a greater ability to affect that person than somebody with a badge.”
Riewestahl said that when the case manager in his office talks with Marsden about people in the deflection program and he hears names he knows from previous interactions with law enforcement, it reassures him that those people have someone in their lives who can make a positive difference.
“Nobody wakes up and says, you know, I want to be homeless, or I want to be a criminal,” he said. “There are a multitude of reasons why somebody ends up in the criminal justice system — underlying traumas, historical trauma, family trauma, mental health, AODA, you name it. The hope is that we can work with that person sooner when the problems and the issues are maybe easier to fix. Because once somebody gets incarcerated and has a criminal record, the barriers just get bigger and harder to overcome.”

title: Whitmer directs state agencies to strengthen privacy protections for reproductive health data
description: In an executive order issued Thursday, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer directed executive departments and agencies to conduct a review of “all policies, procedures, and practices governing the collection, maintenance, storage, and retention of records and data relating to an individual’s reproductive health” and revise any such policies in order to ensure the privacy [...]
text:
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer speaks at a press conference celebrating the enactment of Proposal 3, which enshrines abortion rights in Michigan's state constitution, on Dec. 14, 2022. (Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)In an executive order issued Thursday, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer directed executive departments and agencies to conduct a review of “all policies, procedures, and practices governing the collection, maintenance, storage, and retention of records and data relating to an individual’s reproductive health” and revise any such policies in order to ensure the privacy of that data. 
The review must include, but is not limited to, any precise geolocation information derived from an individual’s internet-connected device and any existing data-sharing agreements or contracts.
“This executive directive is another important step in keeping our patients and providers safe,” Whitmer said in a press release. “Data misuse is a growing threat, and we must make sure that reproductive care data never lands in the hands of people who could weaponize it. I’m proud to sign this executive directive to secure Michiganders’ reproductive health data and strengthen patients’ confidence as they seek reproductive care.”
According to a news release from Whitmer’s office, reproductive care includes, but is not limited to, prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, sterilization, abortion care, miscarriage management, and infertility care. 
Whitmer supports legislation that would protect reproductive health data

The directive, which bars sharing geolocation information and other data with commercial organizations and federal agencies, takes effect immediately and requires departments with relevant records to submit a report to the governor’s office detailing their findings and any policy changes. 
Reproductive rights advocates celebrated Whitmer’s order as she enters the final months of her term, with Planned Parenthood of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear thanking Whitmer for her work in office.
“Nobody should have to fear that accessing sexual and reproductive health care could endanger them,” Thornton Greear said. “That protection reaches someone getting prenatal care, a family going through infertility treatment, a patient managing a miscarriage, a student picking up birth control, and anyone who needs an abortion. Every one of them deserves to know that seeking care in Michigan won’t leave a trail someone can use against them.”
That was a change in tone from earlier this year when Planned Parenthood of Michigan asked Whitmer to provide $5 million to prevent the closure of health centers around the state amid attacks and funding cuts from the Trump administration. 
When the governor said the agency would need to look to the Legislature for assistance, Greear said Michigan patients were “not a football to be tossed around from branch to branch of the government,” and that Whitmer needed “to take responsibility and … drive a solution forward.”
Less than two months later, Planned Parenthood of Michigan announced it was permanently closing clinics in Lansing, Livonia and Warren.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: New rule will bring down drug costs by forcing competition, Ohio expert says
description: An Ohio drug-pricing expert said it was a game changer when U.S. Labor Department officials announced in late October a new rule forcing pharmacy middlemen to show big employers how they make their money. An industry group for the middlemen said it might only make prescription drugs more expensive. The Columbus-based expert, Antonio Ciaccia, has […]
text:
Medications are stored on shelves at a pharmacy. (Photo by Eric Thayer/Getty Images)An Ohio drug-pricing expert said it was a game changer when U.S. Labor Department officials announced in late October a new rule forcing pharmacy middlemen to show big employers how they make their money.
An industry group for the middlemen said it might only make prescription drugs more expensive.
The Columbus-based expert, Antonio Ciaccia, has advocated for years to force more transparency on the middlemen, known as pharmacy benefit managers or PBMs. 
As state legislatures and health agencies have passed laws aimed at shedding light on the practices of the big PBMs, which are part of huge health conglomerates, PBMs simply changed tactics, Ciaccia said.
“This ends the game of whack-a-mole,” he said during a panel discussion that was part of the announcement at the Labor Department in Washington, D.C. 
“It says you can’t hide the ball anymore — that transparency is finally going to be a given for the employer. This is not another instance where the government is creating another program… This is a solution given to employers to finally control their own destinies.”
The PBM industry group, the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, said adequate transparency rules already exist.
“Patients, employers, and unions will have no new meaningful transparency from this action, but prescription drug benefits will now be more expensive,” David Marin, president and CEO of the group said in a written statement.
The Labor Department is finalizing a new rule that requires those in charge of large employers’ self-insured health plans to seek detailed information about how PBMs make their money so the plans can be smart shoppers for their services. It also requires PBMs to turn over that information.
“Wherever there’s a dark corner, somebody’s making money,” Mehmet Oz, administrator of the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said of the need for transparency.
PBMs sit in the middle of prescription-drug transactions. They work on behalf of insurers and contract with drugmakers and pharmacies.
PBMs often extract rebates from makers of patented drugs in exchange for covering them. They use a dizzying array of nontransparent price lists to decide how much to reimburse pharmacies that dispense drugs.
The big three PBMs — CVS Caremark, OptumRx and Express Scripts — collectively control 80% of insured drug transactions in the United States. Each also is part of a Fortune 15 health conglomerate that also owns a top 10 health insurer. 
Critics say the companies’ dual roles as payer and payee in millions of drug transactions create clear conflicts that drive up prices and drive non-PBM-owned pharmacies out of business. 
Critics also say that the rebate system creates a motive to inflate drug prices by giving PBMs a motive to prefer more expensive drugs — for which drugmakers are willing to give bigger rebates — over cheaper ones that serve the same medical purpose. 
Because part of those rebates flow back to companies with self-insured plans, they can seem like a good deal to executives who have little visibility into transactions PBMs are making on their behalf, said Assistant Secretary of Labor Daniel Aronowitz. 
“The word ‘rebate’ makes everyone feel good — money coming back, savings,” he said. “But before anyone around the conference table celebrates, someone needs to ask, what did the plan and our workers pay to get it? A rebate tells you how much money came back. It does not tell you if the price was reasonable in the first place or what your workers paid at the pharmacy counter.”
Aronowitz added, “If a car dealer offered you a generous rebate, you would still want to know the price of the car.”
The new Labor Department rule requires PBMs to disclose all their sources of money prior to entering into or renewing contracts with large, self-insured plans covered under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. It also requires them to make semiannual disclosures and to allow those plans to audit PBMs’ books.
The rule doesn’t begin to apply to all insurance arrangements. But with 136 million Americans covered by the rule, the changes are likely to influence the rest of the marketplace. 
It also requires the plans’ “fiduciaries” — executives responsible for getting the best deal for their workers — to use the new tools to make sure they are. Not only does overpaying for drugs make the plans more expensive, it jacks up workers’ out-of-pocket costs at the pharmacy counter.
“The cost is not a rounding error,” Aronowitz said. “A cholesterol drug for which the pharmacy receives $5.25 can be billed to the plan at $84 — 16 times the price. Multiply that across thousands of prescriptions a year. That is money that can support better health benefits, lower premiums or higher wages.”
Marin of the PBM industry group said he was concerned the new rule “will lead to higher patient costs and less competition, the opposite of the (Labor) Department’s stated intent.”
He also said that it created no additional transparency. Even so, he seemed to hint that the industry might sue.
“We are committed to protecting patients, employers, and unions from the consequences of unnecessary and expensive regulatory overreach, and we will evaluate available pathways to do so,” Marin said.
Ciaccia, the Columbus-based drug-pricing expert, said the rule will provide sorely lacking transparency.
“I’ve been doing this for over 10 years,” he said. “We helped Ohio uncover over $245 million in hidden spread pricing back in 2018. When we caught them, I would have told you this is going to change everything. They’re not going to be able to mark up these drugs anymore.”
But, Ciaccia said, what followed was a long game of cat-and-mouse.
“Now you’re going to be able to see (your PBM charged you) $22,000 for a drug that is being sold by an independent, cash-pay pharmacy for $300,” he said. “There are drugs where that’s literally happening. You cannot manage what you can’t measure. This gives you the ability to measure.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Ohio voters stood up for the power of the people this Election Day
description: Copious content will be written about what happened on Nov. 3, 2026, parsing the polls, interpreting the results, guessing what comes next. There will be plenty of opportunity for political junkies like me to join the fray. But in the bleary-eyed morning after of a stunning midterm election night that ushered in a slew of […]
text:
Early voting in Ohio at the Franklin County Board of Elections. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal) Copious content will be written about what happened on Nov. 3, 2026, parsing the polls, interpreting the results, guessing what comes next. 
There will be plenty of opportunity for political junkies like me to join the fray. But in the bleary-eyed morning after of a stunning midterm election night that ushered in a slew of historic firsts — including first elected woman governor of Ohio, Dr. Amy Acton — all I can think about are the voter lines. 
You saw the pictures. They snaked out the door of many county boards of election and around the building before Election Day. 
Vast numbers of Ohioans lined up and waited, sometimes for over an hour, to cast a ballot. Their determination punctured my cynicism about people not giving a damn about the ship of state or who helms it. 
Apathy is generally the default setting of the electorate in our representative government unless an impending shipwreck threatens to sink the whole experiment. Then Americans focus. Time to save what must never be lost. 
Ohioans rose to the occasion. Across the state, they stood in long lines to vote early. A record-breaking 1.7 million of them voted early in-person and by mail followed by millions more who showed up on Tuesday to cast a ballot. 
The emotional intensity of this referendum on the status quo, inextricably tied to the Trump regime, was off the charts. It surpassed the 2018 midterms, I think. It takes a mountain of pent-up steam to motivate masses of voters to the polls in an off-year election. 
Fury drove turnout this year. It also energized an unprecedented nationwide, bipartisan voter movement. From Trump-supporting rural communities (especially bankrupted farmers) to Democrat-leaning urban constituencies, people were compelled to engage. 
The state of the union was a hot mess. The cost-of-living crisis in the United States is oppressive. Stretching a buck is harder than it was two years ago when Trump promised he’d lower inflation, bring prices down and not start another war. 
Today Ohioans pay more on everyday goods because Trump tariffs jacked up prices. His war of choice with Iran pushed Ohio gas prices to a record high on Election Day even with the state’s gas tax suspended. 
Diesel prices (more than $2 a gallon higher than a year ago) remain elevated so Ohioans spend extra for anything trucked in from milk to lumber. Grocery prices rise every week. 
Affordable healthcare is a pipe dream and new Medicaid work rules, under Trump’s signature rob-the-poor-give-to-the-rich legislation, could leave 356,000 Ohioans without health insurance after January. ACA premiums are expected to jump 13% next year.
As Ohio workers and those on fixed incomes scrimp to survive, the open corruption and brazen enrichment of the president and his family, has not escaped them. 
While people struggle with more month than money and a stack of unpaid bills, Trump and his billionaire cronies are raking in obscene fortunes off the presidency. 
It is also lost on no one that the addled 80-year-old, lording over pathetic Oval Office sycophants like a mob boss, is preoccupied with building monuments to himself. 
Trump has zero interest in problem-solving. He doesn’t care about stanching the runaway costs his policies have inflicted on Americans. He is bored with the lost war he started (and can’t end) and indifferent to its $47.1 billion-and-counting price-tag. 
When Trump isn’t dozing or golfing, the convicted felon works for he/him not Main Street. He makes money on ill-gotten gains and obsesses over a ballroom. 
Before the midterms Trump traversed the country holding bizarre, incoherent rallies, including three in Ohio, to bask in the love of devotees, spew racist slurs for applause, and ogle Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted’s ass. 
Trump riffed about the affordability “hoax,” downplayed sticker shock gas prices — up roughly 44% in Ohio since late February — claimed “inflation is solved,” and wrapped his rambling with “everything’s going good!”  
Not for ordinary Ohioans, it isn’t. 
Trump brushed off their financial pain — “I’ll never apologize for $4 gas” — and called it a small price to pay for an illegal war. That’s a hard sell for strained families watching the Trump clan get rich while they cut coupons. 
Trump pulled in at least $2 billion in the first year of his second term but folks working paycheck to paycheck can’t catch a break on skyrocketing expenses. 
Their fury over broken promises pierced the charade of the Trump roadshow when it came to Ohio. Protests erupted among the red hats.
Righteous anger has stirred in the American soul for months. Ohioans and millions across the country channeled that anger into agency. 
There was a sense of urgency with this election that went beyond economics, a failed war, or health care. Voters understood something bigger than control of Congress was on the ballot. 
America was barreling toward an authoritarian abyss. A megalomaniac, unconstrained by a supine Republican majority on Capitol Hill, had to be checked. 
Trump, who tried to overturn the 2020 election and did his best to manipulate this one, has no allegiance to the law or the republic he dangerously undermines in the 250th year of its founding. 
His autocratic ambitions were enough to get pro-democracy Americans off the sidelines and into the streets. 
Millions marched from coast to coast, in cities and rural villages, conservatives and liberals alike. No Kings was the outcry. No absolute rule, no dystopian playbooks, no paramilitary forces killing Americans with impunity. 
If democratic institutions could not be bulwarks against tyranny, citizens would stand in the breach. And boy, did they ever.
On Nov. 3, 2026, they routed the enablers of the malignant narcissist who torched American exceptionalism, freedom, global leadership. 
It was a wipeout election for the history books in Ohio, Michigan, Georgia, Maine, Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and more. Trump-endorsed candidates who aligned themselves with his trademark hatefulness and cruelty were rejected by voters who aligned themselves with human dignity and decency. 
The sovereign power of the people endured. May it always.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Democrats’ big statehouse wins in Pa. and elsewhere could transform climate and energy policy
description: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here. Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans held more governorships and state legislative seats than Democrats, along with an advantage in state trifectas—unified control of the go[...]
text:
The Seward power plant in Pennsylvania is the nation’s largest waste coal plant, which owner Robindale Energy says provides power enough for 650,000 homes. (Photo by Kyle Bagenstose/Inside Climate News)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans held more governorships and state legislative seats than Democrats, along with an advantage in state trifectas—unified control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature.
That advantage has disappeared, clearing the path for more climate and clean energy legislation, according to analysts and advocates.
Democrats swept the vast majority of competitive races at the state level, flipping control of governors’ offices from Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.
Democrats have a 29-19 edge in governorships, with Kansas too close to call and Alaska likely to take a while to declare a winner.
The party is on track for a net gain of hundreds of legislative seats, potentially giving it control of more nationwide than Republicans for the first time in more than a decade. Going into the election, Republicans had 4,072 seats and Democrats held 3,257, according to MultiState, a research and lobbying firm. Democrats had a net gain of more than 350 seats on Tuesday and are likely to add several hundred more as results continue to be tabulated, according to MultiState.
The Pennsylvania Capitol in downtown Harrisburg on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Democrats won five new trifectas: Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, with Arizona likely to be the sixth once officials finish counting. Those additions would give the party 22 trifectas, with Republicans holding unified control in 18 states and nine with split control. Kansas is yet to be determined.
Republicans lost trifectas in Iowa, Georgia, Texas, New Hampshire and Ohio. Before the election, Republicans had trifectas in 23 states, Democrats had 16 and 11 were under split control.
The implications for climate and energy policy are likely to be profound, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, an advocacy group.
“In the states, we had a generational political window shift to make people’s lives better, to lower costs and to lower climate pollution at the same time,” she said in a conference call.
This was the “affordability election” with concerns about inflation and high energy prices, she said.
Newly elected lawmakers will enter office with energy policy proposals to address voter concerns, she said. She noted that renewable energy is less expensive than fossil fuels and can be developed quickly, promising rapid benefits for consumers. The growth of electric transportation reduces greenhouse gas emissions and shields consumers from the volatility of gasoline and diesel, she said.
Jay Inslee, former Democratic governor of Washington and a prominent advocate for climate and clean energy policies, urged lawmakers to seize this opportunity.
Inslee took a jab at President Donald Trump, calling him the election’s clear loser, even though he wasn’t on the ballot.
“The chief climate denier got his head handed to him,” Inslee said.
John Farrell, co-director of the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, a research and advocacy nonprofit, said in an interview that he is excited to see what comes next with the new trifectas.
“There is this growing sense that more accountability measures are needed in order to rein in [utility] rates, and that utility companies are central to that problem,” he said.
Farrell sees an opportunity for Wisconsin to catch up with neighboring states that have already established climate and clean energy agendas. He’s pleased that Democrats’ legislative majorities in Minnesota are large enough to give the party leeway to propose more ambitious policies. In Michigan, he is encouraged by residents calling for publicly owned utilities and pushing back against the influence of large utilities.
A solar array. (Robert Zullo/ States Newsroom)
In the past, Farrell might have worried that utilities would stave off consumer-friendly policies by showering newly elected Democrats with campaign donations. But he thinks scenarios like this are less likely now because the public is wary of candidates they view as puppets for large companies. And some candidates have shown it’s possible to win without accepting money from utilities.
“We’re in a moment right now where there is enough scrutiny to make it harder for that sort of check-writing strategy to be successful,” he said.
More on the six states that attained trifectas or are on track to do so:
Arizona: Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs cruised to re-election and her party was on track to win majorities in the state House and Senate, although officials are still counting ballots in many races. Analysts said a Democratic trifecta is likely based on available results.
Michigan: Democrat Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, won the governor’s race. Democrats expanded their majority in the state Senate and gained a majority in the state House, with some races still being counted.
Minnesota: Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar was elected governor by a wide margin. The party expanded its majority in the state Senate and turned an even split with Republicans in the state House into a comfortable majority, with counting still underway.
Nevada: Democrat Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, defeated the incumbent Republican governor, Joe Lombardo. Democrats also retained control of the state House and Senate.
Wisconsin: Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, was elected governor. Democrats flipped control of both chambers of the Legislature, with an 18-15 majority in the state Senate and a 53-46 majority in the state House.
Pennsylvania: Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro easily won re-election. His party gained a 26-24 majority in the state Senate and expanded its majority in the state House to 111-88, with four races still being counted.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s picture-perfect autumn includes homelessness and poverty
description: CT must approach homelessness as both an immediate public health and safety concern as well as a long-term policy failure.
text:
Today, I write out of both anger and love for my state. I am inspired by the rich, diverse neighborhoods that span all 169 Connecticut towns, but I am deeply disturbed by the contrast between the beauty we celebrate and the immeasurable suffering experienced by our unhoused neighbors. 
 Each fall, Connecticut transforms into a postcard. New England foliage radiates shades of orange, yellow, and red; families visit orchards and pumpkin patches; and residents welcome the crisp, fresh air. Yet as temperatures drop, what feels refreshing to one resident can become dangerous for another. For Connecticut residents experiencing homelessness, autumn is an urgent awakening to prepare for the harsh conditions ahead. 
 Matthew Desmond, author of   Poverty, by America  , writes, “The end of poverty is something to stand for, to march for, to sacrifice for. Because poverty is the dream killer, the capability destroyer, the great waster of human potential.” His words challenge us to recognize poverty and homelessness not as the inevitable conditions of individual failures, but as preventable injustices that demand collective action. In Connecticut, this responsibility becomes especially urgent as decreasing temperatures expose homeless residents to potential life-threatening conditions. 
The timing is significant. As our harsh winter approaches, so does the legislative session. Our lawmakers have an opportunity to confront this crisis before another season of tolerance and suffering.
 In our legislature’s ivory tower, homelessness is often discussed through estimates, budget proposals, and debates over affordable housing. These conversations are necessary, but they can obscure the immediate reality of surviving without shelter. For someone sleeping outdoors, a cold night is a prolonged period of physical suffering, uncertainty, and, at times, humiliation. People may spend hours at highway exits hoping for enough donations to afford a meal, while others navigate the shame and difficulty of accessing basic needs. 
 The health consequences are equally troubling.   Prolonged exposure to the cold can cause hypothermia, frostbite, and other serious complications.   Existing health conditions, especially for elderly homeless individuals, can make an already dangerous situation even more challenging. When daily survival takes precedence, seeking medical attention or managing chronic conditions can become increasingly difficult. Substance abuse and mental health challenges can further increase vulnerability to dangerous weather. As expressed in conversations with homeless residents, illegal substances and alcohol abuse serve as an unfortunate survival mechanism among harsh temperatures and rampant hunger.  
Connecticut has taken steps to respond through its Severe Cold Weather Protocol , which coordinates emergency resources when temperatures become dangerously low. For instance, dialing 2-1-1 can provide immediate direction to social services. But these resources cannot protect people who do not know they exist, lack access to a phone, or cannot navigate the process of obtaining assistance alone. Shelter capacity, transportation barriers, and eligibility requirements can further limit access. 
In conversations with unhoused residents, I have come to realize that the existence of a service does not guarantee its accessibility. Some people have become so entrenched in the systems of poverty and homelessness that they do not know where to begin with social resources or how to utilize them. Emergency responses are essential, but they should not substitute policies that prevent homelessness and expand access to stable housing statewide. A service is only useful if someone can find it, qualify for it, and apply it.
 Furthermore, the scale of Connecticut’s homelessness crisis makes this more than a seasonal concern. The state’s   2026 Point-in-Time Count   identified 3,847 people experiencing homelessness on a single night in January.   Connecticut’s unsheltered population also increased by 45% between 2024 and 2025.   Although these counts provide a snapshot of homelessness, they do not account for the true total of unhoused residents. Similarly, this snapshot reveals that too many residents remain without stable housing and may become exposed to harsh winter elements in the coming months. 
We must therefore approach homelessness as both an immediate public health and safety concern as well as a long-term policy failure. Poverty and homelessness are shaped by policy decisions. Addressing it requires more than relying on the generosity of Connecticut volunteers, shelters, halfway houses, and nonprofit organizations. Their on-the-ground work is indispensable, but the responsibility cannot fall on them alone.
Connecticut legislators have a duty to consider all residents, not only those who have the privilege to show up to the capital or vote. Legislators should consider the encampments outside of our local grocery store; the hurting men and women who stand in the middle of intersections for hours on end, and the future of our state if homelessness is reduced to an anomaly, rather than a commonly accepted feature of our cities. These immediate interventions must be accompanied by sustained investments in housing developments and affordable housing options, as well as resources that truly help residents secure and maintain stability. 
Furthermore, the homeless population is not only forced to sleep outdoors, but they may be arrested or penalized for doing so. Beyond the immediate dangers of residing in the cold, Connecticut must confront the criminalization of homelessness. 
In the 2024 decision of City of Grants Pass v. Johnson , the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that enforcing public-camping restrictions does not, by itself, violate the Eighth Amendment. This decision gave municipalities greater enforcement opportunities to restrict public sleeping, panhandling, and residing in public spaces, even when homeless individuals  have no other choice. When Connecticut fails to provide adequate alternatives to sleeping outdoors, policies that punish public rest risk penalizing people for the very conditions the state has failed to address. Through fines, displacement, and arrests, the state further entrenches the unhoused population into cycles of poverty, incarceration and homelessness. 
Connecticut lawmakers had an opportunity to address this complication in 2026 through House Bill 5260 , which proposed prohibiting municipalities from penalizing homeless people for certain basic activities of living in public spaces. The bill received favorable votes in the Housing and Planning and Development committees but was ultimately tabled and did not become law. Its failure to advance into law sparks important debates for the next legislative session. Will our state prioritize the safety and dignity of people experiencing homelessness, or continue allowing punitive responses to circumstances that people cannot control? 
Aside from the legislation’s responsibility and the role of community organizations, Connecticut residents also have a role to play. We can support local homelessness prevention organizations, advocate for policies that expand housing affordability, and challenge the stigma that frames homelessness as an individual failure. Most importantly, we must recognize unhoused people as members of our communities rather than strangers that we turn our cheeks to, as a result of our own discomfort and fear. This disconnection only perpetuates the tolerance of homelessness among our state and reduces a homeless person’s dignity as a human-being. Although not every resident can donate to non-profit organizations or speak to policymakers, we can change the stigma by acknowledging homeless individuals as our neighbors rather than an inconvenience at a stoplight.
 Matthew Desmond reminds us that poverty wastes human potential by restricting people’s ability to pursue opportunities, protect their health, and imagine a meaningful future. When someone must devote each day to basic survival, the possibility of pursuing these opportunities becomes distant. We cannot meaningfully claim there is opportunity while ignoring the basic conditions necessary to access it for our homeless population. 
 Connecticut’s autumn will always be beautiful. The leaves will change, the air will grow colder, and another picture perfect winter will arrive. But the success of our state should be reflected in the collective care we have for all of our neighbors, even the ones we cannot see while they reside in tents below the overpass.  
If ending poverty is something worth standing for in Connecticut, the arrival of colder weather must be a call to action. Moreover, we cannot eliminate homelessness in a single legislative session, but our legislators can choose to invest in solutions that make stable housing a possibility and public health a priority. 
Connecticut cannot treat homelessness as an emergency only when winter arrives, nor can it punish people for surviving outdoors while failing to provide adequate alternatives. As we admire the changing seasons, we must ask ourselves and our law-makers a difficult question: What does it mean to celebrate the beauty of Connecticut if we are unwilling to ensure that everyone in our state is safe, healthy, and considered for?
Arianna Martinez of Hartford is a student at Trinity College.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The lost art of statesmanship
description: Governing requires accepting responsibility for everyone, including those who opposed you.
text:
I find it troubling how political discourse has become an exercise in demonizing opponents, too often marked by personal insults, hostility and division. Somewhere along the way, we seem to have confused civility with weakness, compromise with surrender, and political disagreement with personal hostility. Inflammatory rhetoric may attract attention, but it should never be mistaken for strength or effective leadership.

Werner Oyanadel

Part of the problem, I believe, is our failure to distinguish between winning an election and governing. These responsibilities require different kinds of leadership.
Candidates should vigorously debate ideas, challenge one another’s records and make their case to voters. Political competition is essential to democracy. But once an election ends, something important must change. Elected leaders are responsible not only to those who supported them, but to everyone they have been entrusted to serve.
I was encouraged to see two candidates shake hands following a recent gubernatorial debate in Connecticut. It was a small gesture, but one that carried meaning. In Little League, young athletes learn to shake hands with opponents after a game, regardless of the outcome. It is a simple lesson in sportsmanship, respect and humility. Shouldn’t we expect at least the same from those aspiring to lead us? Our children are watching, and the examples we set help shape the leaders of tomorrow.
Winning an election requires persuading enough people to support you. Governing requires accepting responsibility for everyone, including those who opposed you.
Unfortunately, the instincts that help candidates win do not always translate into effective governance. Energizing supporters, drawing sharp distinctions and defeating opponents may produce electoral victories. Governing demands something more: humility, judgment, cooperation and the recognition that no person or party has a monopoly on good ideas.
Connecticut has offered another encouraging example. In September 2023, the University of Hartford hosted a bipartisan conversation about civility in politics, bringing together leaders from different political backgrounds to discuss listening, mutual respect and common ground. Their exchange reminded us that political differences need not prevent cooperation. Respectful disagreement can be a strength in democratic leadership.
Civility does not mean avoiding difficult conversations, suppressing passion or pretending our differences do not exist. It means recognizing the dignity of people with whom we disagree. We can challenge someone’s ideas without questioning their humanity. We can stand firmly on principle without resorting to ridicule or personal attacks. The strength of an argument should rest on its substance, not the volume of an insult.
I’ve always appreciated the analogy of our country as an airplane. We may disagree with the pilot, question the flight plan or wish someone else were at the controls. But rooting for the plane to crash simply because we dislike who is flying it makes little sense. We are all passengers, and the consequences of failure affect us all. That does not mean accepting every decision without protest. It means caring about the country’s well-being even when we oppose its leadership.
Statesmanship also does not mean abandoning convictions or compromising fundamental principles. There are moments when leaders must stand firm, particularly when constitutional rights, democratic institutions or the public interest are at stake. But standing firm on principle is different from refusing to cooperate simply because an idea comes from a political opponent.
I worry that some leaders become so consumed by the competition for power that they fail to recognize when the campaign must give way to governing. The insults that win applause at a rally may undermine the trust needed to work together afterward. And citizens have a role to play, too: We should demand substance rather than spectacle and resist the temptation to treat neighbors who vote differently as enemies.
A great debater may win an election, but it takes a great statesperson to lead a nation.
Democracy does not require us to agree on everything. It requires something harder: the maturity to disagree without becoming enemies, the courage to compromise when appropriate and the wisdom to recognize that our shared future matters more than any individual political victory.
Civility is not weakness. It is the strength to disagree without disrespect, to lead without demeaning others and to recognize that the measure of statesmanship is not simply how well we win, but how responsibly we govern together.
The greatest victory is not when one political party triumphs over another, but when our democracy emerges stronger. When we get this right, our democracy wins — and so do we all.  
Werner Oyanadel lives in Willimantic.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Tribal chairs tell RFK Jr. they need federal resources to improve their own healthcare
description: Native American communities experience some of the highest disparities in healthcare in the country. Tribal chairs are hoping to work with U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who visited North Dakota Thursday, to remedy that.  A major theme of the tribal chairs’ comments Thursday was the need for the federal government […]
text:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during a roundtable discussion with North Dakota tribal leaders at United Tribes Technical College on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Native American communities experience some of the highest disparities in healthcare in the country. Tribal chairs are hoping to work with U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who visited North Dakota Thursday, to remedy that. 
A major theme of the tribal chairs’ comments Thursday was the need for the federal government to provide the necessary resources to support local tribal solutions, not to impose solutions crafted in Washington, D.C. 
“We have survived generations of policies that attempted to diminish our identity, diminish our lands, and take our sovereignty,” said Lonna Street, chair of the Spirit Lake Nation. “We are not simply asking for the healthcare funding. We are advocating for the health and the dignity and the safety of the future of our Native nations.”
Soil health key to improving human health, RFK Jr. says in visit to North Dakota ranch

Garret Renville, chair of the Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate, said the trajectory of chronic health problems in tribal communities is headed in the wrong direction, and the federal government needs to redesign Indian Health Services, an agency under Health and Human Services, to meet the challenge. 
“Are we willing to fundamentally change the role of IHS from an agency that administers healthcare for Indian people into an institution that helps tribal nations build and govern their own healthcare systems?” Renville asked.
Kennedy agreed and said “we need to overhaul” the Indian Health Service to better support tribal governments’ local efforts, rather than directing everything from Washington. 
“I think that gives them agency, gives them a sense of control, gives them the ability to make decisions about their own communities on a day-to-day basis,” Kennedy said. “When the tribes run their own affairs, they do it much better than we do.”
Spirit Lake Nation Chairperson Lonna Street speaks during a roundtable discussion with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. at United Tribes Technical College on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Kennedy was accompanied by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, and Sens. John Hoeven and Kevin Cramer, and the state’s lone U.S. House representative, Julie Fedorchak. He said they were there to listen. 
“We need you to tell us what you need, and we are going to deliver it,” Kennedy said.
Street and the other tribal leaders emphasized that healthcare is tied into a variety of topics, from public safety to economic opportunity, that tribal nations need help with and that everything is tied together. 
“When one child cannot access adequate healthcare, it affects our entire community. When a mother can’t receive proper prenatal care, our entire community is affected,” Street said. “And when a family struggles with addiction, diabetes, unemployment, or inadequate housing, our entire community is affected.”
Street cited a variety of peripheral issues that affect health in tribal communities including unequal funding for education, public safety issues like drug crime, unsolved cases of missing and murdered Indigenous people and a lack of jobs and economic activity. 
She also said there are workforce shortages for healthcare facilities that already exist, a lack of housing for the professionals they recruit, and that funding for the Indian Health Service budget is $8 billion even though “estimated need exceeds $50 billion annually.” 
“These are not separate issues,” Street said. “They’re all connected.” 
Standing Rock Sioux Tribal Chairman Steve Sitting Bear speaks during a roundtable discussion with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. at United Tribes Technical College on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Steve Sitting Bear, chair of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, said his nation has created new initiatives for a variety of areas, from economic development to public safety and housing, because all of those issues affect the health challenges faced by tribes. Now they need the federal government’s support. 
“Our health challenges and problems are directly tied to the economic conditions we were subjugated to,” Sitting Bear said. “We are taking the necessary steps to do what’s needed to be done. We’re just asking for Congress, for the heads of the departments, to do the same.” 
Mark Fox, the outgoing chair of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation, said Kennedy’s ideas are often outside the box. That’s what tribal communities need, even if the HHS secretary receives criticism from others, Fox said. He cited Albert Einstein and said trying the same thing over and over again is the definition of insanity.
“The programs that have been provided, instituted through federal policy in Indian Country, is a reflection of insanity,” Fox said. “Because we do the same thing over and over again, and it doesn’t change. The problem still exists or gets bigger.”
A consistent need cited is help with addiction recovery, substance abuse and mental health services in tribal communities. Tribal leaders said they’ve made strides talking addiction, but significant challenges remain. 
“The drugs are killing us. They’re literally killing us,” Fox said. “We need help. They’re asking you for help. We can’t fund these things on our own.”
Mark Fox, former tribal chair of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation, speaks during a roundtable discussion with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. at United Tribes Technical College on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Fox hailed the success of the MHA Nation’s Good Road Recovery Center. Chris Parisien, a policy specialist for Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa filling in for Chair Jamie Azure, said his community has operated an addiction recovery facility for a little more than a year and they’ve seen good results so far. But he said that isn’t the only issue Native Americans are facing. 
“Our life expectancy is 20% lower than other North Dakotans, and that is because of lack of meaningful access to preventive medical care,” Parisien said. 
Kennedy touted his agency’s accomplishments for tribal communities in the nearly two years since he was confirmed as secretary and his desire to follow through on his family’s decades-old commitment to helping right the wrongs done to Native Americans by the U.S. government. 
“My father had a belief that our country would never live up to its role as an exemplary nation, the exemplary democracy, if it didn’t go back and remedy the original sin that defined our country and allowed us to flourish and to prosper,” Kennedy said. “Which was the treatment, the genocide of the people who were here before us.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.
