name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Bryant elected to lead Arkansas Senate in vote that highlights deep divides
description: Republican Sen. Joshua Bryant was elected Thursday as the Arkansas Senate’s next leader following three hours of deadlocked voting that indicated divisions facing the majority-GOP chamber next year.  The vote for Senate president pro tempore came during the Senate’s organizational meeting and two days after a midterm election where Democrats expanded their r[...]
text:
Republican Senate Pro Tempore Bart Hester shakes hands with Sen. Joshua Bryant in the Senate chamber at the Arkansas state Capitol on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Republican Sen. Joshua Bryant was elected Thursday as the Arkansas Senate’s next leader following three hours of deadlocked voting that indicated divisions facing the majority-GOP chamber next year. 
The vote for Senate president pro tempore came during the Senate’s organizational meeting and two days after a midterm election where Democrats expanded their ranks in the predominantly Republican Legislature. 
Sen. Joshua Bryant (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)
Bryant, a Rogers Republican who has served in the Senate since 2023, was elected following the third round of voting after neither the original president pro tempore designee, Republican Sen. Breanne Davis, nor Republican Sen. Ron Caldwell, received enough votes to claim the chamber’s leadership post.
Sen. Bart Hester, a Republican from Cave Springs, has been the pro tempore since 2023 but declined to pursue a third term. Bryant will still require final approval from the body after senators are sworn in in January.
The Senate currently has 34 senators and senators-elect, with one vacant seat. The vacancy made it possible for no one candidate to receive the required 18 votes. According to several senators, it was the first time the chamber failed to select a pro tempore since it began electing them. 
Davis, a close ally of Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and the Senate sponsor of the governor’s signature education overhaul, was elected pro tempore designee in May. Davis, who was first elected to the Senate in 2018, managed Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton’s reelection campaign.
But Caldwell, who was elected to the Senate in 2012, said earlier this year he would challenge her when the Senate voted on the matter again after the election. Sanders supported a challenger’s vitriolic but ultimately unsuccessful primary bid  against Caldwell, who was one of several GOP lawmakers who opposed the governor’s plan to build a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County. Sanders has put that prison project on hold after facing legislative resistance. 
Senators select the pro tempore, who is responsible for presiding over the Senate in the absence of the lieutenant governor, via a secret ballot. It’s unclear who voted for who. Before the second and third deadlocked round of voting, Bryant was nominated, only for the nomination to be pulled after Davis or Caldwell was nominated again.
After the third round of deadlocked voting, Caldwell made a motion to close nominations after Republican Sen. Scott Flippo nominated Bryant, which no one opposed. With Bryant as the only nominee, no vote took place.
With Arkansas Republicans’ House supermajority lost, a changed dynamic

“Thank you, senators, for putting this trust in me today,” Bryant said after he was named designee. “I will do my best every day at the 96th General Assembly to make sure each one of your voices is heard.”
Republican Sen. Tyler Dees was selected as Senate majority leader after Bryant, who had previously been picked for that post, was elected Senate president. Democratic Sen. Stephanie Flowers was selected as minority leader.
Bryant sponsored a 2023 law that limited local governments’ ability to regulate cryptocurrency mines. After that measure faced a backlash from some communities, the Legislature passed followup legislation by Bryant to add new regulations to the operations.
In 2023, he was the only Republican in the Senate to vote against the initial version of a bill that would have criminalized transgender people using restrooms that match their gender identity. He later voted for a revised version after it was significantly scaled back to remove concerns that it would have been the most extreme bathroom bill in the country. 
Bryant at the time said the original version of the bill went too far by allowing someone to be charged with a crime for being in a public restroom or changing room of the opposite sex when a minor is present, regardless of their intent.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Democrats endorse Matt Ritter, Bob Duff to lead General Assembly
description: CT House and Senate Democrats welcomed 37 new legislators-elect Thursday as they met for the first time to endorse their top leaders.
text:
Name tags might have helped. 
House and Senate Democrats welcomed 37 new legislators-elect Thursday as they met for the first time since Tuesday’s Democratic rout to endorse their top leaders, the necessary first step towards readying the Connecticut General Assembly for the term that opens on Jan. 6.
House Democrats met at the Capitol in the evening to confirm they will be backing Rep. Matt Ritter of Hartford for an unprecedented fourth term as speaker when the session begins in January — if he doesn’t resign before then to become the interim president of the University of Connecticut.
Ritter said he addressed his uncertain status during the closed-door caucus, asking his members for patience, an exchange he called “emotional.” He has been approached informally but noted the timing for resolving his status rests with the university’s board of trustees.
“They have to make a decision. They have their own process. I don’t have an offer,” Ritter said. “I’ve asked the caucus, you know, probably give me a couple of weeks on this thing, and hopefully I’ll have news for them.”
House Majority Leader Jason Rojas of East Hartford, who would become speaker if Ritter departs, stood with him Thursday night as he spoke about the awkwardness of his uncertain status.
“I care a lot about this place and the institution, and Jason’s been a good friend,” Ritter said. “And we understand this — at some point, the wheels of government have to move on.”
Over lunch in New Haven, the Senate Democrats formally endorsed Sen. Bob Duff of Norwalk as their choice for Senate president pro tem, succeeding the retiring Sen. Martin M. Looney of New Haven. Sen. Gary Winfield of New Haven was chosen to succeed Duff as majority leader.
Winfield, a senator for a dozen years, will be the first Black lawmaker to serve as majority leader in either chamber.
In a Republican caucus on the other side of the Capitol complex, House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, was unanimously elected to a fourth term as leader of the GOP caucus.
Pending recounts, Democrats will have majorities of 33-3 in the Senate and 116-35 in the House. The current splits are 25-11 and 102-49.
Senate Republicans have not announced which of their three members will become the Senate minority leader. Sen. Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield, was one of the eight incumbent senators to lose Tuesday.
House Democrats will have 25 new members: 14 who flipped Republican seats and 11 who will be succeeding Democrats who either did not run for reelection or lost a primary. Senate Democrats will have a dozen newbies, including eight who flipped Republican seats.
The 14 incoming House members who won seats formerly held by Republicans are: Francis Lombard, 8th District; Jane Wisialowski, 23rd; Cinzia Lettieri, 35th; Bill Heughins, 43rd;  Bob Fernandez, 48th; Ellen Paul, 55th; Rick LeBorious, 59th; Kim Becker, 62nd; DeWayne K. Wynn Jr., 77th; David Fritz, 90th; Michelle Embree Ku, 106th;  Julie Kerton, 107th; Bryan Lizotte, 113th; Mandy Kilmartin, 122nd.
Another 11 new members won seats already held by Democrats: Kyle Anderson, 5th House; Angie Parkinson, 10th; Tiffani McGinnis, 18th; Olaleye Onikuyide, 19th; Moise  “Moses” Carelus, 31st; Chad Cardillo, 83rd; Samuel Carmody, 85th; Eli Sabin, 92nd; Wildaliz Bermudez, 97th; Tom Labardi, 118th; and Lee Goldstein, 136th.
“There’s a really good energy and good vibe, and now you got to turn the page and you start talking to people about assignments and responsibilities, and it hits pretty quickly for people too,” Ritter said. “All of a sudden, you’re no longer in a campaign. Now you’re a representative-elect and a lot of things attached to that.”
The new senators are: Maryam Khan, 2nd District; David Kiner, 7th; Al Paolillo, 11th; Jack Fazzino, 13th; Joe de la Cruz, 18th; Carolann Reid, 21st; Samantha Nestor, 26th; Rob Blanchard, 28th; Aaron Zimmerman, 30th; Brandi Mandato, 34th; Ethan Werstler, 35th; and Jill Oberlander, 36th.
The only new Republican lawmaker will be Melissa Ziobron, a House GOP staffer who won the open 34th District seat. She held the same seat when she ran unsuccessfully for the state Senate in 2018.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Soil health key to improving human health, RFK Jr. says in visit to North Dakota ranch
description: The top U.S. health official visited a ranch near Bismarck Thursday where he talked about the importance of soil health for human health. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke at a roughly 90-minute roundtable on regenerative agriculture at the Black Leg Ranch east of Bismarck. Reporters were not allowed in […]
text:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., center, speaks during a press conference next to Sen. John Hoeven, left, R-N.D., and Sen. Kevin Cramer, right, R-N.D., at the Bismarck Event Center on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The top U.S. health official visited a ranch near Bismarck Thursday where he talked about the importance of soil health for human health.
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke at a roughly 90-minute roundtable on regenerative agriculture at the Black Leg Ranch east of Bismarck. Reporters were not allowed in except for a 15-minute portion, during which Kennedy talked about how vital soil health is for the human gut, which he said dictates health, emotions, moods, energy levels and “our effectiveness in life.” 
“If we can keep that healthy, we can maintain public health. It’s hard to keep it healthy if the nutrients that are supposed to be in the soils are not making it into the plants, then onto our tables or our plates,” Kennedy said.
Chemicals from farming are hurting the soil and destroying its microbiome, contributing to health issues such as increased cancer rates from nitrates linked to runoff from fertilizers and chemical pesticides, he said.
“Anything that we can do to reduce the intensity of chemical agriculture is just going to be good for the farmer all around,” Kennedy said. 
The Trump administration is pursuing policies for “off-ramps” for farmers to transition to less chemical-intensive agriculture “if they want them,” Kennedy said. Farmers have to be conservative to survive and they “don’t want to do something unless they know it’s going to work,” he said.
Kennedy cited the Doan family’s Black Leg Ranch as a template of regenerative agriculture for other farmers.
Jerry Doan’s great-grandfather started the ranch in 1882. The ranch tries to mimic natural grazing patterns, “bringing back what the good Lord gave us with our natural resources,” Doan said. 
“We had this abundant grassland and season-long grazing has eroded that,” Doan said in an interview. He said better grazing management can improve the diversity of species and water quality and make grasslands more lush.
Popular North Dakota conservation program could attract federal funding

Kennedy also said U.S. children are unhealthier now than when his uncle John F. Kennedy was president in the early 1960s. He said rates of Type 2 diabetes, autism and obesity have increased from decades past. He also linked “an epidemic of depression and behavioral problems” to U.S. food.
America needs to fix its food system and stop the decline in rural areas, he said. 
“We all need to focus on how do we get our food again to be the highest quality in every way,” Kennedy said. “It’s going to start from good soil. Good food, good soil, good human health.” 
Much of the roundtable discussion focused on how to improve soil health, said Burleigh County Soil Conservation District Manager Darrell Oswald, who attended the event. Officials and producers need to realize that “we’re working with a degraded resource,” but there are ways to fix that, he said. 
“When we talk about regenerative agriculture, we’re talking about a more natural system and using the soil health principles to drive the system and build back, if you will, the carbon, the nutrients, the soil organic matter, the microbiome, the microorganisms in the soil, and that’s what regenerative agriculture is all about,” Oswald said. 
The roundtable was a step forward “because when we start looking at the land as a source of life other than a resource, and that’s what regenerative ag is, it’s going to create better health for our communities and better health for our bodies,” said former Standing Rock Sioux tribal chairman Dave Archambault II, who founded Wozu, a tribal food and culture effort.
Wozu is on the Standing Rock Reservation and started with land regeneration. Wozu took on several initiatives such as returning buffalo to the land and connecting people back to the land with programs focused on cultural arts and wellness, food sovereignty and outdoor stewardship.
“I think Indigenous peoples have always had the relationship and the connection to the land, and for somebody like the secretary to come and to hear, it was just an honor,” Archambault said. 
The roundtable included Kennedy, Doan, Archambault, Gov. Kelly Armstrong, U.S. Interior Secretary and former Gov. Doug Burgum, North Dakota’s three-member congressional delegation, Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring and others.
North Dakota to use ‘anchor partners’ to manage Rural Health grants

Later, Kennedy and the congressional delegation participated in a 30-minute rural health roundtable with former first lady Kathryn Burgum, state lawmakers and representatives of hospitals, long-term care facilities and health care associations. Reporters were allowed to attend the entire event.
They talked about focusing on ways to help people recover from addiction, seeking more flexibility for applicants for federal rural health funds and staffing rural hospitals.
Minot-based Trinity Health Vice President of Long-Term Care and Ancillary Services Wade Peterson asked about eliminating some COVID-era regulations – such as reporting cases weekly to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention – given that Trinity has had three COVID-19 cases in the last year and no COVID-19 deaths in over three years.
“We’re still having to do a lot of COVID things. I’d like to see that probably eliminated. The health emergency’s (been) over for three years,” Peterson said.
“Make a list. Get it to me. We’ll get rid of them,” Kennedy said.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

text:
Calvin Schrage, I-Anchorage, waves a sign on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)One day after the Alaska Senate’s bipartisan coalition announced key leadership positions, the incoming majority coalition in the Alaska House announced its leadership including that Anchorage independent Calvin Schrage will be the new House speaker.
The new House majority coalition of the 35th Alaska State Legislature is forming with independent, Democratic and Republican members. While many votes are still being counted,  preliminary election results published Wednesday show independent and Democratic candidates are leading in 23 races for the House’s 40 seats. 
That will produce a larger majority coalition than in the last Legislature, where a 21-member majority held a thin lead over the 19-member Republican-led minority. 
The majority coalition sets the agenda for the House, assigns key committee assignments and decides what legislation will be considered.
Schrage, 35, showed a significant lead ahead of his opponent in House District 12 with 66.5% of the vote on Wednesday, heading for re-election to a fourth term to the House, where he has served since 2022. He served as House minority leader from 2023 to 2024, and as co-chair of the House Finance Committee from 2025 to 2026.
Schrage is set to succeed outgoing House Speaker Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, who is in the race for the Senate seat representing Western Alaska to the Aleutian Islands. 
In an interview on Thursday, Shrage said the “door is still open” for members to join the majority coalition. But he said they have formed quickly after Election Day to begin moving ahead with a bipartisan agenda with members “ready and willing to work across the aisle to move the state forward after a decade of fairly difficult times, austere budgets, outmigration, and, in my view, a really declining sense of hope and optimism about the future of our state.” 
Schrage said the majority coalition’s priorities will include reviving the public pension system, improving predictable and stable education funding, and energy policy — priorities echoed by the incoming bipartisan Senate majority coalition on Wednesday. 
“(There’s) a big interest in addressing the fiscal instability in our state, and also in addressing the high cost of energy, which we’re all expecting to rise in the years to come, and needs to be addressed by the Legislature,” he said. “So, really, in our view, these are kitchen table issues that are front and center for Alaskans thinking about their future here in the state.”
Alaska state oil revenues have surged due to the U.S. war on Iran, but Schrage cautioned that high energy prices have also hurt communities and the state, including the school system. He said he expects the incoming Legislature and governor will also have to address unforeseen expenses from the last year as well, in a supplemental budget.
“I would not be surprised to see significant supplementals emerge through the budgeting process as the new governor steps into his role and discovers fiscal challenges within departments that are inherited from the Dunleavy administration,” he said. 
Schrage said the coalition has not formally met with the Democratic gubernatorial frontrunner Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who received 49.1% of the vote in a four way race as of Wednesday. 
Final election results are scheduled to be certified on Nov. 25.     

House Majority Leader Rep. Chuck Kopp, R-Anchorage, speaks in support of a state pension plan on Apr. 29, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

The majority coalition also named Anchorage Republican Chuck Kopp for another term as House majority leader. He has served in the House 2017, and ran unopposed in this election for a fourth term. Kopp previously served as majority speaker from 2025 to 2026.
Sitka independent Rep. Rebecca Himschoot was named as House Rules chair. She has served in the House since 2023, where she co-chaired the House Education Committee from 2025 to 2026. She led her race with 55.6% of the vote on Wednesday. 
Democrats Rep. Neal Foster of Nome, Rep. Sara Hannan of Juneau and Rep. Ashley Carrick of Fairbanks were named as co-chairs of the House Finance Committee, which is charged with drafting the state’s operating and capital budgets.
Foster has served as co-chair of the Finance Committee since 2018, and has served in the House since 2009, representing the Bering Strait region to the Lower Yukon River. He led his race for re-election with 48.5% of the vote. 
Hannan ran unopposed this year, and is on track to serve a fifth term in the House representing Juneau, where she has served since 2020. 
Carrick led her race with 59.3% of the vote, heading for a third term in the House representing West Fairbanks, where she has served since 2023. 
Schrage said his goal as speaker is to foster a collaborative environment in the House to work across party lines, to tackle the major challenges facing Alaska.   
“I think Alaskans sometimes forget how unique it is in our country to have bipartisan coalitions in the Legislature, and I am incredibly proud that we are once again picking up that mantle of bipartisanship, and that there will be bipartisan coalitions — truly bipartisan coalitions — in both the House and the Senate,” he said. “I think it is a unique thing across our country and is a model for how things can be done better.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama executes Michael Shannon Taylor for the 1991 murder of a couple in Gadsden
description: The state of Alabama executed Michael Shannon Taylor, 54, Thursday for the 1991 murders of Ivan and Lucille Moore in Gadsden. Taylor did not make a final statement. Taylor’s execution was the third in Alabama this year.  Jeremy Tremaine Williams was executed in August and Jeffery Lee in September, both by lethal injection. Gov. Kay […]
text:
Michael Shannon Taylor was sentenced to death for the murders of Ivan and Lucille Moore during a robbery of their home in Gadsden He was executed by lethal injection Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Alabama Department of Corrections)The state of Alabama executed Michael Shannon Taylor, 54, Thursday for the 1991 murders of Ivan and Lucille Moore in Gadsden.
Taylor did not make a final statement.
Taylor’s execution was the third in Alabama this year.  Jeremy Tremaine Williams was executed in August and Jeffery Lee in September, both by lethal injection.
Gov. Kay Ivey commuted the death sentences of Charles “Sonny” Burton in March and Toforest Johnson in October.
Alabama executed five people in 2025, tied with South Carolina and Texas for the second highest total nationwide. Florida executed 19 people that year.
“35 years ago yesterday, Ivan and Lucille Moore kindly opened their home to Michael Taylor. Mr. Taylor repaid the Moores by beating them to death with a metal bar, all to rob them for money to buy clothing and jewelry,” Ivey said in a statement shortly after the execution. “His actions were reprehensible and despite his attempts to evade the consequences, he is facing the Good Lord for final judgement tonight.”
Media witnesses reported no complications with the execution, conducted via lethal injection. Initially Taylor’s eyes were open and looked in various directions. He spoke to his spiritual advisor who appeared to pray and Taylor appeared to say “thank you” to the spiritual advisor and then to his attorney who was seated in the witness room.
The process began at 5:51 p.m. He smiled at his spiritual advisor who appeared to be praying. At 5:53 p.m., Taylor’s eyes rolled back, his breathing became labored and then his eyes closed.
Taylor’s feet moved at 5:56 p.m. and that was the final time his body moved.
The time of death was 6:10 p.m. according to the news release sent by the Governor’s Office.
The family of Ivan and Lucille Moore said in a statement that they thank the Alabama Attorney General’s Office and others who “brought the case to an end.”
“Still, it is very hard for us to understand why it took 35 years,” the family said in the statement. “We know that a person has a right to appeal, but there should come a time when the jury’s decision is final. For all these years, our family has had to live with the waiting, the delays, and the uncertainty.”
Family members also said they have not forgotten the Moores.
“Waiting 35 years for justice has been painful, and no victim’s family should have to wait that long,” the family said.
According to court documents, Taylor received a ride from the Moores while absent without a leave from the U.S. Navy. He asked to use the telephone in their home, and beat them to death during the robbery.
Taylor filed a request for a stay of execution with the Alabama Supreme Court and another appeal with the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals Tuesday, arguing that because he opted into nitrogen gas executions under a 2018 law, the state cannot execute him by lethal injection.
Three judges at the 11th Circuit ruled that the nitrogen gas protocol Alabama planned to use violated Lee’s Eighth Amendment constitutional rights. A federal court then issued a permanent injunction to prevent Alabama from carrying out the execution by nitrogen gas.
After the protocol was blocked, Alabama moved to execute Lee by lethal injection.
Lee also argued that the 2018 law effectively banned the state from using lethal injection when an inmate chose nitrogen gas. U.S. District Court Judge Emily Marks refused to extend the permanent injunction to lethal injection because she said the situation had changed.
The Alabama Supreme Court denied Taylor’s motion for a stay of execution Wednesday evening.
“The man we knew was not the nineteen-year-old who committed this crime in 1991,” said the Federal Defenders for the Middle District of Alabama, which has represented him since 2017. “He was bright and funny, a lover of trivia and sports statistics, a fan of Notre Dame and the Pittsburgh Steelers, and a man who, after years of struggle, found a deep and genuine faith.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Blue wave carries Democrats to supermajority in WA House
description: Democrats in the Washington state House of Representatives are eyeing a supermajority as Thursday vote tallies put them on course to unseat a half-dozen incumbent Republicans and flip a GOP-held seat in the Puget Sound. Those seven pick-ups would give Democrats control of 66 of the 98 seats in the state House, lifting the party […]
text:
People rejoice at the Washington State Democratic Party election night gathering in Seattle, Washington on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard).Democrats in the Washington state House of Representatives are eyeing a supermajority as Thursday vote tallies put them on course to unseat a half-dozen incumbent Republicans and flip a GOP-held seat in the Puget Sound.
Those seven pick-ups would give Democrats control of 66 of the 98 seats in the state House, lifting the party to  a rarefied political plateau; the power to override gubernatorial vetoes and advance constitutional amendments.
“It looks like we’re going to have that supermajority,” House Majority Leader Joe Fitzgibbon, D-West Seattle, said Thursday. “If the late ballots trend our way we could get a few more.”
Democrats last had a supermajority with 67 members in 1949 and came close with 65 members in 1992. Republicans nearly managed it in 1996 when they held 62 of the chamber’s seats.
The likelihood took root as incumbent Republican lawmakers accepted the reality they won’t return to Olympia next year.
Rep. Kevin Waters, R-Stevenson, formally conceded Wednesday night, congratulating his opponent, Democrat Ben Christly, in a lengthy Facebook post.
On Thursday, his seatmate, Republican Rep. David Stuebe of Washougal, along with GOP Reps. John Ley of Vancouver, Gloria Mendoza of Grandview and Deb Manjarrez of Wapato each acknowledged they do not expect to overcome the vote margins by which they trail.
“I’m still in shock,” Stuebe said Thursday afternoon. “I’m sure you can hear the disappointment in my voice.”
Meanwhile, Democrat Renee Hernandez Greenfield of Port Orchard is well on her way to succeeding Republican Rep. Michelle Valdez, who is retiring. Her Republican opponent, Katy Cornell, said she faces a “hurdle to overcome,” but will wait for more votes to be counted before conceding.
“The voters have spoken in the midst of a national blue wave. It is highly unlikely for things to turn around,” said Ley, who is losing to Democrat Deken Letinich by 10 percentage points in the 18th Legislative District in Clark County in southwest Washington.
Rep. Stephanie McClintock, R-Vancouver, who also serves in the 18th district, is also trailing and likely to be unseated. Her Democratic opponent, Randi Knott, said late Thursday that she hasn’t heard from McClintock and isn’t ready to claim victory but believes it’s clear she’ll win. That would propel Democrats to the supermajority.
“We’re going to have no role up there,” said Stuebe, who is also mayor of Washougal. “It would be really tough to serve in that.”
Political headwinds
Christly, of Vancouver, was comfortably ahead of Waters, 55.5% to 44.3% when the lawmaker conceded.
“While the outcome was not what we had hoped for, I am incredibly grateful to everyone who supported our campaign, volunteered their time, and believed in our vision for the future of our district,” he wrote.
Waters also congratulated Diana Perez, who is beating Stuebe by a similar margin.
“I look forward to seeing Ben and Diana represent the people of the 17th District. We are fortunate to call this beautiful part of Washington home, and I sincerely wish them both the very best as they take on this responsibility,” he wrote.
Stuebe didn’t appreciate Waters conceding his race for him: “You don’t do that for me.”
Ley, Mendoza, Manjarrez and Stuebe are in their first terms. All said they could not overcome powerful political headwinds.
“I knew that it was going to be a close race because of what is happening nationally,” said Mendoza, a former mayor of Grandview. “I will continue to represent my district and my state in some capacity.”
‘More voices from more areas’
Christly posted a statement on Facebook on Thursday afternoon.
“From the beginning, we chose to focus on people, not politics. Even when the noise got loud, we stayed positive, treated people with respect, and kept our focus on what really matters,” he wrote. “I’m proud of the campaign we ran and the people who made it possible.”
In the 14th Legislative District in central Washington, Democrat Chelsea Dimas of Sunnyside is beating Mendoza and Democrat Ezequiel Morfin of Toppenish is leading Manjarrez. For years, Republicans have represented the district that includes most of Yakima County, parts of Klickitat, Benton and Franklin counties, and the Yakama Reservation. 
A court-ordered redistricting coupled with an intensified organizing effort by Democrats and the unpopularity of President Donald Trump are propelling the Democrat duo to success.
Dimas expressed her joy on Facebook in which she vowed to be a force for la gente. 
“My parents sacrificed so I could have opportunities they never did,” she began. “And today, their mija, a little Indigenous Mexicana from Sunnyside, is set to make history and FLIP THE 14TH.”
“The first from Sunnyside. The first Indigenous person. The first Democratic Latina. The first Queer person of color..elected to the Legislature from this side of the mountains,” she wrote. 
Winning an election “isn’t the finish line,” she said, but the starting point.
“To the people who didn’t vote for me, I want you to know that I will fight for you, too. Because this seat doesn’t belong to me. It doesn’t belong to any political party. It belongs to la gente,” she wrote.
Fitzgibbon is looking forward to the presence of the many new faces.
Managing a larger caucus “is a good problem to have,” he said. “We’ll have more voices from more areas of the state that we haven’t heard from. It will mean more diversity and it will mean more life experiences.”
Could Dems add more members?
Democrats could potentially pick up several more seats. Here are contests where Republicans were ahead or behind by small margins with Thursday’s ballot count.

Republican Rep. Brian Burnett holds a 110-vote lead on Democrat Stacy Willoughby in the 12th District encompassing communities in Chelan, Snohomish and King counties. Burnett trailed following ballot counts Tuesday and Wednesday.
Democrat David Berg is ahead of Republican Rep. Michael Keaton by 669 votes in the 25th District in Pierce County
Republican Cyndy Jacobsen is clinging to a 222-vote lead on Democrat Jenn Marie Strickling in the 25th District.
Republican Dan Griffey is ahead of Democrat Jim Pierson by 951 votes in the 35th District encompassing parts of Kitsap, Mason and Thurston counties.
Republican Travis Couture is leading Democrat Marla Littlesun by 1,107 votes, also in the 35th District.

Reporter Jake Goldstein-Street contributed to this report.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Landowners petition U.S. Supreme Court in Piedmont power line case
description: A group of Maryland landowners aggrieved by land surveys for a proposed 67-mile electricity transmission line across northern Maryland are petitioning the U.S. Supreme Court to take up their case.
text:
A power transmission line in Frederick County. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A group of Maryland landowners aggrieved by land surveys for a proposed 67-mile electricity transmission line across northern Maryland are petitioning the U.S. Supreme Court to take up their case.
In their request, filed with the nation’s highest court Wednesday, 60 petitioners dispute lower court rulings that allowed surveyors from power line company PSEG Renewable Transmission to enter onto their properties for field studies for the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project.
The landowners are represented at no cost by the Pacific Legal Foundation, a public interest firm focused on individual liberties and property rights that has brought 21 cases to the Supreme Court in its 53-year history, and cites 18 victories before the court.
The landowners “never imagined that protecting their homes, farms, and communities would lead them to petition the United States Supreme Court,” said Joanne Frederick, the resident who leads the advocacy group Stop MPRP, in a statement issued Thursday.
“Their determination has been extraordinary, and this is an important milestone in their fight for property rights,” Frederick said.
PSEG did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest filing in the case.
The landowners have long argued that PSEG should not be allowed to enter their properties before it has received approval from Maryland to build the power line.
Surveys for Piedmont power line can continue, appellate court rules

But in order to get approval from the Maryland Public Service Commission, PSEG needs to finish all of the surveys. So, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals deemed the landowners’ proposal unworkable, and affirmed PSEG’s right to go on the properties for its studies.
In the petition, the landowners contend that the 4th Circuit went “further than any other circuit has dared” in affirming PSEG’s survey access based on the notion that it “likely” possessed the power of eminent domain.
Though the appellate court’s decision may seem like “a procedural quirk,” it has “devastating practical consequences going to the very heart of the fundamental right of private property ownership,” the attorneys representing the landowners wrote. “The Fourth Circuit authorized a private party to enter Petitioners’ property without first establishing that the private party possesses the sovereign power on which its claimed right of entry depends,” reads the petition to the high court.
If approved by the Public Service Commission, the line would be routed through rural areas in Carroll, Frederick and Baltimore counties. Regional grid operator PJM Interconnection deemed the project necessary to prevent power infrastructure issues such as blackouts, amid skyrocketing demands for power from data centers in the region at a time of power plant retirements.
The land surveys have been ongoing since June 2025, when U.S. District Court Judge Adam Abelson granted PSEG a preliminary injunction, allowing it to access properties despite significant landowner opposition. That injunction has since been applied to hundreds of properties with owners who oppose the surveys.
In their Wednesday filing, the landowners argue that the preliminary injunction went too far, since injunctions are meant to “protect rights that exist,” not “let a court create new ones.”
The court could have conducted a proceeding to determine whether PSEG, a New Jersey-based company, possessed eminent domain rights in Maryland. Instead, the court predicted PSEG would prevail in its arguments, and granted the injunction.
“Predictions can be wrong. A court sometimes ‘reaches a different conclusion upon full consideration of the merits,’” the attorneys wrote.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
That decision came with irreversible consequences, the attorneys say.
“In an ordinary case, the final judgment corrects a wrong prediction. Here no judgment can, because the entry will already have happened,” the petition says.
By now, the field studies are nearing completion. In September, PSEG reported that only nine archaeological surveys remained for the properties in the original lawsuit. The studies have also included metes and bounds surveys, forest and wetland delineation surveys, habitat assessments and acoustic bat surveys, according to PSEG’s filing.
But the landowners said in their latest filing that they are requesting a Supreme Court decision in part because the issue may keep arising, whenever out-of-state actors are chosen by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to construct power lines.
The attorneys acknowledged in their filing that Maryland’s Power Plant Research Program would have the power of eminent domain — and therefore would be allowed to conduct the surveys — as would power companies already operating in Maryland.
“When the winner is new to the state, as PSEG is to Maryland, its power of eminent domain may still be unsettled when it needs to survey, and each award like that can raise the question again,” the attorneys wrote.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Swimmers weren’t warned about nearly 30 high E. coli tests at beaches this summer
description: There were 27 instances this summer when a single sample test for E. coli at a state beach came back above the state standard, but state regulators did not issue a swim advisory for the beach.  The Iowa Department of Natural Resources tests lake water at state park beaches for E. coli and cyanobacteria toxins […]
text:
Sunset on Easter Lake in Des Moines. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) There were 27 instances this summer when a single sample test for E. coli at a state beach came back above the state standard, but state regulators did not issue a swim advisory for the beach. 
The Iowa Department of Natural Resources tests lake water at state park beaches for E. coli and cyanobacteria toxins from green-blue algae, weekly from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend. The department issues swim advisories when the tested samples are above a certain threshold. 
The decision to issue a swim advisory is also weighed against a five-year data point that classifies beaches as “vulnerable” “transitional” or “less-vulnerable.” Beaches with a less-vulnerable classification do not receive “swimming is not recommended” advisories when a single E. coli test at the beach comes back higher than the state’s maximum standard for the bacteria. 
Beaches, regardless of classification, will receive a swim advisory if the five-week geometric mean for E. coli exceeds 126 colony forming units, or CFU per 100 milliliters of water.
Tammie Krausman, the communications director for DNR, said because of the way bacteria levels ebb and flow, and the time it takes for the department to receive results on the samples, the department posts advisories when the geometric mean is high or when it’s likely the bacteria levels will remain high at the beach, based on historical data represented in the beach classification status.
Krausman said it takes a day and a half to two days to receive lab results from the sampled beaches, during which time “levels typically return to their average.”
“Because, we are working with essentially expired information we are using more of a predictive model to indicate the likelihood of elevated risk at a beach,” Krausman said in an email. “With that said, because indicator bacteria are used to assess risk at a given time, results below the thresholds never indicate a risk of zero.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colleen Fowle, the water program director with Iowa Environmental Council, said the high E. coli levels in the individual tests indicate a public health risk and swimmers should be informed. 
“If people swim in contaminated water with high levels of bacteria, that can cause acute sickness,” Fowle said. “… Especially when children or people with preexisting health conditions go into water bodies that are high in E. coli, they’re more at risk for those health impacts, and if they don’t even know that there was a high test because there’s not an advisory put out, that’s a public health risk.” 
A beach is not closed when it has a “swimming is not recommended” advisory. Beach goers can still swim, but they are informed that water at that beach may carry a higher risk of causing things like diarrhea, nausea or other acute symptoms.
“We’re not talking about closing an entire state park because a beach has an advisory,” Fowle said “We’re just talking about a sign up at the beach, letting people know. And I don’t think that’s too much to ask, if the standard is exceeded, to put a sign up at the beach.” 


How fluid are E. coli levels?
Claire Hruby, an assistant professor of environmental science at Drake University who researches water quality and E. coli, said it’s fairly normal to see individual spikes in E. coli testing. 
Specific events, like a rain storm, can stir up sediment and cause the E. coli levels to jump up, but Hruby said they will “usually come back down once the water settles.” 
Hruby said data points that would concern her are high, single sample tests early on in the season and those that stick around for a couple of weeks. 
An analysis of DNR’s beach monitoring data, archived by Iowa Environmental Council, shows four instances in the first week of 2026 monitoring where E. coli tests were above the one-time maximum standard of 235 CFU at less vulnerable beaches. 
Throughout the monitoring season, some less vulnerable beaches, like Red Haw, Lake Wapello and Springbrook beaches had back-to-back weeks with levels above the standard. No swim advisories were issued, as the geometric means remained below the threshold. 
“In those situations, I think folks deserve to know that there’s a spike,” Hruby said. “But again – we don’t really know what the cause of it is.” 
Hruby said warm temperatures can cause E. coli in her lab to “grow exponentially” and she’s seen samples taken immediately after a rainstorm that have several thousand CFU because of the stirred up sediment. 
Another cause for the spike in bacteria could be runoff from a nearby source.
In the first week of testing, a sample from Lacey-Keosauqua Beach showed 17,000 CFU/100 mL. Another sample from Geode Lake Beach had 10,000 CFU/100 mL. 
Hruby said she’s “not surprised” when there is an E. coli spike in the middle of summer, because the water is warm and the beach has been stirred up with recreation. 
“But early in the year, that to me says there’s probably a source nearby, something that’s running off the surface,” Hruby said. 
An early season or persistent spike, she said, “deserves some further investigation.” But she emphasized that E. coli numbers “don’t on any given day, necessarily indicate risk.” 
“If we had all the resources we needed, we would go visit those systems, figure out what’s going on,” Hruby said. “… I think there’s a lot more we could do to better understand these situations, and I think DNR does a pretty darn good job of protecting public health with the process that they’re using, so I don’t want to sensationalize it.” 
Beach monitoring protocol
DNR began monitoring state park beaches in 2000. While Iowa statute does not require DNR to publish beach advisories, the law specifies E. coli sample maximum and geometric mean standards with the goal of protecting recreational uses of water segments. These are the same standards used by DNR in its beach monitoring criteria.
Fowle said the statute does not mention “vulnerable” waters and it “seems to be a criterion that DNR established on their own.”
Krausman, with DNR, said the beach classification protocol was implemented in 2005 and was developed in partnership with Iowa’s public health department and the University of Iowa’s IIHR. She said the protocol has been “reevaluated on multiple occasions” since then. The beaches themselves are reclassified each year with the latest data. 
Fowle said DNR should retest beaches that have high single sample results to determine if the levels went down, as it’s assumed they would have at “less vulnerable” beaches. 
“Some of these E. coli spikes do last for a short period of time,” Fowle said. “So if the DNR had more staffing and more funding to perform more tests, they could do that; they could go back, they could take multiple samples.” 
Krausman said that logistically, DNR does not have the capacity to retest beaches that come back with a sample above the maximum. 
“Due to the distances between beaches, the location of the labs and the lag time for analysis, it would be nearly impossible to get updated information before recreation starts on the upcoming weekend,” Krausman said. “Retesting would provide more information; however, based on previous experience when the program included resampling, it would likely have a limited impact on advisory posting.” 
2026 swim advisories
In total, 182 swim advisories were posted in the 2026 monitoring season and 27 of the 41 state beaches had a swim advisory posted at least one weekend between Memorial Day and Labor Day. Two beaches, Lake Keomah and Blue Lake, had a special status this year due to low lake levels or renovations and were not monitored throughout the season. 
As an average and excluding the unmonitored beaches, 69% of monitored state beaches had an advisory at least once during the period, though many of the beaches had multiple advisories. 
Lake Darling Beach had the highest number of swim advisories. A swim advisory was posted in 15 of the 16 weeks that were monitored. 
Backbone Beach had the second highest number of swim advisories, with 14 posted throughout the monitoring season. Backbone Beach also had the highest number of swim advisories in 2025, along with Beeds Lake State Park and Pine Lake State Park beaches.
The majority of swim advisories are issued because of E. coli levels. In 2026, 166 instances of the advisories were because of E. coli bacteria levels, which serve as an indicator that other, more harmful bacteria could also be present. 
Ten advisories were due to microcystin, or green-blue algae, levels and six advisories were issued because of both E. coli and microcystin.
The 2026 monitoring season had one additional week compared to 2025, but historical beach monitoring data collected by the Iowa Environmental Council shows the number of advisories issued at state park beaches increased in 2026.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado voters approve measure to ban trans children from playing school sports
description: Colorado voters approved a ballot measure that will ban transgender children from playing school sports.  The Associated Press called the race at 4:12 p.m. Thursday, when 52% of votes were in support of Proposition 134. The AP estimated 92% of votes were counted at that time.  Proposition 134 will add language in state statute to […]
text:
Election workers organize ballot envelopes at the Adams County clerk and recorder's office in Brighton on Tuesday. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Colorado voters approved a ballot measure that will ban transgender children from playing school sports. 
The Associated Press called the race at 4:12 p.m. Thursday, when 52% of votes were in support of Proposition 134. The AP estimated 92% of votes were counted at that time. 
Proposition 134 will add language in state statute to define boys and girls based on physical anatomy, excluding transgender people. The measure will restrict which teams students play on based on their “biological reproductive system.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Protect Kids Colorado, an organization led by prominent anti-LGBTQ+ activist Erin Lee, led the measure. 
“People from every corner of our state gave what they could — time, treasure, courage and conviction — because our children are worth protecting,” Lee said in a statement Wednesday. “And today, we are sending a clear signal to Colorado’s leadership: when elected officials fail or refuse to protect kids, We the People will come together and do it ourselves. Our voices cannot be ignored.”
Measure on surgeries ahead
Proposition 135, another ballot measure Protect Kids Colorado led, would prohibit health care professionals from knowingly performing any surgery on a minor “for the purpose of altering biological sex characteristics. It was ahead with just under 52% of votes as of 5:10 p.m. Thursday, but the AP had yet to call that race. 
Families Not Politics, an issue committee that opposed both ballot measures, acknowledged the success of both measures Thursday. The committee is led by LGBTQ+ advocacy organizations including One Colorado, Rocky Mountain Equality, the Transgender Law Center and Inside Out Youth Services, as well as Planned Parenthood of the Rocky Mountains and Cobalt, an abortion-rights organization. 
“Colorado’s kids will have to live with the consequences of this election — they will face new barriers to medically necessary healthcare and new, expensive barriers and exclusion from full participation in school,” the Families Not Politics campaign said in a statement. “Their families will now have to navigate laws created by a political campaign that turned their children into a statewide controversy.”
Sports teams sponsored by schools or athletic associations will be required to expressly designate teams for men, women or co-ed participation. Schools and their athletic departments will need to adopt policies implementing the requirements of the initiative by Jan. 1.
Opponents say the definitions of sex and gender in Proposition 134 mean a school cannot rely on its own records or a student’s birth certificate to determine a child’s sex. That could result in more than just trans children being subjected to whatever verification process schools select. 
Families Not Politics said it will “exhaust every option” to defend the rights of trans kids and “keep working toward a Colorado where transgender students are allowed to be kids, not political symbols.”
“Opponents of trans equality used fear and confusion to make scapegoats of trans young people and distract from problems families face every day, including skyrocketing costs of living and lack of access to affordable healthcare,” Jax Gonzalez, political director at One Colorado, said in a statement. “These campaigns are meant to exhaust the people forced to defend their families and their futures.”
Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, a Democrat, on Thursday signaled a willingness to back legislative changes to Propositions 134 and 135.
Bruce Parker, executive director of LGBTQ+ advocacy group Rocky Mountain Equality, said the passage of both measures intentionally leave basic question about how they will be enforced unanswered.
“To every transgender kid and family, we’ve got your back,” Parker said in a statement. “This is your home too. This vote doesn’t change that.”
Another ballot initiative from Protect Kids Colorado, Proposition 133, passed with 62% of the vote. It mandates that anyone convicted of child sex trafficking be sentenced to life in prison without parole.

title: State officials stall $44M Alkali Creek Dam request amid eminent domain worries
description:
Lawmakers table request for more money, time after condemnation backers win Hyattville water board majority.
The post State officials stall $44M Alkali Creek Dam request amid eminent domain worries appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Legislators and state water development commissioners Thursday postponed a northern Wyoming water district’s $44 million request to complete the contested Alkali Creek Dam and reservoir.
State officials asked Nowood Watershed Improvement District and five area landowners to further negotiate over necessary easements and avoid the water district’s taking of private property. The Wyoming Legislature’s Select Water Committee and Wyoming Water Development Commission set a Dec. 17 deadline, when the issue will again be on a joint agenda for the two panels.
The joint boards paused the funding request by the Nowood district without dissent. The district through the Wyoming Water Development Office also sought a time extension to complete the project, which is now estimated to cost $103.4 million.
“The project has cost us financially, professionally, and personally.” Michelle Hamilton
Lawmakers and state water commissioners heard emotional testimony from Michelle Hamilton regarding the stress her family has been under as the district has sought to condemn easements across her property near Hyattville. Condemnation is the formal government process for taking private land for public use. 
“The project has cost us financially, professionally, and personally,” she said. Condemnation: “That is not the Wyoming way.”
The prospect of the district taking private property to complete the project appeared to leave a sour taste in state officials mouths. “Our goal is not to tear communities apart,” one member of the water commission said.
The joint meeting in Casper followed a Nov. 3 election in Big Horn and Washakie counties that preserved the rural water board’s majority that favors condemnation of private property near Hyattville.
The Anita Ditch near Hyattville would be enlarged on private property to carry more water to fill the proposed Alkali Creek Reservoir. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
The election put incumbent directors Mitch Vigil and John Joyce on the board, according to an email from Ashley Coenen, district manager of the South Big Horn Conservation District in Greybull. Todd Jones, who is opposed to the district’s plans for eminent domain against five landowners, will replace Martin Mercer on the Nowood board.
Jones garnered the most votes with 182, according to Coenen’s email. Vigil received 180, Joyce 177.
Mercer, who sold the district the land on which the dam and reservoir would sit, received 158 votes and was unseated. Condemnation opponents Doug Hamilton and Tom Shirran, both of whom are targeted in the eminent domain effort, received 152 and 151 votes respectively
The district offered five landowners a total of $97,000 for right-of-way easements on 35 acres, to be adjusted according to appraisals. If the landowners did not accept the offers, condemnation would proceed, according to water district letters sent to the affected property owners.
Affected landowners, all of whom are upstream of the proposed reservoir, questioned the project’s benefits to them and the compensation for rights of way, among other things. Some of the property eyed for condemnation would be inundated by the reservoir. Other rights of way are necessary for the enlargement and maintenance of the Anita Ditch, which would feed the reservoir.
Among the criticisms of the project: The state doled out funds and the reservoir land was bought before the district obtained necessary easements to complete the project.
Conservation districts in Big Horn and Washakie counties in which the water district lies mailed a total of 453 ballots, district managers said. Each registered voter in the district was to receive one vote, and the owner of each taxable parcel in the district was to receive one vote per parcel.
The dam would be an earth embankment 100 feet high and half a mile long. The resulting reservoir would be 312 acres when full, providing late-season irrigation for some 33 families in eight out of 10 years. It would always have at least a 132-acre pool for recreation. Backers say the project would benefit fisheries in the rivers and creeks.

name: California
title: California’s first carbon capture project shot down in court in setback for climate policy
description: A Kern County judge ruled that approval of California’s first operating carbon capture and storage project — a technology the state is counting on to meet its climate goals — violated state environmental law and must be set aside. Judge Marcos Camacho found that environmental review of California Resources Corp.’s TerraVault project, which Kern County […]
text:
A Kern County judge ruled that approval of California’s first operating carbon capture and storage project — a technology the state is counting on to meet its climate goals — violated state environmental law and must be set aside.
Judge Marcos Camacho found that environmental review of California Resources Corp.’s TerraVault project, which Kern County supervisors approved in October 2024, fell short in several ways. Among them, it failed to analyze the industries expected to supply the project with carbon dioxide. 
Because the judgment is not yet final, it’s not clear when CRC must stop injecting carbon dioxide and suspend the facility’s operations. A real-time project tracker on the company’s website indicates that carbon injection continues. 
Carbon TerraVault 1 — the first of at least nine carbon storage projects the company plans around the state — is designed to collect up to 46 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to CRC. The company is injecting carbon deep underground in a Kern County oil field to keep it from warming the atmosphere. The project began operating earlier this year after a lengthy and controversial approval process. 
Kern County policymakers hoped the project — and others that might crop up nearby to send carbon to the reservoirs — would provide a much-needed infusion to the county’s oil-dependent economy as California moves away from fossil fuels. 
More than 15 similar projects are under development in California, according to a map from the Clean Air Task Force. But for many communities, siting those projects can be a hard sell because of uncertainty and mistrust, and some residents near the project have raised concerns about air pollution and carbon dioxide leaking from the reservoirs or the pipelines feeding it.
What the court found
Environmental groups sued over TerraVault 1 in 2024, alleging the project’s environmental impact report did not adequately consider cumulative environmental and greenhouse gas impacts, among other issues, in violation of the California Environmental Quality Act. Camacho sided with them on several counts.
Among the most significant issues was the potential that polluting facilities could crop up near the storage reservoirs. CRC’s environmental assessment laid out eight industries, such as hydrogen, cement and steel manufacturing, that could someday ferry carbon dioxide to the depleted reservoirs in the Elk Hills oil field. But the review didn’t look at how those plants could affect the surrounding area. The project currently stores only carbon dioxide that CRC strips from gas the company draws from its own oil field.
Leaving out those likely sources, Camacho wrote, “infects the informational foundation for the whole Project.”
Michelle Ghafar, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represented two of the plaintiffs, called the ruling “a pretty resounding win.”
“I was really struck by the decision, which basically said that there are errors running throughout the entire document,” she said.
CRC did not respond to emailed questions about whether it will appeal, how long the reapplication process may take, or if it will suspend project operations.Company president and CEO Francisco Leon said in a statement that the order “is a step in the wrong direction for addressing the impacts of climate change and reflects the weaponization of CEQA by a narrow group of special interests.” The company plans to “aggressively pursue all available options to protect and advance this important project,” the statement said.
What comes next
Plaintiffs, including the Central California Environmental Justice Network, Committee for a Better Shafter and the Center for Biological Diversity, will now prepare a proposed judgment for the court’s approval. They say CRC must suspend operations while the company reanalyzes the project’s impacts and the county reconsiders it. That could take several months or several years, according to Ethan Elkind, director of the climate program at UC Berkeley’s Center for Law, Energy & the Environment.
In a regulatory filing, CRC said Camacho’s ruling was not final and its effect on existing operations was uncertain. A spokesperson for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which approves carbon injection permits in California, said the court ruling has no impact on CRC’s federal permit approvals. A Kern County planning department representative did not reply to requests for comment.
Ileana Navarro, a policy associate at the Central California Environmental Justice Network, called the ruling “a breath of fresh air, both figuratively and literally,” for nearby communities.
“You’re asking community members to gamble their communities, neighborhoods, health and safety on projects that don’t really have a track record,” Elkind said. “That’s always difficult.”
The ruling came as voters weighed Proposition 45, which would set deadlines for environmental reviews and lawsuits on certain “essential” projects — a category that explicitly includes carbon capture and storage — and bar courts from ordering approvals rescinded.
Supporters said the measure would speed construction of housing and infrastructure; opponents said it would weaken environmental protections. It was trailing in early returns. 
Ghafar said the ruling shows why the state’s environmental review law remains an important tool. “We need the law now more than ever,” she said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Lawsuit challenges newly passed initiative to limit corporations’ political spending
description: Fewer than 48 hours after Montanans passed a ballot initiative to ban corporations, organizations and “artificial entities” from contributing to candidates, a lawsuit was filed in federal court alleging it violates the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. The Frontier Institute and the Montana Family Foundation, joined by the Montana Republican State Ce[...]
text:
Voter booths at the Helena Civic Center are pictured on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Fewer than 48 hours after Montanans passed a ballot initiative to ban corporations, organizations and “artificial entities” from contributing to candidates, a lawsuit was filed in federal court alleging it violates the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.
The Frontier Institute and the Montana Family Foundation, joined by the Montana Republican State Central Committee, filed suit Wednesday against the state over the law. The new law utilizes a state’s ability to regulate businesses and nonprofits to prevent them from donating to political campaigns. 
The group behind Initiative 194, Transparent Election Initiative, said a lawsuit being filed over the bill was expected. I-194 passed with 65% of voters in support and will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027. 
TEI said in a press release the groups bringing the lawsuit were “turning to the courts to protect the political spending powers of corporations and other special interests over the will of Montana voters.”
The Frontier Institute is a public policy think tank that often pushes for conservative causes. The Montana Family Foundation is a conservative nonprofit organization focusing on traditional definitions of family and marriage, and lobbies for related bills.
The legal effort is also being supported by the Institute for Free Speech, an organization that has pushed for reducing limits on political spending, saying it’s an infringement of the First Amendment.
The lawsuit was filed in Federal District Court in Helena, and Frontier Institute President Kendall Cotton said he hopes the suit over what’s also known as the “Montana Plan” will move quickly.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs filed in federal court over state district court because they felt it dealt with the First Amendment, the U.S. Constitution and had “federal implications,” Cotton said.
“This is a case that potentially could go to the U.S. Supreme Court,” he added.
He also said he too thinks there’s an issue with political spending in Montana, but the new law is too broad. Cotton said opposition to the Montana Plan has been painted unfairly. 
“We think this infringes on our rights to operate as an organization to advance our mission to be able to educate people about the merits of major policy proposals that are impacting the state,” Cotton said. 
There’s worry, Cotton said, that a company or nonprofit could “completely lose our legal status for simply posting a normal opinion about a local property tax levy or a ballot measure on our Facebook. We think that’s wrong.”
In a press release, Matthew Cochenour, an attorney for TEI and a former Montana acting solicitor general, said they were “confident” in their legal theory.
“This lawsuit is part of a much larger legal campaign to try and silence the will of the people,” said Jeff Mangan, founder of TEI, in a press release. “There will be hearings, decisions and appeals along the way, but no single ruling will determine the future of this movement. Every state that adopts this approach creates another opportunity to make the case.”
The Montana Republican State Central Committee also is one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit and said a newsletter the organization sends out could be banned under the new state law.
The groups challenging the new law say its reach could go far beyond political advertisements and into publishing research and communicating with voters. A release from the Institute of Free Speech, the legal organization that wrote the suit, says the consequences from the law could threaten the organizations’ ability to exist in the state.
“Montana cannot require people to surrender their First Amendment rights simply because they join together to make their voices heard,” said Owen Yeates, an attorney with the free speech organization, in a press release. “This law attempts to accomplish indirectly what the Constitution expressly forbids: Silencing organizations that engage in political advocacy. Calling censorship a restriction on corporate privileges doesn’t make it constitutional.”
