name: Michigan Advance
title: Puri elected House Speaker as Democrats prepare to take control of state government
description: State Rep. Ranjeev Puri of Canton will lead Michigan’s newly elected Democratic House majority as speaker in January, while Republicans chose state Rep. Tom Kunse of Clare to lead their caucus in the minority, marking a new chapter for both parties as Democrats prepare to take control of state government. The respective caucuses in the […]
text:
State Rep. Ranjeev Puri of Canton will lead Michigan's newly elected Democratic House majority as speaker in January, while Republicans chose state Rep. Tom Kunse of Clare to lead their caucus in the minority, marking a new chapter for both parties as Democrats prepare to take control of state government.State Rep. Ranjeev Puri of Canton will lead Michigan’s newly elected Democratic House majority as speaker in January, while Republicans chose state Rep. Tom Kunse of Clare to lead their caucus in the minority, marking a new chapter for both parties as Democrats prepare to take control of state government.
The respective caucuses in the House held their leadership votes on Thursday following a short session day where attendance was taken but no other voting occurred — aside from the leadership elections taking place behind closed doors.
Puri spoke to members of the capitol press corps outside the chamber, and described the last two years as House minority leader as “the most grueling two years of my life.” 
His caucus retaking control of the House was the result, Puri said, of traveling around the state and making the case that a change was needed in state government. 
Those efforts bore fruit in Tuesday’s midterm election, giving Puri and his colleagues what he called “a resounding mandate” for more “stable leadership and prioritizing the needs of Michigan.”
“We’re ready to do that,” Puri said, adding that he was willing to work with Kunse and anyone, really, who is willing to work with his caucus.
Still, he reflected on his past relationship with current House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), as well as the slings and arrows that he had to dodge from the brash and aggressive style of Hall’s leadership.
“The last two years have been led with political divisiveness, and every aspect of it seemed to be on how we could own the other side or win a political point,” Puri said. “In my opinion, that’s not how this institution was designed to run, and so the House Democrats are focused on ‘Team Michigan’ and making sure that we’re making the lives of everyday Michiganders easier and better.”
Michigan House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to members of the news media on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, outside of the House chamber in Lansing, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Puri added that if they had partners on the other side of the aisle, who are willing to put politics aside, they can move forward on that goal.
“The needs of Michigan are transformative, and we need to think about how we tackle systemic issues that are plaguing our state,” he said. “Median household incomes are lagging behind some of our peer states. We still are not seeing population growth in the way that we want. So I’m hoping, with the size of the majority, that we’re able to tackle real issues.”
One thing that Puri doesn’t want to spend time on is litigating culture war issues like “who’s playing in what sport, or who’s going to use which restroom.”
“I’m hopeful that there was some semblance of understanding with the leadership change in the other caucus that maybe that approach wasn’t working,” he said.
In that vein, Puri said he also hoped that the election brought a new set of core values to the House, and that it would have the potential to move the state’s politics “in a direction that is more fair.”
In choosing Kunse, House GOP will try a new approach to working with Dems
Although all eyes were on the Democrats after they secured another government trifecta in the 2026 elections — nabbing the governor’s office, the other two executive branch offices, control of the Legislature and near complete control of the Michigan Supreme Court — the leadership battle on the GOP side of the chamber was of high import.
Hall led the caucus through its minority leader position during the 2023-24 session, in which the Democrats also held a government trifecta, and into the 2025-26 session, where he served at top of the caucus as speaker.
Hall had said before the elections that his caucus would work hard to retain its majority in the House, even if the Senate Democrats were able to retain theirs, and that he could do that all in the face of a highly-favorable Democratic year.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A blue wave, however, swept the nation and Michigan on Tuesday, and that pushed out several key members of the GOP House caucus. Hall faced a serious challenge for his own seat, but prevailed, albeit narrowly, against House District 42 Democratic nominee Nick Rowe, winning only by 3.2 percentage points.
While Republicans chose to move on from Hall’s leadership on Thursday, the speaker will be remembered for his brash and aggressive approach to commanding power in the House, as he routinely mocked his House Democratic colleagues from the bully pulpit of his own press conferences. 
Hall also dared Democrats to blink on all manner of policy points and budget fights over his two years of leading the caucus. In some respects, Hall was successful in doing the latter, especially during the 2025 budget fight.
Kunse thanked Hall for his leadership over the last few years, but said he would do things a bit differently.
“We’re going to do better, and what we’re going to do is show the state of Michigan, number one, that we care,” Kunse said. “We understand that things are expensive, and we understand that education needs to be addressed.”
State Rep. Tom Kunse (R-Clare) speaks to members of the capitol press corps after being an elected Michigan House minority leader on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Lansing, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Kunse said Hall did some good things for the caucus and that there were indeed times when the GOP needed to stand up and say, “No, this is bad policy.”
“I commend him on that,” Kunse said, while also making it clear that he would not blame Hall or any other GOP member for the loss of 11 seats in the 2026 election. “I have nothing but respect for Matt Hall.”
In a break from Hall’s harsh rhetoric, Kunse said his minority leadership in the House would commence with a guiding ethos that “Democrats are not the enemy.”
“Being 45th in education is the enemy,” Kunse added. “Affordability is the issue. There are things that we’re going to work with Democrats on, and there are some things we’re going to have differences on. But what I’m excited about with the team is the professionalism.”
There were many times when Hall used his position as speaker to go after Puri, as well as Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, in a head-on and sometimes personal way. 
Michigan House speaker refuses to reinstate Democratic legislator to Appropriations Committee role

Kunse said the media and the residents of the state won’t be seeing or reading about “our differences on Facebook because we’re going to go into the office and we’re going to say, ‘Listen, we’re not there today, we have a difference of opinion on this.’”
On the House losing its majority, Kunse recognized that they “lost some good people,” but also that “politics is a blood sport.”
“Some of my friends aren’t here anymore,” Kunse said. “I’m sad, I’m angry. I don’t think finding blame is what’s going to be productive. Gov. Snyder had ‘positive, relentless action,’ right? I’m totally stealing that from him. To me, that’s better. Let’s move forward. What are we going to do to get this problem solved? What are we going to do to get back the majority? I don’t have any interest in assigning blame.”
Puri, Kunse give an early look into the priorities of both caucuses
The respective leaders in the House said they are still getting their ducks in a row, meeting their new members and devising battle plans for the road ahead.
Puri’s majority caucus will focus its efforts this year on affordability, household incomes, population growth and the systemic issues that appear to be holding Michigan back. Puri raised utility costs as an area of concern regarding affordability.
Whereas the previous 2023-24 Democratic trifecta that had pushed a large amount of legislation swiftly, Puri said Thursday that “the question is, how do you measure productivity?” 
“I think at times, sometimes it’s on the quantity of how many public acts have been passed, but for me, it’s the impact of the bills that we do,” he said. “There are a number of systemic issues that we can be thinking about and deliberating on what to do.”
Kunse was asked the same question, and landed on it in the same way that Puri did — those plans will come with time.
“Our team has been together for 33 minutes,” Kunse said. “We are working on that. Do I have a detailed plan? No, but I can tell you that education is not acceptable where it’s at. We need to talk about healthcare. The pricing of healthcare is not acceptable. I can’t tell you how we’re going to do it, but I can tell you that these are things that we want to do.”
Detroit Caucus elects new executive board members
New members of the House Detroit Caucus were also elected on Thursday. State Rep. Stephanie Young will again serve as the caucus chair, and state Rep. Tonya Myers Phillips will serve as its vice chair. 
“We are experiencing the dangerous policies from the White House through cuts to Medicaid and SNAP and exorbitant grocery and gasoline prices,” Young said in a statement. “My colleagues and I are laser focused on policies to reverse these devastating decisions and usher in a better Detroit for all of us. I am especially grateful for the team of Detroiters assembled to lead the Detroit Caucus and value our collective voice for positive change over the next two years.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina school facility funding needs climb 37% to nearly $18 billion
description: North Carolina is seeing a steep jump in what it needs to spend on its public school facilities, according to a new report by the state Department of Public Instruction. A newly passed constitutional amendment could make that more difficult.   The 2025–26 statewide facility needs survey, which Vice Chairman Alan Duncan said was “anxiously awaited,” […]
text:
This week the State Board of Education released a new report that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems. (Image: Adobe Stock)North Carolina is seeing a steep jump in what it needs to spend on its public school facilities, according to a new report by the state Department of Public Instruction. A newly passed constitutional amendment could make that more difficult.  
The 2025–26 statewide facility needs survey, which Vice Chairman Alan Duncan said was “anxiously awaited,” outlined nearly $18 billion in projected public school facility needs across North Carolina over the next five years — a 37% increase from the state’s previous survey in 2020–21.
The assessment, conducted every five years, gives state education officials a snapshot of upcoming construction and renovation projects, while establishing a baseline to track how capital demands have grown across all 115 school districts.
Beyond the five-year window, the survey estimates another $14.78 billion in facility needs for years six through 10, bringing total projected needs over the decade to nearly $33 billion.
“Where is the money going to come from?” Duncan asked during the board meeting. 
The report estimates that districts will need roughly $6.2 billion to construct new schools. Inflation has driven up construction costs, with baseline costs for new school construction reaching $350 per square foot in the latest assessment, up from $250 in 2020–21. The $350 figure does not cover furniture, technology, or equipment. 
However, the larger share of projected spending is for renovations, rather than new construction. The report estimates renovation needs will cost  nearly $9.8 billion, a 77% increase from the previous survey. “More renovations-focused is what we’re seeing in the survey,” said Nathan Maune, director of the Department of Public Instruction’s Office of School Facilities, who presented the report’s findings to the board Wednesday. 
North Carolina seeks $40 million to help schools cover rising fuel costs

Local districts reported plans for renovation projects at more than 1,400 schools across 93 of North Carolina’s 115 school systems. Deferred maintenance and repairs, building code and life-safety upgrades, and HVAC improvements accounted for about 80% of all planned work, according to the presentation. 
School districts currently operate more than 6,200 buildings across 2,451 schools. Roughly 67% of those facilities are more than 30 years old, while 29% are more than 60 years old.
The massive renovation estimate prompted Duncan to question whether state and local officials should reassess how they fund work on older buildings. 
“We don’t do this as a state, but you need to take a step back and look at, are renovations really making sense?” he said. “If it’s going up at a 76% rate, and we’re putting $9 billion in renovation and less than that in new schools, that’s a fair question to ask.” 
Funding for these projects relied on a mix of state and local sources over the past five fiscal years. The state provided roughly $2.83 billion through three lottery-funded capital programs between fiscal years 2021–22 and 2025–26, while voters in eight counties authorized $5.88 billion in local school bonds. 
Most of North Carolina’s 100 counties, however, have not passed school construction bonds, leaving rural and lower-wealth districts with limited ways to raise capital locally, Duncan noted. 
He raised concerns over whether a constitutional amendment approved by voters this week could restrict local government property tax revenue typically tapped for school bonds, though the exact financial impacts of the amendment will depend on how lawmakers implement the measure. 
“I think this report highlights, in many ways, the crossroads we find ourselves at,” Duncan said. “And how we respond to that will speak volumes about what we’re saying about the future of our children in this state.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA governor meets with NBA commissioner amid expansion doubts
description: Washington’s governor met again with NBA Commissioner Adam Silver on Thursday to push the case for the return of the Seattle SuperSonics as league expansion here remains uncertain. Brionna Aho, a spokesperson for Gov. Bob Ferguson, described the meeting as “another good conversation” with Silver. She said Ferguson “appreciates the ongoing dialogue about the [...]
text:
A Seattle Supersonics fan dressed as Bigfoot is seen during the game between the Gonzaga Bulldogs and the Kentucky Wildcats at Climate Pledge Arena on Dec. 7, 2024 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images)Washington’s governor met again with NBA Commissioner Adam Silver on Thursday to push the case for the return of the Seattle SuperSonics as league expansion here remains uncertain.
Brionna Aho, a spokesperson for Gov. Bob Ferguson, described the meeting as “another good conversation” with Silver. She said Ferguson “appreciates the ongoing dialogue about the potential for NBA expansion in Seattle,” and is “committed to bringing the Sonics home.”
Ferguson’s office reached out to set the virtual 2 p.m. meeting.
This is the third meeting between Ferguson and Silver this year. They met in February and March ahead of the league’s Board of Governors voting to formally open expansion talks with Las Vegas and Seattle, paving the way for a decision expected by year’s end. 
Fans, who have long salivated for the return of the Sonics, rejoiced. 
At the same time, the news out of NBA HQ in recent weeks hasn’t been encouraging. 
For one, the expansion fee may cost more than earlier estimates. The Las Vegas franchise could cost $10 billion, split among the owners of the 30 other teams. Seattle isn’t expected to be able to fetch as much. Seattle Kraken owner Samantha Holloway is the shoo-in to lead the ownership group for a new NBA franchise. 
Holloway is the obvious choice since her company owns Climate Pledge Arena. A private equity-backed group partnering with the Tulalip Tribes has also come forward, but a team based 40 miles north of Seattle could present pitfalls. Meanwhile, Las Vegas has multiple bidders. The losers could join Holloway in Seattle.
Team valuations have risen this year following the mega-sales of the Los Angeles Lakers and Boston Celtics
NBA owners worry the lower, but still massive, price tag for a Seattle expansion team wouldn’t deliver enough bang for their buck, Bloomberg reported Wednesday. ESPN reported last month that while Silver was a “full-go” on Las Vegas, the league didn’t seem to be happy with the Seattle bids. Some believe league leaders are saber-rattling to drive up the cost of the Seattle team.
Silver has reiterated that the decision at the end of 2026 could deliver only one new team or none at all. The league is planning for the expansion team(s) to start competing in the 2028-29 seasons.
Ahead of the meeting, Ferguson told reporters Wednesday he remains optimistic about the NBA’s return to Seattle.
“I follow the same news that you do about what’s going on with Las Vegas and Seattle,” he said. “So I don’t pretend to have a crystal ball on that and those conversations going on with NBA owners.
“Our bid is strong. We have the right arena. I mean, we check each and every box that the NBA could possibly hope to have for someone bidding for a new team,” the governor continued.
Ferguson has repeatedly emphasized his love of the Sonics since childhood in his push to return a team here. He even mentioned his desire to see the team return in his State of the State address to the Legislature this year.
“As the governor has made clear many times, he’s a diehard Sonics fan from childhood,” Aho said in an email. “He grew up attending Sonics games and the Lenny Wilkens Basketball Camp.”
Seattle has been without professional men’s basketball for nearly two decades, dating back to when Starbucks executive Howard Schultz sold the team, and new owner Clay Bennett shipped it to Oklahoma City to become the Thunder. Seattle came close to getting the Sacramento Kings to move north in 2013, but the plans fell through.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Incoming House speaker recreates committee to eye public corruption
description: House speaker-designate Samuel Garrison Thursday night sent a memo to members announcing two new House standing committees and re-establishment of a third committee focused on public corruption. The memo didn’t include details of who would chair the panels or their membership. Unlike his contemporary, Senate President-designate Jim Boyd, Garrison, a Republic[...]
text:
Front of the Florida Capitol Building, taken on April 25, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)House speaker-designate Samuel Garrison Thursday night sent a memo to members announcing two new House standing committees and re-establishment of a third committee focused on public corruption.
The memo didn’t include details of who would chair the panels or their membership. Unlike his contemporary, Senate President-designate Jim Boyd, Garrison, a Republican from Fleming Island, did not release the names of the House members who would control key committees.
“I am committed to making committee time meaningful. I want you to dig into ideas, hear from the public, and truly study your colleagues’ bills, because behind every bill, every policy, and every budget item are people — our people,” Garrison said in the memo.
Republican House Speaker-designate Sam Garrison. (Via Florida House of Representatives)
“With those goals in mind, we kept most of the current structure and made changes to focus on long-term policy and fiscal impacts, coordination, and emerging issues to help us address problems that extend beyond a single session, term, or time in Tallahassee.”
The Public Integrity Committee Garrison plans is similar to the Public Integrity & Elections Committee, part of the House structure under Chris Sprowls, speaker between  2020 and 2022.
In addition to focusing on public corruption, Garrison said, the panel will look at lobbying, financial disclosure, and conflicts of interest.
The Hope Florida scandal was uncovered in part by the House Health Care Budget Subcommittee, which generally focuses on creating the health care portion of the annual state budget and considers substantive healthcare bills that will require public spending.
The Public Integrity Committee and the other two new legislative panels Garrison announced are all “standing” committees. Standing committees in the House can consider and introduce legislation. By contrast, a “select” committee is created to address a specific task, and whether it can introduce legislation or vote on legislation is tied to the action that created it.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Garrison has created a Policy & Strategy Committee to address issues that transcend one policy area. “Its jurisdiction includes long-range planning and fiscal stability, Garrison said in the memo. 
“I want the House to consider where Florida needs to be in five or 10 or 20 years and what steps we should take now to get there. This committee is where we will do that work.”
The third new standing committee is the Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee. It replaces the Information Technology Budget & Policy Subcommittee created by former Speaker Danny Perez.
“The committee will focus on state technology governance and modernization because we need agencies to be capable of implementing the laws we write. It will also cover artificial  intelligence and emerging technologies, cybersecurity, digital privacy, data governance, and critical  infrastructure security,” the memo noted. 
And, unlike, the committee it’s replacing, the Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee will focus only on policy. Spending decisions, Garrison said in the memo, will be considered by the full Appropriations Committee and its subcommittees.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah House Democrat gains slip slightly as 2 races flip, but GOP still pacing to lose 15 seats
description: As more votes are tallied in Utah’s legislative races, two House races have flipped, putting a few Republican candidates ahead of Democrats that were in the lead on election night.  In the race for Summit and Wasatch counties’ House District 59, Republican Luke Searle is now leading Democrat Celeste Johnson for the open seat being […]
text:
Rep. Tiara Auxier, R-Morgan, talks to other lawmakers on the House floor at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Feb. 19, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)As more votes are tallied in Utah’s legislative races, two House races have flipped, putting a few Republican candidates ahead of Democrats that were in the lead on election night. 
In the race for Summit and Wasatch counties’ House District 59, Republican Luke Searle is now leading Democrat Celeste Johnson for the open seat being vacated by Republican Rep. Mike Kohler, who did not run for reelection. 
‘Blue tsunami’ hits Utah: House Republicans on pace to lose 17 seats, breaking supermajority

Though Searle trailed Johnson on election night, he’s now leading with nearly 51.5% of the vote to Johnson’s 48.5% — ahead by 465 votes — according to election results as of Thursday.
The race for House District 4, representing Morgan, Rich and Summit county areas, also flipped. 
Republican incumbent Rep. Tiara Auxier has pulled ahead of Democrat Zane Woolstenhulme. Auxier had 50.55% of the vote to Woolstenhulme’s 49.45% — a margin of just 141 votes. 
Those races — and several others — remain too close to call with thousands of votes left to be tallied and included in results. Election results are not final until the county and state canvass two weeks after the election. 
If Republicans keep those flipped leads, they’ll chip slightly at Democrats’ projected gains, but the House GOP’s supermajority is still on track to be broken. On election night, 15 Democrats and two unaffiliated candidates were ahead in 17 House races. Now Republicans are down in 15. 
Sen. Emily Buss, a member of the Forward Party of Utah from Eagle Mountain, listens on the Senate floor of the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City. (Courtesy of the Utah Senate)
Utah Forward Party legislator loses tight lead to Republican
In the Senate, another race with razor-thin margins has flipped back and forth several times. Though she was initially in the lead on election night, incumbent Sen. Emily Buss — the Forward Party’s only state legislator — is now trailing her Republican challenger Brooks Benson.
Benson had 50.36% of the vote to Buss’ 49.64% as of Thursday morning — a 169 vote margin. 
Senate Democrats are still pacing to pick up two seats from Republicans. Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore is trailing Democrat Shana Anderson by more than 13 percentage points in the Senate District 11 race, and Democrat “CJ” Christina Hernandez is leading Republican Jill Koford by more than 11 percentage points for Senate District 5. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
If Benson’s lead over Buss holds, Senate Republicans will lose only one seat rather than two since Buss is the Legislature’s only third-party incumbent.
Tight races
Several other legislative races remain tight, but haven’t flipped as of Thursday. They include: 
House District 8: Republican Rep. Jason Kyle, R-Huntsville, was still trailing Democrat Kim James, who had 49.4% (7,208 votes) to Kyle’s 46.43% (6,774 votes) — a margin of 434. Forward Party candidate Libby Shelton had 4.17% (609 votes). 
House District 11: Republican Rep. Katy Hall, R-Ogden, remained ahead of Democrat Dave Calder. Hall had 51.58% (5,520 votes) to Calder’s 48.42% (5,182 votes) — a margin of 338 votes. 
House District 16: Republican Bob Stevenson was still leading Democrat Abigail Treasure with 51.5% (5,523 votes) to Treasure’s 48.5% (5,202 votes) — a margin of 321. 
House District 20: Democrat Phil Graves continued to lead Republican incumbent Rep. Melissa Ballard. Graves had 51.83% (5,470 votes) to Ballard’s 48.17% (5,084) — a margin of 386 votes. 
House District 45: Republican incumbent Rep. Tracy Miller still led Democrat Rod Moser, 52.06% (5,489 votes) to 47.94% (5,055 votes) — a margin of 434.
House District 48: Democrat Benyde Walker continued to lead Republican incumbent Rep. Jake Hunsaker with 52.02% (4,807 votes) to 47.98% (4,433 votes) — a margin of 374.
House District 49: Republican incumbent Rep. Candice Pierucci kept her lead over Democrat Lillian Bowles, 51.37% (4,115 votes) to 48.63% (3,896 votes) — a margin of 219 votes. 
House District 61: Republican Lisa Shepherd continued to lead Democrat Alan Jimenez with 49.32% (2,929 votes) to Jimenez’s 47.5% (2,821 votes) — a margin of 108 votes. Constitution candidate Jennifer Doud had 3.18% (189 votes).

name: Source New Mexico
title: New analyses contend New Mexico US Sen. Heinrich’s permitting bill would cut emissions, costs
description: New analyses of a permitting reform bill U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) has championed say that its provisions would reduce emissions and costs to ratepayers, as well as recover billions of dollars from data center developers.
text:
Newly released analyses of a permitting reform bill sponsored by U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), pictured above pitching the bill in Albuquerque to solar energy developers Oct. 12, 2026, estimate the provisions it contains will cut emissions and reduce household electrical costs. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New analyses of a permitting reform bill U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) has championed say that its provisions would reduce emissions and costs to ratepayers, as well as recover billions of dollars from data center developers. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The analyses, released separately in recent days by four independent nonprofit and industry groups, including the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, modeled what would happen to energy transmission and green energy production with and without Heinrich’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in effect through 2040. 
They found that the bill would lower household electricity bills by $50 to $78 annually by 2040. Moreover, it would reduce power sector emissions by about 20%, which would subsequently help prevent approximately 6,700 deaths and save $54 billion in cumulative public health costs.
Heinrich, the ranking member of the U.S. Senate’s Energy and Natural Resources Committee, announced the proposal along with Chair U.S. Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and other bipartisan senators in recent weeks. He has touted the bill as a way to reform the federal permit review process to reduce delays and give renewable energy developers more certainty and quicker reviews, as well as a way to ensure data center developers don’t pass energy costs onto nearby households. 
The bill has received backlash from tribal and environmentalist groups concerned it will fast-track fossil fuel production and reduce tribal input on sensitive developments. Last week, protesters from the YUCCA Alliance railed against the bill outside Heinrich’s downtown Albuquerque office.
But Heinrich has maintained the bill will prevent vital carbon-free energy and transmission projects from facing years of regulatory delays. His office has pointed to the analyses as proof the bill is necessary to achieve climate goals.
“Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years,” Heinrich said in a statement touting the outside reviews. “These independent analyses show exactly what we stand to gain by fixing our broken permitting system: lower electricity bills, cleaner air, healthier communities, and more reliable energy infrastructure.”
One of those reviews, released Thursday by the nonpartisan Center for Climate and Energy Solutions thinktank, found that passing the bill would reduce annual electricity bills by $2.5 billion by 2035, partially by reducing the queue that power plants, energy storage facilities and energy storage projects idle in before getting approval to connect to the grid. 
“It takes years for projects to connect to the grid and be able to deliver that energy,” the center’s president,  Nat Keohane, said during a virtual news conference. “When demand is growing and supply can’t keep up, costs go up.”
A separate analysis from Grid Strategies, a power sector consulting firm, evaluated provisions in the 417-page bill related to data centers. The bill would require electrical utilities to impose additional costs on data centers, funding that utilities would then use to reduce transmission costs to ratepayers. 
New Mexico students walk out of classes to protest data centers, US Sen. Heinrich’s permitting bill

In total, Grid Strategies estimates that data centers would pay $55 billion to utilities over the next decade if the bill goes into effect, a figure that represents an additional $35 billion more than they would pay under existing policy.
Heinrich and his cosponsors have announced they intend to try to shepherd the bill through both chambers of Congress before the next session begins next year. U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) announced last week that she does not support the bill as written. 
The bill sponsors’ push to pass the bill in 2026 has drawn additional criticism from the bill’s skeptics, who argue Democrats’ new majorities in  the U.S. Senate and U.S. House in Tuesday’s election means a better bill can be achieved.
Moreover, in January, Heinrich may take over as chair of the U.S. Senate’s Energy and Natural Resources Committee, giving him even more power over the bill’s provisions. 
However, in an emailed statement Thursday provided to Source NM, Heinrich said he still thinks the climate and country can’t wait any longer to pass the permitting reform bill. He said if he becomes committee chair that his priorities will be reducing energy costs for New Mexicans and protecting public lands, including in Chaco Canyon and the Pecos River. 
“But our priority right now is passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which would make it illegal for data centers to shift the costs of their grid upgrades and infrastructure onto consumers,” he said. “We’ve been working toward permitting reform for the better part of a decade, and this is the closest we’ve come to getting something signed into law. I’m not going to wait, and I’ll negotiate in good faith, whether I’m the Chair or the Ranking Member.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: House Democrats stick with Fecteau as speaker, select Rana as new assistant leader
description: The bolstered Democratic majority of the Maine House of Representatives re-selected Ryan Fecteau of Biddeford to serve as speaker on Thursday.  The Democratic caucus also kept Rep. Matt Moonen of Portland as majority leader. With former Assistant Majority Leader Rep. Lori Gramlich termed out, Democrats selected Rep. Ambureen Rana of Bangor to assume the role[...]
text:
Maine House Speaker Ryan Fecteau speaks at the No Kings rally in Saco, Maine. Oct. 18, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)The bolstered Democratic majority of the Maine House of Representatives re-selected Ryan Fecteau of Biddeford to serve as speaker on Thursday. 
The Democratic caucus also kept Rep. Matt Moonen of Portland as majority leader. With former Assistant Majority Leader Rep. Lori Gramlich termed out, Democrats selected Rep. Ambureen Rana of Bangor to assume the role. 
The latter was the only contested position when Democrats met behind closed doors in Augusta to decide on their leadership team, though formal votes are held when the Legislature convenes to get sworn in on Dec. 2. Senate Democrats are expected to make their leadership decisions on Friday, as are House and Senate Republicans. 
In a statement, Fecteau said he’s “honored by the continued trust my colleagues have placed in me to lead House Democrats in the 133rd Legislature.”
“Together, we will work steadfast to address the challenges we face – from healthcare to childcare to affordable housing to energy costs – so that every family in Maine can get ahead, not just get by,” he continued.
“As I have done throughout my career, I will continue to work across the aisle, building trust and making sure that we respect people’s time, work productively, and most importantly, deliver results for Maine people.”
First elected to the House in 2014, Fecteau became the first openly gay speaker and one of the youngest to hold the leadership position at age 28 when he assumed the role in 2020. His caucus selected him as speaker again in 2024, when he returned to the House after being term-limited in 2022.
The speaker presides over chamber sessions, appoints all committee members and committee chairs in conjunction with the Maine Senate president and oversees the flow of legislation, among other responsibilities.  
Moonen, a leader in progressive politics in the state, is entering his seventh non-consecutive term in the House. He served as the House majority leader during the 129th Legislature and in the most recent 132nd Legislature, a role in which he represents the party on the chamber floor and helps direct legislative priorities and debate. 
Finishing her second term in the House, Rana previously served on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, which sets the state budget. Before becoming a legislator, Rana worked with the Health Equity Alliance and as a community organizer with Maine Equal Justice.
With each of these leadership positions also comes a seat on the Legislative Council, which is responsible for the overall management of the legislative branch and has authority over whether to approve after deadline bills. 
After Tuesday’s election, Democrats have at least 85 seats in the 151-member House, up from 76 last session, based on races called by The Associated Press so far.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Supporters of Colorado’s graduated income tax measure declare victory
description: With their narrow lead holding steady with an estimated 90% of the statewide vote counted, proponents of a ballot measure to establish a graduated income tax system in Colorado declared victory on Thursday, heralding the most seismic shift in state fiscal policy in decades. Amendment 87 would remove the Colorado constitution’s flat-tax requirement and establ[...]
text:
Supporters of Amendment 87, a graduated income tax measure, celebrated in Denver's La Raza Park on Thursday, as election results showed the measure on track to be narrowly approved by voters. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)With their narrow lead holding steady with an estimated 90% of the statewide vote counted, proponents of a ballot measure to establish a graduated income tax system in Colorado declared victory on Thursday, heralding the most seismic shift in state fiscal policy in decades.
Amendment 87 would remove the Colorado constitution’s flat-tax requirement and establish a tiered system under which higher earners pay higher marginal income tax rates. With more than 2.4 million ballots counted as of 4 p.m. Thursday, the measure’s lead stood at 1.5 percentage points, a slight increase since late on election night, and many of the ballots remaining to be counted are in populous Front Range counties where the measure has been running ahead.
Unlike other constitutional amendments on the ballot this year, because it only repeals, and does not add, constitutional language, it needs only a simple majority to pass. Its tiered income tax structure would be added to state statute.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This is a huge day for Colorado,” said Chris deGruy Kennedy, president of the liberal Bell Policy Center and one of the leaders of the campaign in support of the measure. “It’s a signal by voters that we are fundamentally changing the direction of how we are going to make sure Colorado’s economy supports every hardworking person, every older adult, every child and everyone in between.”
Supporters of the Protect Colorado’s Future Coalition, who included many progressive lawmakers at the state Capitol, said the new revenue will put an end to years of painful cuts, including those forced on the state by President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans’ 2025 package of tax and spending cuts. Kathy White said the GOP-backed law had delivered a “body blow to our state budget.”
“We are looking at next year cutting $600 million out of Medicaid alone,” said White, speaking at a press conference held by proponents at Denver’s La Raza Park. “We have a $1.6 billion budget deficit, on the back of a $1 billion budget deficit last year, and the year before that. And that stops today.”
Sweeping set of changes
Amendment 87 proposes to hike corporate and individual income tax rates to 7.4% for income above $500,000 and gradually increase the rate to 8.4% for income above $1 million. Those higher rates would apply to the top 3% of earners, while the 97% of Coloradans who earn less than $500,000 per year would see a slight income tax reduction. A fiscal analysis by nonpartisan state legislative staff estimated that the measure would raise $2 billion in additional revenue for the state by the 2027-28 fiscal year.
Together with Proposition NN — a measure also approved by voters this year to raise the annual revenue growth cap established by the state constitution’s Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights — Amendment 87 marks the most sweeping set of changes to Colorado tax policy since voters passed TABOR in 1992.
In the decades since, advocates for public education, healthcare and other social spending programs have struggled to surmount TABOR’s strict anti-tax requirements, including its revenue cap and its requirement that all tax increases be approved at the ballot box. Two previous attempts to pass a progressive income tax, 2013’s Amendment 66 and 2018’s Amendment 73, were rejected by voters.
Lisa Weil, executive director of advocacy group Great Education Colorado, was involved in both efforts, and said Thursday that Amendment 87 will allow Colorado to “turn the page” on an era of scarce public funding. She applauded the years of organizing that preceded Protect Colorado’s Future Coalition’s victory.
“It may look like stars aligned, and suddenly this happened in Colorado,” Weil said. “That is not how it works. Stars do not align by themselves — it requires shoving. And there are some incredible star-shovers in this group.”
Chris Kennedy, center, president of the Bell Policy Center, spoke as Amendment 87 supporters declared victory at a press conference in Denver’s La Raza Park on Thursday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Conservative opposition
To win, proponents of Amendment 87 needed to overcome a powerful, deep-pocketed network of Colorado conservative policy advocates, who have increasingly prized TABOR and the ballot initiative process as one of their last remaining checks on a state government dominated over the last decade by Democrats.
Led by Advance Colorado, a “dark money” nonprofit that does not disclose its donors, opponents sought to block Amendment 87 at every possible stage, including challenging it at the state’s Title Board and suing the secretary of state to remove the amendment from the ballot in a case that was decided just days before Election Day.
Conservative groups spent millions on an opposition campaign that blasted Amendment 87 and Proposition NN as multibillion-dollar “blank checks” for state government, and spread the false claim — repeated by Democratic Gov. Jared Polis, who also opposed the measure — that Amendment 87 would eliminate deductions for Social Security income and other state tax breaks.
Finally, Advance Colorado backed a countermeasure, Proposition 136, which aimed to block Amendment 87 by capping income tax rates at their current level of 4.4%. The measure was on track Thursday to lose by a 5-point margin.
Advance Colorado didn’t respond to a request for comment.
“Whenever we organize, we turn out. Whenever we turn out, we win,” said Christina Soliz, executive director of New Era Colorado and another campaign co-chair. “The volunteers, the organizations who were part of this, who were on the ground since Day 1, making sure this was a truly people-powered measure, deserve this win today.”
The Protect Colorado’s Future Coalition relied on a combination of volunteers and paid canvassers to collect the signatures necessary to qualify a constitutional amendment for the ballot, including signatures equal to 2% of the registered voters in each of Colorado’s 35 state Senate districts. As of Oct. 28, the campaign had reported $3 million in contributions from donors including the Bell Policy Center, the Colorado Fiscal Institute and philanthropist Merle Chambers.
Unlike amendments 66 and 73, this year’s progressive income tax campaign did not receive support from the Colorado Education Association, which instead backed Proposition NN, referred to the ballot by Democratic majorities in the Legislature. Proposition NN was on track Thursday to pass by a nearly 12-point margin after a $10 million campaign overwhelmingly funded by teachers unions.
In addition to Polis, Democratic Gov.-elect Phil Weiser announced last week that he opposed Amendment 87, adding that if it passed, he “will implement it effectively.” Both Polis and Weiser backed Proposition NN.
State Rep. Lorena Garcia, a Democrat from Westminster and director of the Colorado Statewide Parent Coalition, alluded to the doubts the campaign faced throughout the process as she addressed the dozens of supporters and volunteers on hand for Thursday’s victory celebration.
“When they said, ‘Not this year,’ what did we say? We said, ‘Yes, this year.’ When they said, ‘You’re gonna get in the way of other things,’ we said, ‘No, we are adding to it,'” Garcia said. “When they said, ‘OK, you barely got it on the ballot. Now how are you going to win?’ Like this. It’s with people.”

name: VTDigger
title: For new taxes, only room at the inn
description:
“Any time you hear the word tax, that's got a negative connotation to a lot of people,” Bennington Selectboard Chair Tom Haley said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  For new taxes, only room at the inn.
text:
People hold signs for candidates and ballot measures at Essex Middle School in Essex Town on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Photo by Brendan Kinney/VTDigger

Local option taxes met a mostly chilly reception in Bennington, Hinesburg and Essex on Tuesday, with only one — a rooms tax  — passing in a preliminary vote.
“People feel the stress of increased gas prices,” said Ted Brady, executive director of Vermont League of Cities and Towns. “They feel the stress of the cost of inflation, and they seem to have questioned whether adding another percent to their shopping bill would have made sense to them.”
Although all seven proposals were touted as a way to provide property tax relief, town officials and experts said local option taxes faced an uphill climb this November due to high economic pressures for Vermonters. 
The failures do not necessarily signify a trend because local option taxes are typically more successful in Town Meeting Day votes, they added.
The local option tax ballot questions — votes on whether to implement a 1% increase to state taxes on meals, alcoholic beverages, rooms or sales in individual municipalities — failed on all fronts in Bennington and Hinesburg.
In Essex, the rooms tax prevailed with 60% support on a preliminary vote despite controversy after the town failed to notify residents in time for the vote in accordance with state law. The rooms tax in Hinesburg was also the most popular option. It received 46.3% of the vote as opposed to 27.4% for sales and 34.7% for meals and alcohol.
“When we look at it, the rooms tax is one that is clearly for people that are visiting our town,” said Shannon Jackson, chair of the Essex selectboard.
Bennington bundled the three elements of the tax into a single proposal, which failed by a margin of 2,292 to 3,136 on Tuesday.
“Maybe three separate votes might have been the better way to go, I don’t know,” Haley said. “That’s Monday morning quarterbacking at this point, which we’re going to do a lot of.”
Local option taxes met a different fate in the March votes earlier this year. Almost 20 municipalities proposed the tax, and the measures passed fully or partially in all but six municipalities. Brady said Tuesday’s votes do not necessarily indicate a larger trend.
“The economic climate wasn’t that different in March, and several towns passed local option taxes,” Brady said. He said the contrasting results had more to do with the individual town residents and the issues that each town is dealing with. 
The electorate that turns up for the midterm elections also tends to be slightly different than a Town Meeting Day, Brady said.
“I don’t think a lot of people showed up at the midterm elections to vote specifically on the local option tax,” Brady said, “where I think when you get to a Town Meeting ballot, oftentimes that might be the reason you’re showing up. That’s the only controversial thing that’s on the ballot.”
Some controversy surfaced in Bennington in the lead-up to the vote, Haley said, including questions about whether the revenue would just drive up city spending, driven by individuals whom he deemed “keyboard warriors.” But there was also some confusion on how exactly the proposal could benefit Bennington’s residents.
“Any time you hear the word tax, that’s got a negative connotation to a lot of people,” Haley said. “And the idea of using a tax to reduce another tax, I think, is, it’s weird, right?”
The local tax option proposal is tabled for now in Hinesburg, according to Todd Odit, Hinesburg’s town manager. It is too early to say how the selectboard will proceed in Bennington, Haley added. Essex will take a final vote on the rooms tax on March 2, 2027, which will be binding.
The recent election results encouraged Jackson, since the rooms tax didn’t pass on a “razor-thin margin.”
“They did want a very clear victory margin for the rooms,” Jackson said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Attorney Whitney Lipscomb announces run for secretary of state
description: Republican Whitney Lipscomb announces her candidacy for secretary of state at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Whitney Lipscomb, the general counsel for the Republican Attorneys General Association, announced Thursday that she is running for Mississippi secretary of state next year in the Republican primary. 
“I am more convinced now more than ever that Mississippi needs leadership with unwavering conservative convictions, a deep desire to make a difference and the ability to get things done,” Lipscomb said at a press conference at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in Jackson. 
While this is her first time running for office, Lipscomb has spent much of her career in Republican politics and government. 
Lipscomb was deputy chief of staff and an attorney for former Gov. Phil Bryant. She served as deputy attorney general for about five years under AG Lynn Fitch, who is running for governor next year.
“I have spent my career in the fights that matter to Mississippi because I love this state,” Lipscomb said, citing her work under Bryant and Fitch, both of whom were seated in the front row during her announcement.
The secretary of state’s responsibilities include overseeing state elections as well as managing business formations and managing state-owned land. Lipscomb said her top priorities are cutting red tape for business owners and protecting “every lawful vote” in elections. 
“We’re going to continue to protect the integrity of Mississippi’s elections. If people do not trust elections, they won’t trust their government,” Lipscomb said. “Process matters and the rules must be followed. We are seeing exactly how important that is right this very moment.”
Lipscomb’s campaign committee filed its initial paperwork in May 2026.
Shuwaski Young, the Democratic nominee for secretary of state in 2023, has said that he is running again for the position next year as a Republican. No Democratic candidate has announced a run for the office. 
Current Secretary of State Michael Watson is running for lieutenant governor next year. Current Lieutenant Governor Delbert Hosemann is term-limited.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Board: Nursing home worker stole dozens of painkillers from residents
description: After being convicted of stealing the medication of multiple nursing home residents, a nurse from Preston has agreed to surrender her license. In June 2025, licensed practical nurse Jaci Moore, now 33, was charged by Waterloo police with third-degree theft after it was alleged she stole 74 items, putting some in her purse and some […]
text:
Heritage Specialty Care in Cedar Rapids. (Photo via Google Earth)After being convicted of stealing the medication of multiple nursing home residents, a nurse from Preston has agreed to surrender her license.
In June 2025, licensed practical nurse Jaci Moore, now 33, was charged by Waterloo police with third-degree theft after it was alleged she stole 74 items, putting some in her purse and some in a shopping cart, worth $847. She later pleaded guilty to the charge and received a deferred judgment.
In October 2025, Linn County prosecutors alleged that Moore was working at the Heritage Specialty Care in Cedar Rapids in September 2025 when she “mis-administered and/or took” approximately 43 oxycodone pills by falsely claiming the patients had requested the medications and then falsely claiming she had administered the drugs.
When interviewed by police, Moore allegedly admitted that she had an oxycodone addiction and also admitted stealing 10 or 12 of the patients’ oxycodone pills. She was charged with felony prohibited acts involving controlled substances.
In December 2025, Linn County prosecutors charged Moore with a second count of prohibited acts. In that case, prosecutors alleged that an investigation by the state’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit found that while Moore was working as a nurse for the Harmony Cedar Rapids nursing home in January 2025, she stole “dozens of tablets of oxycodone from residents” and tried to conceal the theft through false reporting in home’s narcotics log.
There were at least three Harmony Cedar Rapids residents from whom she stole the painkillers, prosecutors alleged. As with the previously filed case, prosecutors alleged Moore confessed to the theft and to an oxycodone addiction.
In July 2026, Moore pleaded guilty to both counts of prohibited acts involving controlled substances and received a deferred judgment that will wipe both convictions from her record after the successful completion of three years of probation.
In January 2026, the Iowa Board of Nursing filed disciplinary charges against Moore and, in September 2026, filed additional charges based on her criminal convictions.
The board charged Moore with misappropriating patient medications, committing an act that may adversely affect a patient’s welfare, failure to accurately document a patient’s condition and being convicted of an offense directly related to the practice of nursing.
The board then agreed to settle the case by accepting Moore’s voluntary surrender of her license, with the understanding that she can seek reinstatement after one year.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Moore for comment.



Other recent nursing board cases
Other Iowa nurses recently sanctioned by the Iowa Board of Nursing include:
Jessica Larson of Lime Springs — The board alleged that while working as a registered nurse for the Federal Bureau of Prisons, Larson was assigned to the Federal Medical Center in Rochester, Minn. According to the board, in April 2024 Larson “engaged in an inappropriate personal, emotional, and sexual relationship with an inmate.” When confronted by prison officials, the board alleges, Larson lied about the nature of the relationship.
In March 2025, she was indicted by a federal grand jury for abusive contact with a ward and providing a false statement to authorities. She later pleaded guilty to the false-statement charge and the charge of abusive contact with a ward was dismissed. In January 2026, she was sentenced to six months of incarceration.
The board subsequently charged Larson with having sexual contact with a patient, engaging in a sexual relationship with a former patient, engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum and pleading guilty to a crime directly related to the practice of nursing. The board recently agreed to settle the case by accepting Larson’s voluntary surrender of her license, with the understanding that she can seek reinstatement after one year.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Larson for comment.
Angela Veenstra of Clive — In July 2025, the board charged Veenstra, an advanced registered nurse practitioner, with unethical conduct or practicing in a manner that is harmful to the public by violating patient confidentiality, performing nursing services that are beyond her authorized scope of practice, committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare, prescribing or dispensing drugs in an unsafe manner and prescribing or administering drugs to patients outside her area of specialty.
The board alleged that from August 2022 to April 2024, while Veenstra was working at a central Iowa outpatient mental health clinic the board has opted not to publicly identify, she treated patients with a variety of psychiatric conditions although she was not licensed as a psychiatric nurse practitioner.
In addition, the board alleged, Veenstra prescribed for patients a combination of medications that did not meet the expected standard of care given the potential interactions among those medications. She was also accused of taking a list of patients with her when she resigned from the clinic and then sending those patients a “mailer” of some kind.
Veenstra and the board recently settled the disciplinary case with an agreement that calls for her to complete 35 hours of educational training and for her license to be placed on probationary status for three years.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Veenstra for comment.

This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Al final, no fueron hombres siniestros rellenando urnas ni agentes federales quienes causaron disturbios la noche de las elecciones en el bastión republicano rural del condado de Shasta, en el norte de California.
Fue la aparente incompetencia de Clint Curtis, el responsable electoral del condado que niega los resultados de las elecciones y que pronto se quedará sin trabajo. Periodistas, entre ellos Shasta Scout, colaboradora de CalMatters, han reportado numerosos problemas con el recuento de votos en el condado de Shasta, ubicado a dos horas y media en coche al norte de Sacramento. Informaron sobre urnas desbordadas, escasez de personal, trabajadores que colocaban las papeletas en los contenedores equivocados , fallos informáticos y votantes que llegaban a sus centros de votación y encontraban carteles que indicaban que la ubicación había sido cambiada.
 La mayoría de los condados publicaron los resultados iniciales justo después de las 8 de la noche, cuando cerraron las urnas, pero Shasta no informó de ninguno hasta alrededor de las 10 de la noche, ya que los funcionarios electorales no habían configurado correctamente su sistema informático, lo que lo convirtió en el único condado del estado que el miércoles por la mañana no había terminado de contar las papeletas de quienes votaron en persona.
 Un reportero del Shasta Scout le preguntó a Curtis el martes por la noche por qué el personal adicional que, según él, había contratado en los últimos meses, no recogió las papeletas de los buzones. El propio Curtis abandonó la oficina electoral para recoger papeletas cuando debería haber estado supervisando el recuento.
 “Porque soy estúpido”, dijo Curtis a Shasta Scout . “Así que cuando veo que hay que hacerlo, simplemente lo hago yo mismo”. Curtis no respondió de inmediato a la solicitud de entrevista de CalMatters el miércoles.
 Los problemas en el condado de Shasta son una excepción en California. No se reportaron problemas importantes en los otros 57 condados de California, a pesar de la preocupación previa a las elecciones de que la administración Trump pudiera intentar interferir en el recuento de votos después de que funcionarios federales hicieran amenazas sin precedentes a los trabajadores electorales de California. 
Curtis llevó al FBI al condado de Shasta
Debido a Curtis, este otoño parecía que el condado de Shasta podría convertirse en el epicentro de la guerra del presidente Donald Trump contra las elecciones en los estados demócratas, ya que sus fiscales buscaban demostrar las antiguas afirmaciones de Trump de que los demócratas están manipulando las elecciones en su contra.
Curtis, quien durante mucho tiempo ha negado la veracidad de las elecciones en Estados Unidos, hizo afirmaciones descabelladas de que actores malintencionados habían llenado las urnas con papeletas falsas en las primarias de junio. Perdió su candidatura para un mandato completo en esas elecciones.
El año pasado, Curtis redujo el número de urnas para depositar votos en el condado de Shasta de 13 a cuatro. Luego, tras las elecciones de junio, Curtis afirmó que se estaba tramando un complot para rellenar las urnas después de que él y su equipo encontraran papeletas que, según ellos, tenían un papel con un aspecto, tacto y olor extraños.
 Sus afirmaciones llamaron la atención de altos funcionarios encargados de hacer cumplir la ley en la administración de Trump.
 En septiembre, las autoridades enviaron un equipo de agentes del FBI a la oficina electoral del condado con cizallas para entrar en una habitación donde se guardaban papeletas antiguas que Curtis había cerrado con candado y tirado la llave. Curtis afirmó que los agentes no confiscaron ninguna papeleta.
Se desconoce el estado de la investigación federal en el condado de Shasta. El Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos no ha confirmado siquiera la existencia de una investigación.
El sustituto de Curtis asumirá el cargo en enero
 Curtis, una figura de poca relevancia entre los negacionistas electorales del movimiento MAGA de Trump, nunca había desempeñado un papel oficial en las elecciones antes de que los miembros de extrema derecha que controlaban la Junta de Supervisores del Condado de Shasta en 2025 lo designaran.
 Curtis, abogado y excandidato demócrata al Congreso en Florida y California , perdió las primarias de junio ante Joanna Francescut, una exfuncionaria electoral del condado de Shasta que ayudó a dirigir la oficina electoral antes de que Curtis la despidiera.
 Francescut asumirá el cargo en enero.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi GOP chair vows to ‘fight like hell’ in Senate midterm vote counting
description: Mississippi Republican Party Chairman Mike Hurst speaks about the U.S. Senate race between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic candidate Scott Colom during a news conference outside the Hinds County Circuit Courthouse in Jackson on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
As Democrat Scott Colom narrowly leads incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a race for U.S. Senate, it appears Mississippi will see a partisan legal fight over thousands of affidavit ballots that will decide the outcome.
Mississippi Republican Party Chairman Mike Hurst vowed at a Thursday press conference to “fight like hell” to ensure that only “legally cast” ballots are counted and that the process to review and count the outstanding ballots is aboveboard. 
READ MORE: Thousands of affidavit ballots outstanding in Mississippi Senate election. Campaigns prepare for legal fight
“Let me be clear: This race is far from being over,” Hurst said. “Right now, we estimate that there could be approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted.” 
Hurst said, without providing evidence, that the areas where a large number of affidavit ballots remain outstanding are traditional Republican-leaning areas of the state. When asked if he would name those specific counties, he declined. 
Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The razor-thin margin of votes between Hyde-Smith and Colom in a state considered a Republican stronghold has sent shockwaves across the nation, but it remained too close to call on Thursday. Only 1,764 votes separated the two candidates. The Associated Press reported that Colom led 466,226 to 464,502, with 96% of the vote counted.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee, the fundraising arm of the Senate GOP, sent letters to circuit county clerks and election commissioners asking them to preserve and set aside affidavit ballots. 
Kyle Kirkpatrick, former head of the elections division at the Mississippi secretary of state’s office, questioned on social media how productive that exercise would be because once affidavit ballots are scanned, it is “impossible to determine” what voter that ballot was associated with. 
Gerard Henderson, Colom’s campaign manager, said in a statement that the NRSC letters were a “desperate stunt” and signaled Republicans knew they were about to lose the race. 
“We’re confident that when every lawful ballot is counted, Scott Colom will be Mississippi’s next U.S. senator,” Henderson said.  
PODCAST: When will we know who won Mississippi’s Senate midterm election?
Election attorneys, voting rights advocates and reporters from around the globe have descended on Mississippi over the past 48 hours, scrambling to make sense of what remaining ballots were left, when they would be counted and how Colom found himself in striking distance of pulling off a victory in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in over four decades.  
Fair Fight Action, a voting rights advocacy organization, said the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Democratic election attorneys from Elias Law Group have deployed hundreds of volunteers and local lawyers across all 82 counties to oversee the final rounds of counting. 
Mississippi has no automatic recount law. A recount would happen only if a court ordered it. For that to happen, a campaign or political party would have to file a lawsuit against a county or county election commission. 
A state judge would likely hear the case on an expedited basis, and the lower court’s decision would be appealable to the Mississippi Supreme Court. 
After the election results are certified, campaigns can conduct ballot box examinations, which can be used as evidence in a lawsuit. The dispute over which affidavit ballots are accepted and rejected would likely be the subject of litigation. 
If a court fight ensued, it could be a disjointed, chaotic process. Mississippi law does not establish a system for challenging ballots on a statewide scale, only on a county-by-county basis. 
The Republican Party chairman declined to say in which specific county he’s considering filing a lawsuit, but he referenced Hinds County, Mississippi’s largest county and a Democratic stronghold, as a likely option. 
“It’s no surprise that this is a traditionally Democratic county, and I don’t think it’s any surprise that this election commission, in particular, has had a number of issues in the past that frankly are not just Republican issues, but even Democratic election commissioners have complained about how the electoral system in Hinds County has operated,” Hurst said. 
The press conference displayed the awkward and surprising position the state GOP currently finds itself in, a Deep South state that has consistently sent Republicans to the U.S. Senate for the last four decades. 
For the first time in a generation, an incumbent Republican senator in Mississippi running for reelection has been caught flat-footed and put on the defensive after Black voters turned out in droves and many Republican voters crossed over to vote for Colom. 
Hurst, who also serves as general counsel for the Republican National Committee, acknowledged that Democratic candidates did “pretty well” around the country and this was the closest Senate race that reliably conservative Mississippi has had in a “very, very long time.” 
Though he claimed that Hyde-Smith would ultimately win the election, Hurst said he would accept the results of the election if the votes show Colom lawfully won.
Voters have until Nov. 10 to correct issues related to presenting a voter ID at their local circuit clerk’s office, which is also the same date election officials have to count late-arriving mail-in ballots that were postmarked by Election Day.

title: Arkansas attorney general seeks end to order establishing majority-Black judicial districts
description: Attorney General Tim Griffin asked a federal judge Thursday to end a 35-year-old order establishing multiple majority-Black judicial districts in Arkansas, citing a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that weakened a key part of the Voting Rights Act. The Republican attorney general asked a judge to terminate the 1991 consent decree that created 10 judicial seats […]
text:
Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin briefly takes the stage at the Republican Watch Party on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the North Little Rock Event Center in North Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Attorney General Tim Griffin asked a federal judge Thursday to end a 35-year-old order establishing multiple majority-Black judicial districts in Arkansas, citing a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that weakened a key part of the Voting Rights Act.
The Republican attorney general asked a judge to terminate the 1991 consent decree that created 10 judicial seats in predominantly Black subdistricts. The order was issued in a lawsuit that had been filed by Black residents who said the state’s system of electing judges violated the Voting Rights Act.
In his filing, Griffin said the decree should be terminated because of significant changes to the law and because of the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais ruling in April that said the Voting Rights Act does not require states to create majority-minority districts. 
“The consent decree should independently be terminated because defendants have fully complied with the consent decree in good faith since it was entered and any vestiges of past discrimination have been eliminated to the extent practicable,” the filing said.
In a news release, Griffin said the consent decree is “premised on racial stereotypes and contrary to equal protection mandates,” and that it unconstitutionally divides voters by race.
Griffin’s filing was criticized by civil rights advocates who said the decree ensured a more representative judicial system.
“I think it’s an attack on the Black judges that are doing an outstanding job right now across Arkansas,” said Barry Jefferson, president of the NAACP Arkansas State Conference. “I think this is something that we really need to stand up and fight against because we can’t let this continue to happen throughout our country.”
The NAACP Legal Defense Fund said it planned to oppose Griffin’s motion and noted that Black judges had not been elected in Arkansas before the 1991 consent decree.
“So we’re talking about a justice system that was being doled out by people who didn’t look like the people who were receiving that justice, and that’s pretty fundamentally unfair…It’s an important decree that’s led to a more representative bench, and I think that should be important to everybody in Arkansas,” said Kathryn Sadasivan, senior counsel for the Legal Defense Fund.

text:
U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley spoke at a Westside Conservative Club meeting Oct. 14, 2026 in Urbandale, Iowa. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley, 93, does not plan to resign before Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds leaves office, to allow her, instead of Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand, to appoint someone to fill his seat, a spokesperson said Thursday.
There is no immediate need for Grassley, an Iowa Republican who has served in the U.S. Senate since 1981, to vacate his position before the end of his term in 2028. But the senator would be 95 years old when his current term ends, and some Iowans have raised questions about who would be appointed to replace him if he resigned or died in office.
Some have speculated that Grassley might opt to leave office early, allowing a Republican governor to appoint his successor — perhaps U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, whose time in D.C. is ending after an unsuccessful run for Iowa’s open Senate seat, or Grassley’s grandson, Pat Grassley, who currently serves as Iowa House speaker.

Grassley himself spoke about the possibility on the 2026 campaign trail as he rallied voters to support GOP gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn over Sand. In September, he told Republicans, “I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor.”
A spokesperson for Grassley said in a statement that he does not plan to leave his role.
“Senator Grassley is not resigning. He remains committed to delivering for the people of Iowa, who overwhelmingly elected him to a six-year term in 2022,” the spokesperson said.
Speaking with Iowa News Now earlier in September, Sand said he’d “be interested in an independent” to fill an Iowa U.S. Senate seat if a vacancy happened during his term.
Beginning in January, there will be only one other Iowa Republican in Iowa’s Washington delegation — Chris McGowan, the Republican elected to represent Iowa’s 4th Congressional District. Democrats won Iowa’s other three U.S. House seats in Tuesday’s election, as well as the U.S. Senate seat currently occupied by Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Grassley is set to serve alongside Josh Turek, the Council Bluffs Democrat who won the Senate race.
Grassley, who currently chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee, will lose the top position as Democrats take over the majority next year. He has served as the committee’s ranking member twice, from 2011 to 2015 and from 2021 to 2023.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘We will not be intimidated’: 3 anti-ICE protesters plead not guilty to federal charges
description:
Their attorney said he intends to file a motion to throw out the charges on several grounds, including that they violate his clients’ First Amendment rights.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘We will not be intimidated’: 3 anti-ICE protesters plead not guilty to federal charges.
text:
From left: Sherri Wormser, Henry Prensky, and Peter Booth read from a joint statement to supporters outside of federal court in Burlington on Thursday, November 5, 2026, following their arraignments on charges stemming from anti-ICE demonstrations in Williston. Photo by Alan J. Keays/VTDigger

BURLINGTON — Three people have denied federal charges stemming from demonstrations where they allegedly blocked doors at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surveillance facility in Williston.
Peter Booth, 58, of Jericho; Henry Prensky, 80, of Burlington; and Sherri Wormser, 57, of Colchester, appeared Thursday in federal court in Burlington for their arraignments on misdemeanor charges.
Attorney Robert Appel, representing all three, entered not guilty pleas on their behalf, and they were each released on a condition that they not violate any federal, state or local laws.
All three are charged with obstructing access to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center at the White Cap Business Park in Williston during anti-ICE demonstrations earlier this year.
VTDigger has previously reported that, according to federal records, information at that facility is reviewed and collected from publicly available sources, such as social media, and assists ICE officers with investigations.
The U.S. attorney’s office in Vermont filed the charges in September against the three defendants as well as two other people — Lexington Kennedy, 22, of New York City, and Roan Wade, 23, of Red Hook, New York — in connection with the anti-ICE demonstrations in Williston.
Kennedy and Wade are to be arraigned on similar misdemeanor charges as the three arraigned Thursday.
According to charging documents, Booth, Prensky, Wormser, Kennedy and Wade went into the atrium of the White Cap building Feb. 9 and blocked the doors between the atrium and the federal facility with their bodies. They ignored orders to move, according to the documents. 
Then on May 14, the documents say, Booth and Prensky blocked the doors again. Kennedy and Wade are charged with similar conduct on July 24, according to the documents. 
By blocking the doors to the federal property, the defendants obstructed its “usual use, enjoyment and access,” according to the documents. 
Each offense carries up to 30 days in prison and up to a $5,000 fine. 
Appel, speaking to reporters after the hearing, said he was told by a prosecutor to expect an offer to resolve the cases that did not include jail time. Appel added that if he does receive a plea offer, he is obligated to present it to his client for their consideration.
Booth, Prensky and Wormser read a joint statement outside the federal courthouse to a group of about 30 supporters.
“The purpose of these prosecutions is to intimidate,” Wormser said, adding, “We will not be intimidated.” 
Activists say they plan to continue protesting ICE’s presence in Vermont. Organizers have announced a mock funeral procession Friday starting at the Williston facility in remembrance of people who have died in ICE custody since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The event will be followed by a sit-in, according to a press release.
The filing of the federal charges is the latest prosecutorial turn following many anti-ICE protests and demonstrations in Vermont.
Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George has declined repeatedly to press state charges against anti-ICE protesters after their arrests at demonstrations in the county, contending that it didn’t serve justice to prosecute them. 
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark, who also has the authority to bring state criminal charges in Chittenden County, has since filed trespass-related charges against protesters stemming from demonstrations at the White Cap facility. 
Appel, the attorney for the three people who appeared in federal court Thursday, told reporters outside the courtroom that it is extremely rare for prosecutors to bring federal charges in such cases. He said that he would seek to have the charges thrown out on several grounds, including that they violated his clients’ First Amendment rights.
“A potential problem I see is that this is not a federal facility,” added Appel, a former head of the Vermont Human Rights Commission. “It’s rented space in a public building that offers a variety of other services.” 
Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathanael Burris, the prosecutor, requested a condition of release prohibiting the defendants from coming “within 50 feet of federal facilities or property occupied by the United States Department of Homeland Security” in Vermont, without prior court approval.
Magistrate Judge Kevin Doyle said he wouldn’t impose that restriction, adding that he was concerned the request was too broad and could result in violations for being at airports or ports of entry where Homeland Security may be located as well.
