name: Maryland Matters
title: Ex-campaign treasurer for Luke Clippinger faces embezzlement, theft charges
description: The Office of the State Prosecutor on Thursday charged Melissa Ann Smith, a former campaign treasurer for Del. Luke Clippinger (D-Baltimore City), with stealing more than $87,000 from his campagn account. Clippinger serves as the House speaker pro tem..
text:
The Baltimore County Circuit Courts Building in Towson. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)A former campaign treasurer for a top Democratic lawmaker faces embezzlement charges, prosecutors announced Thursday.
Melissa Ann Smith, who served for more than a decade as the treasurer of Friend of Luke Clippinger, is accused of stealing more than $87,000 from the campaign, according to charges filed by the Office of the State Prosecutor Thursday.
The charges come 11 months after Maryland Matters raised questions about more than a dozen checks allegedly cashed by Smith, then known as Melissa Evans, over a four-year period. Del. Lukc Clippinger (D-Baltimore City) serves as House speaker pro tem and was elected Tuesday to a fifth term in the House.
“Treasurers of campaign finance committees have an important role in ensuring funds raised to support a political candidate are used to benefit the purpose of the campaign,” said State Prosecutor Charlton T. Howard III. “Our Office strives to hold individuals in positions of public trust in the electoral process accountable if they violate that trust for personal financial gain.” `
The Office of the State Prosecutor filed the charges Thursday in Baltimore County Circuit Court. An initial hearing has not been scheduled.
Online court records do not list an attorney for Smith. She did not respond to a request for comment.
Clippinger, in a text, declined comment because it is an open criminal case.
Del. Luke Clippinger (D-Baltimore City) is the No. 2 Democrat in the Houser as Speaker pro tem. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
In all, Smith is accused of stealing more than $87,000 from Clippinger’s campaign account. Prosecutors allege Smith deposited 47 checks into three personal bank accounts between 2018 and 2025.
As a result, she faces charges related to a theft scheme as well as embezzlement. A conviction on theft charges carries a sentence of up to 10 years in prison and up to a $15,000 fine. Conviction on the embezzlement charge carries a sentence of not less than one year by not more than five years in prison.
She faces two additional accounts of perjury for filing campaign finance reports in 2025 and 2026. Prosecutors allege Smith attempted to cover up the diversion of funds by filing inaccurate reports that did not include checks she allegedly wrote to herself.
Conviction on perjury charges each carry a 10-year sentence.
In January, Maryland Matters raised questions about more than a dozen checks totaling $44,000 drawn on Clippinger’s campaign account between 2020 and 2024.
Checks obtained by Maryland Matters were made out to Melissa Evans. All of the checks appeared to have been endorsed by Smith and deposited into her personal bank accounts. The checks range in amounts from $500 to two for $10,000. One of the checks was a bank check drawn on the Clippinger campaign account payable to Melissa Evans.
Clippinger, in a statement issued in January, told Maryland Matters he discovered four additional checks “written in the past month by my treasurer that were not authorized and not legitimate campaign expenditures.”
He said at the time that he immediately forwarded the matter to the Office of the State Prosecutor and would cooperate with their investigation. He also hired an outside accountant to begin a review of his account.
At the same time, Clippinger announced he had fired Smith from the position she had held since 2013.

title: RI Senate begins judicial nominations process. House hearing on McKee’s Supreme Court pick pending
description: The Rhode Island Senate returned Thursday for a rare fall session to begin the advice and consent process for eight magistrate nominations and formally read in Gov. Dan McKee’s nominee to the state’s Supreme Court. “As we convene in the Senate chamber, let us once again contemplate our reason for being here,” Sen. John Burke, […]
text:
Senators gather for a rare fall floor session at the State House on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The Rhode Island Senate returned Thursday for a rare fall session to begin the advice and consent process for eight magistrate nominations and formally read in Gov. Dan McKee’s nominee to the state’s Supreme Court.
“As we convene in the Senate chamber, let us once again contemplate our reason for being here,” Sen. John Burke, a West Warwick Democrat, said during the opening invocation of the six-minute floor session.
Return of the lame-duck session with RI General Assembly set to reconvene after November election

McKee in August selected Superior Court Judge Luis Matos to fill the vacancy created by Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg’s retirement in the spring. But Matos’ official paperwork was not transmitted to the House and Senate until Wednesday, Nov. 4, which triggers a 60-day window for lawmakers in both chambers to act.
“Judge Matos brings extensive judicial experience and a vast record of service to the bench, and the governor looks forward to his nomination moving into the advice and consent process,” Olivia DaRocha, a spokesperson for McKee’s office, wrote in a statement announcing the submission. 
The 62-year-old Providence resident, who immigrated from Portugal in 1969, has served on the Superior Court since 2012. A former federal prosecutor in Rhode Island and Delaware, Matos has extensive experience prosecuting health care fraud, white collar crime and public corruption cases, according to his resume. 
Since 2020, he has served on the Judiciary’s Committee on Racial and Ethnic Fairness in the Courts, helping improve internal policies and public outreach to promote fairness in the judicial system.
McKee repeatedly praised Matos as the “most qualified” of the five applicants he interviewed when he announced his judicial selection Aug. 12. The shortlist also included former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi, who will vote on Matos’ confirmation should the nomination reach the House floor.
State law requires a seven-calendar-day waiting period before lawmakers can begin considering a Supreme Court nomination. The Senate Committee on Judiciary has hearings for all potential judicial picks planned for Nov. 17 and 18, chamber spokesperson Greg Paré confirmed in a text message to Rhode Island Current.
Sen. Matthew LaMountain, a Warwick Democrat who chairs the judiciary panel, declined to say when the committee would consider Matos’ nomination. “I’ll defer to the House,” he said in an interview after the Senate went into recess. “Historically they go first in the process”
The House Committee on Judiciary has yet to schedule a hearing on Matos’ nomination as of Thursday.
Rep. Carol Hagan McEntee, a South Kingstown Democrat who chairs the House Judiciary Committee, said she expects one to take place within the next month but noted a final date is still being worked on with House leadership.
“We haven’t got anything definite yet,” McEntee said in a phone interview.
The House has yet to schedule a Judiciary Committee hearing on Matos’ nomination. Rep. Carol Hagan McEntee, a South Kingstown Democrat who chairs the committee, said she expects a hearing within the next month, though a final date is still being worked out with House leadership.
“We haven’t got anything definite yet,” McEntee said in a phone interview Thursday.
For now, the Senate will proceed with the five magistrate nominations before it.
Superior Court Presiding Justice Joseph A. Montalbano on Oct. 23 recommended Timothy G. Healy and Kara Hoopis Manosh for magistrate positions in the state’s highest trial court, subject to Senate advice and consent. All Rhode Island magistrates serve 10-year terms, unlike judges, who receive lifetime appointments.
Also before the Senate are Robert A. Ragosta and Therese M. Picard, whom Family Court Chief Judge Michael Forte recommended for magistrate appointments in August. 
The Senate is also expected to consider the reappointment of Traffic Tribunal Magistrate Erika Kruse Weller, recommended by the Supreme Court in January, along with David Lapatin, Eric A. Batista and Nicole McCarty — each of whom were nominated at the end of October.
Beyond those appointments, McKee has several other judicial vacancies to fill.
The governor has yet to announce his selections for two Superior Court vacancies from a pool of eight candidates recommended by the Judicial Nominating Commission on Aug. 12. The openings arose when Montalbano became presiding justice and Jeffrey Lanphear retired.
McKee is also considering five candidates recommended Friday by the Judicial Nominating Commission for District Court chief judge. The vacancy was created by the Oct. 9 retirement of Jeanne E. LaFazia, who stepped down after 16 years on the bench.
McKee’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his remaining judicial selections.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma turnpike tolls to rise, increasing the cost to travel to Tulsa by about 35 cents
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Tolls on Oklahoma turnpikes are set to increase Jan. 5. For PikePass customers traveling on the state turnpike system, the cost will increase by about a penny to 8 cents for every mile driven.  The toll increase will bring the cost for PikePass holders traveling from Oklahoma City to Tulsa in a […]
text:
A street sign marks the interchange of Interstate 40 and the Kilpatrick Turnpike. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Tolls on Oklahoma turnpikes are set to increase Jan. 5.
For PikePass customers traveling on the state turnpike system, the cost will increase by about a penny to 8 cents for every mile driven. 
The toll increase will bring the cost for PikePass holders traveling from Oklahoma City to Tulsa in a passenger vehicle to $5.75, up from $5.40, said Lisa Shearer-Salim, a spokesperson for the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority.
The agency on Thursday approved the toll increase to pay for a 15-year, $9 billion turnpike expansion and improvement project, called the Advancing and Connecting Communities and Economies Safely Statewide, or ACCESS.
The increase is designed to generate a 6% revenue increase for the turnpike authority, said Mary Biswell, the agency’s director of revenue assurance.
“We anticipate coming back every two years to consider another 6% increase,” Biswell said.
The hike keeps revenues adjusted for inflation and pays for the significant reinvestment into the system, Biswell said.
The last toll hike was in 2025, Biswell said.
The agency’s governing board also approved a toll hike for the Gilcrease Expressway, which is not on the turnpike system due to how it was financed.
The increase for PikePass passenger vehicles will be about 15 cents if they travel the entire five miles of the roadway, Shearer-Salim said.
“Even with this increase going into effect Jan. 5, we will still have the ninth lowest toll rate in the nation for a transponder,” Shearer-Salim said.
Turnpike customers can use the agency’s toll calculator to look up rates, she said. It will be updated to reflect the new rates when the increased tolls take effect.
The ACCESS project was to initially cost $5 billion, a figure that later rose to $8.2 billion due to inflation. 
It is now projected to cost about $9 billion as additional projects, such as eight-laning the Turner Turnpike from Bristow to Oklahoma City, have been added, she said. It had originally planned for six lanes, she said.

name: VTDigger
title: Washington County voters approved $54.9 million bond for new career center
description:
Residents in Washington County advanced the effort to build a new Montpelier campus for the Central Vermont Career Center, expanding its enrollment size. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Washington County voters approved $54.9 million bond for new career center.
text:
An architect’s drawing shows the proposed site plan for the new facility on the U-32 campus. Image courtesy of CVCC

Voters in Washington County supported an effort to nearly double the Central Vermont Career Center, approving a $54.9 million bond to build a new campus. 
The current technical education center at Barre’s Spaulding High School only has space for about 250 students. Last year more than 400 kids applied, according to Jody Emerson, the center’s director. 
With a new building in Montpelier, which voters also approved on a special ballot vote Tuesday, the career center could enroll about 450 students across two campuses, Emerson said. 
Votes from across the county’s 18 towns were tallied Thursday, with 60% of voters approving the bond for construction, according to an announcement from the career center. Residents approved the bond 9,753-6,609. 
The new technical center in Montpelier is slated to be built next to the U-32 Middle and High School. County residents approved a 30-year lease from the Washington County Unified Union School District in a separate ballot question, with 62% voting in-favor. 
Construction on the new building could begin as soon as spring 2028, Emerson said, with doors opening to students in fall 2030. 
Last year, voters rejected a more expensive proposal — a $149 million bond — to build a new career center building in Barre. After the measure was rejected, leaders at the center planned to build a smaller campus while maintaining its space at Spaulding. 

READ MORE

The rising demand for technical education in Washington County is emblematic of a larger statewide trend. Demand for career and technical education is growing around the state at a rate that outpaces districts’ ability to provide programs for students, according to The Other Paper. About a quarter of high schoolers in the state enroll in career and technical education centers, The Other Paper reported. 
Emerson said that the center often lacks the capacity to cater to specific high demand interests. For example, more than 70 kids apply to the automotive program, she said, but there are only 16 seats in the class. 
“Even if I had a second auto instructor, there’s not enough room in the auto shop and the auto classroom to actually serve a lot more students,” she said. 
With the new career center in Montpelier, Emerson said the district plans to split its program offerings between the U-32 campus and its site in Spaulding, Emerson said. 
Classes for heavier trades like construction and transportation will stay at the career center in Barre, Emerson said, while classes for hospitality, arts and health pathways will be offered in Montpelier. 
Where students take classes, Emerson said, will depend on their interests.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: As Democrats gain power in Pa., some business leaders wonder about moderation
description: A GOP Senate forced moderation in Pennsylvania's legislature, according to some — so what will Democrats do now?
text:
The Pennsylvania State Capitol on March 19, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)In the next legislative session, Democrats in Pennsylvania will not necessarily have to compromise with Republicans to pass laws. On Tuesday, voters handed both chambers in the General Assembly and the governor’s office to Democratic candidates.
The results were part of a nationwide “blue wave” that ousted GOP lawmakers on the state and federal levels across the country. 
“The outlines of this race, the contours, were very clear: voters were deeply unhappy with their economic circumstances,” said Berwood Yost, who has long studied where the state’s voters stood on issues.
Berwood Yost, Director of the Center for Opinion Research (Courtesy of F&M College)
Yost is the director of the Floyd Institute for Public Police and Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster. He was part of a virtual panel Thursday organized by RKL, an advisory firm. 
Having a Democratic majority for the first time since 1993 — which, Yost noted, only happened at the time because a member changed their party affiliation — is “a sea change in Pennsylvania politics.” 
Having that Republican Senate for so long has “moderated” policies in the commonwealth, Yost continued.
“It has forced there to be compromise,” co-panelist Luke Bernstein, the president and CEO of the Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry, agreed. “No bill has been signed in the last four years that has not been bipartisan … we are in a much different environment now.”
Bernstein claimed that “significant positive economic movement in the last four years” were the result of bipartisan policies like lowering the corporate net income tax, which he credited for attracting recent major investments from Chobani, Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson and Merck. 
That cut was a “significant policy win” that was bipartisan, but was “led by the Republican Senate,” he said. “Without that force on that side, what does this come to?” 
He said that the legislative body “has been a pro-business majority … for a number of years,” and that having a divided government protected the commonwealth from extreme legislation. 
The first agenda item for Democrats, increasing the state’s minimum wage from $7.25 to $15/hour, required more nuance, he claimed. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“From a business community standpoint, we want Pennsylvanians to earn more. And while we should suggest — I would say — different approaches, I understand that this is a policy priority for lawmakers in this new trifecta,” said Bernstein. “From our standpoint, we’re certainly willing to work toward some type of compromise that … mitigates negative impacts on businesses.”
He pointed to a 2025 study from the National Federation of Independent Business, which projected “more than 101,000 jobs would be lost over the next 10 years,” more than half of which would be small business posts. 
The bill studied would have doubled the wage by 2026, rather than phasing in a $15/hour wage, and tie future increases to inflation. 
Bernstein pointed to other considerations, such as tip credits — which allows tips to be counted toward the minimum wage for tax purposes — and consistency with federal law.

Raising the minimum wage would also increase prices, he argued, running counter to campaign promises to make life more affordable for everyday Pennsylvanians. Supporters argue that higher wages “may lead to a small increase,” but employers will save money because turnover will fall and employee morale will improve.
He criticized several other measures advanced by House Democrats, like increasing nursing ratios, capping return on equity for publicly traded companies, paying unemployment benefits to striking workers and the “Fair Share Tax Plan,” the last of which he said would quadruple small business taxes. 
“These are all bills that have passed in the state House under Democratic control the last four years that are concerning,” he continued. 
 Data centers and maintaining power

A recent focus for the state chamber has been making “The Case for Data Centers” and turning public opinion, which has soured on projects in communities across the state. But voters overwhelmingly voted to restrict data centers in 44 ballot measures across the country, with just one pro-data center initiative advancing. 
“How we’re approaching this is, ‘Data centers are part of the critical infrastructure of today and tomorrow’s future economy.’ We truly cannot have the type of medical advancements, the type of communication opportunities, the type of innovation (we have) without a strong critical infrastructure. And data centers are a huge part of that.”
Voters across the country reject data centers

He emphasized a need to build responsibly, pointing to “efficient” technology that uses fewer resources. 
Bernstein said there was mis- and disinformation swirling around data centers, especially in some campaigns, but hopes “now that the temperature is lowered, we could really have a factual discussion on what are the challenges and how do we mitigate some of those challenges.” 
Yost noted that as many as 80% of people will say they oppose data center development, but he thinks “public opinion data overstates how much opposition there is.”
“Their knee-jerk (reaction) is to oppose it, but what they really want and what really bothers them is that they don’t know anything about them,” Yost continued.
Sentiment changed, he said, when people were given more information. People also don’t like feeling “forced” to accept a project. 
“I think part of the problem with data centers is no one knows what goes on inside them,” Yost said. “It’s the black box that people are reacting to, and I think there may be opportunities for that to change.” 
Putting “guardrails” around data centers was identified as a priority for a Democratic trifecta by Senate Minority Leader Jay Costa (D-Allegheny) on Wednesday. He is in line to hold a leadership position when the new Democratic majority takes power.

He and others will be under pressure to deliver quickly, though Yost wondered if Gov. Josh Shapiro’s rumored presidential aspirations might force some moderation. 
“They’re going to move faster than we typically see. There probably will be more legislative output than we’ve seen in recent years,” Yost said. “I think (Shapiro’s) primary brand, for lack of a better word, has been as someone who’s pretty pragmatic and tries to address issues in a way that solves problems. I wonder if that has a constraining force as he thinks of higher office.”
Democrats’ ability to hold on to their majorities in the 2028 election will also depend on whether Pennsylvanians feel like the party delivered on their promises — which may also act as a moderating force, he continued. 
“It really depends on what kind of progress voters think has been made between now and then,” Yost said. “The farther the legislature strays from enacting policies that people perceive as helping them, the more likely we are to be back here in two years having a webinar about how Republicans flip things back.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico utility regulators advance transfer of troubled water company that ran dry last year
description: New Mexico utility regulators on Thursday approved an expedited process for reviewing a potential takeover of a small-town water company that suffered a “complete” water outage in 2025.
text:
After experiencing a complete outage in 2025, Albuquerque hauled drinking water to Melody Ranch, a small community near Edgewood. The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission on Nov. 5, 2026, expedited a process that could let a regional water authority take control of Melody Ranch Water Co.'s operations. (Photo courtesy of County Line Feed and Supply)New Mexico utility regulators on Thursday approved an expedited process for reviewing a potential takeover of a small-town water company that suffered a “complete” water outage in 2025.
For much of this year, the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission has received regular updates about Melody Ranch Water Co., a utility that serves a small town outside of Edgewood. One of the company’s primary wells didn’t produce enough water to keep up with demand last year, resulting in a widespread water outage. In a 2025 email to the commission, company representatives said they had depleted much of their financial reserves to address the problem.
The commission unanimously voted Thursday to accelerate its review of a proposal that would let the Estancia, Moriarty, Williard and Torrance County Regional Water Association take control of Melody Ranch Water Co.’s operations. The commission will notify Melody Ranch customers by Nov. 9 and give interested parties until Nov. 16 to weigh in.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The commission could consider a final decision as soon as Dec. 3, according to a PRC news release.
If approved, the regional water association would take control of Melody Ranch’s water system, wells, equipment and water rights at no cost, but would not assume the company’s debts or add new fees to customers’ bills. It would also let the association build a new well and connect Melody Ranch’s system to Moriarty’s with a pipeline. Earlier this year, the state Legislature dedicated $4 million to water infrastructure improvements. 
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham had previously signed an executive order that facilitated hauling water to the community. However, that agreement is set to expire at the end of the year.
While commissioners voted on the expedited review with little discussion, they said finding a permanent solution — such as connecting Melody Ranch to Moriarty with a pipeline — is a top priority.
“I share the sense of urgency…for me, it’s just making sure that whatever we do sticks,” PRC Chair Pat O’Connell said during Thursday’s meeting.
Melody Ranch officials have already signed a transfer agreement with the regional water authority, according to a recent PRC filing, and in 2025 requested PRC support in expedited measures to restore service.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: August ICE raids stoked fear in Danbury schools, uneasy silence elsewhere
description: The Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation sent shockwaves through the city and changed how students perceive the agency's role.
text:
Erin Daly said the anxiety was already building at the start of summer break. That’s when some of her students told her they were “going into hiding” or said they wouldn’t be allowed to play outside.
“‘Getting caught’ and ‘rounded up’ were words that my students were using amongst themselves in conversations,” Daly said.
Then came the first week of school, and the Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation that sent shockwaves through the city of Danbury, where two-thirds of K-12 students are Latino. One story in particular grabbed the attention of students and teachers: Agents had approached a bus stop to detain parents dropping off their kids.
Daly is a third grade teacher and the president of NEA-Danbury, the district’s teachers union. She said after the ICE raids, one of her students refused to stand for the Pledge of Allegiance.
“I asked him why, and he said … ‘The flag does not keep me safe, and I’m not doing it anymore,’” Daly recalled. “It unleashed a huge assortment of emotion in my class from my other students.” Half the class, she said, was in tears.
“I’ll tell you one thing,” she said. “That bus stop incident from the first week of school traumatized so many of our kids, and I’m hearing that from all of my colleagues.”
“I’ve had students that have demonstrated a lot of negative behaviors in the classroom that they ordinarily wouldn’t have, or that they didn’t demonstrate in younger grades,” she added.
When asked for comment on those detentions, a representative for ICE shared a link to a statement released on Sept. 11, roughly two weeks after the Danbury arrests. The statement said agents with ICE’s Boston field office had arrested “118 illegal aliens,” of which “numerous have been charged with crimes.” It listed five specific individuals alongside their pending criminal charges or previous convictions.
The agency representative, who responded from a general email address and did not provide their name, did not say whether ICE is detaining green card holders or what individuals with legal residency can do to avoid being detained by agents.
NEA-Danbury Vice President Julian Schafer, who teaches high school social studies, said students’ opinions of ICE have changed markedly since the August enforcement operation. Last year, he said, a fair number of his students expressed the belief that ICE was focused on removing dangerous criminals from the country.
“I think the blinds on that were ripped off this first week of school,” Schafer said. “It was clear mass enforcement — you know, parents being taken from a bus stop.”
The view from behind the stage at a rally to protest ICE in Danbury, Connecticut on September 2, 2026. Credit: Molly Ingram / WSHU
On Sept. 2, Danbury teachers, advocates and city leaders held a rally alongside U.S. Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy to condemn ICE and show support for the city’s immigrant community. Schafer was one of the speakers. 
In his speech, he recounted how some of his students had seen ICE agents making arrests out the windows of their buses. A video of Schafer’s speech posted on Facebook drew over 100 comments, some defending ICE’s actions.
“Well, if they’re here legally, then these families have nothing to fear,” one user wrote.
“When laws getting enforced scares people, it implies that they know that they have been violating the law,” another wrote.
In early October, a group of masked protesters appeared outside Danbury police headquarters holding a sign reading “Keep New England White.” Daly described them as a “white nationalist neo-Nazi group.”
“Another level of hate being brought into our community,” she said in a text message.
The Connecticut Mirror spoke with several teachers in the Danbury area, and none expressed support for the scale of ICE arrests taking place under the Trump administration.
Schafer said he worries the detentions could potentially hurt Danbury’s tax base, which the city relies on to fund local services — including schools. “When, let’s say, an immigrant family is renting an apartment or a home, they’re paying a landlord property taxes through their rent,” Schafer said. “I’ve seen the local economy … struggle in the wake of these deportations because folks are not out patronizing local businesses.”
Julian Schafer goes over a documentary clip with students during a social studies class at Danbury High School West on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Outside Danbury, the impact of the late August ICE raids is less clear. In Windham, in Eastern Connecticut — which also has a majority-Latino student body — attendance during the first 10 days of school was actually 2% higher than the same period last year, according to District Superintendent Iris Gomero.
“The trends that I’m seeing is that our students are coming to school,” Gomero said. Those are “very intentional efforts that are happening from across the district. And it starts with students knowing that they’re going to be safe in our schools.”
That safety, Gomero said, comes in part through ensuring students and parents know the school’s policies around who is and is not allowed in the building.
“They know that if someone was to show up at our doors, that there’s a process and a protocol in place. That we would ask for ID, we would ask for judiciary subpoenas,” Gomero said. “And if that is not the case, then … we wouldn’t allow them to have access to our students.”
About 20 minutes west of Danbury via I-84 is Brewster, a New York town of fewer than 3,000 residents with a large Latino population. The proximity of the two municipalities means some people work in one and live in the other — as is the case for Tom Mullane, a Brewster social studies teacher and Danbury resident.
When immigration enforcement agents first started showing up in August, Mullane said, one of his close friends became afraid to leave the house, worried that the color of her skin could put her at risk of arrest.
Mullane said his friend is a Mexican citizen with permanent legal status in the United States. In the past, Mullane said, she was a visible participant in community events in Danbury, but ICE’s actions made her too scared to even shop for groceries alone.
The atmosphere in Brewster was entirely different. Although more than half of the students are Hispanic or Latino, Mullane said ICE wasn’t on their minds at the start of the school year. Instead, everyone’s attention was on something decidedly ordinary: The district’s new class schedule.
Below the surface, there are signs of disruption. Shannon Riley — a colleague of Mullane’s who also happens to be chair of the Brookfield Democratic Town Committee in Connecticut — said there are students in Brewster the district has yet to see this year.
“We’ve reached out to find out where they are and haven’t gotten any information,” Riley said. “They either have picked up and moved or they’re just afraid and don’t trust us to protect their identities.”
Mullane said he’s aware of a couple of isolated immigration cases. He’s written a letter of support for one student and talked to another whose relative was deported. And he feels there’s a sharp political divide in the community, as evidenced by opinions his students have expressed. 
Mullane said he and his colleagues have become skilled in moderating political conversations when they occur in the classroom. But ICE is one topic he’s not sure they can manage.
“I feel bad saying this, but I really, I’ve avoided it,” Mullane said. “I’m worried that [these conversations are] going to go badly, even though I know that I facilitate them well.”
And the relative calm of the moment may be fragile.
“If ICE does in Brewster what they just did in Danbury, call me back and we’ll be having a very different conversation,” Mullane said.

title: Vets Town Hall events will highlight veterans’ stories in November
description:
“The veterans who speak are our neighbors, colleagues, friends, and family members. Attending a Vets Town Hall is a chance to learn about some of the experiences that have been meaningful to them,” said Kristen Eaton, deputy director of Vets Town Hall.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vets Town Hall events will highlight veterans’ stories in November.
text:
Veteran Larry Stoneking speaks at a Vets Town Hall event in Colchester in 2022. Photo by Megan Humphrey/Waterbury Roundabout

This story was first published in the Waterbury Roundabout on Nov. 2, 2026.
The Vermont nonprofit organization Vets Town Hall will host 10 community storytelling events in Vermont and New Hampshire from Nov. 6-15 to increase community understanding between veterans and nonveterans.
The public is invited to attend, regardless of whether one has any ties to military service. At each Vets Town Hall, any veteran may speak about their experiences serving in the military and the impact of those experiences. At a Family Vets Town Hall, immediate family members of veterans and service members are invited to speak as well.
The events are free to attend and nonpolitical in nature; all perspectives are welcome.
“The stories shared at these events are as varied as the veterans who share them,” said Kristen Eaton, deputy director of Vets Town Hall, in an announcement. “This is a way for Vermonters, whatever their views on U.S. foreign policy, to support veterans as individuals. The veterans who speak are our neighbors, colleagues, friends, and family members. Attending a Vets Town Hall is a chance to learn about some of the experiences that have been meaningful to them.”
The Vets Town Hall concept was launched in 2015 by author Sebastian Junger (“The Perfect Storm,” “War,” “Tribe”) with U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton in Marblehead, Massachusetts. Two years later, Eaton organized the first Vets Town Hall in Vermont. In 2022, Junger, Eaton and Bristol resident and U.S. Marine Corps veteran Jon Turner founded the nonprofit Vets Town Hall, which works to increase understanding between veterans and nonveterans by facilitating these events both in Vermont and elsewhere around the U.S.
The upcoming series has dates in Barre on Saturday, Nov. 7, and South Burlington on Sunday, Nov. 8. Others are planned for Bennington, Brattleboro, Charlotte, Rutland, St. Johnsbury and Wilmington, as well as in Hanover, New Hampshire. The Family Vets Town Hall will take place in Middlebury on Nov. 12.
Veterans and family members of veterans who would like to speak at any of the November events can indicate their interest when registering. Time permitting, there will also be a chance at the events to sign up to speak.
Community partners for the events include public libraries, arts venues, veterans groups and community organizations. Vets Town Hall events are supported in part by Vermont Humanities and the Vermont Veterans Fund.
The full schedule of events and registration forms are online at vtvetstownhall.org. Registration is not required, but organizers appreciate it.

description: South Dakota utility regulators unanimously approved a rate increase Wednesday that will add about $16 to the typical Black Hills Energy residential customer’s monthly electric bill, while an additional request from the company to add a $20 surcharge is pending. The South Dakota Public Utilities Commission approved a settlement allowing the company to collec[...]
text:
South Dakota regulators approved a rate increase that will add about $16 to the typical Black Hills Energy residential customer’s monthly electric bill. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)South Dakota utility regulators unanimously approved a rate increase Wednesday that will add about $16 to the typical Black Hills Energy residential customer’s monthly electric bill, while an additional request from the company to add a $20 surcharge is pending.
The South Dakota Public Utilities Commission approved a settlement allowing the company to collect an additional $27.4 million annually from its roughly 75,000 customers in western South Dakota. That’s less than the $50.6 million the company sought, which would have been a $25 monthly increase for the average residential customer. 
The higher monthly increase took effect on an interim basis in August. The new rate will take effect in December, and customers will receive refunds for the overages they’ve paid the last several months.
Montana Public Service Commission postpones vote on merger of Black Hills Energy, NorthWestern

The commission’s staff negotiated the settlement with the company and a group representing large electric customers, including Monument Health; Pete Lien & Sons, which makes concrete and other construction materials; Wharf Resources, which operates a gold mine near Lead, and others. The settlement includes lesser increases for some types of commercial and industrial customers.
During a public meeting Wednesday in Pierre, Commissioner Kristie Fiegen described receiving numerous messages from Black Hills Energy customers who “are struggling with inflation and healthcare costs, and these are the people that necessarily didn’t have a lawyer at the table, but had the PUC staff at the table.” Fiegen said the staff did its due diligence in representing the residential customers.
In response to a commission question, staff attorney Amanda Reiss said the commission cannot reject a rate increase solely because customers are struggling. She said the commission is legally obligated to allow utilities to recover reasonable costs and earn a return on their investments, and she described the settlement as defensible.
The company has said the rate increase is necessary to cover infrastructure improvements, inflation and rising operating costs. The company’s rates had not increased since 2014.
The settlement prevents another rate increase from taking effect before August 2030. However, other charges on customers’ bills can still change.
The increase is separate from another pending Black Hills Energy request for a surcharge to recover costs associated with the $320 million Lange II natural gas power plant under construction in Rapid City.
That surcharge, which would add an estimated $19.70 per month to a typical residential bill, is scheduled to take effect on an interim basis in December. If the commission later rejects or reduces the surcharge, customers would receive refunds.

title: Wealth shouldn’t fast-track a private runway in Lincoln
description:
Regulators approved an airstrip for Beta’s CEO without giving neighbors and town officials an open hearing.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Wealth shouldn’t fast-track a private runway in Lincoln.
text:
Dear Editor,
Few would dispute that Beta Technologies is a boon to Chittenden County employment and its economic environment. However, the company’s CEO, Kyle Clark, would like to be able to fly to and from his $3.5 million home in Lincoln, a 45-minute drive from Beta’s headquarters at Burlington International Airport. The planes could include traditional fuel-powered aircraft and not just quiet, nonpolluting electric planes.
Vermont should hold public hearings about a private airport proposal, as has been done for many private landing area and airport applications in the past. To date, the Federal Aviation Administration, Vermont Transportation Board and Vermont Agency of Transportation have only considered the safety of the aircraft. 
Despite opposition from two local municipal boards and many abutting and near-adjacent residents, formal legal objections on behalf of 19 residents, and opposition from the Lincoln Selectboard and its lawyer, state and federal agencies have granted approvals without holding public hearings, conducting a public safety review or considering the safety of neighboring homes, local schools and public recreation areas and an immediately adjacent recreational trail.
I write this as a concerned Vermonter. I’m seeing the subversion of the public process, born from wealth and power, that may have negative repercussions in our state far beyond this incident.
Krister Adams
Waterbury, Vt.

text:
Jamie Davis, the Democratic candidate in Louisiana's U.S. Senate race, addresses supporters at his election night party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Baton Rouge. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)Jamie Davis’ narrow loss to U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, has given Louisiana Democrats hope they could unseat a slate of Republican statewide elected officials next year, including Gov. Jeff Landry. 
“Jeff Landry, you’re on notice, buddy,” Davis told his supporters on election night, later confirming to reporters he is mulling a run for governor. 
Davis’ loss to Letlow by about 25,000 votes — less than a two-point margin — was remarkably better than any Democrat has fared in a Senate race since former Sen. Mary Landrieu was elected to her last term in office in 2008. 
The narrow loss was among the strong Democratic turnout in this week’s midterm elections, when they were elected en masse in red states across the South. 
“Jeff Landry should [praise] God that he was not on the ballot right now because if he was on the ballot today, Jeff Landry would have been a one-term governor,” said Public Service Commissioner Davante Lewis, D-Baton Rouge. “But I think we’re still going to make him a one-term governor because the investment shows that the South is back.” 
Lewis, whose seat on the five-member PSC makes him the Democrat in Louisiana who represents the most constituents, is among the Democrats who could throw their hat in the ring for a gubernatorial run next year. Other candidates speculated to run include State Sen. Jay Luneau, D-Alexandria, former State Sen. Gary Smith, D-Norco, former state Treasurer candidate Dustin Granger and former Gov. John Bel Edwards, though his candidacy is dependent on whether a just-passed constitutional tweak restricting governors to two terms is determined to be retroactive. 
Landry and Republican Attorney General Liz Murrill both said Wednesday they are not worried about their re-election bids next year. 
“I will tell you that I feel very confident. I’m happy to put my record against the Democrats’ record next year. In fact, I look forward to it,” Landry said. “The senate candidate made some mention of me on the stage. I would implore him to get into the governor’s race. I’d be happy to debate him.” 
Unlike Letlow, who had to face a Democratic opponent head-on due to newly reinstated party primary elections for federal offices, Landry, Murrill and other state-level Republicans will face their challengers in a jungle primary. 
In these elections, all candidates, regardless of party, are on the same ballot. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the top-two vote getters advance to a runoff election. 
Usually that means the top Republican and top Democrat face-off, but in 2023, Landry was easily elected on the first ballot and did not have to face any candidate in a runoff. 
Landry was also elected with a much lower voter turnout than came out for the senate race. About 49% of registered voters in Louisiana turned out for the midterms, compared to about 36% who voted in 2023. 
The Black voter turnout was also much higher this election cycle. 
To repeat and build off of Davis’ success, Democrats are considering coalescing around a single Democrat. 
“We were all rowing in the same direction, and so we do need to figure out strategically how we recreate this same energy, the same synergy, because that’s one of the main reasons why we were so competitive,” progressive commentator Quenton Anthony Anderson said of Davis’ performance. 
Louisiana Democrats will have the benefit of Louisiana being one of a small number of states holding statewide elections next year. 
That means more attention, and more money, potentially coming Louisiana’s way. 
Davis received essentially no money from national Democratic donors and groups, such as the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee, leading many Democrats to wonder what could happen for Louisiana if there were more investment. 
“If Jamie loses by two points, we are going to get up Wednesday morning, and we are going to wonder where the hell were you [national Democrats]?” Democratic campaign consultant James Carville said in an interview with the Illuminator before the election. 
Julie O’Donoghue contributed to this report

text:
Matt McCarville, chief information officer for the State of Nebraska, at an inaugural public roundtable of Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen's cabinet. April 20, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s chief information officer, Matthew McCarville, has resigned after serving in the role since 2024. The position is part of Gov. Jim Pillen’s cabinet.
The announcement from the Governor’s Office came the day after the general election where voters reelected Pillen to another four years.
Pillen issued a brief media statement: “Matt has been with the state since 2024. I appreciate his public service in fulfilling the role of CIO. I wish Matt the best as he moves forward with his career.” 
The statement did not provide a reason or a comment from McCarville. 
In a LinkedIn post, McCarville called the return to his home state to lead its technology transformation an “extraordinary privilege” and said his team made “substantial progress.”
He described numerous achievements in the office during his tenure, including further modernizing decades-old systems, reducing reliance on contractors, expanding data analytics and developing statewide cybersecurity (he pointed out the deployment of the National Guard Cyber Protection team for the first time).
For now, McCarville said in the post, he was “enjoying some much needed time with my young family through the holidays and am excited to share where I’m going soon.”
Department of Administrative Services Director Lee Will will serve as interim head of the Office of the Chief Information Officer, a division that is under the DAS purview.
Additional information about filling the vacancy is to be provided later. Will told the Examiner that McCarville’s state service is to conclude in early December and that he will use his accrued vacation time through that date. 
McCarville earned a $262,502 annual salary, according to a public payroll database by Flatwater Free Press. He was not at his state office when a reporter called Thursday, and could not be reached for comment. 
Raised in Omaha and previously an information technology leader at the University of Colorado, McCarville had led the Nebraska information division since Pillen appointed him in April 2024 pending formal legislative approval.
During a July confirmation hearing before a legislative committee, lawmakers questioned McCarville’s ability to remain politically impartial in his government role and with staff and potential contractors. A point of discussion was an email that had been sent on McCarville’s behalf “encouraging” his workforce to participate in a legislative hearing on Pillen’s plan for property tax reduction.
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln at the time had sent a complaint to the Nebraska Accountability and Disclosure Commission identifying the email as part of a series of incidents by Pillen, his staff or executive branch that potentially violated state statute by misusing or commingling personal, campaign and public resources.
Even before Conrad and other committee members laid out concerns during the hearing, McCarville apologized for the email, calling it an “accident” and a “mistake.” He said he had asked his assistant to send the message, and didn’t mean to “advise a position.”
The Nebraska Legislature later voted 36-0 to confirm McCarville’s appointment (nine state senators chose not to vote). Conrad at that time said a “rather strange timing” of events clouded earlier discussion of McCarville’s “incredible” educational background and compelling personal story.

name: WyoFile
title: Google commits to spending $17B on AI data centers in Wyoming
description:
The tech giant promises to capture carbon dioxide emissions and "minimize strain on local water resources."
The post Google commits to spending $17B on AI data centers in Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Technology giant Google will build its first data center in southeast Wyoming, and potentially invest $17 billion in computing centers here.
The company confirmed its Equality State data center plans Thursday afternoon, “designed to deliver lasting benefits for Laramie County families and businesses.”
“We’re committed to partnering with communities to build data centers the right way,” the company said in a prepared statement. “We will pay for 100% of the power we use, and when we build data centers, we’ll cover the infrastructure needs directly driven by our growth.”
It was unclear as of press time Google’s timeframe for building the first facility and how long it might take to complete its $17 billion buildout near Terry Ranch Road in Laramie County. 
The news comes amid a whirlwind of data center speculation throughout much of the state, including in the Cheyenne area, where the industry is already established, with 10 in operation and more than a dozen on the planning books.
The bevy of data centers has provoked a backlash in Wyoming and elsewhere. Prominent politicians, including Secretary of State and soon-to-be Congressman Chuck Gray, have come out in opposition to new AI data centers in Wyoming. A University of Wyoming poll published last week found only 30% of residents here supported allowing the construction of more large data centers for AI technology.
Google says it is partnering with natural gas pipeline company Tallgrass Energy, electric utility Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and data center developer Related Digital for the “long-term” investment plan.
The first step is a 702-megawatt facility, powered by fuel-cell technology — converting natural gas into electricity — and a plan to permanently sequester electrical generation emissions deep underground, the company said. Tallgrass is already developing a carbon dioxide sequestration hub in Wyoming, it noted.
Regarding water consumption — a major concern among Wyomingites — Google said, “our Wyoming data center will be air-cooled to minimize strain on local water resources.”
Prior to Thursday’s announcement, Google officials met with “more than 200 residents in Laramie County” to gather feedback to tailor its plans, the company said.
Local officials have been in discussions with Google and its partners for the past year, Cheyenne City Councilman Larry Wolfe told WyoFile. Project partner Tallgrass has already begun some dirt work in preparation, he said, and Thursday’s announcement feels like a confirmation from Google.
“You know, we’re not easily dazzled anymore,” Wolfe said. “I will tell you that it’s $10 billion here, $20 billion there. What it’s done is it has made us really cynical about projects that aren’t of that magnitude.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Thursday: What races the AP has not yet called in contests for Senate and governor
description: Stickers are in place for voters at the G. Chastaine Flynt Memorial Library in Flowood during the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WASHINGTON — There are just four races for U.S. Senate and governor that The Associated Press has not yet called as of Thursday.
Contests in Alaska, Kansas and Mississippi have narrow margins with votes still outstanding even as the scale of Democrats’ midterm victory across the country comes into focus, ensuring the party will control the House and the Senate next year.
LIVE: 2025 Mississippi election results
In the House, 35 races in which party control of the seat is at stake have yet to be called.
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow the trailing candidate to close the gap.
In Mississippi’s Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom has seen his lead of a few dozen votes over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith grow to 1,145 votes with 96% of ballots counted.
Several thousand provisional ballots are expected to be counted in the race, and the state has until Nov. 10 to resolve those ballots. Those votes will be decisive. In 2022, the state counted about 5,700 provisional ballots. Mississippi does not have an automatic recount process, but a challenger can seek a court order for one.
The AP also has not called Alaska’s Senate contest between incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who had a 637-vote lead over Sullivan with an estimated 74% of votes counted. Peltola had 48.2% of the votes, to Sullivan’s 47.9%. Under Alaska law, if neither candidate gets more than 50% of the votes then it goes to ranked-choice tabulation.
Also in Alaska, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has a 20-percentage-point lead over Republican Bernadette Wilson in the governor’s race. Kreiss-Tomkins had 49.2% of the vote with an estimated 74% of the ballots counted.
Like the Senate contest, the governor’s election advances to another round if no candidate gets more than 50% of the votes.
In Kansas, Democrat Cindy Holscher has less than a 1-percentage-point lead over Republican Ty Masterson in the governor’s race. Holscher’s 7,045-vote lead with an estimated 99% of votes counted comes after Democrat Adam Hamilton became the first member of his party to win a Senate seat in the state in nearly a century.
Holscher and Masterson both serve in the state Senate, where the Republican serves as its president.

He will lead a caucus of just 15 Republicans after Democrats swept the election on Tuesda[...]
text:
Sen. Julian Bradley (R-New Berlin) was chosen to lead Senate Republicans. Bradley speaks at a press conference in February 2025. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Senate Republicans chose Sen. Julian Bradley (R-New Berlin) to lead them as minority leader when lawmakers return in January following the midterm elections.
Bradley succeeds Senate Majority Leader Devin LeMahieu (R-Oostburg), who decided against running for reelection. He will lead a caucus of just 15 Republicans after Democrats swept the election on Tuesday night. Democrats added three seats to their caucus, winning a total of 18 seats to take the  Senate majority for the first time since the 2008-09 legislative session. 
Bradley said in a statement that the election results had “changed the math in the Senate, but they didn’t change what we believe or who we work for.” 
Three Republicans were reportedly running for the position, according to WisPolitics. They were  Sen. Mary Felzkowski (R-Tomahawk), who had served as Senate president, Sen. Patrick Testin (R-Stevens Point), who led Senate Republicans’ election efforts and had served as president pro tempore, and Sen. Eric Wimberger (R-Gillett).
Bradley was not one of the names reported in WisPolitics ahead of the caucus meeting, but he emerged as the chosen leader. He has served in the state Senate since 2020 and is the first Black Republican to serve in the Wisconsin Senate. 
“Wisconsin families still want safe communities, good jobs and a government that lives within its means. We’re going to keep fighting for those goals and our state,” Bradley said. “I’m grateful to my colleagues for the trust they’ve placed in me. Leading this caucus is a responsibility I don’t take lightly.” 
Bradley said the caucus will be focused on “protecting taxpayers and expanding opportunity for every Wisconsinite” in the new session. During his time in office, he has served on the Joint Finance Committee, as the vice chair of the administrative rules committee and as the chair of the utilities, technology and tourism committee. 
Bradley, 45, was born in Baltimore before moving to Wisconsin in 1992. He was previously a professional wrestler and a realtor and operations manager for Northwestern Mutual and CenturyLink.

name: VTDigger
title: Lighten up and let ’em fly
description:
An airstrip and float planes have shared a quiet Grand Isle road for years without trouble, so why can’t Lincoln live with a 900-foot runway the FAA has already cleared?
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Lighten up and let ’em fly.
text:
Dear Editor,
I keep reading with fascination about the ongoing contention over Beta Technologies CEO Kyle Clark’s desire to build an airstrip on his land. I live in Grand Isle, where there is an airstrip on my road as well as float planes on the lake. 
There has never been a problem. Not one. The noise is minimal and certainly far quieter than the F-35 training runs that can happen here several times a year. Seeing a plane in the air so close is almost magical. And when our neighbor sees us, he gently tips the wings in greeting and flies off, and we don’t hear the plane again for hours. These small planes and probably some electric planes — which kind of puts a crimp in the noise complaint issue — are hardly going to ruin anyone’s day. 

READ MORE

I’m having a hard time understanding the fear around this. If Clark is a licensed pilot and the Federal Aviation Administration has signed off on the plan, why is that not good enough? Is the expectation that there will be dozens of flights every day? The planes that fit a 900-foot runway are quieter than the overnight commercial flights that seem to fly over many days a week at night when Clark will be prohibited from flying. 
Lighten up and let ’em fly. 
Josie LeavittGrand Isle, Vt.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Death row inmate is competent for execution, SC Supreme Court says
description: Attorneys for another inmate at the end of his appeals asked for a pause in issuing death warrants for the winter holidays.
text:
The state death chamber at the prison complex in Columbia, S.C., as seen from the witness room. (Courtesy of the S.C. Department of Corrections)COLUMBIA — A death row inmate convicted of raping and killing his neighbor is competent for execution, the South Carolina Supreme Court decided this week.
The high court also turned down a rehearing request for inmate Steven Bixby, who the court already decided was competent.
Gary Terry, 58, was convicted in 1997 of raping and killing Urai Jackson in her West Columbia home two years yearlier. He ran out of ordinary appeals in his case in 2022, but his execution has been on hold so that judges could decide whether he had an intellectual disability.
A Lexington County judge last year said he didn’t, and the state Supreme Court agreed Wednesday.
The court also turned down Bixby’s latest appeal. The court had already ruled Bixby, who was sentenced to death in 2007 for fatally shooting two police officers during a daylong standoff at his parents’ Abbeville home, was competent for execution.
Bixby’s attorneys said they intend to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, according to a Wednesday court filing.
Whether any executions are imminent, though, is unclear. Attorneys for Bixby asked justices Wednesday to wait until after the holidays to issue a death warrant.
If Bixby receives a death warrant Friday, which is the earliest possible day the high court could issue it, his execution would be scheduled for Dec. 4.
That would require his attorneys, the state’s attorneys and state Supreme Court staff to work through the week of Thanksgiving, as death warrants usually bring on a flurry of last-minute appeals.
“The preparation for and carrying out of an execution during a time of year that is so important to families will take a substantial toll on all involved,” Bixby’s attorneys wrote.
The court has paused executions for the holidays before.
In 2024, amid a spate of back-to-back executions, justices agreed to halt all death warrants in November and December. Bixby’s attorneys asked for a similar pause this time, which would push back any potential warrants until at least Jan. 8.
SC Supreme Court denies death row inmate’s appeal of incompetence

Gary Terry’s case
Terry’s attorneys argued he had an intellectual disability because of brain damage likely caused by a small stroke. That damage affected parts of his brain responsible for controlling focus and behavior, his attorneys argued in court documents.
A Lexington County judge decided the attorneys failed to prove Terry had enough damage in his brain to keep him from execution. Terry’s legal team appealed to the state’s highest court, which agreed with the circuit court judge in a one-sentence order issued Wednesday.
People with intellectual disabilities generally can’t be put to death. The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled executing someone with an intellectual disability is cruel and unusual punishment, which violates the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment.
According to court filings, Terry struggled significantly in school as a child and spent several years in special education classes before dropping out of school in ninth grade. Between then and his 22nd birthday, Terry suffered multiple head injuries, including from sniffing glue, falling out of a tree, and crashing his motorcycle, his attorneys wrote.

Court documents also say that Terry struggled as an adult to care for himself, do basic chores around the house, or hold down a job.
Experts at the time of Terry’s 1997 trial and again in 2024 found his intellectual functioning to be in the “low-average” range, according to court filings.
Evidence in 2024 relied on little more than anecdotes and bad grades in school, which don’t rise to the level of making someone incompetent for execution, lawyers for the state attorney general’s office argued to the state’s highest court.
After more than a year of written arguments from attorneys on either side of the case, the state Supreme Court’s justices agreed.
Wednesday’s order said only that justices voted to deny the appeal. It was not signed by the justices or include a vote tally.

title: ‘He could barely hear me’: Deacon recounts Indiana death row inmate’s final hours
description: Jeffrey Weisheit’s spiritual adviser said prison staff kept him outside the condemned man’s cell during their final hours of prayer together, then allowed him only a few minutes at Weisheit’s side in the execution chamber early Thursday. Deacon Brian Nosbusch, who had ministered to Weisheit for about 13 years, described struggling to communicate through thic[...]
text:
Deacon Brian Nosbusch speaks outside the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis on Oct. 19, 2026. Weisheit’s longtime spiritual adviser urged clemency ahead of the scheduled Nov. 5 execution. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Jeffrey Weisheit’s spiritual adviser said prison staff kept him outside the condemned man’s cell during their final hours of prayer together, then allowed him only a few minutes at Weisheit’s side in the execution chamber early Thursday.
Deacon Brian Nosbusch, who had ministered to Weisheit for about 13 years, described struggling to communicate through thick glass before being separated from him for roughly 90 minutes on Wednesday night. When prison staff brought him into the execution chamber, Weisheit was already strapped to a gurney with intravenous lines in his left arm.
Nosbusch said the execution appeared “calm.” But he left Indiana State Prison troubled by the restrictions on their time together and how little of the process anyone outside the execution team could see.
Former Rep. Andrew Ireland, a Republican death penalty supporter, also called Thursday for greater transparency in the process.
Death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit (Photo courtesy the Indiana Department of Correction)
“My prayer was through that window,” Nosbusch told the Indiana Capital Chronicle of their hours outside the chamber. He leaned toward a small opening in the glass to speak and pray with Weisheit.
“He could barely hear me, and I had to sit outside the cell,” Nosbusch continued.
His account offers a closer look at an execution that other witnesses could see for only three minutes through a small, tinted window. Still unknown are when Indiana began administering pentobarbital, how much was used and what happened before witnesses were allowed to look inside.
Hours after the execution, Gov. Mike Braun defended carrying out Weisheit’s sentence but suggested that state lawmakers could examine Indiana’s execution secrecy provisions and difficulties acquiring lethal injection drugs.
“When it comes to even the transparency, that evidently is engulfed in our own code, that might be worthy of a legislator looking at,” Braun said Thursday morning.
The Department of Correction also released a temperature log Thursday showing six of seven recorded readings below the log’s stated target range of 68 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit in the days preceding the execution.
DOC had not yet provided the Capital Chronicle with an updated inventory log showing how much pentobarbital was used for Weisheit’s execution, however.
Weisheit was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. Central Standard Time for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a 2010 house fire near Evansville. Their mother, Lisa, was working overnight and had left the children in his care.
Victims were also allowed up to five witnesses in a separate room but their identities are protected.
Braun denied clemency Monday. His office did not publicly announce a decision on the attorneys’ separate requests for a temporary reprieve and an independent investigation of Indiana’s lethal injection procedures and drug procurement before the execution.
Praying through glass
Nosbusch, a Catholic deacon in the Diocese of Gary, said he visited Weisheit about twice a month for years and increased those visits to three times a week during his final month.
They talked about reconciliation, forgiveness and anger. They prayed for Weisheit’s parents and sister, for the children he killed and for the children’s mother and family.
About three months before the execution, Nosbusch said, a priest visited the prison to baptize and confirm Weisheit and give him Holy Communion.
Nosbusch had also served as spiritual adviser to Roy Lee Ward, whom Indiana executed in October 2025. During Ward’s final evening, he said, he was permitted to sit inside the holding cell with him.
He expected similar access Wednesday.
Indiana executes Jeffrey Weisheit for 2010 murders of two children

Instead, after arriving at the prison around 6 p.m., Nosbusch said a masked staff member told him he had not been informed that the deacon could enter Weisheit’s cell. Nosbusch said his requests to contact a supervisor did not resolve the issue.
Nosbusch said he had called the prison’s new warden, Erik Kruper, several times beforehand to clarify arrangements for the execution. He did not know why staff had not received instructions allowing him inside Weisheit’s cell.
He sat outside the glass, leaning toward a small opening to make himself heard. He could pass Communion through the opening and hold Weisheit’s hand, but said the arrangement made conversation and prayer difficult.
Nosbusch said prison staff stood nearby talking and repeatedly went in and out of the room, making it harder to hear Weisheit or have a private exchange.
“It was not personal,” Nosbusch said. “It was not anything.”
He said Weisheit tried to reassure him as he grew frustrated.
“Jeff calmed me down,” Nosbusch recalled. “He said, ‘Brian, don’t worry about it. It’ll be fine.’”
Nosbusch said he plans to write to prison leadership after taking more time to reflect. He wants to explain why he found their final hours together disappointing and ask for greater consideration of the spiritual adviser’s role.
At about 11 p.m., staff moved Nosbusch into another room at the state prison, he said. He waited there until approximately 12:30 a.m., wondering at times whether the governor might have granted a reprieve.
Nosbusch did not see Weisheit being moved into the chamber, restrained or fitted with intravenous lines.
Once brought inside, he said, he immediately began the prayers and Gospel reading he had prepared. He placed a hand on Weisheit’s shoulder and later touched his hand.
Nosbusch estimated he was in the chamber for six minutes at most.



Quotation







It was not personal. It was not anything.


– Deacon Brian Nosbusch


He said he saw two intravenous lines in Weisheit’s left arm but did not examine the right. Weisheit had told him beforehand that he intended to keep his eyes closed, Nosbusch said, and the deacon said he did not see him open them.
Nosbusch described a slight movement of Weisheit’s head when he touched his shoulder, followed by stillness. Toward the end, he said, Weisheit’s hand felt cold and his lips appeared to be turning blue.
Nosbusch was escorted from the chamber before DOC’s reported time of death and did not witness the official pronouncement.
“But it was very peaceful — very peaceful, from what I saw,” Nosbusch said.
He remained in the chamber only briefly after the witness room blinds closed.
“I was in there about a minute longer, so I prayed again and blessed him,” Nosbusch said. “And that was it. Then they took me out.”
The Capital Chronicle’s reporter, who witnessed Weisheit’s execution, saw no visible movement during the three-minute viewing period. The blinds opened at 12:34 a.m. and closed at 12:37 a.m., eight minutes before DOC’s reported time of death.
DOC spokesperson Noelle Russell declined to provide a detailed execution timeline early Thursday morning, citing security concerns, but said the process begins shortly after midnight and proceeds slowly to ensure nothing is rushed. Asked whether Weisheit showed any reaction suggesting complications, Russell said, “Not at all.”
“I am told he did not move at all,” she said.
Indiana does not guarantee journalists access to executions. The Capital Chronicle, which is challenging those restrictions alongside other news organizations, was the only media outlet to witness Weisheit’s execution. Its reporter attended via Weisheit’s personal witness list.
New storage records — and more questions
The November temperature log DOC provided Thursday lists a desired range of 68 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit — the same recommended storage range listed in prescribing information for Nembutal, the brand-name pentobarbital product.
The state received six 50-milliliter vials of pentobarbital on Oct. 29.
Its seven entries run from Nov. 1 through the morning of Nov. 4. Readings range from 65 to 68 degrees, with only one — the evening entry for Nov. 2 — reaching the stated range.
Story continues below.
20261104121633961_Redacted
 
Nembutal’s prescribing information also permits brief temperature excursions between 59 and 86 degrees.
All seven readings fall within that broader interval. But the twice-daily entries do not show how long temperatures remained below 68 degrees, and the log does not indicate whether those conditions affected the drugs’ quality.
The Capital Chronicle was still awaiting an updated drug inventory to determine how much pentobarbital was used in Weisheit’s execution as of late Thursday. Earlier inventory records obtained by the newsroom have documented the state’s purchases, use and destruction of execution drugs.
Dr. Jonathan Groner, an emeritus professor of clinical surgery at Ohio State University’s College of Medicine, said the limited viewing period left important questions about the procedure unanswered.

“When pentobarbital is properly administered as an IV bolus, it should cause rapid unconsciousness — 30 to 60 seconds,” Groner told the Capital Chronicle.
Groner did not attend the execution. Neither the witnesses’ observations nor Nosbusch’s account make clear when the drug was administered or whether Weisheit was conscious while witnesses could see him.
Weisheit’s attorneys had sought testing and storage records before the execution, raising concerns about the Indianapolis pharmacy they identified as the supplier, Pharmaneek Inc. The pharmacy is on probation and faces further disciplinary proceedings. Those proceedings do not establish that the execution drugs were contaminated or ineffective.
The Indiana Professional Licensing Agency confirmed Thursday that Pharmaneek’s disciplinary hearing has been postponed to Dec. 14 after its new counsel requested a continuance last week because of a scheduling conflict.
Before the execution, DOC said it remained confident in its ability to carry out the sentence humanely. The attorney general’s office likewise expressed confidence it could proceed safely and lawfully. Both cited state confidentiality law in declining to discuss supplier information.
Braun signals possible legislative review
Asked Thursday morning whether lawmakers should revisit capital punishment, Braun said the three executions carried out during his administration involved clear cases and lengthy court proceedings.
“I think going forward with it made perfect sense,” Braun said. “I think most Hoosiers would agree with it.”
He said the death penalty was not a particularly high priority but could be examined, including the transparency restrictions written into state law.
“But I think here, the way that drug is acquired certainly looks like it’s not easy, and the whole discussion probably needs to be looked at more broadly, and we’ll see where that goes,” Braun said.
The discussion would return to a Legislature changed by Tuesday’s election, which defeated two Republicans who approached capital punishment from different directions but supported greater scrutiny.
Gov. Mike Braun speaks to reporters at the Statehouse Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)
Ireland, R-Indianapolis, who lost his reelection bid Tuesday night, additionally called attention Thursday to the Legislature’s failure to pass execution transparency language.
“One regret this last legislative session was not getting our death penalty transparency language passed,” he wrote.
Ireland said supporting capital punishment should also mean allowing reporters to observe whether executions are carried out lawfully, rather than requiring news organizations to sue for access.
Rep. Bob Morris, R-Fort Wayne, who also lost Tuesday, has been a vocal Republican opponent of capital punishment and sought more transparency around execution procedures.
After unsuccessfully seeking repeal in 2025, Morris introduced legislation this year that would have required execution teams to consist of volunteer legislators and made their names public records.
Lawmakers also considered expanding the methods Indiana could use to carry out death sentences. A House firing squad bill fell short in a narrow 48-47 vote in January, failing to secure the required 51 votes. A separate Senate proposal stalled without a committee vote.
Despite those unsuccessful efforts, DOC confirmed to the Capital Chronicle in June that the new prison in Westville was designed to accommodate both lethal injection and firing squad executions. The agency declined to provide design details, citing security concerns.
Indiana currently authorizes only lethal injection.
Groner said the public has an interest in understanding how the state carries out death sentences.
“If capital punishment is portrayed as a public good, then the public should be allowed to know how executions are performed,” he said.
For Nosbusch, the immediate concern is continuing a ministry that has taken him inside the prison for more than two decades. He intends to keep visiting men on death row and in protective custody.
After leaving the prison early Thursday, he sat in his car to gather his thoughts, then stopped for coffee before driving home.
Nosbusch described Weisheit as a friend. Accompanying him through the execution was difficult, he said, but he was grateful he had been there.
“It makes it hard,” he said. “But I’m so glad I did it.”
