name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Unlikely political newcomer unseats NC powerhouse despite big challenges
description: LaKesha Womack is anything but a textbook political candidate. She had never run for office before, had very little funding or outside support, and had even been unhoused at one point. She also has an outstanding felony charge that could theoretically leave her unable to vote in the U.S. House.  None of that stopped her […]
text:
Lakesha Womack. right, and Shivawn Mitchell, left. pose with campaign sign. (Photo: Courtesy of campaign)LaKesha Womack is anything but a textbook political candidate. She had never run for office before, had very little funding or outside support, and had even been unhoused at one point. She also has an outstanding felony charge that could theoretically leave her unable to vote in the U.S. House. 
None of that stopped her from riding a blue wave on Election Day to unseat one of the state’s most powerful politicians, Republican U.S. Rep. Tim Moore, who, before being elected to Congress nearly two years ago, served five terms as speaker of the N.C. House.
Former N.C. House Speaker Tim Moore (Photo: NCGA.gov)
Moore was one of the architects of the state’s 2023 redistricting process, which redrew many districts to favor Republicans. His district was designed to be a safe seat district for the GOP.
The redistricting maneuver backfired.
NC Newsline reached out to Moore for comment, but did not receive a response from him before this story was published.
Womack, a political newcomer who moved to North Carolina in 2016 to campaign for Hillary Clinton and never left, credited the victory to “amazing volunteers and county party chairs” who helped us “get out and knock on doors and have conversations” with voters in the 14th Congressional  District.
“We had lots of meet-and-greets and town halls, and we held listening sessions,” Womack said. “Right now, there are so many people who just feel like they’re not being heard and that their issues are not being taken seriously.” 
Womack is a consultant who helps design loan products for underserved small businesses. She’s a native of Alabama and a graduate of Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee.
The newly elected congresswoman’s district includes Gastonia, Shelby, Morgantown, and parts of far south Charlotte.
Former Rep Wesley Harris, D-Mecklenburg. (Photo: NCGA.gov)
Wesley Harris, former state lawmaker and chairman of the Mecklenburg County Democratic Party, said Womack’s win was a welcome surprise.
“When you look at the map, it shouldn’t be competitive, but when you started looking at early votes, the early vote was heavily, heavily favoring Democrats in that entire district,” Harris said. “LaKesha ran a great campaign. She didn’t have a bunch of money, but she went everywhere, and she talked to everybody.”
Across North Carolina, Harris said Democrats won in places they shouldn’t have won. 
“We ran some great people, but that only comes from just a backlash of voters who were sick and tired of those in power,” Harris said. “It was a full repudiation of the Republican Party, and it was the biggest signal ever that folks were ready for a change.” 
Womack’s decision to enter the congressional race revealed a nearly decade-old skeleton in her closet, which Moore highlighted in campaign ads.
Womack was served with a felony warrant at a campaign event last month. The warrant stated that she rented a 2019 Toyota Corolla from Budget Car Rental in October 2019 and did not return it by the agreed-upon date.
Womack’s legal troubles have raised questions about her ability to serve if convicted. Members of Congress convicted of an offense that could result in two or more years’ imprisonment cannot vote or participate in committee activities, according to an internal rule. Those privileges can be restored if the member is reelected to Congress. 
Her first appearance hearing is scheduled for Nov.10.
Voters lined up at the Durham County South Regional Library for the last day of early voting on Oct. 31, 2026.(Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)
Womack did not respond to a request for comment on the matter Thursday before this story was published. She did, however, address it on her campaign website last month.
“Candidates for public office should be held accountable, and voters deserve transparency,” Womack said. “Accountability, however, must be grounded in facts, fairness, and due process rather than speculation or sensationalism. As an attorney, Congressman Moore knows that any ongoing legal matter should be addressed through the appropriate legal process.”
Harris said he hopes the legal matter can be resolved quickly.
“We’re going to take that one day at a time and let the process work itself out,” he said. 
On the campaign trail, Womack also revealed to voters that she became unhoused with her young son after moving to North Carolina in 2016, when a medical emergency related to her Type 1 diabetes left her hospitalized in intensive care.
“I know firsthand what it’s like to experience some of these challenges,” Womack said. “A lot of these situations, from food insecurity to housing insecurity, are things that I’ve had to deal with myself.” 
Access to health care has been a major plank in her platform because, like her, too many Americans are just one medical crisis away from financial ruin, she said.
“When we’re looking at how policy decisions impact these issues, it is important to have people at the table who have actually dealt with these issues so that we can understand what the solutions are, and we’re not just throwing money at a problem versus giving people the help that they actually need,” she said.
Womack said she was encouraged to see so many Black women run competitive races in districts where “people would traditionally think that they couldn’t win.”
She believes Moore took reelection for granted.
“Tim Moore was not out doing town halls,” she said. “He wasn’t out talking to the voters, and he wasn’t answering for a lot of the votes that he had taken while he was in Congress, and so it allowed me to provide a great contrast to my leadership style to his.”
Strong Democratic turnout flips at least 5 US House seats across North Carolina

Womack doesn’t discount the role the Democrats’ historic night played in her win. The party won control of the House and Senate in what pundits say was an unqualified rebuke of President Donald Trump’s policies, many of which have been blamed for making life more expensive.
“I focused my campaign on being present for the community and making sure that they knew that I was not only listening to them, but also helping to connect their issues with actual policy decisions that were being made in Washington, D.C.,” Womack said
Womack says she’s eager to head to Washington to begin delivering on campaign promises. But she said voters should “temper their expectations.” 
“Just trust that we have a great group of people around the country who are going to Washington, and we really want to straighten out a lot of the chaos that led people to vote in such record numbers across the country,” Womack said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Senate Republicans choose new leaders as election losses reshape chamber
description: Missouri Senate Republicans will return to Jefferson City in January with fewer seats, a flood of newcomers and new leaders who say they heard voters’ frustration Tuesday — even as they have yet to settle on what to do about it. Sen. Jason Bean, a Republican from Holcomb chosen Thursday to serve as Senate president […]
text:
State Sen. Nick Schroer, a Republican from Defiance, right, speaks Thursday with state Sen.-elect Sam Alexander, a Republican from Bolivar, after being elected Senate Majority Leader for the upcoming session (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Missouri Senate Republicans will return to Jefferson City in January with fewer seats, a flood of newcomers and new leaders who say they heard voters’ frustration Tuesday — even as they have yet to settle on what to do about it.
Sen. Jason Bean, a Republican from Holcomb chosen Thursday to serve as Senate president pro tem, said the election results made clear the party needs to reassess its approach.
“They weren’t real fond of what we’ve been doing,” Bean said of voters. “So we’re going to look at changes.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sen. Nick Schroer, a St. Charles County Republican selected as majority floor leader, offered a more specific diagnosis: Republicans lost because they failed to deliver on their promises, not because their agenda was too conservative.
“Voters are sick and tired of spineless politicians that promise the world and produce nothing,” Schroer said.
Democrats, meanwhile, believe the election was a rejection of the GOP’s priorities, not simply its ability to accomplish them.
“Voters are screaming that they don’t like what Republicans are doing in Jefferson City,” said Democratic Sen. Stephen Webber of Columbia, who was chosen Thursday as minority floor leader.
The competing interpretations will help shape a legislative session that begins under significantly different political circumstances.
Democrats flipped two Senate seats Tuesday, defeating Republicans in eastern Jackson County and Springfield to end the GOP’s two-thirds supermajority. Republicans will hold 22 of the chamber’s 34 seats.
The losses were part of a broader Republican setback that also saw Democrats flip 16 House seats and end the GOP’s supermajority in that chamber.
‘We’ve got to listen’: Missouri Republicans confront fallout from historic election losses

House Republicans interviewed Wednesday were divided over whether their losses reflected national political headwinds or voters’ frustration with an unpopular legislative agenda. Some have urged the party to abandon personal pet projects and focus on issues that matter more to constituents.
Schroer rejected the suggestion that Republicans need to move toward the political center, arguing that even moderate GOP lawmakers suffered defeats Tuesday.
Democrats didn’t win on Tuesday, Schroer said, “I think, in my opinion, Republicans lost.”
He said Republicans should focus on delivering tax cuts, education reform and policies addressing public safety and the cost of living.
Bean was less willing to draw conclusions about what went wrong. Asked specifically whether he shared Schroer’s view that the party needed to be bolder rather than more moderate, he declined to embrace either interpretation.
“Let’s let the dust settle,” Bean said. “Let’s take a look at everything, look at what the people voted for, what they didn’t vote for.”
Republicans will gather next week in Kansas City to discuss their priorities for the coming session.
Webber argued the losses cannot be explained solely by a national political backlash against Republicans.
He pointed to the overwhelming defeat in August of Republican-backed proposals to overhaul the state’s tax system and make constitutional amendments harder to pass, followed Tuesday by voters rejecting a proposed abortion ban and a Republican congressional map.
“It was a national dumpster fire that Missouri Republicans poured gas on,” Webber said.
The election also imposed new constraints on the GOP’s legislative agenda.
Voters approved Amendment 6, which sharply limits lawmakers’ power to alter citizen-approved measures and prohibits them from weakening the initiative petition process. Any legislative proposal to change a voter-approved initiative now requires support from 80% of both chambers before going back to voters.
Schroer said Republicans still intend to pursue changes to the initiative petition process and policies aimed at restricting abortion, despite voters rejecting their proposals on both issues.
But he acknowledged Amendment 6 could complicate those efforts, saying attorneys are examining its legal implications and the possibility of a court challenge.
“What happens with Amendment 6,” Schroer said. “I think will dictate what happens with the life issue in and of itself.”
 A Senate full of newcomers

Beyond the political disagreements, the new leadership team faces the practical challenge of managing a chamber in which nearly half the senators will be newcomers.
Bean said his immediate priority is building relationships, particularly among lawmakers who have never served together.
“I’m a big believer in getting to know people outside of politics,” he said, describing plans for dinners and opportunities for senators to learn about one another’s families.
He also wants incoming senators to spend time presiding over the chamber and learning its procedural rules.
Schroer, whose role as majority floor leader will give him control over which legislation comes up for debate, promised a “no nonsense” approach to negotiations.
“If you’re going to negotiate in bad faith, lying, you know, dragging your feet to try and address an issue, there are going to be consequences,” he said.
Missouri Republicans suffer biggest electoral setback in a generation

But he also stressed the importance of communication across party lines, citing his friendship with former Democratic Sen. Karla May of St. Louis as an example of lawmakers who can clash over policy while maintaining a productive relationship.
The budget could provide an early test.
Schroer said lawmakers must confront the state’s fiscal problems after years of spending he believes was excessive.
He pointed to video lottery terminal legislation as another issue that will require negotiations across party lines.
“The budget iss going to be key,” he said. “That’s one that we’re going to have to have buy-in from both parties.”
Sen.-elect Keri Ingle, a Lee’s Summit Democrat who defeated Republican House Speaker Jon Patterson on Tuesday, agreed that the budget should be a priority but blamed Republican fiscal policies for threatening public education and Medicaid.
She also identified child welfare as an opportunity for bipartisan cooperation, saying she intends to pursue recommendations from Gov. Mike Kehoe’s task force examining the state’s troubled child protection system.
“I certainly hope that people can put politics aside and do what’s best for the children of the state,” Ingle said.
Webber said he is optimistic about working with the incoming Republican leadership, provided the majority is willing to focus on affordability and public schools.
The enlarged Democratic caucus, he said, will bring additional experience and a stronger voice to those debates.
But the greater opportunity may come from the sheer number of new senators, giving both parties a chance to reconsider how the chamber operates after years of bitter partisan and intraparty disputes.
“I think it’s a really good opportunity for the Senate,” Webber said. “It’s an opportunity for us to sort of reset.”
The Independent’s Rudi Keller contributed to this story.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas United uses election to build familiarity and support for new party
description: TOPEKA — Political candidates who receive 4% of the vote aren’t usually happy about the accomplishment. But for Scott Morgan, his success as a United Kansas candidate isn’t — yet — all about the numbers. It’s about building recognition for a new political party. “For a five-month campaign with very little money, I feel very […]
text:
Scott Morgan, shown here speaking at a Leading Age candidate forum on Sept. 24, 2026, in Salina, was pleased with his secretary of state campaign for United Kansas. Although he garnered few votes, he was able to familiarize people around the state with the new centrist political party. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Political candidates who receive 4% of the vote aren’t usually happy about the accomplishment.
But for Scott Morgan, his success as a United Kansas candidate isn’t — yet — all about the numbers. It’s about building recognition for a new political party.
“For a five-month campaign with very little money, I feel very good about the response that we got out there,” he said.
Morgan received 4% of the vote in the secretary of state race, which hasn’t been officially decided. The count is close between Democrat Jennifer Day with 47% of the vote and Republican Pat Proctor with 48%, as of Thursday.
As executive director of United Kansas, Morgan dismissed the idea that his fledgling party pulled votes from Day. He said people called him a “spoiler” and caused her to lose the race.
“The ones really worried about spoiling are really pretty hardcore Democrats or Republicans,” Morgan said. “Most people don’t understand why we don’t have more choices.”
He said he received several “nasty notes” from Democrats criticizing him for running and pulling votes from Day, although he pointed out that a Democrat has only won the secretary of state race once in 165 years — in 1948. That, Morgan added, was because a guy with the same last name ran against the 81-year-old incumbent in a four-way race.
In looking at votes reported so far, Morgan said, he took more votes from Proctor than Day.
“If you take out my votes and distribute them to the other two based on how they did in each of those counties, Proctor’s numbers go up,” Morgan said, noting that he did better in the counties outside of Kansas’ five largest, which was where Day dominated as a Democrat.
“She was 70% in the five largest, and 29% out there, and so they look at my 45,000 votes, almost 46, and think, well, that’s the difference,” he said. “But that so misunderstands Kansas voters. How many would just never vote for her? How many don’t like either party and vote for me?”
Choice is better for Kansans, Morgan said, and his party wants to give that to voters.
Founding a new party is a long process, he said, and the party had to run at least one political candidate and get 1% of the vote to meet state requirements. He ran because he had past political experience, after running and losing in the 2014 GOP primary for secretary of state against Kris Kobach. He also lost as the GOP nominee for the 2nd District congressional seat in 1990.
“The idea was we wouldn’t run other candidates. We would use this opportunity to start getting the name known, and as I traveled around the state to build pockets for it,” Morgan said. “The existing parties have precinct people everywhere, or at least county chairs everywhere, and we have none of that.”
He called that work a “major success.” 
“I had very good luck out there finding people, connecting with them, giving them a sense that we had direction at this point because we have this two-year, we have a four-year plan,” Morgan said. “We knew this wasn’t going to happen overnight, and people really liked that.”
United Kansas was recognized as a political party in 2024, and in April, it merged with the Free State Party. Morgan had been an organizer of Free State, and when the two merged, he became executive director at United Kansas.
United Kansas party leaders will soon gather to determine which districts they want to target, based on where they found interest and people who want to be involved. 
“Where we have possibilities,” Morgan said.
When a new political party starts, it is frequently tied to other groups, such as unions and environmental groups on the left or religious or gun groups on the right,” Morgan said.
“Moderates aren’t big on organizing,” he said. “They’re big on organizing things like school carnivals, but they haven’t had a need for that. We are trying to create something from scratch with a group that are very busy, very engaged. And I think it’s taken us a while to wrap our heads around that.”
Morgan said he hopes people see “less yelling and more doing” with the party.
“We’re still going to argue. I mean, it’s not like this is some fairyland where we’re just all going to get along and hold hands, and it’ll be sweet and beautiful,” Morgan said. “The idea is that we will respect that we are a group of people with different views and, in our mind, the center left and center right, and that’s a broad spectrum.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire ballot question to eliminate defunct position fails, according to preliminary results
description: A ballot measure meant to eliminate a defunct county-level position within the state’s judicial system just barely failed in Tuesday’s election, preliminary results show. According to the Associated Press, 64.7% of voters opted to abolish the register of the probate, with 96% of votes counted. That’s just shy of the two-thirds majority needed. The New […]
text:
Tuesday’s result means that the state will continue electing and paying 10 registers of probate every two years.(Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)A ballot measure meant to eliminate a defunct county-level position within the state’s judicial system just barely failed in Tuesday’s election, preliminary results show.
According to the Associated Press, 64.7% of voters opted to abolish the register of the probate, with 96% of votes counted. That’s just shy of the two-thirds majority needed.
Two questions, shown here in a screenshot of a sample ballot from the Secretary of State’s Office, were on the ballot for New Hampshire voters in the Nov. 3, 2026 midterm elections. The first, which would’ve eliminated a defunct county position, failed to receive the needed two-thirds majority. (Screenshot)
The New Hampshire Constitution mandates that every New Hampshire county elect a register of probate. The position, now defunct, used to complete administrative tasks for the courts. However, in 2011, the state completed a major overhaul of the court system that included transferring register of probate duties to other staff. Because it’s still in the constitution, the position appears on ballots every two years and the winner accepts an annual $100 salary to do nothing. Ballot Question 1, if successful, would’ve eliminated the role.
The question’s technical language could have created some confusion.
Question 1 appeared on ballots as follows: “Are you in favor of eliminating the office of register of probate by amending articles 71 and 81 of the second part of the constitution to read as follows: [Art.] 71. [County Treasurers, County Attorneys, Sheriffs, and Registers of Deeds Elected.] The county treasurers, county attorneys, sheriffs and registers of deeds, shall be elected by the inhabitants of the several towns, in the several counties in the State, according to the method now practiced, and the laws of the state, provided nevertheless the legislature shall have authority to alter the manner of certifying the votes, and the mode of electing those officers; but not so as to deprive the people of the right they now have of electing them. [Art.] 81. [Judges Not to Act as Counsel.] No judge shall be of counsel, act as advocate, or receive any fees as advocate or counsel, in any probate business which is pending, or may be brought into any court of probate in the county of which he or she is judge. (Passed by the N.H. House 325 Yes 15 No; Passed by the Senate 23 Yes 1 No) CACR 13.”
Tuesday’s result means that the state will continue electing and paying 10 registers of probate every two years. Because it’s in the constitution, lawmakers cannot legally eliminate the position themselves. Instead, per the constitution, they must take it to the voters, who must approve the change with a two-thirds majority.
This is not the first time voters have weighed in on the question. In 2022, a similar measure received the approval of only 63% of voters.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: CAIR ends operations in Florida as domestic terrorist designation takes effect
description: The Council on American Islamic Relations (CAIR) has suspended operations in Florida, the organization has announced. It did so after a federal judge rejected an emergency request Wednesday by the Muslim civil rights organization to stop the state from designating the group and its state chapter as domestic terrorist organizations, allowing the designation t[...]
text:
Hiba Rahim, interim executive director for CAIR-Florida, speaking in Tampa on Dec. 16, 2025. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)The Council on American Islamic Relations (CAIR) has suspended operations in Florida, the organization has announced.
It did so after a federal judge rejected an emergency request Wednesday by the Muslim civil rights organization to stop the state from designating the group and its state chapter as domestic terrorist organizations, allowing the designation to take effect while its legal challenge, litigated by the ACLU and the Southern Poverty Law Center, continues.
Federal Judge Allen C. Winsor of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida denied CAIR and CAIR Florida’s request to reverse the designation. In a ruling released Wednesday night, Windsor said the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed at this stage on their claims that the designations under a new law (HB 1471) violates their due process and First Amendment rights.
The judge did issue a narrow form of preliminary relief, stating that Florida prosecutors cannot enforce the law against CAIR and CAIR Florida, their employees, or third parties with respect to provision of legal services to the groups.
That designation took effect Thursday. As a result, both groups say they have been forced to shut down their advocacy and operations in Florida.
“Today’s ruling is deeply disappointing and we are appealing it,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project.
“Today’s decision upholds state officials’ sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorist,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. Florida officials have been relentless in seeking to silence our clients’ civil rights work and advocacy, damaging not only them but also their community. We cannot allow this dangerous and sweeping censorship regime to stand.”
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier hailed the ruling Thursday. “Great win by our Solicitor General’s office and for the people of Florida!” Uthmeier wrote on X.
DeSantis and other members of the Florida Cabinet voted to designate CAIR and CAIR Florida as domestic terrorist organizations on Sept. 29. They contend the group operates as a front for Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood.
Attorneys for CAIR have vehemently denied the allegation, contending its mission, “rooted in faith, is to enhance the public’s understanding of Islam, protect civil rights, promote justice and empower American Muslims.”
The designation in late September came months after DeSantis signed legislation approved by the Legislature earlier this year that gave five Florida executive officials — the head of domestic security (the commissioner of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement), the governor, and the three members of the state Cabinet — power to designate and eliminate groups operating in the United States without filing any legal charges or submitting their case to a jury.
 Students targeted 
The legislation prohibits any state agency, political subdivision, or public school district from expending or accepting state funds to support groups thus designated. It bans public schools or school districts from spending state or federal funds or maintaining programs on campus that “promote” a designated group.
The law also says any college or university must report information relating to the status of a student attending that school on a student visa if the student “promotes” a terrorist-designated organization. Students found to have promoted the group can be expelled.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.The ACLU, the ACLU of Florida, and two other legal groups representing CAIR and CAIR Florida filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the legislation in July in the Northern District.
“As Florida chief of domestic security, I know there are imminent dangers to public health, safety, and welfare due to increasing risks from foreign and domestic terrorist groups,” then-FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass said on Sept. 11. Glass has since been replaced by Larry Keefe.
DeSantis has been attempting to put CAIR out of business for nearly a year. He issued an executive order in December designating CAIR and CAIR-Florida as terrorist organizations, directing state and local agencies to block them and their supporters from public contracts, funding, and benefits. After the groups sued, a federal judge issued a temporary injunction blocking the order in March.
Shortly afterwards, the Legislature passed and DeSantis signed HB 1471.
CAIR and CAIR-Florida say the impact on the communities they serve will be “immense.” They say they provide a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suffer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system.
“CAIR-Florida categorically rejects Florida officials’ baseless designation of us,” said Hiba Rahim, executive director of CAIR-Florida, in a written statement. “Nevertheless, we are heartbroken that we have no choice but to close our doors to protect our staff and people of all faiths who support our work.”

title: Denver Democrat James Coleman elected again to be Colorado Senate president

James Coleman of Denver to continue his role as state Senate president.  The majority party first elected Coleman as president following the 2024 election.  “It has been the honor of my life to serve this chamber and to be able to make it so that we can get good things […]
text:
Colorado Senate President James Coleman, a Denver Democrat, delivers opening remarks on the first day of the 2025 session at the Capitol. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Senate Democrats elected Sen. James Coleman of Denver to continue his role as state Senate president. 
The majority party first elected Coleman as president following the 2024 election. 
“It has been the honor of my life to serve this chamber and to be able to make it so that we can get good things done for the state of Colorado,” Coleman said. “The most important thing is that if you are in a leadership position, no one should outwork you serving others, and the higher up you go in leadership, the greater the servant.”

Sen. Cathy Kipp of Fort Collins nominated Coleman, who ran uncontested for the role. 
The caucus also elected Sen. Kyle Mullica of Thornton as the next president pro tempore and Sen. Dylan Roberts of Frisco as majority leader. Others elected to leadership positions: Sen. Democrats claimed supermajorities in both the House and Senate following Tuesday’s election.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham opts in to Trump education tax credit, prompting rebuke from educators
description: New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced Wednesday that the state will join a new federal scholarship tax program created by the Trump administration, a move New Mexico teachers’ unions are describing as a “betrayal.”
text:
On Nov. 4, 2026, New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced the state would opt in to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, a decision that drew immediate backlash from teacher unions in the state. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced Wednesday that the state will join a new federal scholarship tax program created by the Trump administration, a move New Mexico teachers’ unions are describing as a “betrayal.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, established in President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act enacted last year, allows eligible taxpayers to receive a federal tax credit of up to $1,700 annually for charitable contributions to qualified nonprofit “scholarship granting organizations.” Those organizations then award scholarships to eligible K-12 students in public and non-public schools to cover qualified educational expenses such as tutoring, special education services, instructional materials and more. States can opt in to the program, which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
The Treasury Department issued rules for the new program last month.
The new program has sparked controversy nationally as the Trump administration has made significant cuts to federal funding for public education. Education experts and advocates in September urged Congress to repeal the program, and expressed concerns that it would divert money away from public schools and to private institutions.   
With Lujan Grisham’s decision, New Mexico becomes the 32nd state to opt in to the program, and she becomes the third Democratic governor to do so, alongside New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Colorado Gov. Jared Polis. Democratic Minnesota Gov. Mike Walz and Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek declined to opt in, two Democratic governors in Wisconsin and Arizona vetoed state legislation that would have required their states to join and 15 states, including Washington D.C., have yet to make a decision.
“At a time of diminishing federal investment in education, New Mexico must take advantage of every dollar we can to bolster public education and continue our state’s upward trajectory in literacy and student achievement,” Lujan Grisham said in a statement. 
The New Mexico Public Education Department will now establish a process for scholarship-granting organization certification in the coming weeks and SGOs can apply to participate once guidelines are released, the governor’s office said.
State Rep. Rebecca Dow (R-Elephant Butte), who lost her reelection bid Tuesday to Democrat David Mooney, urged the governor last March to opt into the program. On Thursday, she praised the move in a phone call with Source NM. “The governor has done the right thing,” Dow said, adding that “public schools and charter schools are eligible to receive these funds to build programs on their campuses without costing the New Mexico taxpayer a dime.”
The governor’s decision also earned praise from state Sen. Gabriel Ramos (R-Silver City), ranking member of the Senate Education Committee, who issued a statement that said opting into the program “is common sense. It puts more opportunities in front of New Mexico students and lets parents choose the tutoring, services, or school that fits their child’s needs. Every student learns differently, and this gives families the tools to help their kids succeed in the classroom and in whatever career path they choose.”
But in a Wednesday joint news release, both Whitney Holland and Bethany Jarrell — presidents of the American Federation of Teachers New Mexico and National Education Association New Mexico unions, respectively — called the governor’s decision to opt in “nothing short of a betrayal” to students and families in the state’s public schools.
Both teacher unions called the tax program “a voucher scheme” that promises “tax credits to well-off individuals who can donate thousands of dollars” to so-called “scholarship-granting organizations” in order to “reduce their individual federal taxes.” They added that Lujan Grisham “lowered herself” to partnering with Trump and Education Secretary Linda McMahon “as they dismantle federal educational supports and programs.”
Jarrell told Source NM that she was “shocked” when she saw Lujan Grisham’s announcement. She added that NEA-NM had been talking with her over the last few months and had “educators reaching out and asking her not to.”
“I expected her to listen to constituents and the people who helped get her in office and supported her, so it was devastating that she would make that decision,” Jarrell said. 
Source NM has a pending request to the governor’s office for a response to the unions’ criticism. 
“Every child deserves a well-funded, fully supported public school in their community, and this is just not the way to do that,” Jarrell said.

name: California
title: What Gavin Newsom’s commutations mean for the death penalty in the U.S.
description: If approved by the California Supreme Court, the number of people sentenced to death nationwide would drop by nearly a third.
text:
In summary
If approved by the California Supreme Court, the number of people sentenced to death nationwide would drop by nearly a third.


California Gov. Gavin Newsom today moved to commute the death sentences of all 548 people facing execution in the state, allowing them to instead serve life sentences without the possibility of parole.The California Supreme Court must approve some of these commutations. If it does, Newsom’s action would be responsible for the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history.
“I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” he wrote in an open letter to Californians. 
Newsom’s decision, which his office said would benefit 529 men and 19 women, does not guarantee they will all be resentenced. The justices will have to decide whether to approve commutations for people convicted of multiple felonies, more than half of those in question.
Nationwide, only about 440 people on death row have received commutations since 1972. As a result of Newsom’s announcement, the entire population of people sentenced to death in the United States could drop by nearly a third, according to a Marshall Project analysis of data on death sentences collected by scholar Frank Baumgartner and the Death Penalty Information Center. 
The Marshall Project previously reviewed data on 9,000 U.S. death sentences and found inequities in California dating back 50 years. Death sentences in the state are more common among Black and Hispanic people, and defendants in some counties are far more likely to face execution than those in others. 
Newsom has spoken out about disparities in death sentences throughout his time as governor, and reiterated his concerns in an open letter announcing the commutations.
“By every measure, California’s system for administering the death penalty is a failure,” Newsom wrote. “It has not been and cannot be fairly applied and has resulted in the conviction of innocent people.”
Newsom, whose term ends in January, is considering a run for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.Shortly after he became governor in 2019, he declared a moratorium on executions. California later transferred people off death row to live among the general population at other prisons. But the punishment can only be abolished in California through a public referendum, so prosecutors across the state continue to seek death sentences. A future governor could choose to reverse course and revive the state’s death chamber.
Newsom’s decision illustrates how governors can take a more active role in stopping executions, at a moment when federal courts have proven less likely to do so. From the 1970s through the 2000s, the U.S. Supreme Court issued numerous rulings that limited who could be sentenced to death. But the court’s current conservative supermajority almost never halts executions; the Death Penalty Information Center reported that the high court did not grant a single stay of execution last year.
That leaves more room for governors to stop executions through clemency. Newsom’s move will invariably add fuel to calls on other governors on their way out the door to save people from execution, including Republican Mike DeWine of Ohio and Democrat Laura Kelly of Kansas, both of whom have criticized the death penalty in the past.
A few commutations have recently come from red state governors in the middle of their terms, like Kay Ivey of Alabama and Kevin Stitt of Oklahoma, in cases where the person facing execution was an accomplice, rather than directly responsible for the murder in question.
Historically, Democratic governors have commuted large numbers of death sentences right before leaving office, although Newsom’s closest predecessor was a Republican. In 2003, Illinois Gov. George Ryan commuted 167 death sentences as he left office. He had previously supported capital punishment, but had been shaken by exonerations of innocent people from his state’s death row. 
Criticism of Newsom’s action — from victims’ groups, prosecutors, and police — began last month, after the governor signaled an interest in commuting sentences on his podcast. 
“Baby killers, cop killers, spree killers and serial killers have all found an ally in Gavin Newsom,” Marc Klaas, the father of Polly Klaas, a 12-year-old girl who was kidnapped and murdered in 1993 by a man who later received a death sentence, told Fox News Digital. 
Meanwhile, Klaas’ sister, Jess Nichol, issued a statement after Newsom’s announcement describing her support for the decision. 
“I used to think the man who killed my sister deserved execution,” Nichol said. “But over time I’ve realized that whether he’s executed has absolutely nothing to do with my recovery or with real public safety.”
In his open letter, Newsom said he consulted with crime victims and survivors, public safety experts and religious and civil rights leaders on his decision. He wrote that he chose not to exclude any prisoners from the commutations, because it would “inadvertently create two classes of murder victims” and each victim “experiences their loss as the worst of the worst.”
“I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss,” Newsom wrote.
Advocates are praising Newsom’s action and hailing it as a victory for death penalty opponents. The New York Times reported that anti-death penalty groups are sponsoring a minute-long commercial that will air nationwide. 
The New York Times reported that he minute-long commercial casts the governor’s decision as an act of courage and leadership inspired by the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Dolores Huerta and Robert F. Kennedy. It will air on dozens of news and political shows nationwide, said Dan Newman, a Democratic strategist who advises both Mr. Newsom and the anti-death penalty groups sponsoring the ad.
Not everyone on Newsom’s commutation list may celebrate. Although many people under a death sentence in California did not have lawyers to work on their appeals — due to a statewide funding crisis — they were entitled to lawyers, and now they won’t be. Last year, two federal death row prisoners tried unsuccessfully to refuse clemency from President Joe Biden, saying they wanted to keep trying to prove their innocence in court, and would only get funding to do so while under a death sentence.
When California voters last considered abolishing the death penalty in 2016, prisoner Kenneth Hartman argued, writing for The Marshall Project, that replacing death sentences with life sentences robs people of lawyers while replacing one kind of death sentence with another. “Life without the possibility of parole is the death penalty, pure and simple,” he wrote. 
After Newsom leaves office, prosecutors will likely continue to pursue death sentences in areas where they have historically been popular, like Riverside and San Bernardino counties in Southern California.
California’s incoming governor, Democrat Xavier Becerra, has said he would extend Newsom’s moratorium on executions. But if Californians do not vote to abolish the death penalty, and Becerra does not revive executions, the state could eventually be in the same quandary that Newsom was facing: People will be sentenced to death in a state that refuses to execute them — a broken system that satisfies neither side of the debate. 
This article was published in partnership with The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook.

title: State moves to revoke EMT’s license, citing criminal charges of grooming
description: The state of Iowa has proposed revoking the license of an emergency medical services provider criminally charged with grooming minors. In September 2026, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services’ Bureau of Emergency Medical and Trauma Services proposed revoking the EMS certification of Jeremy Dean McCormick of Indianola. At the time, the bureau charg[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)The state of Iowa has proposed revoking the license of an emergency medical services provider criminally charged with grooming minors.
In September 2026, the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services’ Bureau of Emergency Medical and Trauma Services proposed revoking the EMS certification of Jeremy Dean McCormick of Indianola.
At the time, the bureau charged McCormick with knowingly making misleading, deceptive, untrue or fraudulent representations in the practice of the profession or engaging in unethical conduct or practices that are harmful to the public.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The board also charged McCormick with betrayal of a professional confidence and willful or repeated violations of laws or regulations, and with having his certification to practice emergency medical care sanctioned – an apparent reference to a previous emergency suspension of McCormick’s certification.
As justification for the charges against him, the bureau has alleged that McCormick was “convicted of two counts of grooming two teenage girls, ages 15 and 16” after being criminally charged in April 2025. The bureau has also alleged McCormick was charged with grooming in a separate case that was initiated in June 2025.
McCormick was given 20 days to request a hearing with the bureau, and if no request was made, the proposed revocation was scheduled to become effective immediately and constitute the bureau’s final action in the matter. It’s not clear whether McCormick requested a hearing.
There is no publicly available court record of McCormick being convicted of grooming in the state of Iowa.
Court records detail two Iowa cases in which McCormick has been charged with grooming — one initiated in January 2025, and one initiated in June 2025. Both cases are still open, with no pleas or convictions entered, and McCormick has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges.
In the January 2025 case, the Warren County Sheriff’s Office charged McCormick with two counts of grooming. The sheriff’s office alleged that in October of 2024, McCormick took a 15-year-old female and a 16-year-old female on a shopping trip to eastern Iowa and purchased underwear for both of them at Victoria’s Secret. One of the girls said McCormick asked her to send him photos of her in the underwear he had purchased for her, the sheriff’s office alleged.
In the June 2025 case, Indianola police alleged they were contacted by an individual who said she had previously worked for McCormick and, while she was underage, he had offered her a drink of some kind and had offered to take her to a Victoria’s Secret store to “get something sexy.”
According to police, McCormick then asked the individual to delete written communications they had shared, stating, “I’d rather it not be stumbled upon by a parental figure, lol.” McCormick was also accused of placing “police-grade handcuffs” on the individual and hugging her for “an irregular amount of time.”
Pretrial conferences in both criminal cases are scheduled Nov. 10, 2026.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach McCormick for comment.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Here’s what Denise Powell said about her victory in Nebraska’s 2nd District
description: Powell’s victory in Nebraska's most politically divided and diverse congressional district was part of a historic night for Democrats
text:
Denise Powell greets supporters at her watch party turned victory in Omaha-based 2nd Congressional District. The Nov. 3 event was in downtown Omaha at the Hilton at 10th and Cass streets. (Photo by Ailyn Adame for Nebraska Examiner) OMAHA — Denise Powell’s victory in Nebraska’s most politically divided and diverse congressional district was part of a historic night for Democrats nationally, as voters across the country delivered a significant rebuke to the Trump administration.
Nebraska’s 2nd District often has had barn-burner races decided by a few points — that wasn’t the case Tuesday as Republican Brinker Harding conceded roughly an hour after the polls closed. Powell won by a margin of 15 percentage points.
The margin of the race could hint at a new era for the so-called swing district – though Powell isn’t counting on it. She said she can’t “ever, ever, ever take anything for granted in this district.” 
“From your lips to God’s ears … I think a big part of our success was people’s frustration with this current administration,” Powell told reporters at her campaign headquarters Wednesday. “I know that my job over the next two years is to show the people of this district that I am truly going to fight for the things that I said that I was going to fight for.”
Her victory is also historic because she is the first woman to represent the 2nd District and the first Latina to hold a federal office in Nebraska. Powell said her campaign was triumphant because she stayed on message about concerns they were “hearing in the district”: affordability, access to healthcare, grocery costs and gas prices. 
The campaigns tried to paint each other as extreme throughout the campaign. In the last few weeks of the race, the two candidates each accused the other of benefiting from PAC spending and making late tax payments.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Harding consistently attacked Powell for alleged support for “sex education” for kindergartners and “transgender surgeries” for minors. During one of their debates, Powell said that wasn’t true. 
“I think it’s really easy to get pulled in lots of different directions in politics because folks want to throw all kinds of issues around like Molotov cocktails,” Powell said. “I’m really proud of the way that we stayed really focused on that (affordability) messaging.” 
Harding, while conceding the race at his Tuesday watch party, acknowledged the political environment deteriorated for Republicans.  Harding, an Omaha City Council member, said Wednesday, “Voters in Nebraska and across the nation spoke loud and clear last night, and it’s incumbent upon the Republican Party to listen.” 
“We need leaders who are focused on pocketbooks, public safety, and bringing people together,” part of Harding’s statement said.
Republicans across the nation were swept away by a blue tsunami, which included Senate contests in states Trump won by double digits just two years ago. Some had not elected Democrats in decades: Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina, Ohio and Texas. Powell said she hopes the election results show President Donald Trump that he “needs to listen to the voice of the American people” because voters from across the political spectrum said “enough is enough, and we need to get this country back on track.” 
Nebraska saw a splash of the tsunami as registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn lost his bid to Sen. Pete Ricketts, Gov. Jim Pillen won another term, and Rep. Mike Flood survived a closer-than-expected race against Chris Backemeyer. 
During the GOP watch party in Omaha, several Republican elected officials called Nebraska a “firewall” from the great night for Democrats. 
Powell said making “progress” is a long-term play and statewide candidates should feel proud of their performances. 
“I think again Nebraska is a state where we don’t win everything with just Democrats. …We need to figure out a way to work within this broad coalition,” Powell said. “That is the reality of the state, and it’s one of the things that makes the state special.” 
Looking ahead, Powell said one of her first priorities would be to seek reversal of Medicaid cuts. Powell hopes to land a spot on the House’s agriculture, energy and commerce committees. Democrats gained more than 30 seats Tuesday, more than enough to have control of the chamber. 
She starts her two-year term next year.

name: Delaware
title: AI gives citizens a new way to check what government tells them
description: Delaware’s latest government efficiency report shows how artificial intelligence can help voters look beyond official press releases, examine the facts and make better-informed decisions about government performance.   DOVER, Del. — For generations, voters have relied on government officials, news organizations and political campaigns to explain how governme[...]
text:
Delaware’s latest government efficiency report shows how artificial intelligence can help voters look beyond official press releases, examine the facts and make better-informed decisions about government performance.
 
DOVER, Del. — For generations, voters have relied on government officials, news organizations and political campaigns to explain how government is performing and how their tax dollars are being spent.
But those explanations often come through press releases designed to highlight accomplishments, defend policies or promote the priorities of elected officials.
The full story may be buried in lengthy government reports, budgets and financial documents that few citizens have the time or expertise to examine.
Artificial intelligence is beginning to change that relationship between voters and government.
Today, an ordinary Delaware voter can upload a government press release and the full report behind it into an AI tool and ask a simple question: “Does this press release accurately represent what the report says?”
What once might have required hours of research can now begin in minutes, giving voters a new opportunity to evaluate government claims for themselves.
Delaware LIVE recently tested that capability using Gov. Matt Meyer’s Nov. 5 announcement of the state’s 2026 Government Efficiency and Accountability Review (GEAR) annual report.
The results demonstrate how AI could become a valuable tool for government accountability — particularly for voters who want to judge elected officials by results rather than political messaging.
The $117 million question
The governor’s two-page press release highlighted approximately $117 million in estimated lifetime savings from 164 government improvement projects.
It pointed to reductions in state real estate expenses, the elimination of underused government vehicles, faster permitting and improved public services.
Those accomplishments are supported by the underlying 79-page GEAR report.
But when the press release and full report were compared using AI, an important qualification emerged.
The full report explains that the $117 million represents planning estimates rather than savings actually recorded in state budgets.
That’s a distinction taxpayers should understand.
Reducing the time employees spend processing government paperwork may make an agency more efficient. Eliminating unnecessary vehicles or negotiating lower rents can directly reduce spending.
But making an existing employee more productive does not automatically mean government costs taxpayers less.
The press release correctly described the savings as estimated, so the claim itself was not false. However, the full report provided information that could change how voters interpreted the number.
AI made that difference easier to discover.
What voters might not have learned from the announcement
The AI comparison also identified significant financial issues discussed in the full report but omitted from the governor’s announcement.
Among them:

A technology modernization initiative expected to cost more than $150 million. Delaware has already appropriated $130.5 million toward replacing aging state financial, payroll, pension and human resources systems. The report says total costs may exceed $150 million.
Rapidly rising state employee health benefit expenses. Gross spending on GLP-1 weight-loss medications is projected to increase from $84.1 million in fiscal 2026 to $127.5 million in fiscal 2027.
Additional costs associated with handgun permitting. The report estimates that implementing Delaware’s permit-to-purchase law would require 29 additional civilian employees and 10 sworn personnel positions.
The possibility of another permanent government office. GEAR proposes transitioning toward a multidisciplinary service-improvement operation, with decisions about permanent staffing and funding potentially coming in fiscal 2028.

None of these omissions establishes that the administration was deliberately misleading voters.
Government press releases are intended to summarize selected accomplishments, not reproduce every finding in a comprehensive report.
However, the comparison illustrates something important: What government chooses to tell voters may be accurate without being the complete picture.
And voters now have a practical way to investigate that difference.
Voters no longer have to accept the summary
For years, one of the challenges of government transparency has been that information can technically be public while remaining difficult for ordinary citizens to understand.
A school district may publish a 200-page budget. A county government may release a complicated financial review. State agencies may post reports filled with statistics, technical language and explanations of programs unfamiliar to most taxpayers.
Making those documents public is important. But availability alone does not guarantee understanding.
AI tools can help close that gap.
A voter can ask an AI system to explain a government budget in plain English, identify spending increases, compare current and previous reports or distinguish actual savings from projected financial benefits.
The same tools can help residents examine campaign statements, legislative proposals and the financial implications of public policies.
For example, a Delaware voter might ask:

Did this agency actually reduce spending, or did it simply spend less than originally projected?
Does the governor’s announcement describe accomplishments from the current administration or include work completed under previous governors?
What important financial risks appear in the full report but not in the public announcement?
Has a new government program achieved the goals that were promised when it was created?
How much will a proposed law cost taxpayers to implement?

These questions are not inherently Republican or Democratic.
They are the questions citizens should be able to ask of any government, regardless of which political party is in power.
A new advantage for the independent voter
The opportunity may be especially valuable for voters who do not automatically accept the interpretation offered by either political party.
Campaigns and elected officials naturally emphasize their accomplishments and criticize their opponents. Political organizations select facts that support their arguments.
Voters are left to determine which claims are accurate, which are exaggerated and which leave out important information.
AI cannot eliminate political bias, and AI systems can introduce inaccuracies or biases of their own. But when used to examine original documents, they can help voters move beyond competing political messages and focus on evidence.
Consider Delaware’s GEAR report.
A voter skeptical of government spending can use the document to question whether projected efficiencies have actually reduced the cost of state government.
A voter supportive of the administration can point to legitimate improvements in permitting, property management and public services.
Both conclusions can be informed by the same report.
The important development is that voters no longer have to depend exclusively on someone else’s interpretation to begin examining the evidence.
The technology still requires a skeptical eye
AI is not an infallible fact-checker.  It can misunderstand financial information, overlook important context, misinterpret tables or reach incorrect conclusions.
A responsible voter should ask the system to identify the specific page or passage supporting an answer, then check that information against the original document.
When AI identifies a difference between a press release and the underlying report, that finding should prompt further questions rather than an immediate accusation of dishonesty.
The GEAR comparison is an example.
It revealed legitimate accomplishments, important financial qualifications and significant information that the press release did not discuss.
It did not establish that the governor or his administration falsified the report.
That’s an important distinction in a political environment where accusations can spread much faster than corrections.
The goal should be better-informed voters, not faster accusations.
Government accountability between elections
Voters generally have an opportunity to hold elected officials accountable at the ballot box every two or four years.
But the decisions that determine government performance happen throughout those years — when budgets are adopted, contracts are awarded, programs are expanded and regulations are implemented.
AI creates new possibilities for citizens to follow those decisions without needing advanced training in public finance or government administration.
A parent could examine whether increased school spending produced better educational outcomes.
A homeowner could compare county reassessment claims with underlying property and tax data.
A business owner could evaluate whether promised permitting reforms actually shortened approval times.
A taxpayer could review whether government efficiency initiatives eliminated expenses or simply moved employees and resources to different activities.
And as voters become more comfortable examining original documents, public officials may face greater pressure to provide clear, measurable and defensible explanations for their decisions.
That could strengthen accountability even when no election is approaching.
A more informed Delaware electorate
Delaware’s small size makes this opportunity particularly relevant.
State government, county councils, school boards and local municipalities make decisions that directly affect taxes, education, economic development, public safety and the cost of living.
Many of those decisions are documented in reports that are publicly accessible but seldom closely examined outside government.
AI will not replace informed judgment, public debate or independent journalism.
But it can put powerful research capabilities directly into the hands of voters who previously lacked the time, resources or expertise to examine government claims on their own.
The recent GEAR announcement demonstrates both the opportunity and the responsibility that comes with those capabilities.
The administration highlighted approximately $117 million in estimated efficiencies. The full report supported the figure but added important qualifications about what those savings represent.
Neither document needed to be dismissed. Instead, the comparison provided a more complete understanding of both.
For voters, that may be the most important lesson.
Government transparency is no longer simply about whether officials make information available. It is increasingly about whether citizens can use that information to independently evaluate what their government tells them.
And with AI, Delaware voters have a new way to do exactly that.



Editor’s note: Delaware LIVE used artificial intelligence to compare the Meyer administration’s Nov. 5, 2026, press release with the full 2026 GEAR annual report. The comparison examined financial claims, qualifications and significant information not included in the announcement. It was a document-based analysis, not an independent financial audit. AI-generated findings require verification against original sources.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Fresh off reelection win, Moore names new chief of staff
description: Fresh off his reelection victory Tuesday, Gov. Wes Moore on Thursday announced the departure of chief of staff Lester Davis and named Emmanuel "Manny" Welsh to replace him, a possible start to staff shuffling ahead of Moore's second term.
text:
Manny Welsh becomes Gov. Wes Moore's third chief of staff, succeeding Lester Davis who takes over as the interim CEO of TEDCO. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Fresh off his reelection victory Tuesday, Gov. Wes Moore on Thursday announced the departure of chief of staff Lester Davis and named Emmanuel “Manny” Welsh to replace him.
Davis, who was named Moore’s top aide in September 2025, leaves after 14 months in the State House to become the interim CEO of the Maryland Technology Development Corp., what he called the “opportunity of a lifetime” in statement announcing the changes.
For the last year, Welsh has served as principal deputy chief of staff and chief administrative officer for Moore, who said Welsh has been “invaluable” to the administration since joining initially as the liaison to the Board of Public Works.
“His encyclopedic knowledge on how to pull the levers of state bureaucracy to tackle complex problems and find innovative solutions is exactly what Maryland needs right now,” Moore said in the statement.
Manny Welsh leans in to speak to Gov. Wes Moore at a Board of Public Works meeting. Welsh is Moore’s liaison to the board. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Welsh has effectively been second in command to Davis. As such, Welsh was responsible for the day-to-day operations of the office. He also worked with Moore’s Cabinet and senior staff members as well as Moore’s procurement policy and the Board of Public Works.
Before joining Moore, Welsh worked for then-Comptroller Peter Franchot (D). Welsh, who was born in the Philippines, joined Franchot’s communication staff in 2015 and within a year, he was assisting the comptroller with the Board of Public Works, a three-member panel — the governor, comptroller and state treasurer — that approves state contracts. By 2020, Welsh was named Franchot’s chief of staff.
Welsh earned a bachelor’s degree in political science from Towson University and a master’s degree in public administration from the University of Baltimore.
Welsh takes over his new role effective immediately.
Welsh’s ascendance and Davis’ departure is part of a shuffling of Moore’s second-floor staff ahead of the start of his second term.
At TEDCO, Davis will replace Troy LeMaile-Stovall, who has led TEDCO since 2020.
Lester Davis leaves his role as Gov. Wes Moore’s (D) chief of staff to to become interim CEO of TEDCo. (File Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
“TEDCO is where this state’s economic agenda becomes lasting: Backing new companies, supporting entrepreneurs in every region, and getting research out of the lab and into the market,” he said in a statement.
Davis joined the Moore team fresh from a three-year stint as vice president and chief of staff for CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield. He also served on transition teams for Moore and for Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott.
Davis joined Moore’s team at a time when there was some grumbling that the governor’s office was not always responsive.
“When Lester joined my team as Chief of Staff, he inherited some of the longest standing, thorniest problems we needed to solve quickly,” Moore’s statement said. “He implemented new processes and creative solutions to help deliver real results, and so much more. Lester has made State government work better for the people of Maryland, with integrity, discipline, and heart.”

title: Every Minnesota House district shifted left in 2026
description: The national wave of anti-Trump fervor that swept the country Tuesday seems to have permeated every geographic region of Minnesota: Every Minnesota House district shifted leftward in 2026 compared to 2024, with several districts moving left by over 15 percentage points. In 10 districts, that meant voters who chose Republican legislators in 2024 voted for […]
text:
Attendees celebrate as results roll in at the DFL watch party, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in St. Paul, Minnesota. Every Minnesota House district voted more blue than in 2024, leading to a DFL trifecta in the state government. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The national wave of anti-Trump fervor that swept the country Tuesday seems to have permeated every geographic region of Minnesota: Every Minnesota House district shifted leftward in 2026 compared to 2024, with several districts moving left by over 15 percentage points.
In 10 districts, that meant voters who chose Republican legislators in 2024 voted for a Democrat in 2026, ousting several Republican incumbents. In six districts, Trump-voting legislative districts voted for a Democrat for the Minnesota House in 2026.
The Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party will take control of both the House and the Senate in the Minnesota Legislature, which, along with Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s victory in the governor’s race, gives the Democrats another “trifecta” after two years of sharing control with Republicans.
Districts where the two parties didn’t both have candidates in 2024 or 2026 — all blue districts, except District 21A, which didn’t have a Democratic candidate in 2024 — are excluded from the Reformer’s analysis of voting shifts.
The outcome could be a function of voters changing their allegiance, but also a different electorate from two years prior. That is, Republican voters may have been more likely to stay home this time.
The districts that shifted left the most were districts that voted red in 2024 and continued to vote Republican in 2026, but by a smaller margin this time. Many are still comfortably red. District 12B in central Minnesota shifted 20 points leftward, the most in the state, but Republican state Rep. Mary Franson, R-Alexandria, still defeated DFL candidate Michael Gardner by a margin of 35.8 percentage points in 2026 — compared to her 2024 win by a margin of 56 percentage points.
One north metro suburban district that was solidly red in 2024, 32A, is now facing a recount after Rep. Nolan West, R-Blaine, won by a margin of just 22 votes.

name: California
title: Mayor-elect Nithya Raman inherits a Los Angeles full of promise and burdened by challenges
description: Nithya Raman positioned herself as an outsider to mainstream Los Angeles politics. The mayor-elect will quickly face an array of significant challenges.
text:
Los Angeles, once California’s most reliably Republican stronghold, now faces a future under the leadership of a democratic socialist. Incumbent Mayor Karen Bass has lost her reelection bid to a friend-turned-rival, Councilmember and Mayor-elect Nithya Raman. 
Her election ushers in a new era for California’s largest city, decisively breaking it from the history that preceded it. Raman’s victory was unusual in some respects — she rode a national blue wave that toppled Republicans from Maine to California and, along the way, ousted the liberal, Black woman serving as mayor of Los Angeles — but natural, even overdue, in others. Raman, a 45-year-old Indian immigrant and mother of twins, was carried into office by younger voters and newer arrivals to L.A., those least burdened by the expectations or limitations of the city’s past.
Raman will face significant challenges: Homelessness is a grinding human tragedy that resisted her predecessor’s best efforts; housing is expensive and likely to remain so at least for a while; the 2028 Summer Olympics are fast approaching; the city’s police department and public safety strategies are a source of contention. 
Meanwhile, some of Raman’s campaign pronouncements may prove difficult to execute and even contradictory. She has vowed, for instance, to support a smooth run-up to the Games and promised to remove the city’s police chief. These two goals may bump into each other.
Still, she arrives at the post on the heels of a largely positive, uplifting, even joyful campaign. Her election night party at the Greek Theater in Griffith Park was an outpouring of exuberant energy that her supporters hope to carry with them into office.
“Are you ready for an L.A. that loves you back?” she asked those supporters. Their answer was obvious, and their excitement was real.
First, though, what happened to Bass, who will become only the second mayor in modern Los Angeles history to be shown the door by voters after one term. The first, James Hahn, defied his political base — an unusual combination of Valley moderates and Black voters — by opposing Valley secession and denying Police Chief Bernard C. Parks a second term at the helm of the LAPD. That left Hahn in 2005 without allies to face Antonio Villaraigosa in a rematch of their 2001 contest. Hahn was easily defeated.
This race was not so easy for Raman, and Bass did not fold as quickly or decisively as Hahn did. But some noteworthy events conspired with some of Bass’ executive weaknesses to create the conditions for her downfall.
Foremost was one over which she had no control. Dry conditions and furious winds descended upon Los Angeles in January 2025. Once brush and homes began to ignite, nothing could have stopped the inferno that swept across the city — and, simultaneously, over land outside the city, notably in nearby Altadena. The Palisades and Eaton fires were not Bass’ fault, but they were crippling crises that turned a mostly sedate electorate into an enraged one. Her approval ratings plummeted, and she was suddenly vulnerable, especially because she happened to be out of town when the fires erupted. She struggled to regain her footing once she returned.
If it was unfair to blame Bass for the fires, other aspects of her leadership were more susceptible to criticism. She gave police officers a gigantic raise, and the city’s police union became one of her most conspicuous supporters, fueling the critique that she was in cahoots with her backers. She appointed some mediocre deputies and often second-guessed them, delaying decisions on important matters. She frustrated allies by letting problems linger and resisting new ideas in the area of homelessness, for instance. 
Perhaps most importantly, though, she suffered from a politicians’ worst enemy: bad timing. Bass chased off potential rivals in the run-up to her reelection, but Raman jumped in late and then flourished as the national electorate was growing more restive. Rising prices, hostility toward immigrants, a general tone of nastiness in national discourse all were the work of President Donald Trump, whom Raman and Bass loathe equally, but those sources of unhappiness made this a bad time to be an incumbent on the ballot.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass speaks at an election night event in Los Angeles on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Jill Connelly, AP Photo
Bass conceded defeat Thursday morning. In a statement, she took credit for progress while also acknowledging the mounting votes against her.
“Coming out of the pandemic, when encampments lined our streets and businesses were trying to reopen — we got Angelenos off the streets, made our neighborhoods safer, built more affordable housing and created new opportunities for working families,” Bass said. “We stood together through devastating wildfires and protected our immigrant communities when Donald Trump sent federal troops into our streets to spread fear and intimidation. That progress belongs to all of us.”
Raman’s campaign, by contrast, was fresh and positive. She successfully positioned herself as an outsider to the mainstream of Los Angeles politics. 
Running both as a member of the council and as the alternative to the status quo gave Raman the luxury of claiming credit for city progress — she boasted of the decline in street homelessness in her district last year — while also distancing herself from the city’s struggles. She did not run a perfect campaign — a few late gaffes gave the Bass camp room for optimism as Election Day approached and the mayor closed the polling gap on the council member.
In the end, however, Bass’ negative ratings — about two-thirds of city voters disapproved of her performance in office — outweighed Raman’s — about half of voters disapproved of hers.
Raman now inherits a city full of promise and potential as well as one burdened by challenges.
Homelessness will top the agenda, and Raman has made herself susceptible to clear accountability: She has promised to reduce street homelessness in the city by 50% over the next two years. That’s a measurable goal, and one she may find hard to meet. Bass, no less committed to solutions in this area, managed to bring down street homelessness about 17% over four years.
But Raman is nothing if not smart, and her background in urban planning and her experience on council give her a fresh perspective on this ancient and frustrating problem. She will certainly be less singularly committed than Bass to Inside Safe, a program that Bass initiated but that has proved very expensive and only incrementally successful. 
Much has been made of Raman’s lack of support from her council colleagues, and it is true that they lined up against her mayoral bid, reflecting a combination of professional disagreements, assessments of her work and flat-out jealousy. There, however, the transition may not be as rough as some suggest. 
Relationships at City Hall are not friendships in the way most people experience friendship. They are commonalities of interest, and the same council members who did not appreciate Raman as a colleague will find ways to mend fences now that they need her. Necessity has a way of papering over differences. 
The issue that may most complicate her new life, however, is public safety. During the campaign, Raman struggled with questions about the LAPD and its leadership. She repeatedly asserted that Chief Jim McDonnell had lost public confidence and that she would seek to replace him. But she never said how she had reached that conclusion or how she would approach replacing him.
At first, she equivocated, saying that the process for firing a chief was complicated by the roles of the council and Police Commission. But that was a dodge, and she knew it. Here’s the process: The mayor appoints the Police Commission and can direct the commission to fire the chief. The chief could appeal to the council, but likely won’t. So, yes, the mayor can fire the chief.
Whether the mayor should fire the chief is another matter. Crime is down significantly since Mayor Bass and Chief McDonnell moved into their positions, so disrupting that progress risks creating a problem where none exists. Moreover, Raman’s insistence that LAPD is doing too much to share information with federal authorities is both historically inaccurate and infuriatingly vague.
Her wisest course there may be to look for an out and to recognize that the police department requires firm civilian oversight. The values she represents as a (politically) young democratic socialist have a place in public safety, but change merely for the sake of politics is unwise.
