title: Republicans win in Public Service Commission races
description: Republican Montana Public Service Commissioner Annie Bukacek won re-election against Democrat Kevin Hamm and will serve four more years on the regulatory body. “I have been known by many for decades as one who can be trusted to stand up for Montanans,” Bukacek said in a text message Thursday. “That includes keeping the lights and […]
text:
Montana Public Service Commission (via PSC Twitter account). Republican Montana Public Service Commissioner Annie Bukacek won re-election against Democrat Kevin Hamm and will serve four more years on the regulatory body.
“I have been known by many for decades as one who can be trusted to stand up for Montanans,” Bukacek said in a text message Thursday. “That includes keeping the lights and heat on at the best possible price.”
Bukacek, also a medical doctor based in Kalispell, represents district No. 5, which covers part of northwest Montana.
A photo of Dr. Annie Bukacek (Photo via Annie Bukacek for PSC website).
Bukacek won 53% of the vote and Hamm earned 47% of the vote with all precincts fully reporting.
In district No. 1, a large portion of eastern Montana, Republican Jeff Pattison won 65% of the vote against Democrat Angeline Cheek, who earned 35%.
Pattison works in agriculture, and in a statement on social media about his win, he said he’ll take lessons from farming and ranching to his role on the PSC.
“I’ve spent most of my life planting seeds, fixing fences, caring for livestock, and praying for rain,” Pattison said. “And I’ve learned that you don’t always control the harvest. But you are responsible for how faithfully you tend the field.”
He said that’s how he will approach his responsibility on the Public Service Commission.
Republican Jeff Pattison, center, won the a Public Service Commission race. (Provided by Pattison’s campaign site)
The PSC regulates monopoly utilities, including NorthWestern Energy and Montana-Dakota Utilities.
It is made up of five commissioners elected by district, and this week’s election results mean it will remain an all-Republican commission.
The PSC has come under scrutiny in recent years as Montanans have seen increases in power bills and worry they’ll be forced to subsidize energy costs for data centers.
It is handling a significant caseload, including a case for how to address data centers and a multibillion-dollar merger proposal between NorthWestern and South Dakota-based Black Hills Corp.
The PSC also is facing a lawsuit filed by 17 groups demanding it “recognize its constitutional duty to consider climate change” in regulating utilities.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Sen. Chris Murphy ‘making remarkable progress’ after stroke
description: A spokesman for Chris Murphy said the senator continues to improve since having a stroke but didn’t elaborate on his condition or recovery.
text:
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy continues to improve five days after he was hospitalized with a stroke, according to a spokesman who said he’s “making remarkable progress.”
Murphy, the 53-year-old junior senator from Connecticut, was hospitalized on Saturday, a day before he planned to return to the campaign trail on behalf of Democratic candidates running in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
“He’s continuing to improve and heartened by the outpouring of well wishes,” Murphy communications director Josh Sorbe said in a statement.
He didn’t provide further details when asked about his condition, recovery or hospitalization.
Murphy experienced arm numbness while attending his son’s hockey game on Saturday, Oct. 31, and was taken to a hospital. He was later transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital where his doctors said they were “encouraged by his progress.”
“Yesterday afternoon, Sen. Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game,” Murphy chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement the following day.
“He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” she said. “He is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”
Murphy, who was not on Tuesday’s ballot, was campaigning the past several weeks in Connecticut and a handful of swing states for Democratic candidates competing in the midterms. And in early October, Murphy made a trip to the Middle East amid the ongoing war with Iran.
He was supposed to campaign in New Hampshire on the final weekend before Tuesday’s election. Murphy had also planned to attend Connecticut Democrats’ election night party in Dunkin’ Park in Hartford. That night, Gov. Ned Lamont went on to win a third term and Democrats across the board made massive electoral gains both locally and in Congress.
Murphy was in the hospital during Election Day, but he had cast an early vote in Connecticut’s elections.
He’s seen as a potential 2028 presidential contender or someone who can ascend in Senate leadership. And Murphy became a go-to campaign surrogate this election cycle.
Over the past few days, Democratic lawmakers and officials noted Murphy’s absence and credited his campaigning and fundraising as a key contribution to the blue wave that swept the party back into the majorities in both chambers of Congress. 
At a post-election event outside the state Capitol on Wednesday, Connecticut Democrats highlighted Murphy’s long-term work as a campaigner.
“Chris is somebody who has always, always fought to not just help the people running for office in this state, in this country, but to really drive towards serious change in this country, whether that was when he was in the state legislature or now as a member of Congress,” State Comptroller Sean Scanlon, who’s a former Murphy staffer, said Wednesday. “And I know Chris is paying attention and watching.”
“No one is with us more in spirit right now than my great friend and colleague Chris Murphy,” U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Tuesday night from the election watch party in Hartford.
“I will tell you when I go back to Washington to fight Donald Trump and this corrupt administration, Chris Murphy will be on my side,” he continued. “I look forward to welcoming him back to the United States Senate to continue this fight as a partner, as a colleague, as a wonderful friend.”
After a month-long recess for lawmakers to campaign, the U.S. Senate returns to Washington on Monday for about five more work weeks in the lame-duck session before the new Congress begins early next year.
Murphy is one of several senators to experience a stroke in the past several years.
In January 2022, U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., suffered a stroke when he was 49 and returned to work full-time about five weeks after. Several months later that year, U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., was hospitalized for about a week after a minor stroke when he was 63. 
Also in May 2022, John Fetterman, who was a 52-year-old Senate candidate in Pennsylvania, suffered a near-fatal stroke just days before the Democratic primary. He went on to win the primary and has served in the U.S. Senate since winning in November of that year.

title: Braun: Election results a ‘wake-up call’ for GOP
description: Gov. Mike Braun hinted Republicans should pick statewide candidates through public primaries, backed off mid-decade redistricting and dismissed concerns about his administration’s performance in wide-ranging comments Thursday about this week’s midterm election results. The governor described Democrats’ sweeping gains Tuesday as a “wake-up call” and an “oppor[...]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun speaks to reporters about midterm election results at the Statehouse Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle.)Gov. Mike Braun hinted Republicans should pick statewide candidates through public primaries, backed off mid-decade redistricting and dismissed concerns about his administration’s performance in wide-ranging comments Thursday about this week’s midterm election results.
The governor described Democrats’ sweeping gains Tuesday as a “wake-up call” and an “opportunity” for Republicans to refocus their agenda on issues of affordability, speaking of his desire to reach across the aisle to Democrats on issues like healthcare, education and childcare. 
But Braun, who is expected to announce his re-election campaign Nov. 16, repeatedly blamed the GOP’s losses on national issues rather than a referendum on his administration, saying voters were preoccupied with inflation.
“They were cranky, irritable and we did not read that well,” Braun said.
Indiana Democrats broke the GOP supermajority by flipping 16 seats in the House, ousted House Speaker Todd Huston and picked up seats in the state Senate. The party also claimed two statewide offices and picked up a congressional seat.
Indiana House Republicans pick new leader after big election losses

Braun suggested Republicans suffered fewer losses in Indiana than in states like Texas because his administration paid more attention to inflation, touting his gas tax suspension and firings at the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission as examples.
“That is a question I anticipated, and I think that is where you’re completely wrong, because here, what they say out of the gate, it was nationalized, and my administration has done nothing other than emphasizing the big issue out there,” he said.
Still, Braun conceded Republicans lost support in places like Hamilton County because “we weren’t listening enough there.”
He seemingly retreated from his support of mid-decade redistricting — months after backing President Donald Trump’s retribution campaign to oust Republican state senators who opposed the effort last year.
“I think that was probably clearly litigated by the results of the election Tuesday,” he said.
Braun also suggested support for selecting future statewide GOP candidates through public primaries following the election of Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh and Comptroller-elect Jessica Bailey — the first Democrats elected to statewide office since 2012.
Currently, state convention delegates choose the GOP’s nominees for secretary of state, attorney general, comptroller, treasurer and lieutenant governor. But the top post of governor goes through an open primary.
“When it comes to our system, which uses a convention, that’s a few people. We’ve done it traditionally. I had to run in a primary. To me, the more you open anything up to the people, you’re probably going to get a better result,” Braun said. “That’s going to be a big discussion for our party, because we still, at this point in time, have all those levers to play with. And again, the more you democratize how you pick people, I’m going to be for it rather than doing it behind closed doors, or where fewer people can weigh into it.”
Some Republicans believe convention delegates — the hard core party faithful – are choosing nominees that aren’t best suited to win in a General Election environment.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: 3M settles chemical contamination claims for $7.35 billion, while admitting no guilt
description: 3M, which is responsible for widespread groundwater contamination from so-called forever chemicals in the eastern Twin Cities metro, will pay $7.35 billion to settle the vast majority of outstanding personal injury claims against it. The Minnesota corporate behemoth and a group of plaintiffs’ lawyers announced the settlement on Tuesday. As many as 120,000 pe[...]
text:
Sprinklers spray water over the grass on 3M's Maplewood headquarters Monday, Sept. 12, 2022. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)3M, which is responsible for widespread groundwater contamination from so-called forever chemicals in the eastern Twin Cities metro, will pay $7.35 billion to settle the vast majority of outstanding personal injury claims against it.
The Minnesota corporate behemoth and a group of plaintiffs’ lawyers announced the settlement on Tuesday. As many as 120,000 people who say they were injured by PFAS and similar chemicals in firefighting foam, drinking water and other sources could be eligible for compensation under the agreement.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said the settlement was a long time in coming.
“For the thousands of victims who have sought answers and accountability for nearly a decade, 3M’s $7.35 billion settlement is welcome news” and a “favorable result for victims who are in urgent need of support to cover the mounting medical bills and other costs frequently associated with toxic PFAS exposure,” attorneys Fred Thompson and David Hoyle said in a joint statement. Both are partners with Motley Rice, a South Carolina law firm.
The settlement, valued at $5.8 billion for accounting purposes, “addresses approximately 99% of current personal injury claims” related to PFAS, 3M said. Payouts will come over nine years, with the bulk arriving from 2028 to 2033.
As is common in negotiated settlements, the agreement includes no admission of wrongdoing from 3M. The company “is prepared to continue to defend itself in litigation” if the settlement falls apart, it said in a securities filing Tuesday.
The settlement nonetheless resolves a significant source of uncertainty that has dogged Maplewood-based 3M for more than a decade. 3M’s stock price rose about 10% on Wednesday, the first day of trading after the announcement.
William Brown, 3M’s chairman and CEO, said in a prepared statement that the agreement was “a significant milestone for 3M and substantially reduces litigation uncertainty.”
Like international oil companies that knew about the planet-warming effects of their products for decades before admitting the connection, 3M and fellow chemicals giant DuPont were aware as far back as the 1950s that PFAS compounds from their products were accumulating in human and animal tissues, according to internal company documents reviewed by the Reformer in 2022. 
But state and federal environmental regulators didn’t begin actively investigating the connection until 1999, when a 3M toxicologist resigned in protest and alerted the U.S. Environmental Protection Administration.
The following year, 3M said it would voluntarily phase out some PFAS compounds in its products. As of 2025, it no longer manufactures any PFAS compounds anywhere in the world — though forever chemicals from products previously produced by 3M and other industrial companies will remain in the environment, and people, for the foreseeable future. 
PFAS compounds are or were once found in an array of consumer and industrial products, including nonstick coatings, food packaging, dental floss and firefighting foam. They are useful because they are resistant to heat, oil, stains, grease and water. 
In 2023, 3M announced a sweeping $10.3 billion settlement with U.S. public water suppliers to fund present and future PFAS remediation “at any level” in drinking water systems and to support nationwide PFAS testing in clean water supplies. This year, it reached a separate, $450 million agreement with the state of New Jersey to remediate PFAS groundwater contamination there.
Several Minnesota cities, including Lake Elmo and Hastings, have discovered PFAS in drinking water wells since the early 2000s. 
In 2010, then-Attorney General Lori Swanson sued 3M, alleging the company harmed Minnesotans by dumping the chemicals in the east metro. The state and the company eventually settled for $850 million for east metro water supplies. 
The Legislature enacted some of the nation’s tightest regulations on PFAS in 2023, including a law named after Amara Strande, a young advocate who died of a rare cancer she suspected was caused by PFAS exposure. As one graduate of Tartan High School told the Reformer in 2022, Oakdale — where 3M dumped PFAS into unlined pits until 1959 — featured the nerds, the jocks and “the cancer kids.” 
The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency has found PFAS in surface water and fish tissue in Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota lakes, too. And a citizen analysis of contaminant testing by MPCA and other state agencies points to significant potential gaps in fish-tissue testing statewide, the Reformer first reported last month.
PFAS compounds’ infamous durability means the issue is unlikely to go away soon, even if most of the active claims against 3M appear to be resolved. The company’s settlement announcement describes the resolved complaints as “legacy claims,” and the agreement’s fine print includes a $680 million reserve fund for future claims. 
It also anticipates a court order “establishing evidentiary and timing requirements for plaintiffs who may seek to litigate in the future.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Camilleri named Senate majority leader by Democratic caucus, Hauck chosen to lead Republicans
description: Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) was named the next Senate majority leader by the Democratic caucus on Thursday afternoon. While he will not officially assume the role until voted in by the full chamber in January, his nomination by the Democrats makes that a formality. Talking to reporters after the vote, Camilleri repeatedly said that his […]
text:
Incoming Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) and outgoing Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) speak on the Senate floor prior to caucus leadership elections on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton) was named the next Senate majority leader by the Democratic caucus on Thursday afternoon. While he will not officially assume the role until voted in by the full chamber in January, his nomination by the Democrats makes that a formality.
Talking to reporters after the vote, Camilleri repeatedly said that his goal is to ensure that the upcoming legislative session is “the most productive legislative session in our lifetimes.” He later went on to say that his metric for that was having the most “meaningful” bills signed into law.
“My caucus was sent here with a mandate to lower the cost of living for our residents, to address the many problems that Michigan has not been able to address for the last two years, and get things done for working people,” he said. “We are incredibly excited at the chance for us to take on a big, bold agenda with our brand new Democratic trifecta, and be in a position to solve as many problems as we can.”
Camilleri will assume the majority leader role with a 23-15 majority in the chamber — significantly larger than the last session, where Democrats held just a single seat majority for most of the term and did not control the House, and larger than the session prior, in which Democrats had a trifecta but only a two-seat margin in the Senate.
State Senate Democrats take a selfie in the Senate chamber prior to caucus leadership elections on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
With such a large majority in the Senate, as well as a large Democratic majority in the House, Camilleri said, “Our goal will be to make sure that we can again do big bold things in this new trifecta. I can’t again give you a list today, but I do believe that because we have returned with stronger majorities than we’ve ever really had, we’ll have a chance to do a lot more.”
A significant portion of the Democratic caucus is new to the state Senate, and many members are new to the Legislature completely. Camilleri said their wide breadth of experiences and backgrounds will help inform legislative priorities for the next two years, though some will have to get up to speed on the workings of the Legislature.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sen. Kevin Hertel (D-St. Clair Shores), who was chosen by the Democrats as the next Majority Floor Leader, will play a role in that, Camilleri said.
“We want to make sure with this diverse caucus that everybody, everybody’s ideas are on the table, that every voice is being heard, and that we are being extremely productive,” Hertel told reporters. “That’s the role of the floor leader to make sure everything’s moving in a smooth fashion. That the caucus is getting the information that they need.”
Lt. Governor-elect and outgoing Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said she feels “great about the handoff” and emphasized the importance of having wide margins in both chambers of the legislature to help the executive leadership push through their agenda. 
Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson also expressed support for Camilleri’s leadership, telling reporters, “My ask of all of them was to be bold. Let’s take big swings together. Let’s transform our state. And the other thing I said was that I intend to be collaborative. I know they all have great ideas. They come here representing their communities with a vision for what they want to achieve. I want to have them achieve it.”
Incoming Senate Minority Leader Roger Hauck (R-Mt. Pleasant) speaks to reporters following caucus leadership elections on Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Republicans chose Sen. Roger Hauck (R-Mt. Pleasant) as their caucus leader. While some had speculated there might be a contentious leadership election in the minority, Hauck said his election was unanimous and that he “put that to rest.”
“Obviously, we start out in a bad situation. We only have 15 members, right, and they have 23, so they’re not going to need us as much,” he told reporters after his selection. “But I promised the majority leader and Senator Hertel that I would work with them.”
Republicans also announced their full leadership team in a press release. Sen. Thomas Albert (R-Lowell) will serve as Republican Floor Leader, Sen.-elect John Wetzel (R-Grand Haven) as Republican Whip, Sen.-elect Gina Johnsen (R-Portland) as Republican Caucus Chair, Sen. Michele Hoitenga (R-Manton) as Assistant Republican Leader, Sen.-elect Mike Murphy (R-Howell) as Assistant Republican Floor Leader, Sen.-elect Donni Steele (R-Orion Township) as Assistant Republican Whip, and Sen. Jonathan Lindsey (R-Coldwater) as Assistant Republican Caucus Chair.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Former Columbia mayor, White House adviser funds USC leadership scholarships, speakers
description: The University of South Carolina is naming its leadership center after former Columbia Mayor Steve Benjamin, who donated $1 million to his alma mater.
text:
Former Columbia Mayor Steve Benjamin is seen during the Mark Anthony Brewing grand opening and ribbon cutting event in Columbia, S.C. on Thursday, May 12, 2022. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Steve Benjamin, the former mayor of South Carolina’s capital city and adviser to President Joe Biden, donated $1 million to his alma mater to promote student leadership and community service.
In response, the University of South Carolina named its leadership center, located inside the Russell House student union, in his honor. The center houses the school’s more than 700 student organizations and student government.
“As a student, I saw firsthand how mentors, service and a community that believes in you can help turn potential into purpose. My hope is that the Stephen K. Benjamin Leadership and Service Center will give students the same opportunities to learn, listen and serve alongside their neighbors while using their voices and talents to create meaningful change,” Benjamin said in a statement.

Students walk past Russell House student union on the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia, S.C. pictured on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/SC Daily Gazette)

Benjamin earned a bachelor’s degree in political science in 1991 and a law degree three years later, also from USC.
While an undergraduate student, he was elected student body president and joined USC’s historic chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi fraternity, founded in 1970 as the campus’ first Black, Greek-letter fraternity.
During law school, Benjamin was president of the Student Bar Association.
From 1999 to 2003, he led the state Department of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services under Gov. Jim Hodges, South Carolina’s last Democratic governor.
Voters first elected him mayor in 2010, making him Columbia’s first Black mayor. He tenure officially ended Dec. 31, 2021, after he decided not to seek a fourth term.
Then in February 2023, Biden made Benjamin his senior adviser and director of the White House Office of Public Engagement.
Benjamin’s gift to the university will pay for scholarships and lecture series on leadership, civic engagement and community impact.
“Students are the heart of this campus, and their leadership and service make a lasting impact on our university and community,” Ambra Hiott, associate vice president for student life, said in a statement. “We are deeply grateful to Mayor Benjamin for his investment in our students and for the example he continues to set through his commitment to service, civic engagement and leadership.”
Benjamin’s wife, U.S. Appeals Court Judge DeAndrea Benjamin, also graduated from USC’s law school. She graduated in 1997. She attended Winthrop University for undergrad. Before the U.S. Senate confirmed her to the federal bench in February 2023, she was a circuit court judge in Richland County.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: A former state lawmaker, Clark now ready to help set US House agenda
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: Top Democrats agree their agenda will focus on ways to lower costs including reversing Medicaid cuts and opposing tariffs proposed by President Donald Trump.
text:
US REP. KATHERINE CLARK and fellow Democrats eyeing leadership roles in the US House and Senate will be busy over the next several weeks solidifying an agenda they hope will help the party hold onto, and possibly expand, its base of support over the next few years.
Top Democrats agree their agenda will focus on ways to lower costs including reversing Medicaid cuts and opposing tariffs proposed by President Donald Trump.
Asked by a reporter on Wednesday about priorities, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is favored to become the next House speaker, said “we have been focused relentlessly on dealing with the affordability crisis and driving down the high cost of living.”
That includes extending Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired last year, lifting Trump’s tariffs, reversing cuts to Medicaid and ending the “reckless and costly war” that has driven up gas prices.
“We ran as affordability Democrats, and every single campaign had that at its center: lower costs, make sure every American has health care when and where they need it, that they can afford and hold those who are enriching themselves through corruption at taxpayers’ expense accountable and that’s exactly what we’re going to do,” Clark said during a press conference on Wednesday.
“The priority, the agenda – we cannot wait to get this big caucus together and help set that with the speaker’s vision and guidance. But I can tell you this: that every week when we come to the floor, it is going to be the people of this country who are going to be the focus of the work we do and the campaign promises made are going to be promises kept,” she said.
State lawmakers are processing a supplemental budget that features appropriations to cover explosive Medicaid spending and any changes to that program will be watched closely for fiscal impacts on the state budget and those covered by the sweeping health insurance and safety net program. Legislators now have members of the state’s congressional delegation poised to help set national policies in 2027 and 2028, although their offerings could be vetoed by President Trump.
Clark served in the Massachusetts House from 2008 until 2010 and in the state Senate from 2011 until 2013. A Revere Democrat and current minority whip, she is favored to become the next majority leader – and the first woman to hold the role – after Democrats won back control of Congress on Tuesday.
US Rep. Richard Neal, who’s viewed as the next chair of the US House Ways and Means Committee, told the News Service that he’d like restoration of ACA credits to be one of the House’s first actions. He also believes that some Republicans, who will now be in the minority party, can feel freer to oppose tariffs that President Donald Trump proposes.
“We’re likely to have a substantial majority, and they’re likely to be able to read what happened to them at this last election,” Neal said.
Neal said he and Clark are on the same page and meet regularly.
“We convene for breakfast, the Democratic leadership team every Wednesday morning at 8:15 a.m., and Katherine and I actually sit next to Hakeem Jeffries. So it’s been a good, strong relationship that we’ve had,” he said.
Democrats flipped 31 US House seats to secure 240 spots to Republicans’ 147 with 48 races yet to be called as of about 9:45 a.m. on Thursday, according to The Associated Press. In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats for a majority of 54-44 with two races undecided.
And as top Democrats still need the caucus’s backing to solidify their leadership roles, they will have to focus more efforts on understanding the priorities of newly elected members that flipped seats in areas that have been dominated by Republicans, said James Messner, former deputy political director for US House Majority Leader Steve Scalise.
“They’re there because of the large majority that these members in Trump-won districts have provided them, and they haven’t been on the ground talking to voters like these new members have, so they’re going to learn a lot over the next couple weeks of what is it exactly that these voters want done from these new members, and it’ll adjust the priorities,” Messner said, adding that the cost of living will likely remain House Democrats’ top priority.
Neal is aware of this reality and said he wants to craft legislation that those members can feel good about supporting as well as include them in the legislative process.
“I think there’s a reminder there for the Democratic caucus, and I think Hakeem Jeffries has understood it quite clearly, and that is that many of these members that got elected last evening – they come from purple districts. They’re likely to have major opponents in two years,” he said.
Also, while some Democrats have called for impeaching Trump, Jeffries has been less enthusiastic about the idea.
“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic caucus talk to me about impeachment,” he said. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability because the House is a separate and co-equal branch of government, we recognize that we don’t work for Donald Trump, we don’t work for J.D. Vance, we don’t work for the Supreme Court.”
“House Democrats are going to lead a Congress that does serve as a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch,” Jeffries said, adding that he has not “heard from President Trump.”
To cement the caucus’s support, Clark and Jeffries – along with others seeking leadership roles – are also expected to be spending the next several days and weeks contacting newly elected members of Congress.
“Those relationships are largely intact well before Election Day, and they’re spending today calling them directly to find out  ‘how can I support you in staffing your office?'” said Messner. “…A lot of these members are going to need assistance, and Jeffries and Clark are going to be that main point of contact to help them get set up.”
The idea of Jeffries and Clark leading the caucus is not new – in 2022, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi endorsed the pair along with California Rep. Pete Aguilar as the next trio of top Democrats. Also, experts say the reelection campaigns for those seeking leadership roles have also doubled as unofficial internal campaigns as they spent much of the election cycle fundraising and backing candidates. 
“In a sense, that was their campaign. They were out there over the past two years proving to their colleagues that they deserve to have these leadership positions and they were raising resources, recruiting candidates, coaching those candidates, traveling to those districts, supporting them, so that when it comes time to take this vote in early January, that that it’ll be a no-brainer,” said former Democratic New Hampshire US Rep. Annie Kuster.
That’s largely the case for Neal, who was first elected to Washington in 1988. He was elected chair of the House Committee on Ways and Means in 2019 and held that post until 2023 when Republicans took control of Congress. Neal, the committee’s ranking member, told the News Service that he’s maintained “pretty good loyalty with Democratic members” and helped dozens of candidates throughout the election.
“I would anticipate that,” Neal said when asked if he viewed his support for other candidates as an unofficial campaign for chairmanship. “I also would point out that I had a pretty good run the last time I was chairman, and I would intend to certainly build upon what we did.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Thousands of affidavit ballots outstanding in Mississippi Senate election. Campaigns prepare for legal fight
description: Election lawyers from across the country have descended on Mississippi as the national Democratic and Republican parties scrutinize the final count of the midterm Senate race between Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Local election officials on Thursday continued processing thousands of outstanding absentee and affidavit ballots as the nation watched to see who will win Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race.  
The razor-thin margin between Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom has already shocked many across the nation, but it remained too close to call on Thursday. Colom led by 1,764 votes with nearly 1 million cast.
A likely legal fight over the count also continued brewing on Thursday.
Colom’s campaign said he is clearly on track to win, and the voting rights organization Fair Fight said the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Democratic election attorneys from Elias Law Group have deployed hundreds of volunteers and local lawyers across all 82 counties to oversee the final rounds of counting. 
LIVE: 2026 Mississippi election results
The National Republican Senatorial Committee sent a letter on Thursday to county election commissioners and circuit clerks in Mississippi, demanding they separate and preserve all affidavit ballots cast. 
“As the democratic process continues to play out, we are committed to ensuring that every single lawful ballot is accurately counted and the voices of all Mississippians are heard,” said NRSC Regional Press Secretary Samantha Cantrell. 
The letter demands that election officials preserve a wide range of records, pointing to future litigation.  
The state Republican Party was set to address reporters in a press conference in Jackson later on Thursday. 
How many votes are left to count?
Secretary of State Michael Watson on Wednesday said that 3,600 outstanding mail-in absentee ballots could be processed, though realistically not all of these ballots will reach local election workers by the statutory Nov. 10 deadline. 
Between 14,000 and 18,000 affidavit ballots remain outstanding throughout the state, according to Lisa Ross, a local voting rights attorney who is leading the effort to monitor election officials processing the remaining ballots. 
Election attorneys, voting rights advocates and national reporters have descended on Mississippi over the past 48 hours, scrambling to make sense of what remaining ballots are out, when they would be counted and how Colom found himself in striking distance of pulling off a victory in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in decades.  
At a breakfast event in Jackson on Thursday morning, Colom greeted a throng of jubilant volunteers and said he had little doubt the race was breaking in his direction. 
“Anybody out there that does an analysis knows where this is going. The affidavit (vote) is always moving in Democratic favor in Mississippi,” Colom said. “You look at the ballots that are left, it’s going in our favor, absolutely.”
Spokespeople for Hyde-Smith’s campaign did not immediately offer a comment about where the number stood on Thursday. 
The Associated Press showed about 10% of the vote remained uncounted in Hinds County, the most populous area of the state and a Democratic stronghold. Election officials in Hinds County have said they expect the review of remaining ballots, most of which are absentee and affidavit ballots, to take days. 
Ballots also remained uncounted in areas along the Mississippi Gulf Coast and in the Jackson suburb of Rankin County, both areas Hyde-Smith won. 
Colom did not speculate how long it would take for the remaining ballots to be counted, but said he is confident “Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction.” 
“I’m proud of the lawyers that we’ve got, the organizers we have that are on the ground making sure the law is followed, and that you know we do what we can,” Colom said. “I’m very excited where we are.”  
Election lawyers descend on Mississippi
Lauren Groh-Wargo, Fair Fight’s CEO, said in a statement that “Mississippians turned out in historic numbers” and that the organization would work to “defend the will of the people.” 
“Right now, Scott Colom is ahead, and we are confident that when the votes are tallied, he will be Mississippi’s next U.S. Senator.”
Semafor congressional reporter Nicholas Wu reported on Thursday that the U.S. House Black Caucus’ political arm is “aggressively fundraising for recounts in Mississippi” and a congressional race in North Carolina. 
Mississippi has no automatic recount law. A recount would happen only if a court ordered it. For that to happen, a campaign or political party would have to file a lawsuit against a county or county election commission. 
A state judge would likely hear the case on an expedited basis, and the lower court’s decision would be appealable to the Mississippi Supreme Court. 
After election results are certified, campaigns can conduct ballot box examinations, which can be used as evidence in a lawsuit. The dispute over which affidavit ballots are accepted and rejected would likely be the subject of litigation. 
If a court fight ensued, it could be a disjointed, chaotic process. Mississippi law does not establish a system for challenging ballots on a statewide scale, only on a county-by-county basis. 
How Democrat Colom pulled ahead of a GOP senator
The razor-thin margin has national pundits wondering how a Democrat is on the cusp of managing a stunning upset in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat in over four decades or elected a Black person to the chamber since Reconstruction. 
Colom managed to crack the GOP’s iron grip on the state by turning out large numbers of Black voters, flipping several crucial swing counties blue and convincing Republicans to cross over and vote for him. 
The most surprising feat was Colom winning DeSoto County, a reliably Republican stronghold in a Memphis suburb, by seven percentage points, something Democrats would have viewed as unthinkable last year. 
In 2020, Hyde-Smith won the county with 56% of the vote, while Democrat Mike Espy got 40%. Now Colom has flipped the script and carried the county by 51%, while Hyde-Smith trails at 45%. 
Colom also tempered his losses in Harrison County, a populous coast county that has swamped statewide Democratic candidates over the last decade and become a red firewall for the state GOP. 
In 2020, Hyde-Smith trounced Espy in Harrison County by 17 percentage points. This year, only four percentage points separate Hyde-Smith and Colom. 
The Democratic nominee also managed to flip Lafayette and Madison counties, two majority-white, affluent areas of the state that have become swing areas in recent elections. Brandon Presley, the Democratic nominee for governor in 2023, lost those two areas, but Colom narrowly won them 
Colom said he dramatically overperformed a “generic Democrat” in counties across the state and believed Hyde-Smith’s negative ads had backfired because he visited so many voters in person.

text:
The Florida Senate chamber on May 29, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Senate President-Designate Jim Boyd released on Thursday released details about his planned inner circle during his two-year rein as leader of the Florida Senate and confirmed an organizational session will be held in Tallahassee on Tuesday, Nov. 17.
There was no mention of a special session on a taxpayer bill of rights, as Gov. Ron DeSantis advocated, in Boyd’s announcement.
During the organizational session, new and returning senators will be sworn in and Boyd, a Republican from Bradenton, will officially be elected to preside over the chamber. The Senate also will adopt rules that it will follow during Boyd’s two-year term.
 
House Speaker-Designate Sam Garrison, left, and Senate President-Designate Jim Boyd, right, converse between their two chambers in the Florida Capitol. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
Incoming House Speaker Republican Sam Garrison, meanwhile, had made no announcement about any of his appointments to leadership positions.
Boyd tapped Miami Republican Sen. Ana Maria Rodriguez and Sen. Nick DiCeglie, a Republican from Indian Rocks Beach, to serve as Senate president pro tempore and Senate majority leader, respectively.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.In terms of high-profile committee assignments, Boyd announced that Zephyrhills Republican Sen. Danny Burgess will head the powerful Senate Committee on Rules.
Republican Jay Trumbull, of Panama City, who is anticipated to succeed Boyd as Senate president, was named chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations.
It’s a role he is familiar with, having served as chair of the House Appropriations Committee between 2020 and 2022 under former House Speaker Chris Sprowls.
Lakeland Republican Sen. Colleen Burton was named chair of the Committee on Fiscal Policy.
In a prepared statement, Boyd said that panel will provide an “alternative path to the Senate Calendar for bills with a fiscal impact. This structure allows time for robust discussion and debate on both budget items and policy initiatives prior to consideration by the full Senate.”
The announcement didn’t include any other committee assignments.

name: California
title: Gavin Newsom clears death row, commutes sentences for hundreds of prisoners
description: Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted death sentence for 548 state prisoners, saying "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values." Victims rights advocates criticized his decision.
text:
In summary
Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted death sentence for 548 state prisoners, saying “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values.” Victims rights advocates criticized his decision.


Gov. Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of 548 people, clearing the California death row for the first time since the state conducted hangings in the late 19th century. 
It is a monumental move in the history of capital punishment in America: The prisoners represent more than a quarter of the nation’s condemned inmates. 
And it is a decision Newsom has spoken about in starkly personal terms. In 2019, shortly after taking office, he issued a moratorium on executions just three years after voters rejected a ballot measure to abolish the death penalty and instead approved one to speed them up. But at the time, the governor said he couldn’t be responsible for killing another person. 
“After nearly 30 years in office I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish,” Newsom wrote in a letter addressed “to all Californians.” “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us.”
Since 2024, death row has been a metaphorical place. The male prisoners were cleared out of their individual cells in San Quentin State Prison and distributed among other 24 facilities. Twenty female prisoners condemned to death were moved to general population at the Central California Women’s Facility that year. Even before Newsom’s 2019 moratorium, it had been more than a decade since the state performed an execution. 
Some of the decisions Newsom made Thursday will need court approval. For those convicted of multiple felonies, four of seven judges on the Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations. 
Newsom said those with the commuted sentences will not be eligible for new Board of Parole Hearings commutation and resentencing regulations. That addresses some concerns prosecutors, victims’ groups and supporters of the death penalty had expressed as they anticipated Newsom’s decision: that those newly sentenced to life might get a chance later to be released. 
His anticipated decision garnered sharp condemnation in recent weeks from those groups, who argued it flew in the face of juries and judges that had upheld the death sentences, and voters who have upheld the practice. 
“I don’t think he or any person should undo the sentence rendered by a jury and signed off by a judge because of his personal beliefs or feelings,” said Topo Padilla, president of Crime Victims United, last week. 
Newsom said in his letter that the decision is among the most difficult of his career, “not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families.” He said after meeting with them over the years, he considered commuting only some sentences but “that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims — those whose perpetrators deserve the death penalty and then the rest.”
Natasha Minsker, former director of the American Civil Liberties Union of California’s Center for Advocacy and Policy, said the death penalty is now a forgotten part of California politics. “I’m shocked, when I talk to legislators and tell them to oppose it, they say we don’t have the death penalty in California,” she said. 
Mary McComb, the former state public defender, said from her first case defending a man with intellectual disabilities who was charged with a capital offense, she has found a moral reason to oppose the death penalty. 
“One can always hope, but without the commutations, it’s not always guaranteed that governors would continue to have the courage to (maintain a moratorium),” McComb said.
In an interview before the decision was made, Polly Klaas’ father Marc Klaas said the prospect of the commutations “upsets me terribly.” After years of appeals, Klaas said he had already given up the expectation that Davis would be executed one day, at the time of Newsom’s moratorium. 
“But I was still secure in my mind that he and the rest of them would be on death row for the rest of their lives,” he said. 
However Polly’s sister said in a statement Thursday that she used to think Davis deserved execution but came to realize that his killing won’t help her recovery or public safety. 
“The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need,” said Jess Nichol. 
This is a developing story that will be updated.

(Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse on Thursday asked Democrats in the House of Representatives to select him for the fourth highest-ranking role in the chamber’s incoming majority. 
Neguse, of Lafayette, is now the assistant minority leader in the House. The assistant speaker position is his current role’s equivalent in the majority party.
“With our decisive and overwhelming victory this week, it is more important than ever for the House Democratic Caucus to be unified in the 120th Congress, and to repay the faith that the American people have put in us to lower costs, end corruption, and deliver for working families,” Neguse said in a letter asking House Democrats to support him for the role.

If elected assistant House speaker, Neguse said he wants to expand training programs for district directors, launch a technical assistance program for subcommittee chairs and enhance mentorship and transition programs for new members of the caucus.
He is only the second Colorado lawmaker to serve in senior leadership, and he’s now the highest-ranking Colorado lawmaker since the 1930s. If elected, he will be the youngest member of Congress to ever hold the role. In the 119th Congress, he also served as chair of the House Democrats’ litigation task force.
“From our successful amicus briefs in multiple cases, our groundbreaking lawsuit against ICE, and regular programming opportunities for member engagement with legal experts, I’m deeply grateful to the many members of our caucus who made the Task Force’s work so consequential and impactful,” he said.
Voters in the 2nd Congressional District elected Neguse to his fifth term in Congress on Tuesday. The district is anchored in Boulder, stretching west along the Interstate 70 corridor and north to include Fort Collins. After being elected in 2018, he succeeded then-Rep. Jared Polis, who is Colorado’s outgoing governor.
Neguse became assistant minority leader after South Carolina’s Jim Clyburn decided to step down in early 2024 to create opportunity for new leadership.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Incoming Democratic House leader not sure of special session on property taxes
description: The new leader of the now-larger House Democratic caucus hopes her GOP leadership colleagues will decline Gov. Ron DeSantis’ call for a special legislative session to implement Amendment 3, following its passage into Florida law earlier this week. The governor on Wednesday called for a special session before the end of the year to implement […]
text:
The Fourth Floor Rotunda in the Florida Capitol. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix)The new leader of the now-larger House Democratic caucus hopes her GOP leadership colleagues will decline Gov. Ron DeSantis’ call for a special legislative session to implement Amendment 3, following its passage into Florida law earlier this week.
The governor on Wednesday called for a special session before the end of the year to implement the far-reaching homestead property tax reduction measure approved Tuesday by more than 62% of Florida voters. DeSantis said in a press conference that he wants lawmakers to prevent local governments from doing “an end-run around the amendment” by shifting how they can continue to collect revenue from their constituents.
State economists have estimated that local government revenues could be reduced ultimately by as much as $12 billion five years after the amendment goes into effect.
Christine Hunschofsky via Florida House
“I am hoping that this will not be a special session,” Florida House Democratic Leader Designate Christine Hunschofsky said during a remote press conference with reporters. “Those haven’t always worked out so well.”
Hunschofsky said it’s her understanding that there has not been any decision to convene a special session by incoming House Speaker Sam Garrison or incoming Senate President Jim Boyd, despite DeSantis’ announcement. Neither Republican leader has yet to publicly comment on his suggestion. As the Phoenix reported earlier this week, both leaders told the “Between the Lines with Dara Kam” podcast before the election that they weren’t ready to commit until next year.
Haste
The haste with which the Legislature reviewed and approved of the proposal sent by the governor’s office earlier this year was troubling, Hunschofsky said. She believes it would be more appropriate to review the upcoming law in a “thoughtful, methodical way” during the regular session, which is set to begin next March.
That’s when lawmakers would have sufficient time to review updated data and all of the amendment’s potential impacts “so that we do not do anything that would create implications that we did not foresee,” she said.
The amendment will increase the homestead exemption for non-school taxes from $50,000 per year to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.Hunschofsky hosted a group of newly elected House Democrats on the press call on Tuesday. Florida Democrats netted 15 additional seats in the House, and that could soon go to 16 if House District 33 Democratic candidate Daniel McDow survives a recount in his race in Brevard County against Republican incumbent Monique Miller. The Democrats flipped 16 Tuesday, losing only the House District 87 seat in Palm Beach County to Republican Jon Maples that Democrat Emily Gregory had won in March in a special election.
If McDow makes it through his recount, there’ll be 70 Republicans and 50 Democrats in the 120-member body.
The Democratic caucus is no longer in superminority status because of its successful night Tuesday. That means Republicans will now need Democratic votes to get a two-thirds vote on certain legislative procedures such as waiving the rules, placing constitutional amendments on the ballot, and overriding vetoes by the governor, Hunschofsky said.
Closer margins can make it easier to reach agreement on bipartisan matters, she said. “And with us having more numbers, it makes it more important that on those really important bipartisan issues that we all come together and that our caucus has a seat at the table.”
With additional reporting by Jay Waagmeester.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump administration grants 6-month reprieve for Arkansas Medicaid expansion
description: Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion will get a six-month grace period starting Jan. 1 while state officials consider a replacement for the program providing health coverage to more than 200,000 low-income residents, the state Department of Human Services announced Thursday. The state asked the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for a two-year reprieve [...]
text:
Secretary Janet Mann (left) and Division of County Operations Director Mary Franklin (right) of the Arkansas Department of Human Services answer questions from the Arkansas Legislative Council’s Hospital, Medicaid, and Developmental Disabilities Study Subcommittee on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion will get a six-month grace period starting Jan. 1 while state officials consider a replacement for the program providing health coverage to more than 200,000 low-income residents, the state Department of Human Services announced Thursday.
The state asked the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for a two-year reprieve in August after the federal agency verbally denied a five-year extension of the Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME. The current waiver for the hybrid program, which uses private insurance to cover low-income residents, expires Dec. 31.

Temporary_Extension_ARHOME_Signed.11.04.2026 
CMS notified Human Services Secretary Janet Mann that the program will remain in effect until June 30, 2027.
Mann and Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders expressed gratitude for the six-month grace period in a Department of Human Services news release.
“Our commitment to responsible stewardship of resources and connecting eligible Arkansans to quality health care will remain our focus,” Mann said.
The Trump administration’s rejection of renewing the expansion spawned from new guidance under last year’s federal tax and spending cut legislation known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. It requires the expansion program to not cost the federal government more than would be projected without the program.
“CMS will request additional information from the state needed for budget neutrality certification,” the agency wrote in Thursday’s letter to Arkansas.
In 2013, Arkansas became the first Southern state to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, but used a first-in-the-nation model that used expansion funds to purchase private insurance for those eligible.

Medicaid expansion in Arkansas: A timeline of the first-in-the-nation hybrid model


Arkansas adopted the hybrid model as a conservative alternative to Medicaid expansion when state government was divided between a Democratic governor and a Republican Legislature.
The program has survived multiple attempts to kill it, winning reauthorization each year despite the three-fourths vote needed in the House and Senate. The program easily won reauthorization in the Legislature earlier this year.
The future of Medicaid expansion is expected to be one of the Republican-led Legislature’s top priorities in the session starting in January.
Arkansas Democrats broke Republicans’ House supermajority in Tuesday’s elections, giving Democrats more leverage in discussions of how to spend taxpayer dollars. The supermajority that had been in place since 2016 allowed Republicans to pass most budget bills along party lines with at least 75 House votes.
House Minority Leader Andrew Collins said Thursday that he believes Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program has been important for individuals and the state’s healthcare system, and it needs to continue in some form.
During a virtual call with reporters about Democrats breaking the supermajority, Collins said details about what the state’s Medicaid expansion program will look like are underway and will continue during next year’s legislative session.
Collins also said the six-month extension granted by the federal government was a shorter timeframe than he expected.
“So we are going to have to work very fast and work very smart to both make sure that we have something in place and that we don’t have gaps that make life more difficult for people as they transition from ARHOME into whatever comes next,” he said.
Mann told lawmakers in August that nixing Medicaid expansion completely is not an option.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act put in place work requirements for Medicaid expansion recipients that Arkansas will start enforcing Jan. 1. Negotiations over the future of Medicaid expansion will not impact the Department of Human Services’ implementation of the work requirements, which apply to able-bodied Arkansans between the ages of 19 and 64, Thursday’s news release states.
In October, the Department of Human Services entered a three-year, $48 million contract with the Arkansas Foundation for Medical Care to set up a customer service center that will field questions about the agency’s programs, starting with Medicaid expansion.
Deputy Editor Antoinette Grajeda contributed to this story.

name: VTDigger
title: Porter Medical Center nurses sign new 3-year contract
description:
The contract extension — which includes slight wage increases — caps a bargaining session that started last summer.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Porter Medical Center nurses sign new 3-year contract.
text:
Porter Medical Center in Middlebury seen on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by John Flowers was first published by the Addison Independent on Nov. 2, 2026.
MIDDLEBURY — Porter Medical Center nurses have agreed on a new three-year contract that grants them annual wage increases of 3.25% in each of the first two years and 3.5% in year three, as well as additional gains in such areas as shift differentials, incentive pay and bereavement leave.
The agreement, confirmed by Porter Federation of Nurses & Health Professionals and Porter administrators, caps several lengthy bargaining sessions since July. The union a few weeks ago brought in a mediator to avert a possible strike; the nurses’ previous three-year deal expired Sept. 30.
Wages emerged as the major sticking point, and the union pared back its original demands in that area to make gains in other parts of the contract. As previously reported by the Independent, the union had recently pitched a 3% base-pay bump during each of the three years of the new pact, while Porter had countered with 1.5%.
It should be noted that the base pay figure doesn’t include an additional 2% “step” pay increase accorded to experienced registered nurses. So all told, the union ask would have amounted to 5% annually for experienced nurses, while Porter’s offer would have amounted to 3.5%.
“The obvious shortcoming of this contract is the wage increase,” registered nurse Finn Yarbrough, vice president of the union, stated in a post-ratification message to nurses. “By itself, I fear it will not keep up with inflation, and there is no way to sugar-coat this truth. Since midsummer we have all fought both as hard and as strategically as we could to win a wage increase for all that would bring us into parity with our colleagues at (the UVM Medical Center in Burlington). We did not succeed in this goal, and our strategic calculus ultimately was that it would hurt nurses more to recommend a strike: leaving us with losses rather than gains.”
But Yarbrough also touted contract gains, as did labor organizer MacArthur Stine, lead field representative/organizer for the American Federation of Teachers Vermont. The Porter nurses union falls under the AFT umbrella.
Stine said the new deal in effect raises wages by 10% over the three-year contract, mandates the construction of a registered nurse career ladder with two 5% increases built in, provides paid time off to recover after staff are assaulted physically or otherwise at work, increases retirement benefits by 2%-6%, “lays the foundation for safer staffing” and “improves job security,” among other things.
Yarbrough added that the pact will create a “more powerful” Nursing Practice Council combined with Labor Management Committee “to confront front-line issues of patient care and establish enforceable staffing ratios.”
“Over the course of the bargaining process, we have won significant ground in ways that cement our power to collectively determine the future of our careers,” Yarbrough told colleagues.
The new contract covers 143 full- and part-time nurses at Addison County’s healthcare hub.
Yarbrough said around 70% of local nurses union members voted on the new deal, and of those, 80% endorsed the new agreement.
It’s a deal that also drew praise from management at Porter Medical Center and the University of Vermont Health network, of which Porter is an affiliate. Vermont’s healthcare system has been in austerity mode for the past few years, as the number of privately insured Vermonters continues to decline while those covered by federal programs like Medicaid and Medicare — which don’t cover the true costs of medical service — increase.

READ MORE

As previously reported by the Independent, UVM Health in September eliminated a combined 199 jobs among its affiliates, including around 20 on Porter’s Middlebury campus. Most of the local job cuts (15) were at Helen Porter Health and Rehabilitation, which lost $5 million last year. Still, Porter has proven itself as one of the most solvent UVM Health units.
“This agreement is the result of months of thoughtful work between Porter and our union partners,” said Bob Ortmyer, president of Porter Medical Center, in a statement. “Nurses care for our neighbors, friends and family members every day and are vital to Porter’s mission. This agreement recognizes their essential contributions and reinforces our commitment to them, our patients and the long-term strength of Porter as a trusted health care resource for our community.”
Disclosure: John Flowers’ son is a Porter Hospital nurse.

title: Flores selected as new Nevada Senate majority leader
description: Democratic State Sen. Edgar Flores was selected as the next Senate Majority Leader, the Nevada Senate Democratic Caucus announced Thursday.  Flores, an immigration attorney, was first elected to the state Senate in 2022 and previously served in the Assembly.  “Our state faces urgent challenges, and working-class Nevadans are counting on us to deliver real so[...]
text:
Democratic state Sen. Edgar Flores. (Photo: Trevor Bexon/Nevada Current)Democratic State Sen. Edgar Flores was selected as the next Senate Majority Leader, the Nevada Senate Democratic Caucus announced Thursday. 
Flores, an immigration attorney, was first elected to the state Senate in 2022 and previously served in the Assembly. 
“Our state faces urgent challenges, and working-class Nevadans are counting on us to deliver real solutions from expanding access to affordable housing and health care to investing in our neighborhood public schools and making sure our economy works for everyday people,” Flores said in a statement. “I am excited to get to Carson City and work with our colleagues in the Assembly and Governor-elect Aaron Ford to build a Nevada where every community has the resources and opportunities to thrive.”
He will replace current Nevada State Senate Majority Leader Nicole Cannizzaro, who won her race to be Nevada’s next attorney general.
Flores won his general election bid, which was uncontested. He earlier had faced a tough primary election this year against North Las Vegas City Councilman Isaac Baron. 
The election centered around failed efforts by state lawmakers to massively expand the state’s existing film tax credit program, which Cannizzaro supported, Flores opposed. 
The $1.8 billion subsidy would have been tied to a planned film and production studio in the Summerlin neighborhood of Las Vegas. Legislative staff warned the proposal would lead the State of Nevada’s general fund off a fiscal cliff.
The proposal died in the Senate, falling short by just one vote.
Labor unions warned those opposed to the bill that there would be political consequences and Laborer’s Local 872 funneled a combined $20,000 to Barron’s campaign to unseat Flores.
Flores beat Barron with nearly 55% of the vote.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: MWRA pulls largest water transfer request in history after drawing backlash from Quabbin communities
description: The MWRA’s request landed the agency in even more hot water among Quabbin communities, which mobilized to kill the proposal.
text:
THE STATE’S BIGGEST drinking water provider has nixed a groundbreaking request to draw an additional 20 million gallons of water per day out of the Quabbin Reservoir in a nod to the outrage it prompted within central Massachusetts communities. 
The Massachusetts Water Resources Authority, which serves 61 municipalities mostly in and around Greater Boston, had pursued its plan — by far the largest withdrawal request in its history — in order to meet growing demand from new communities like Weymouth and Wayland looking to join the system.  
But in addition to the size of its proposal, which totaled 10 percent of average annual demand, the agency faced fierce backlash for the process it deployed to win approval from state regulators at the Water Resources Commission. The proposal added fuel to an escalating feud with the small rural towns surrounding the Quabbin and their representatives on Beacon Hill.  
Water transfers like the one the MWRA pitched here are governed by the 40-year-old Interbasin Transfer Act, in which state officials ensure that the move is environmentally sound and meets demonstrated need for both what’s known as the donor basin, the resource sending water elsewhere, and the receiving basin, or the area taking in more water. 
Yet for the first time in state history, the MWRA sought the greenlight from state regulators on its donor basin proposal separately, before any receiving basin requests that may come in the future in an effort to streamline the process and cut red tape. If advanced, the MWRA could have had donor basin approvals in hand by the time new communities attempt to receive the water and join the system. 
“It is clear that the use of that regulatory option added to confusion and concern, rather than allaying it,” Stephen Estes-Smargiassi, MWRA’s interim executive director, wrote in a letter to the Water Resources Commission on Thursday.  
Estes-Smargiassi said the agency will “commit” to returning to the traditional process under the law, in which donor basin and receiving basin analyses are considered simultaneously.  
But the decision may not kill the underlying drive to win approval for future requests to support system expansion.  
Jonathan Gulliver, who was recently named the agency’s full-time executive director, supports withdrawing the request and “pursuing a more focused submission that addresses the demonstrated needs of the communities currently seeking admission to the MWRA system,” according to the letter.  
The MWRA’s request landed the agency in even more hot water among Quabbin communities, which mobilized to kill the proposal.  
Those small towns themselves don’t drink water from the reservoir, creating a cruel irony as private and municipal wells near the largest water body in the state dried up and towns instituted water restrictions during recent years’ record drought while MWRA customers faced few limits. 
Plus, these communities are barred from developing — and therefore taxing — large sections of land around the reservoir to protect the water source from which they don’t benefit. The glaringly little state compensation they do receive for stewarding that land has further laid bare the intense fiscal shortfalls those towns confront as they cut public school workers, consolidate emergency services, and navigate local water crises of their own that in some cases render municipal buildings unusable.  
To these towns, the MWRA’s water transfer request could feel more like an end run to expedite its expansion efforts in the eastern part of the state than a legitimate push to reduce bureaucracy.  
Sen. Jo Comerford, who represents the Quabbin towns at the State House and is spearheading legislative reforms to boost payments to these communities and grant them a permanent seat on the MWRA board, said in a statement that the agency’s decision to pull back its transfer request is a “powerful recognition of the significant concerns” the towns raised. 
“Arm in arm with statewide partners, constituents and the state legislative delegation showed up, raised our voices, and made clear that regional equity, the voices of watershed communities, and a shared potable water future must be centered in all decisions involving the Quabbin Reservoir,” Comerford said. 
Gov. Maura Healey, who won a second term Tuesday, sided with the Quabbin communities’ concerns earlier this year — even though the MWRA argued the transfer request would help meet ambitious state housing goals that Healey has stressed are necessary to tackle a sweeping affordability crisis.
“Every day, these watershed communities provide an invaluable public service to the communities served by the MWRA system,” Healey wrote in a letter to the agency. “They continue to help protect the watershed’s natural resources while navigating infrastructure constraints, including limitations on their own water supply and economic development.” 
Even with this transfer request off the table, Gulliver will step into the top spot at the MWRA in January amid major expansion plans and continued discontent from the communities surrounding the agency’s main water source.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: War, high prices, typical midterm backlash spurred NJ GOP losses, party says
description: Republicans took a drubbing nationally and lost two of their three New Jersey House seats Tuesday. Now they're asking why.
text:
Republicans took a drubbing nationally and lost two of their three New Jersey House seats Tuesday. GOP officials say high prices and the Iran War are to blame. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)New Jersey’s top Republican party official said a dour national political climate and economic fallout from the Iran War helped seed the party’s broad losses Tuesday, but she said it is too soon to chart the GOP’s course into the future.
The electoral losses cost New Jersey Republicans two of their three House seats and cemented for national Democrats their largest congressional majorities in nearly 20 years.
“I would say that it’s, No. 1., you have the midterm backlash, which is normal, and then on top of that, you have a war, you have high gas prices,” said Republican State Chair Christine Hanlon, who is also Monmouth County clerk. “I don’t think it’s too difficult to look at what was going on, to come up with the reasons why people were not happy.”
Democrats must deliver on their affordability promises

On Tuesday, Democrats swept congressional races across the country. They won at least 54 seats in the Senate and have claimed at least 247 seats in the House, a feat not seen since a wave of Democrats entered Congress on President Barack Obama’s coattails in 2008.
New Jersey Republicans’ losses included House seats held by Reps. Tom Kean Jr. and Jeff Van Drew, as well as losses further down the ballot, including for county offices in Monmouth, Cumberland, and Morris counties.
Republicans had been bracing for Kean’s loss to Democrat Rebecca Bennett but were stunned when Van Drew was ousted by Zack Mullock, the Democratic mayor of Cape May City.
Sen. Jon Bramnick (R-Union), a frequent and longtime critic of President Donald Trump, said Trump’s brand is corrosive in New Jersey, adding that Republicans need to return to moderation and fiscal conservatism. Trumpism “just doesn’t work in New Jersey,” he said.
“Stop making excuses. Stop blaming fraud in voting and start to accept the fact that you win when you follow traditional Republican values,” he said.



Quotation







Right now, we’re at the point of not being a viable entity, and we can’t let that happen.


– Ocean County Republican Chair George Gilmore


Bramnick has for years sparred with Trump allies in New Jersey over whose brand of Republicanism is more favored in the Garden State.
The president’s allies were sure they won that argument in 2024, when Trump came closer to winning New Jersey in that year’s presidential election than any other Republican in decades, but the following year the party’s Trump-supporting gubernatorial candidate lost in a landslide.
Hanlon acknowledged decisions made in Washington, D.C., had a “real impact” on New Jersey’s races but said Republicans need to regroup first before looking forward. The state party had limited success getting its own messaging out, she conceded.
“Our legislators have been banging the drum,” she said, adding, “We’ve been trying to have a New Jersey message, and it kind of gets drowned out in the national. “
Ocean County Republican Chair George Gilmore likewise acknowledged Trump contributed to Tuesday’s results, but said the GOP needs to do a better job of matching candidates to districts and financially supporting its office seekers.
Further, the disparate Republican campaign arms need to better coordinate their plans and spending, both to keep hold of GOP ground that has progressively shrunk over the last two years and bolster Republican organizations whose control has waned in counties like Bergen and Somerset.
“What I want to see is progress all the way around, in the Senate, in the Assembly, in the state committee, and among the county chairs to work together to make the Republican Party viable again,” Gilmore said. “Right now, we’re at the point of not being a viable entity, and we can’t let that happen.”
For Bramnick, the path forward is a clean break with Trump, even if that split proves electorally costly for members in heavily Republican districts, like those based in Ocean County or the state’s northwest.
“They have to get over self-preservation and start thinking about the Republican Party as a whole in New Jersey,” Bramnick said. “I don’t know how you do that. People have to be selfless, and they have to say, ‘Look, here are the results. Stop.’”
The Republican Party has limited time to find its path forward. Every seat in the New Jersey Legislature — that’s 40 in the State Senate and 80 in the General Assembly — is up for a vote next year. Democrats, who control the Senate 25-15 and the Assembly 57-23, have controlled the Legislature for more than two decades.
Bramnick’s anti-Trump stance has already drawn a 2027 primary challenge from Peapack-Gladstone Councilman Conor Sweeney. Bramnick represents the 21st Legislative District.
Gilmore said Republicans need to adapt their candidates to the districts they are running in, warning that Sweeney could win that primary but could cost Republicans the district’s Senate seat in the general election.
The 21st is a suburban district long targeted by Democrats. Last year, Democrats ousted Republican Assembly members there, marking Democrats’ first win in the district since 1989.
“Don’t tell me there’s going to be some miracle wave that comes into everybody’s mind and in Bramnick’s district they’re going to vote conservative next year,” Gilmore said. “It’s not going to happen, so why set yourself up for failure?”
