French Hill, a Republican, answers questions during the debate against Democratic opponent Chris Jones on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill has won a seventh term, fending off his challenger Chris Jones despite efforts from national Democrats to flip the seat.
The Associated Press called the race Thursday at 11:01 a.m.
Jones hoped to capitalize on the sour national mood toward Republicans, with voters deeply unhappy about the cost of living and stubbornly high gas prices amid the war in Iran. He conceded the race to Hill Thursday afternoon.
“More than 123,000 of you voted for us, we got the closest anybody has ever come to beating Congressman Hill, and we put a crack in that Arkansas glass ceiling,” Jones said in a statement. 
“Now, this isn’t the outcome we worked for, but being your candidate has been one of the great honors of my life. I’ll carry the stories you shared with me at your kitchen tables for a long time.”
The 2nd Congressional District was the most competitive of Arkansas’ four House races, covering central Arkansas, including most of Little Rock. But Democrats were unable to capitalize on the blue wave that swept across much of America Tuesday night. Redistricting in 2021 made the map more favorable to Hill, who won reelection in 2024 with 59% of the vote.
“This election was about lowering costs for families, growing the economy and keeping America strong,” Hill said in a statement Thursday afternoon. “I look forward to continuing my work on those priorities in the U.S. Congress and delivering results for Arkansans.”
Democrats have tried for years to unseat Hill, who first took office in 2015. Polling from Hendrix College and Talk Business and Politics found Jones with a slim lead over Hill in August, though the results were within the poll’s margin of error. 
Hill outspent and outraised Jones throughout the campaign, which saw congressional Democrats’ campaign arm spending more in the final weeks.
President Donald Trump won the district by more than 15 percentage points in 2024.
Chris Jones (D), answers questions from Arkansas journalists during the debate against U.S. Congressional District 2 incumbent Rep. French Hill (R) on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
During the campaign, Jones criticized Hill as being too closely aligned with the president.
Hill has split with Trump on some issues, including opposing the president’s plan to allow more beef imports into the U.S.  Hill, who chairs the House Financial Services Committee, sponsored the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a bipartisan bill that became law in July without Trump’s signature.
Democratic Party Chairman Marcus Jones, who unsuccessfully challenged Hill in 2024, said he was disappointed with the race results, but proud of the campaign Chris Jones ran.
The chairman said splitting up Pulaski County along racial lines during the redistricting process was done to protect Hill, but Democrats still made it a close race.
“I think it sent a message to Republicans and to Congressman Hill,” he said. “He got quite a shock out of this because he almost lost, and had it not been for the state legislature saving him through that gerrymandering, he would have.”
In his concession, Chris Jones cited the redrawing of the district’s boundaries and called on Congress to pass legislation named after the late congressman and civil rights leader John Lewis that would restore protections enshrined in the Voting Rights Act.
“I ran for Congress because I wanted to cast a vote to restore the Voting Rights Act,” he said. “I won’t get to cast it in January, so I’m asking the people who have that opportunity to get it done.” 
Despite failing to flip Hill’s seat, Democrats made gains in the state Legislature, breaking a supermajority Republicans have held in the state House for the past decade. The gains mean Republicans won’t be able to pass most budget bills along strictly party lines. 
The entire state shifted to the left as well, as voters took out their anger over affordability and the war in Iran at the ballot box. 
Hill was the most vulnerable of the five congressional Republicans on the ballot Tuesday, all of whom won reelection. Democrats have not won a statewide congressional race in Arkansas since 2010 — though the party eroded into the Republican Party’s margins. U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders won by less than they did when they were first elected.
Deputy Editor Antoinette Grajeda contributed to this story.

title: After Democratic legislative endorsements, Republican wins Hancock County sheriff’s race
description: The Republican beat out the Democrat in the sheriff’s race in Hancock County, which otherwise mostly went blue on Tuesday. The county’s Democratic legislators wanted that outcome.  “I was pleased that people did their research and looked at both candidates,” said Democratic Rep. Nina Milliken of Blue Hill, who was re-elected with almost 70% of […]
text:
Republican Corey Bagley, a detective with the Ellsworth Police Department and former sheriff’s chief deputy, won the race for Hancock County sheriff after he was endorsed by several local Democratic legislators. (Photo courtesy of Nina Milliken)The Republican beat out the Democrat in the sheriff’s race in Hancock County, which otherwise mostly went blue on Tuesday. The county’s Democratic legislators wanted that outcome. 
“I was pleased that people did their research and looked at both candidates,” said Democratic Rep. Nina Milliken of Blue Hill, who was re-elected with almost 70% of the vote. 
Milliken, Rep. Gary Friedmann of Bar Harbor, Rep. Holly Eaton of Deer Isle, and Sen. Nicole Grohoski of Hancock County endorsed Republican Corey Bagley, a detective with the Ellsworth Police Department and former sheriff’s chief deputy, who won the race according to the unofficial results from the municipalities. 
They did so because the Democrat, Dakota Dupuis, currently a lieutenant at the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office, only recently switched parties and the current sheriff, Scott Kane, a Republican, backed Dupuis. 
“I think Corey is a pretty respected member of law enforcement,” Milliken said. “He and I have had many interesting conversations. We don’t agree on many things, but he had a more progressive pitch.”
In trying to get Dupuis elected, Kane, the outgoing sheriff, had published an attack website against his own party’s nominee to replace him. The website also took aim at County Commissioner William Clark, the county’s previous sheriff and a supporter of Bagley. Kane and Clark have long sparred since Clark accused Kane of forcing him out in 2023 to hire his brother. 
“I think the sheriff’s office in Hancock County has lost a lot of credibility with other law enforcement agencies in the county, and with many members of the public,” Milliken said. “I think the biggest thing that I would hope would change would be that they become a more respected law enforcement agency and rebuild some trust.”
Following his win, Bagley said in a statement that he was humbled by the support. 
“It was a long, hard campaign,” he said. “I’m glad that it’s over. Now I can look to the future and what’s best for the sheriff’s office and what’s best for Hancock County.”
Dupuis said in a social media post that while the outcome is not what he hoped, he respected the results. 
“Regardless of political affiliation or who someone supported, it is time to set politics aside,” he wrote. “The focus should be on the Sheriff’s Office providing the best possible service to the citizens of Hancock County.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: 3 Kansas counties that helped Hamilton win US Senate seat have majority Latino populations
description: TOPEKA — Ford, Finney and Seward counties in western Kansas historically haven’t been Democratic strongholds. But three cities in each county are home to large Latino populations, in part because of meatpacking industry jobs, and those three cities were hit recently with sweeping federal immigration raids that led to children not showing up to school, […]
text:
U.S. Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton gives a victory speech on Nov. 3, 2026, in Overland Park after he defeated Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in the 2026 midterm election. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Ford, Finney and Seward counties in western Kansas historically haven’t been Democratic strongholds.
But three cities in each county are home to large Latino populations, in part because of meatpacking industry jobs, and those three cities were hit recently with sweeping federal immigration raids that led to children not showing up to school, delayed start times at meatpacking plants and instigated fear across the communities.
Republicans, in the wake of these immigration raids, doubled down on the need for immigration enforcement. Meanwhile, Democrats were quick to condemn the effects of the raids and paid visits to Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal.
Democrats’ efforts paid off. While official data is still pending, early indications show Latino and Black voters across the state boosted Democratic candidates’ vote totals, leading to historic victories. 
Among the Republicans who ran on strict immigration enforcement was U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, the incumbent who lost to Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, and Attorney General Kris Kobach, who, by early indications, lost his reelection bid to Democratic attorney Chris Mann.
Around half or more of registered voters in Finney, Ford and Seward counties are Latino, according to state voting data. Hamilton won all three, along with eight other counties to secure his victory. 
Hamilton said in his victory speech Tuesday night that he supports immigration enforcement, but only on the grounds that it does what it was created to do.
“That is to keep dangerous people from blowing up buildings and hurting people,” he said. “They were not commissioned to arrest preschool teachers in front of their children.”
He said one woman told him that when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents showed up in western Kansas, parents didn’t pick up their children from school because they were afraid.
“Those children just stayed there at school,” Hamilton said. “This was not OK.”
At the time, Marshall encouraged local and federal law enforcement to work together while Hamilton said something had “gone very wrong” to incite fear among schoolchildren and shutter local businesses.
While results in three statewide races, including the governor’s race and the attorney general’s race, are undergoing an audit, unofficial results showed Democrat Cindy Holscher and Mann leading. Mann visited cities in western Kansas multiple times on the campaign trail, and won Finney and Seward counties, in addition to more traditional Democratic strongholds near Wichita and Kansas City, per unofficial vote counts. Holscher appeared to win Seward County, home to Liberal.
Mann said in a statement after the election he thought his efforts to traverse 50,000-plus miles across 75 counties made a “real difference” in the race. Those trips also involved sitting down with law enforcement, farmers, business owners and community leaders, he said.
“In every community I’ve gone to, Kansans have made it clear they are tired of politics as usual,” he said. “They want their elected leaders to show up, and to listen.”
A Democrat also won in a state House race in Garden City, defeating Republican incumbent Bob Lewis, who had served since 2023.
 
6 months, 3 counties, 1 win
Latino voters make up 49% of registered voters in Ford County, 48% in Finney County and 60% in Seward County, according to data from Ike Lab, a voting data and analysis site by professors at Wichita State University. Registered Democrats only make up between 23% and 24% of voters in each county.
According to a New York Times voter trend analysis, 75% of Latino voters in Kansas voted for Hamilton.
Melissa Morales, president and founder of Somos PAC, a political advocacy arm of the Latino voter engagement group Somos Votantes, said on election night other Democratic candidates should take note of Hamilton’s campaign.
“Today, hardworking Kansans showed up at the ballot box to collect on a long-overdue debt: promises that were never delivered,” Morales said.
She said Somos was the only political group talking to voters in Latino-heavy areas in the state.
“Kansas’s motto, ‘Ad Astra per Aspera’, rings truer tonight, when voters in one of the reddest states in the country lived it,” Morales said. “Today, we are one step closer to that promise.”
Hamilton in his victory speech hypothesized how in six months — from when he declared in late April to Election Day — he was able to get elected. 
“I think I got elected because Kansans were saying we’re tired of the bullies. We’re tired of the chaos,” Hamilton said. “There are a lot of Kansans saying, ‘Let’s love our neighbors as we love ourselves.’ See, Kansans are decent people. They’re good people. They care about each other. That’s who we are in Kansas.”

title: After flipping Michigan’s 4th District, McCann plans bipartisanship approach in Congress
description: As state Sen. text:
State Sen. Sean McCann faults Republicans in Washington, D.C. for rising costs while rallying voters on on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo By Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)As state Sen. Sean McCann prepares to make his way to Washington, the Kalamazoo Democrat is committing himself to listening and delivering for his constituents, whether they voted for him or not.
“We’re going to put together a top-notch constituent service organization in the district, one that doesn’t care if someone’s a Republican or a Democrat. We do everything we can to make sure that people get the full support that they need from the federal government,” McCann told reporters at a press conference on Wednesday.
Riding the blue wave of Democratic lawmakers winning elections all across the country, McCann unseated U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Holland Township), who has served in the U.S. House of Representatives since 2011.
The Associated Press called the race for McCann at 1:13 p.m. Wednesday. Unofficial results showed McCann with 50.1% of the vote and Huizenga with 48.3%.
With Democrats poised to take control of both chambers of Congress,, party leaders have taken these sweeping victories as a mandate from the American people to deliver the economic relief that President Donald Trump and Republicans promised in 2024.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
However, delivering on that mandate could be difficult, as Trump retains control of the executive branch.
When asked about navigating that dynamic in Washington, McCann took inspiration from Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.
“One of my role models, Governor Whitmer, has always said she’ll work with anyone to get things done,” McCann said, noting her willingness to work with the president as well as Republicans in Michigan to deliver for the state.
“That’s really what we think people expect at the end of the day, and my approach has been not about partisan bickering or trying to be divisive,” McCann continued. “It’s been returning to sort of that Carl Levin, Fred Upton model of working across the aisle when it makes sense, building relationships with your colleagues, whether they’re Democrat or Republican, because eventually you hopefully can work together to get results for the people that you represent.” 
As someone who’s served in the state Legislature as a member of the minority party, the majority party and under divided government, McCann said the Democratic majority still has to see if there’s a place to work with Trump to deliver for the nation’s residents. He also recognized that the balance of power could shift back toward Republicans if Democrats fail to deliver.
“We’ve got to hit the ground fast and running to show that we’re going to be able to keep those promises to people.”

text:
On Nov. 15, schools, libraries, families, writing groups and individuals around the country will mark I Love To Write Day, a grassroots campaign founded in 2002 by Delaware writer and author John Riddle.
I Love To Write Day returns Nov. 15, encouraging people of all ages to put their thoughts on paper
WILMINGTON, Del. — A Delaware writer’s idea scribbled on a diner napkin more than two decades ago has grown into a nationwide invitation to write.
On Nov. 15, schools, libraries, families, writing groups and individuals around the country will mark I Love To Write Day, a grassroots campaign founded in 2002 by Delaware writer and author John Riddle.
The premise is intentionally simple: Write something.
It could be a poem, a letter, a greeting card, an essay, a short story or perhaps the opening sentence of a book someone has been thinking about for years.
“I Love To Write Day continues to grow as more people discover the enjoyment and importance of putting their thoughts on paper,” Riddle said.
The idea itself came while Riddle was traveling to teach workshops at the Blue Ridge Mountains Christian Writers Conference near Asheville, North Carolina.
He stopped at a diner for lunch and wrote four words on a napkin: “I Love To Write Day.”
“A few months later, the grassroots campaign was launched,” Riddle said.
Since then, Riddle says thousands of writers, teachers, librarians, students, families and community organizations across the United States have taken part.
The campaign also has a notable Delaware connection beyond its founder.
In 2008, then-U.S. Sen. Tom Carper of Delaware recognized I Love To Write Day in the Congressional Record. Riddle also says governors in nine states have issued proclamations recognizing Nov. 15 as I Love To Write Day.
Riddle, a Delaware freelance writer, author and ghostwriter, said the campaign’s mission has remained largely unchanged since its beginning.
“My goal for I Love To Write Day remains the same as it was when I launched the campaign,” he said. “People of all ages are encouraged to write something.”
That could include beginning or finishing a novel, writing a family story, sending a letter to someone important or simply taking a few minutes to record thoughts that otherwise might never make it to paper.
Schools and libraries can organize writing activities, while families can write stories or letters together. Businesses, churches, senior centers, bookstores and community groups also can create their own programs.
Riddle said the value of the day is less about producing polished work and more about giving people permission to begin.
“You never know what might happen when someone is encouraged to write,” he said. “A young person may discover a lifelong love of words. An adult may finally begin the book they have always wanted to write. Someone may write a letter that becomes a treasured family keepsake.”
Riddle also created the “I Love To Write Day Creative Writing Journal,” featuring 30 writing challenges and advice about creativity from more than 80 writers, authors, artists, musicians, actors and other creative professionals.
For Riddle, however, the most important part of Nov. 15 still comes down to the idea he first wrote on that diner napkin in 2002: Sit down and write something.

When: Nov. 15
Who can participate: Anyone, including students, families, schools, libraries, businesses, churches, senior centers and writing groups
How to participate: Spend time writing a poem, letter, story, essay, journal entry or another piece of your choosing

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: While Democrats are celebrating, pollsters are breathing sighs of relief
description: The fact that the results broadly matched pre-election surveys has to be heartening for pollsters, an often-beleaguered and much-criticized cohort.
text:
THE CRUCIAL TEST for preelection polls is whether they broadly indicate how voters are likely to decide. By that fundamental measure, the 2026 midterm polls largely succeeded in anticipating outcomes on Election Day.
If somewhat tentatively, the polls overall had been signaling important gains for Democrats. And that is what voting produced.
It was, perhaps, polling’s most reassuring performance since accurately anticipating Barack Obama’s presidential election in 2008, an outcome cited in my book, Lost in a Gallup: Polling Failure in US Presidential Elections.
This is not to say the 2026 preelection polls offered precision estimates before returns poured in. They appear to have underestimated support for Democratic candidates in some Senate races.
But spot-on precision, while enviable, is not what polls can be expected to produce, considering the many ways error can infiltrate opinion surveys. Given their checkered record in recent national elections, pollsters and media analysts tended to couch their end-of-campaign assessments in measured tentativeness.
For example, Nate Cohn, chief political analyst for The New York Times, wrote just before the election that “it’s reasonable to wonder whether the polls might be overestimating Democratic strength yet again. This is a real possibility. President Trump’s supporters are relatively unlikely to respond to polls, which introduces the ever-present risk of a polling misfire.”
That risk was mostly unrealized, as Republican candidates were swept in a red wipeout.
The 2026 polls tended to confirm the truism in American politics that midterms typically are rough on candidates of the party that holds the presidency.
Another truism, again reaffirmed, is that a president’s approval ratings often are useful in gauging the country’s mood before midterm elections. President Donald Trump’s preelection approval ratings hovered at or below 40 percent, according to survey data compiled by RealClearPolitics.
The US war with Iran, launched by Trump, was a major factor propelling the unenviable ratings. The conflict went unresolved while fuel prices surged, bringing pain to consumers.
Those and other problems prompted polling analyst Nate Silver to write that Trump “almost seems to have a death wish in these midterms. And the one superpower he has – turning out low-propensity voters in presidential years, the sorts of voters who apparently are often missed by pollsters – has never really worked when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot.”
And it didn’t work this time, either, even though throughout the campaign Trump encouraged supporters to pretend his name was on the ballot and turn out to vote.
When examined closely, the polls delivered some disagreement in the days before the election. Pollsters offered ranges that, in some races, were sizable.
For example, was Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton up by 1 percentage point in Texas late in the campaign, or was he down 7 points? Paxton lost by double digits to Democrat James Talarico, a margin that no pollster anticipated.
Similarly, was long-serving Republican Sen. Susan Collins ahead by 2 points in Maine or was she losing by 9 points? The outcome was closer to the latter reading, with Democrat Troy Jackson winning by more than six points.
In Minnesota, was Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan up by 14 points, or by just 2 points? With most votes counted by the day after the election, Flanagan’s margin of victory was about 10 points.
Such polling gaps in high-profile races offer a reminder to not focus on any single survey but, instead, to consider overall polling averages, which tend to remove or reduce the effects of outliers.
None of this necessarily is to declare that pollsters have resolved their persistent problems in sampling, especially in interviewing hard-to-reach voters. But big polling misses like that in the Texas governor’s race – where Democrat Gina Hinojosa won by double digits, although polls had shown Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ahead by a few points – were few this election cycle.
Meanwhile, the electorate’s broad inclinations were plainly if not precisely depicted.
That outcome has to be heartening for pollsters, an often-beleaguered and much-criticized cohort.
W. Joseph Campbell, is professor emeritus of communication at American University School of Communication. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

title: Vermont invested in her. Now she’s coming back.
description:
A Curtis Fund scholarship closed Makayla Towne’s college funding gap and opened the door to more than a degree. Now a Clark University senior preparing for medical school, she plans to return to Vermont as a psychiatrist serving neurodivergent teens—and give back to the community that raised her.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont invested in her. Now[...]
text:
Two out of three young Vermonters say they want out, according to a 2026 Campaign for Vermont survey, citing costs, taxes, and a lack of opportunity. Makayla Towne plans to come back. The Curtis Fund helped make that possible.
Makayla grew up in Manchester, where money was always tight. She received new clothes once a year from her grandparents. Anything else, she earned through jobs at camps, after-school programs, mentoring—whatever paid.
Home carried other challenges, too. Her mom cycled through doctors for an illness no one could name. One brother, who has autism, spent a year in residential treatment; another, who has ADHD, struggled after he left. Some weeks, neighbors showed up with groceries or found extra work for her dad.
That’s where Makayla learned what community really means. In a recent psychotherapy class exercise, students were asked to rank their values. “Making a difference” and “community” landed at number one and two.
College was always the goal, but paying for it felt nearly impossible. Makayla spent high school searching for scholarships with mentors through Burr and Burton Academy’s Success Program. She had no co-signer for a parent or private loan, making every scholarship critical.
At BBA’s Scholarship Night, Makayla kept getting called to the stage. After her fourth award, she had already done the math: what she owed, what federal loans would cover, and what would still have to come from a private lender.
Then they called her name again.
“As each scholarship came in, it was like a load being taken off my back,” she says. “When I found out I got The Curtis Fund’s Northshire and Mettawee Valley Scholarship, I looked at my mom and said, ‘Mom, I have enough. I’m not taking out any private loans.’”
One scholarship closed the gap.
Without it, Makayla says she might have taken a gap year or worked two jobs just to stay enrolled. Instead, the scholarship gave her room not simply to attend college, but to fully participate in it.
Today, Makayla is a senior at Clark University, double majoring in biology and psychology, with minors in chemistry and health science and society. Her honors thesis explores the experiences of people assigned female at birth who were diagnosed with autism after age 16—a topic shaped in part by her own family experience and work with neurodivergent young people.
Outside the classroom, she serves on student council, participates in two honor societies, and created a mentoring program for first-generation students after recognizing how difficult her own transition to college had been. She also continues working with neurodivergent children in Vermont through Onward Rising.
After graduation, Makayla plans to work as a licensed behavioral technician while studying for the MCAT, then attend medical school and become a psychiatrist specializing in neurodivergent teens.
And then she plans to come home.
Vermont faces a shortage of child psychiatrists, and Makayla hopes eventually to open a practice here and offer free weekly sessions to families who otherwise could not afford care.
“I feel a responsibility to give back to the community that raised me,” she says. “They made what seemed impossible, possible.”
For Makayla, the scholarship was never just about earning a diploma. It gave her the freedom to mentor other first-generation students, conduct research that matters to her, serve neurodivergent children, and prepare for a career she intends to bring back to Vermont.
That is the return on a Curtis Fund scholarship: opportunity given to one Vermonter, multiplied through the lives and communities they go on to serve.
The Curtis Fund awards over 600 degree scholarships each year to Vermonters like Makayla, and another 250 scholarships to students pursuing certificates through short-term professional training programs. Since 1910, more than 14,000 Vermonters have been able to pursue post-secondary education because of it. For the Towne family, that number just went up by one.

Delaware-founded fintech has added nine employees and says its new Iron Hill Corporate Center office can support continued expansion
NEWARK, Del. — Delaware-founded financial technology company GradBridge has opened a new headquarters in Newark, establishing a base for a planned expansion that could add nearly 50 full-time jobs over the next five years.
The company officially opened its 9,321-square-foot office at 750 Prides Crossing in the Iron Hill Corporate Center on Wednesday, Nov. 4, with state, county and business leaders attending a ribbon-cutting and open house.
GradBridge, which specializes in what it calls “second-look” private student lending, launched its lending platform in March. The company announced in June that it planned to create 49 full-time, salaried, benefits-eligible positions in Delaware over five years.
Nine full-time employees have recently joined the company, bringing GradBridge’s workforce to 19 people, including six contractors, according to the company.
“Delaware has a longstanding reputation of being a leader in the financial services industry. This opening builds on that by growing our innovation economy and attracting fintech investment,” Delaware Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez said.
She said the company’s decision to build its headquarters in Delaware reflects confidence in the state as a place for financial companies to invest and grow.
GradBridge’s new office will house executive leadership as well as finance, compliance, credit, data and analytics, and management operations.
The company said it spent more than $290,000 with six local contractors and suppliers to build out the space, which includes offices, shared work areas, conference rooms and employee facilities.
New Castle County Executive Marcus Henry said the company represents the type of entrepreneurial growth county leaders hope to encourage.
“GradBridge recognized a need and built a business around helping address it,” Henry said. “That’s the kind of innovation and entrepreneurial spirit we want to see in New Castle County.”
A Delaware fintech connection
Founder and CEO Jen O’Donald has deep ties to Delaware’s financial services industry.
O’Donald said she received her education in Delaware and has spent more than 25 years working in the state’s financial services sector.
“Less than two years ago, GradBridge was just an idea,” O’Donald said. “Since then, we’ve turned that vision into reality, launching an innovative lending platform, building a talented team and now opening our new headquarters.”
Delaware has long been home to major banking, credit card and financial services companies, giving startups such as GradBridge access to a workforce experienced in lending, credit analysis, compliance and financial technology.
O’Donald said the company intends to build on that base as it expands nationally.
“I’m especially proud to be building a company that creates meaningful career opportunities, contributes to Delaware’s growing fintech community and helps students across the country achieve their educational goals,” she said.
A ‘second look’ at student borrowers
GradBridge is targeting a specific segment of the private student loan market: upperclassmen and graduate students who are turned down under traditional lending criteria but are making progress toward earning a degree.
The company says more than 1 million students each year are declined for private student loans because they fall outside traditional credit standards.
GradBridge’s underwriting approach considers academic progress along with conventional credit factors in an effort to identify borrowers the company believes have a strong likelihood of completing their degrees.
“At GradBridge, we believe a student who is making progress toward a degree deserves a meaningful opportunity to finish,” O’Donald said.
The company says its focus is not on replacing federal student aid, but providing another private lending option for students who might otherwise be unable to secure financing needed to complete school.
The Newark headquarters marks the next stage of the company’s expansion after launching its lending platform earlier this year.
O’Donald credited Gov. Matt Meyer’s administration, New Castle County, Delaware Prosperity Partnership and other organizations with assisting the company.
“This celebration is about more than opening an office,” she said. “It’s about building a company that creates opportunity for our employees, our community and the students we serve.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge temporarily halts efforts to revoke Canton school’s charter
description: Buses arrive to pick up children attending SR1 College Preparatory and Stem Academy at the end of the school day, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Canton.
text:
Efforts to revoke the charter of a Canton school are on pause for at least a month.
On Monday, Hinds County Chancery Court Judge Tametrice Hodges-Linzey granted SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy a temporary restraining order against the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board. School leadership requested the order on Oct. 30, four days after the board voted to revoke its charter for severe financial mismanagement.
This is the first time the state is revoking a school’s charter — and navigating an appeal of that decision — since 2013, when Mississippi’s charter school law went into effect.
SR1 school leadership is appealing the board’s decision and filed its restraining order request in Hinds County chancery court because the authorizer board is based in Jackson. Jamie Travis, the school’s attorney, argued in the recent court filing that authorizer board staff should not be allowed to start the process of revoking the school’s charter while an appeal is pending. 
The board voted on Oct. 26 to revoke the school’s charter. The authorizer board mandated that the school cease operations by the end of the year. 
Read more: Dysfunction put Canton school’s charter at risk
Travis contended in the Oct. 30 court filing that authorizer board members did not adequately prove mismanagement. He said the board was unwilling to wait on the school’s latest audit, which came out Oct. 7. Instead, the board held a hearing in May to determine whether to revoke the school’s charter. The audit lacked serious findings and would clear up concerns about the schools’ finances, Travis said. Travis also argued that the authorizer board did not provide enough technical support to charter school leaders.
Travis also argued in the court filings that the authorizer board is driving away students and staff before an appeal can be heard. He described an Oct. 28 incident as an example of interference by the board. 
A sign for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy is shown Thursday, Dec. 19, 2025, in Canton. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
That day, Lisa Karmacharya, the authorizer board’s executive director, showed up at the school during an internal staff meeting. Tamu Green, the school’s chief executive officer, opened the door for Karmacharya, but she had not been invited, Travis said. 
Authorizer board policy mandates close-out procedures start within a day of the vote to revoke a school’s charter, and board staff must hold meetings to close out school finances and provide information to parents and staff. State law and agency policy also allows authorizer board staff to conduct on-site inspections of schools. In an interview Wednesday with Mississippi Today, Travis disputed whether state law supports unannounced on-site visits.
School officials must also secure financial records and schedule time for school finance team members and charter authorizer board staff to review the closed-out records. There must be a separate meeting between staff of the authorizer board and school to discuss the details of the school’s operating status.
School officials must also provide contact information for parents and staff so the authorizer board can notify them about the school’s operating status. Board policy requires notifying parents and staff within five and 10 days, respectively. However, SR1 charter school officials did not provide the necessary contact information by the agency’s deadline, according to Karmacharya. 
Karmacharya told Mississippi Today on Wednesday she felt it was important that school staff gain clarity about the authorizer board’s decision to revoke the school’s charter.
Dorlisa Hutton, the school’s vice president, did not respond to a request for comment. She hung up the phone when Mississippi Today contacted her Wednesday. Green did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hodges-Linzey will need to rule on whether to overturn the authorizer board’s decision to revoke the school’s charter.
Appeals of agency decisions made after administrative hearings, or judicial reviews, are limited to certain criteria in Mississippi. Travis, on behalf of SR1 CPSA, must prove that the authorizer board’s decision was arbitrary, capricious, unsupported by fact, exceeded the agency’s authority or violated the school’s constitutional rights.

title: 48 Nebraska judges all leading up-or-down votes to stay in office six more years
description: LINCOLN — Voters across Nebraska favored keeping all 48 of the judges who faced up-or-down votes on remaining in office for an additional six years, keeping alive a 16-year streak of no booted jurists. Depending on the county where they live, Nebraska voters saw at least two judges or as many as 15 on their […]
text:
Many state judges, at right, and Nebraskans joined in the Nebraska State Capitol Rotunda for the investiture of Nebraska Supreme Court Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke. Nov. 22, 2024. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Judicial Branch)LINCOLN — Voters across Nebraska favored keeping all 48 of the judges who faced up-or-down votes on remaining in office for an additional six years, keeping alive a 16-year streak of no booted jurists.
Depending on the county where they live, Nebraska voters saw at least two judges or as many as 15 on their ballots. The most are in Nebraska’s most populous county, Douglas, which is Judicial District 4. State law provides that district with the most judges.
No Supreme Court justices faced retention. On the Court of Appeals, only Judge Michael W. Pirtle of Omaha faced retention; he represents part of Douglas County. He led in his district 62%-38% as of 6 a.m. Wednesday.
Since 1964, judges have gone to voters for retention at the first general election at least three years after their appointment. Nebraska has nearly 150 judges in total. 
Current terms in office end Jan. 7, 2027.
The last time a Nebraska judge was not retained in office was in 2008. Should votes hold, judges could serve until January 2033 and could file for retention again in 2032.
The closest race was for Douglas County District Judge Marlon A. Polk, who joined the bench in 2005 at the appointment of then-Gov. Dave Heineman. He made history as the first Black person to be appointed as a judge of a district court. By 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, Polk led with 56% of the vote to retain him, a margin of nearly 19,000 votes.
The Douglas County Election Commission said Wednesday evening election workers have nearly 16,000 more ballots to process by Nov. 16. The total includes more than 6,000 early vote ballots, which will be counted Friday; 550 early vote ballots requiring additional research, such as replacement ballots or those with questionable signatures; 4,000 provisional ballots case during in-person early voting or on Election Day and 5,000 resolution ballots that can’t be scanned by ballot-counting machines and will be replicated by a bipartisan team of election workers.
The Nebraska State Bar Association each year polls attorneys who work before the judges. Of the 48 up for retention this year, attorneys recommended that all but one be retained in office.
The one exception was Lincoln County District Judge Cindy R. Volkmer. She received a performance evaluation of 38.5% of attorneys recommending she be retained. Election results had her with 75% of the vote to keep her in office, or nearly 15,000 in favor of retention.
Of Nebraska’s nearly 150 judges, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen has appointed more than 30, and three of his judges faced up-or-down votes Tuesday. He was reelected to four more years.

title: Maine’s 2nd District race heads to ranked choice runoff. Here’s what to expect.
description: Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is officially headed to a ranked choice runoff, the Secretary of State’s Office announced Thursday morning. Though only two candidates, Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage, were on the ballot, the one declared write-in prompted ranked choice voting, meaning voters could rank three names on their ballot.  Accordi[...]
text:
U.S. House candidates Democrat Matt Dunlap (left) and Republican Paul LePage (right) met for the second time on the debate stage on Oct. 15. (Photos by Jim Neuger and Andrew Clark/ Maine Morning Star)Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is officially headed to a ranked choice runoff, the Secretary of State’s Office announced Thursday morning.
Though only two candidates, Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage, were on the ballot, the one declared write-in prompted ranked choice voting, meaning voters could rank three names on their ballot. 
According to results from the Secretary of State’s Office, of the 341,248 ballots cast in the district, LePage received 49.894% of votes and Dunlap received 48.307% — both failing to get the more than 50% needed to avoid the runoff. 
The announcement comes a day after LePage declared victory in the race. He said his team “has been calling all the towns that haven’t come in yet, and there is no path to victory for my opponent.” 
Dunlap quickly responded that the race was still too close to call. “This race is very close and there are plenty of ballots left to count,” he said.
Polling ahead of Election Day had LePage in the lead, but a strong showing from Democrats nationally likely buoyed Dunlap in Maine’s more conservative 2nd District. The party succeeded in winning both the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in response to President Donald Trump’s declining approval.
“The first step in the process will be to verify the vote totals from every municipality to ensure accuracy,” Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said in a statement Thursday. “Once the election night totals are verified, assuming neither candidate received a majority of the votes, which is what we are observing now, we will proceed to the ranked choice voting tabulation.”
The tabulations will begin on Monday at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters in Augusta.
Maine’s elections are run by municipalities. This is a more hyper-local structure than most of the country, where elections are often run at the county level. While municipalities informally report results to the state and media on election night, under Maine law, they have two days to report official counts to the Secretary of State’s Office. 
Ranked choice voting only applies to federal races in the general election, though primary elections for state and federal offices in Maine can use it. 
Like elections past, the tabulation process in Maine will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State’s YouTube page. The public is also invited to watch the process in-person. 
Maine’s 2026 November ballot lists the candidates for the 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage, along with space for a write-in candidate. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)

Why is a runoff needed?

A race goes to a ranked choice runoff if no candidate receives more than 50% of votes on Election Day. That calculation is based on total ballots cast, including blanks and write-ins. 
Gregory Ward is the sole declared write-in candidate in the 2nd District, and the secretary’s office said he received 123 votes in Tuesday’s election, and another 6,017 ballots were blank. 
Blanks led to a runoff in 2024. Golden won a plurality of first-choice votes against Republican Austin Theriault, but received just under 49% of total votes. Golden eventually won the runoff and was officially declared winner after a recount Theriault requested.
And in 2018, Golden defeated incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Poliquin in the nation’s first congressional election to use ranked choice voting to determine the winner. 
Golden announced last November that he would not seek reelection. LePage had already announced his campaign, and faced no Republican primary challengers. Dunlap had intended to challenge Golden, and went on to defeat three other candidates in a ranked choice runoff in the June primary. 
The process
If ranked choice tabulations take as long as they have in elections past, the outcome should be known by next Friday. 
“We are hoping to expedite the process so that we can have results more quickly, if at all possible,” Bellows said before the election. 
The bulk of that time will be the secretary of state’s staff logging results from every ballot and checking multiple times to ensure the totals line up. 
For example, during the June primary runoffs, the Friday and Monday after the election were spent scanning ballots into a tabulator, uploading thumb drives from municipalities that have in-house tabulators, and hand entering votes on any of those ballots that failed to scan. 
On Tuesday and Wednesday, staff checked the votes in the computer against the forms sent in by the municipalities and resolved any discrepancies. While not a requirement, the results from the counties farthest away are typically logged first, so there is adequate time in case any missing materials need to be retrieved. 
“We have some communities that are only reachable by boat,” said Deb McDonough of the nonpartisan League of Women Voters. “It’s just a fact that it’s a complicated logistical task to get all of those votes transferred from the scanner or the paper ballots from the community, such that all of that information is now in a single computer that’s prepared to run the tabulation software.”
That runoff included statewide gubernatorial primaries, and required ballots from every municipality in the state. The gathering process may be quicker for this runoff, because it will only be the 2nd District municipalities. 
On the final two days of the primary runoffs, staff reconciled what is called the cast vote record with the reports from municipalities. The cast vote record is the electronic record, an excel spreadsheet where each line represents one ballot. This reconciliation took a while in June since there were five different runoffs happening, two gubernatorial primaries, a congressional primary and two legislative primaries.  
Actually running the ranked choice tabulation formula produces results in a matter of minutes.
Last-place candidates are eliminated first and votes are then redistributed to a voter’s next choice. If your first choice makes it to the final round, your ballot will stay with your first choice throughout the tabulations. That’s repeated until one candidate receives more than 50% of votes.
Following the ranked choice tabulation, the losing candidate may request a hand recount. 
The software used is available at no charge from the Ranked Choice Voting Resource Center. Voters can therefore run the tabulations themselves once the Secretary of State’s Office publishes the cast vote records.
